News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could face legal demand to testify in US about friendship with Epstein
News.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could face legal demand to testify in US about friendship with Epstein

The former Prince, who has denied all wrongdoing, could be called to testify in the US as Democrats pledge to further plumb the depths of the Epstein files following the Midterms

View 3 Images Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could be called to testify in the US (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor could be called to the US to testify over his links to Jeffrey Epstein if Democrats win big in the country's coming November elections.

A new push for investigation into the Epstein files by opposition politicians is taking shape ahead of the midterms, which will decide who has control of the House and Senate in the US Congress. If they win, one top Democrat has said, they will help British police investigating the paedophile financier gain access to the unredacted files, allowing them to bypass a critical barrier impeding their inquiries.

Suhas Subramanyam, ranking member for military and foreign affairs on the House Oversight Committee, has vowed that, on top of this, he would make a legal demand for the former Prince to testify about his relationship. Andrew has continuously denied any wrongdoing in regards to his relationship with Epstein.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor would try to block searches at his homes READ MORE :

View 3 Images US Representative Suhas Subramanyam has called for Andrew to testify (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Speaking to The Sun, Mr Subramanyam said his party would "demand answers" from the ex-Duke, and called on him to testify. He said: "Democrats will continue to investigate Epstein’s crimes and demand answers from Andrew and anyone else involved. We will use the full subpoena power of Congress to get justice for the survivors and transparency for the American people.

"I called on the former Prince Andrew to testify and will continue to do so in the next Congress. I also fully support giving British law enforcement the Epstein files and assisting with any other criminal investigation." Mountbatten-Windsor has faced growing pressure over the last year to appear before Congress, with multiple other high ranking Democrats, including Ro Khanna and Teresa Leger Fernandez lodging similar calls.

View 3 Images Andrew was arrested at Royal Lodge (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Andrew, a former friend of the disgraced financier, was arrested in the UK by Thames Valley Police on February 19 after the US Department of Justice published documents showing his connections to Epstein. He was accused of misconduct in public office after officers executed warrants at his former Royal Lodge property in Sandringham, Norfolk.

Article continues below

Lawyers for the King's brother successfully argued in court last week that those warrants were unlawful, although the investigation continues ahead of a 2027 ruling as to whether items seized as a result of the warrants can be used as evidence.

It is alleged that when he worked as a UK trade envoy he may have forwarded Epstein official reports from visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.

Another claim stemming from the US DoJ files held that Mountbatten-Windsor briefed Epstein on Afghanistan investment opportunities. The documents also mentioned a suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor met with a private investment firm and later suggested to Epstein that he might invest in the company.

News.title: Man City charges LIVE: Points deduction timeframe as appeal 'decision date' predicted
News.content:
Football finance expert Kieran Maguire has claimed Manchester City must be deduced "multiple double figures of points" after breaching Premier League financial rules.

Maguire said: "The redacted report sets out year by year how much the sham contracts contributed to the artificial commercial revenue. Over the rolling three-year period, in some years we could be talking about a £350million difference. That would shatter all records for PSR compliance.

"Everton and Nottingham Forest's deductions covered a single breach in a single year, an overspend of no more than £20million. So is there a ceiling on what can be deducted? And the sanctions hearing could already have taken place. Because City are appealing and everyone has NDAs, we might not know the sanction until the appeal result. But it has to be multiple double figures of points, before you start the calculations.

"I worked out that if you add up nine years of Champions League non-participation for individual clubs at an average of £50million a time, around £20million for the Europa League, plus potential claims from players who missed bonuses, the Premier League's legal fees and a fine, we're talking in excess of a billion pounds regardless of the points deduction.

When asked about the possibility of City being kicked out of the Premier League, Maguire responded: "I think it would be a very unusual vote. We did see Bury get expelled from League Two some time ago but I think that the other clubs would have to bear in mind that Manchester City would probably take legal redress and that could prove to be very expensive if they are expelled without the verdict being held and without the appeal. So it's a risky path to tread, but the strength of feeling does vary from club to club.

"Certainly some of the other elite clubs are very unhappy with the delay in the situation because they feel it has an impact upon their ability to qualify for the Champions League. I think some of the more mid-tier clubs who don't see Manchester City as a threat, their main concern is, is this going to further increase the already sky-high legal costs that have been incurred by the Premier League and they don't want any part of it.

"So, they want a quick resolution and then they can get on with the rest of their season and focus on their own clubs."

News.title: Warning update for sertraline, citalopram and fluoxetine after number of deaths
News.content:
Warning update for sertraline, citalopram and fluoxetine after number of deaths

A coroner warned that action should be taken to prevent future deaths

View 3 Images Lady Gabriella Windsor and Thomas Kingston leave after marrying in St George's Chapel

Antidepressants are to come with more “prominent” warnings about risks of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, the medicines regulator has announced. It comes after it emerged that four prevention of future death reports concerning the prescribing of antidepressants, or their safety information, have been sent to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) since 2020.

‌



‌



The prevention of future deaths report issued after the death of Thomas Kingston, the husband of Prince and Princess Michael of Kent’s daughter, Lady Gabriella Kingston, questioned whether there is “adequate communication of the risks of suicide associated with the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) medications”.

‌



Mr Kingston died by suicide in 2024 when he was 45 years old. The inquest into his death at Gloucestershire Coroner’s Court was told he had been given sertraline , a drug used to treat depression and mental health problems, and zopiclone, a sleeping tablet, by a GP at the Royal Mews Surgery, a practice at Buckingham Palace used by royal household staff, after complaining of trouble sleeping following stress at work.

‌



View 3 Images Millions take the pills every day in the UK

Mr Kingston returned to the surgery saying the drugs were not making him feel better and his doctor moved him from sertraline to citalopram. Both of these drugs are SSRIs. In the days leading up to his death, Mr Kingston had stopped taking medication and toxicology tests showed caffeine and small amounts of zopiclone in his system.

In her prevention of future deaths report, senior coroner for Gloucestershire, Katy Skerrett, said that Mr Kingston “had recently been experiencing anxiety, but had not expressed any suicidal ideation”. She wrote to the MHRA saying that matters of concern arising from the inquest include: “Whether there is adequate communication of the risks of suicide associated with the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) medications.”

‌



She warned that action should be taken to prevent future deaths. Mr Kingston’s parents, Martin and Jill Kingston, called for changes in how patients are prescribed SSRIs, saying that both the patient and the people close to them should be told more explicitly about the potential side effects of the medication, including what can happen if they stop taking it.

The changes announced by the MHRA follow a review by the Commission on Human Medicines, which took place after patients and families raised concerns about how information is communicated in patient safety leaflets on suicidal thoughts and behaviours and sexual dysfunction that continues after treatment is stopped.

View 3 Images A box of Citalopram

‌



Patient information leaflets for antidepressants will be updated, including a new “boxed warning” with information on suicidal thoughts and behaviours, “making information easier to find”, the regulator said. A new patient safety card is expected to be included in or on the medicine box to reinforce safety messaging, MHRA added.

And patient information leaflets for certain antidepressants will be updated to include the term “Post SSRI Sexual Dysfunction” to explain the risk of symptoms continuing after treatment. Meanwhile, an additional safety leaflet is being developed by the MHRA, which will be given to patients at their first appointment discussing antidepressants when it becomes available in 2027.

Dr Alison Cave, MHRA’s chief safety officer, said: “Patients need clear and accessible information about the benefits and risks of medicines so they can make informed decisions. We are incredibly grateful for the valuable contributions of patients, families, clinicians and experts to this review.

‌



Benefits and risks

“These measures will help ensure patients, carers and healthcare professionals can have more informed conversations about the benefits and risks associated with antidepressant medicines, and better support people throughout their treatment.

“Antidepressants are effective medicines for the treatment of depression and other conditions. When used appropriately and under clinical supervision, for the vast majority of individuals, the benefits outweigh the risks. The aim is not to discourage use, but to improve the prominence and clarity of the existing warnings.

“It’s imperative that patients do not stop taking these medicines without first speaking to their healthcare professional.”

‌



Earlier this week, health minister James Frith said that revised patient information leaflets and patient cards would be available online from October and hard copies will be in packs around three to six months later. He said in a written answer to Parliament that in the interim the MHRA is working to evaluate the feasibility for earlier access to hard copies via pharmacies.

Asked about prevention of future death reports – which coroners write if they are concerned future deaths may occur – Mr Frith added: “The MHRA logs all Prevention of Future Deaths reports it receives and can confirm that since 2020, four reports concerning the prescribing of antidepressants, or their safety information have been sent to the MHRA.”

A new drug safety update has also been issued on the topic, which advises healthcare workers on the information to give to their patients, including what to tell them if they feel suicidal, and the potential for sexual dysfunction with some antidepressants.

Article continues below

Patients should be told that “these are not new risks for these medicines, but it is important to be aware of them”.

And they should be advised: “Do not stop taking your medicine without first speaking to your healthcare professional”.

When life is difficult, Samaritans are available day or night, 365 days a year. You can call them for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org.

News.title: Reform mayor Luke Campbell accused of showing staff member naked pictures of himself
News.content:
Reform mayor Luke Campbell accused of showing staff member naked pictures of himself

The former Olympic gold medallist boxer 'firmly denies any wrongdoing', according to Reform, after it emerged he allegedly called a female employee to his desk and showed her the images

View 3 Images The Olympic gold medallist became the first elected mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire in May 2025 after winning 35.8% of the vote (Image: Donna Clifford/HullLive)

Reform mayor Luke Campbell is under police investigation for cyberflashing, an allegation he 'firmly denies'.

The 39-year-old former Olympic boxing gold medallist is accused of allegedly showing naked pictures of himself to a female member of staff on a computer. It is understood he denies any wrongdoing. A Reform spokesperson said: "Luke firmly denies the allegations. They come from a disgruntled employee attempting to leverage a settlement in a meritless workplace dispute."

Hull and East Yorkshire mayor Mr Campbell allegedly called a female employee over to his desk and showed her four fully "naked and sexualised images" of himself on a computer in an office in central Hull in May, reports the Observer. She was reportedly left feeling "shocked, embarrassed, and humiliated" afterwards, as Campbell allegedly mocked her reaction.

View 3 Images Mr Campbell was pictured with Reform leader Nigel Farage at an event in Hull in February last year (Image: Getty Images)

The Observer claim that employment tribunal documents show the woman alleged: "I was deliberately exposed to naked and sexualised images involving the mayor in the workplace, without my consent, and was laughed at when I was visibly embarrassed. In my view, this was unwanted conduct of a sexual nature which violated my dignity and created a humiliating, degrading and offensive working environment."

A second filing seen by The Observer allegedly includes testimony from a witness who confirmed seeing Campbell and two other male colleagues ushering a female officer to look at his laptop, on which was "a naked man with a tattoo", which the witness said left them feeling "uneasy".

Other alleged incidents have involved Campbell lowering his trousers’ waistband to show a tan line and revealing a tattoo on his lower abdomen to a woman. It is understood Mr Campbell was interviewed by Humberside Police officers earlier this month in relation to the alleged incident. No arrests or charges have been made.

View 3 Images Mr Campbell won a gold medal in the bantamweight boxing competition at the 2012 Olympic Games in London and was later awarded an MBE (Image: Getty Images)

Mr Campbell became the first elected mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire in May 2025 after winning 35.8% of the vote. He won a gold medal in the bantamweight boxing competition at the 2012 Olympic Games in London and was later awarded an MBE for services to the sport. He also competed on Dancing On Ice in 2013, finishing third.

Article continues below

The Hull and East Yorkshire Combined Authority confirmed a police investigation is under way and are now conducting an internal probe. A spokesperson said: "As with all public authorities, the combined authority has a standards process that can be engaged to deal with complaints about members and a complaints procedure that can be used to deal with complaints about officers. The standards process and the complaints procedure must be carried out in a fair and independent manner."

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, which is responsible for governance at local authorities, told Hull Live: “Whilst we cannot comment on individual allegations, Mayors should be held to the highest possible standards in elected office and combined authorities must have appropriate arrangements for protecting their staff, with the right safeguards in place when allegations are made. We have established processes in place to intervene in cases where they fail to meet these standards and will not hesitate to use them where required.”

Humberside Police and Reform were contacted for comment.

News.title: 'I thought my symptoms were a bad cold but it was aggressive cancer'
News.content:
'I thought my symptoms were a bad cold but it was aggressive cancer'

Ashley Grey, 59, collapsed when he got to hospital

View 5 Images Ashley Grey in hospital

A grandad who thought he just had a "bad cold" when he felt unwell and couldn't stop shaking was diagnosed with an aggressive cancer. Ashley Grey, 59, started to feel unwell in December 2022 and by Christmas he had a fever and was shaking, so his wife called 111 and he was sent to Northern General Hospital.

‌



‌



Tests showed his blood counts were "on the floor" and he was taken to the Royal Hallamshire Hospital where he was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia on New Year's Day 2023 - after a bone marrow biospy. Ashley went through months of chemotherapy and on May 16, 2023, underwent a stem cell transplant and is now in recovery.

‌



Ashley, a patient transport worker from Hillsborough, Sheffield, said: “I thought I’d just had a bad cold, and I’d even carried on working. Whilst I was at home, I started a fever and was shaking, so my wife called 111. It was Christmas week, and the walk-in was shut, so we were sent to A&E. When I got there, I collapsed, and tests showed all my healthy blood counts were on the floor. I had absolutely no idea.”

‌



View 5 Images Ashley Grey with his grandson

At Royal Hallamshire Hospital, he received blood transfusions and his diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia was confirmed. H e then underwent several rounds of gruelling chemotherapy, losing his hair, and remaining as an inpatient for seven weeks before being given the all-clear to continue his treatment after discharge.

‌



Thanks to the generosity of a stranger, he received his life-saving stem cell transplant on the May 16, his daughter’s birthday.

“I had side effects like sickness, diarrhoea and tiredness throughout my chemotherapy, and a nasty rash during my transplant, and I lost all my hair which affected me much more than I thought it would," Ashley said. "But the haematology team were superstars, and I had so much gratitude, and that’s when I decided I wanted to do something more worthwhile with my life.”

View 5 Images Ashley Grey enjoys camping with his grandchildren

‌



A few months after his transplant, he was well enough to go back to work as a lorry driver on a part-time basis and it was here that he spotted a job as a non-emergency patient transport worker. He now helps transport disabled, elderly, sick or vulnerable people to and from outpatient clinics, day care centres and routine hospital admissions.

Three years on, he remains cancer-free and continues to enjoy the job. Ashley said: “I really enjoy getting people home and talking to people. One of the best things was when I first went back up to the O2 day ward in my job rather than as a patient and I saw one of the nurses that treated me there.

‌



“To be there and to be better and doing something for others, it meant so much. Everybody and everyone in the hospital team have been absolutely brilliant. I can't thank them enough.”

View 5 Images Ashley Grey with his daughter

‌



Around 3,100 people are diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia in the UK every year. A stem cell transplant is often the only hope of a cure. Dr Alex Kanellopoulos, Consultant Haematologist at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, said: “Sheffield is a major centre for stem cell transplantation and everyone here is so proud of Ashley and all he has achieved following treatment.

"Although treatments for acute myeloid leukaemia have remained largely unchanged for the last few decades, there have been significant breakthroughs in recent years, including genetic techniques which allow us to track DNA changes and patient-specific markers of the disease in the blood and bone marrow, improving outcomes. New maintenance therapies have also helped to lower the risk of relapse.

View 5 Images Ashley Grey is now an ambulance worker

Article continues below

“Our ambulatory care service also allows certain patients to receive a variety of treatments, including high-dose chemotherapy, without the need for an overnight hospital stay. This helps patients retain much-needed normality and independence during highly intensive treatments."

News.title: Households urged to put old socks in their garden in autumn
News.content:
Households urged to put old socks in their garden in autumn

Gardening experts have claimed how repurposing old socks could help attract a common type of wildlife.

View 3 Images Households urged to put old socks in their garden in autumn (Image: Nozdracheva via Getty Images)

If your laundry basket has a mysterious pile of single socks, it's worth knowing that they're surprisingly useful in the garden if you're keen on attracting birds.

‌



‌



While you might come across a wonderful array of birds during a pleasant walk outdoors, many of these feathered creatures can actually be enjoyed right from your own back garden. There's something truly magical about having a garden that's packed with birds.

‌



These charming animals bring vivid colours, cheerful sounds, and a wonderful energy to our outdoor spaces, and they're also incredibly useful at keeping common garden pests such as caterpillars and aphids under control. Certain bird species will even tuck into slugs and snails.

‌



Your garden can also serve as a vital refuge for birds, providing them with food, safe spots to rest, and perfect locations for nesting. This means that turning your garden into a bird-friendly haven creates a brilliant situation where everybody wins. Gardening experts at Gardening Know How have recommended a clever trick to draw birds in, and it involves putting your old socks to good use.

View 3 Images Households can put old socks to use for feeding birds

There are countless household items you can repurpose for birds, from teacups as feeders to juice cartons for nests; but old odd socks have their own part to play.

‌



The experts suggest copying commercial finch feeders, which are usually made from breathable mesh and packed with tiny seeds such as nyjer. The concept is that small birds can grip onto it and peck through the material.

To create your own version, simply fill a clean sock with bird seed, tie a knot at the top, and hang it from a tree branch or hook. The soft fabric gives small birds something to hold onto while they feed.

Just like with any bird feeder, make sure you inspect it regularly and replace the sock whenever it becomes wet, develops mould, or gets particularly dirty. It's advised to keep feeders clean to help prevent diseases from spreading among your feathered visitors.

‌



Position feeders somewhere birds can access easily but where they have some shelter from the weather and predators. A spot with nearby bushes or a hedge can offer useful cover.

However, avoid placing feeders too close to dense vegetation such as hedges where cats can lurk and pounce on feeding birds.

View 3 Images If you only want to buy one type of bird food, sunflower hearts are “a good place to start” (Image: Marcia Straub via Getty Images)

‌



What foods should you put in your sock bird feeders?

Sunflower hearts

If you only want to purchase one type of bird food, sunflower hearts are "a good place to start", according to the experts at Otter Garden Centres. They are the kernels inside sunflower seeds, so birds don't have to waste time removing the husk.

They're especially popular with finches, including goldfinches and greenfinches, as well as blue tits, great tits, house sparrows, robins and other small garden birds. They're also tidier than whole sunflower seeds because there are no piles of discarded husks left beneath the feeder.

Suet balls

Foods high in fat can be especially helpful when birds like robins and goldfinches require additional energy, particularly during chilly weather in autumn.

Article continues below

Suet balls, pellets and other fat-based foods are favoured by a broad variety of other garden birds, including sparrows, starlings, woodpeckers and nuthatches.

News.title: France protests turn violent as 1,200 arrested, looting breaks out and buildings burn
News.content:
Protests against the cost of living in France have turned to riots with Limoges city hall and Lyons tourist office among buildings destroyed while a young man had his hand blown off by a grenade

A city hall and tourist office were among buildings set on fire and completely destroyed as protests across France turned violent with police making at least 1,200 arrests.

The French government said there had been an "escalation in violence" as an estimated 550,000 took to the streets.

In Lyons, a tourist office was completely destroyed after it was set on fire and the same fate befell the city hall in Limoges where a 143-year-old spire collapsed. Tens of thousands protested in Paris alone with police firing tear gas and turning a water cannon on crowds in the Place de la République. In Marseille, a town hall was invaded and barricades set on fire as footage appeared to show people attacking a bank.

The mayor of Saint-Étienne said a young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" and France's interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said looting or attempted looted had been recorded in multiple cities.

Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters are demanding more investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and rundown buildings.

The latest protests are about wider problems in France, including the state of the education system.

News.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children will be a priority, says health secretary
News.content:
The NHS must take urgent action to stop children receiving treatment in hospital corridors, Health Secretary Yvette Cooper has told the BBC.

Cooper told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she has asked NHS England to draw up urgent plans to eliminate what is known as "corridor care" for children as a priority, and to introduce new standards for how children should be treated at A&E.

It comes after more than a dozen health groups urged the health secretary to take action to end corridor care.

The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.

Cooper said the way this data is collected will be changed to have the number of children included in the figures.

"I'm clear that child health needs to be a much greater priority for the NHS," says Cooper.

The government has an aim of ending corridor care more broadly by the end of this parliament, she added.

Kuenssberg highlighted the case of Finlay Roberts, a two-year-old boy who died in 2024 after spending the final hours of his life in a crowded A&E corridor.

Finlay's father David Roberts told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family briefly moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to Finlay in the corridor because there was no other option.

After hearing their story, Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS.

"No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor," she said.

The Whittington Health NHS Trust where this happened said they extended their condolences to Finlay's family.

They said they continue to experience periods of exceptional demand across emergency care and at times some patients may receive care in temporary clinical areas, including corridors.

They said: "Our staff work tirelessly to provide safe and compassionate care in extremely challenging conditions."

On Friday, 16 health groups - including Age UK, Marie Curie and the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) - sent a letter to Cooper, urging her to take action on ending corridor care.

It said the practice is fundamentally incompatible with NHS care standards and it would require "whole-system action" to eradicate it.

Before speaking to Kuenssberg, Cooper had warned the NHS was facing a more challenging winter than normal, after multiple heatwaves led to its busiest summer on record in England.

She announced Â£140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.

The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.

Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from, while the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) England said the funding was "just another sticking plaster".

In a statement, Cooper said: "Winter will be more challenging for our NHS this year, after such a heavy summer.

"That's why we have been preparing early and investing in extra urgent care capacity to help get patients the care they need."

It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.

Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.

NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.

Swords said earlier this month there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year.

"And unfortunately, people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she added.

RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome in the short term but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point".

"The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.

The waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row, according to the latest data.

An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

These were the highest numbers since October 2025, and have raised questions as to whether the NHS will meet the government's target to treat 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.

News.title: Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests
News.content:
A clock tower spire has collapsed in a ball of flames in the French city of Limoges amid nationwide protests.

The local prefecture said the town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze started deliberately.

Fire crews were still battling the blaze late into the night, while eyewitnesses captured the dramatic moment the tower's turret fell.

News.title: Police officer in hospital after being shot in Nottingham
News.content:
A police officer is being treated in hospital after being shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is now being treated for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a firearm was recovered and that two suspects, a man and a woman, fled the scene.

Angel Row is currently closed and a large police scene remains in place.

News.title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy but is it already out of control?
News.content:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than Â£20m on new players.

The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of Â£8.5m.

That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when Â£100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.

All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than Â£300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.

It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.

But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.

News.title: Making murder fun: How the Traitors' soundtrack sets the tone
News.content:
Suspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.

But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.

Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.

As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.

Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning.

"I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).

Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach.

"They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."

News.title: The playground murder - trauma, loss and a love that endured
News.content:
As we spoke, beside her on the sofa was her husband, Andy Thomson.

It took me a moment to take it in when they told me that Andy had been Alan's best friend.

That through all the tragedy and trauma, this couple found solace in each other and they've been married for 34 years.

Their little grandson is the light of their lives.

"We were kids and I got what she was going through because I was so close to Alan," says Andy.

"And then obviously when Alan passed away, it just drew the two of us even closer.

"And we're 34 years together, we're still going strong and always have been. And always will be."

"No one gives you a book on how to cope with trauma when you're a teenager," Pauline says.

"We were left to cope, and we helped each other. Our life hasn't been all trauma â not at all. But it has been a part of it.

"The most important thing for us was we wanted to talk about Diane and Alan, not just the names in the newspapers.

"For people to have a better understanding of them as kids â because that's what they were, they were kids. Just normal teenagers who should still be here."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

News.title: The turbulent backstory of one of Turkey's biggest girl groups
News.content:
A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night.

As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers.

The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya PÄ±nar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal YelekÃ§i and main dancer Esin Bahat.

But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions.

"After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal YelekÃ§i, playing on the group's name.

manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 TÃ¼rkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group.

They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including GÃ¼lÃ§in ErgÃ¼l, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show.

The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify.

News.title: Dubois destroys Wardley in two rounds to retain WBO title
News.content:
Daniel Dubois underlined his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain his WBO title in London.

The 29-year-old floored Wardley with a straight right inside the opening 20 seconds of their eagerly anticipated rematch at the O2 Arena and continued his relentless assault.

Wardley survived the opening round but was overwhelmed by another sustained attack in the second, prompting his corner to throw in the towel.

Dubois registers a second successive stoppage victory over Wardley, just five months after climbing off the canvas twice to dethrone his British rival in a thrilling 11-round contest in Manchester.

This time, there was no such drama for the champion, who was dominant from the opening bell as he extended his professional record to 24 wins - 23 by knockout - and three defeats.

"Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time and my era. I had my intentions, bad intentions from the beginning," Dubois said.

"My back was against the wall the first time, this time we just had to go out there and show that we mean business, which is what we did tonight."

Wardley, 31, suffered the second defeat of his 23-fight professional career.

"I have always thrown myself in with the best competitors out there, the best in the business, the biggest, hardest, meanest guys around so, there is no shame in a loss when you're testing yourself against the best," he said.

News.title: Reform activist suspended after reportedly saying Muslims cannot be British
News.content:
Reform UK has suspended a party activist who reportedly said that you cannot be Muslim and British in footage recorded by an undercover reporter from ITV News.

It is also investigating two of its councillors who appear to have advocated for the mass shooting of grooming gang members in the footage.

The party's response follows the latest allegations from undercover filming by ITV News, external, which has led to Reform facing questions over its vetting procedures for candidates.

A party spokesperson told the BBC it was pursuing legal action against ITV and the documentary's production company which had used undercover reporting to obtain its material.

Reform said in a statement to ITV there is "no room for racism" in the party, and added that it has opened investigations where activists or members had "clearly behaved inappropriately".

In the ITV documentary Undercover: A Year in Reform - set to be broadcast on Sunday - party activist Jason Powell reportedly says: "You cannot be Muslim and British, it's like oil and water."

In the footage, Powell, who has applied to be a Reform parliamentary candidate, also says he believes migrants who arrive illegally should be kept in "concentration camps" if they cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Reform said Powell has been suspended from party membership while an internal investigation takes place.

Reform is also investigating two councillors who represent the party in the London borough of Hounslow.

In the footage, Councillor David Kerr advocates machine gunning thousands of grooming gang members.

His colleague Councillor Adam Parkins suggests if he became prime minister he would conduct Sunday morning executions in the Downing Street rose garden.

Mr Parkins told the BBC that advocating the death penalty for men who "systemically groomed and raped young girls" was a perfectly legitimate opinion.

Mr Kerr has been contacted for comment.

Reform UK has said it has prioritised and improved its vetting procedures.

On Wednesday night, ITV News broadcast undercover filming which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

Responding to the broadcast, Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.

News.title: Boy, 14, stabbed in shopping centre attack
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy has been stabbed in a car park at Manchester's Arndale Centre shopping mall.

Greater Manchester Police said the boy was injured on the 9th floor of Manchester's Arndale Centre just after 15:00 BST on Saturday.

The force said his injuries were not believed to be life threatening or life changing. The Arndale was closed for several hours after the stabbing.

Det Insp Sam Jones said: "This is believed to be an isolated incident with no risk to the wider public."

The BBC understands a row with other males had taken place beforehand.

No arrests have been made in connection with the stabbing so far and inquiries were continuing.

News.title: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
News.content:
This was a more emotional speech than we are used to from John Swinney.

His voice quivered as he explained that his personal commitment to the cause is for the future of his 15-year-old son, Matthew.

Then the autocue stalled and the SNP leader is heard saying under his breath "oh, come on".

A period of silence was broken by the conference crowd who came to his rescue with a standing ovation.

Without the prime minister's name being mentioned, this section of the speech seemed to be a response to Andy Burnham's emotional appeal for the union in memory of his father at the Labour conference in Liverpool.

News.title: Comedian Paul Whitehouse mugged at London cash machine
News.content:
Actor and comedian Paul Whitehouse has fought back against someone who tried to steal his card at an London cash machine, according to his wife.

Dr Mine Conkbayir posted on Instagram that her husband had gone out to get some medication on Friday, when he was mugged at a cash machine behind a Sainsbury's in Islington.

"He did fight back and retrieved his card, with the perp scuttling away empty-handed," she wrote, warning people to be "super vigilant" out there.

The Welsh comedian, 68, is known for his work on The Fast Show and BBC's Gone Fishing.

In her post, Conkbayir said Whitehouse was picking up medication for her after she had a bad reaction to some treatment.

"Well, a horrid start to the weekend, would be an understatement," she wrote, adding that she had been encouraged by her husband to make the post "in the hope that it might help folk to be more aware when out and about".

Friends and fans alike have flooded to the comments of Conkbayir's post, condemning the attack and wishing Whitehouse a speedy recovery.

Among them were fellow comedian Dawn French, who wrote that the incident in Islington was "utterly not okay", and Angela Barnes, who said it was a "horrible thing to happen" and she was "sending love to you both".

Whitehouse is best known for his work on Gone Fishing, which he presents alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer.

The BBC Two series began in 2018 and sees Whitehouse and Mortimer discuss life while fishing. It has been nominated six times for a Bafta TV award.

The comedian has also been cast as Hogwarts caretaker Argus Filch in HBO's upcoming Harry Potter television series.

News.title: More NHS staff sacked over attacks victims' records
News.content:
Further members of staff have been sacked by an NHS trust for inappropriately accessing medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims.

Nottingham students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

In May, Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had dismissed 11 members of staff and, in an update on Friday, said a total of 15 people had now been sacked as part of its investigation.

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "I am appalled, it's time to get a handle on these failures."

He added: "Clearly, the way that the highest confidential data, which is medical data, is being looked at by voyeuristic people in the NHS is disgraceful."

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, medical director at NUH, said: "There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason and I hope this sends a really clear message â we will investigate and we will take action.

"To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough.

"I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members."

News.title: UK must protect against Russian 'hybrid attacks', ex-national security adviser says
News.content:
The government must do more to protect key infrastructure against "hybrid attacks" from Russia, a former national security adviser has told the BBC.

Lord Ricketts said more money should be spent on the defence budget, as well as improving the resilience of energy, transport and air traffic control.

He warned hybrid attacks were becoming "more reckless, more dangerous" and that people could end up being killed.

It comes after MI5 chief Sir Kevin McCallum said in his annual speech earlier this week that threats from foreign states, including Russia and Iran, had quadrupled in the last decade.

Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that ministers had to warn British people about what might be coming.

"Not only is [Russian President Vladimir] Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he's also trying to undermine morale in European countries," he said.

He said there had been a stark warning from the head of MI5 that there could be worse to come in terms of hybrid attacks in the UK or on other Nato territory.

Responding to a question about the impact of disruption by Russia, Lord Ricketts said: "I'm not saying there's going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain.

"But yes these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous...people are going to end up getting killed somewhere."

Hybrid attacks tend to use non-military methods, such as hacking, in an attempt to destabilise a country.

Moscow is suspected to be behind many such attacks in Europe since the start of the war in Ukraine, but it has always denied involvement.

As well as cyber-attacks, hybrid attacks can include attempts at sabotage and efforts to spread misinformation.

Lord Ricketts's warning comes after US President Donald Trump blocked sanctions on Russia. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said the decision "only encourages him [Putin] to keep attacking" Ukraine.

The former national security adviser, who also previously ran the Foreign Office, said the UK's focus should be on putting more effort into the coalition of the willing, rather than attempting to act as a bridge between Zelensky and Trump.

"I don't think in Trump's current mood there is any influence Britain can have in the short term," he said.

A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.

Last month, Germany said Russia was responsible for a drone attack on an airport in Leipzig, in which an explosive failed to detonate close to Ukrainian cargo planes.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned in September that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France had intensified.

News.title: Husband calls for PM to intervene after wife detained in Egypt
News.content:
The husband of a woman who was detained by the Egyptian authorities has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to get involved and help with her release.

Eman el-Shazly, from Handsworth Wood, in Birmingham, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo two months ago, allegedly in relation to her sister's online activism.

Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said that their family felt "very helpless" and that their "only possible solution" was for Burnham to "make a phone call to Egypt" to end the detainment.

The BBC has approached the Egyptian consulate in London for a response. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said it was in contact with authorities in Egypt.

Moustapha said he had had "no contact whatsoever" with his wife, but had heard from her mother that her health had deteriorated due to a lack of food and medical assistance.

"It's not a five-star hotel, there's 30 individuals sleeping in a cell with one toilet and one shower," he said.

He told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.

News.title: House that looks like boulders to be built on moor
News.content:
Plans for a house designed to look like rocks on a famous Yorkshire moor have been approved.

The contemporary structure, which has large irregular-shaped windows and a natural outdoor pool, looks similar to the landmark Cow and Calf Rocks in Ilkley, West Yorkshire.

The house will be built on green belt land which is the garden of a home off Heber's Ghyll Drive, and will be eco-friendly, to an ultra-low energy standard called Passivhaus.

Harrogate-based architects Shaw & Jagger said the scheme was eventually passed by HM Planning Inspectorate through the country house clause, which allows development on green belt for buildings of "exceptional quality".

The architect Matt Masserella-Gill was commissioned to design the home by the landowner David Rasche.

He said the design was "arguably the most complex country house application ever made in this country".

The house has been named Fomorian - meaning a supernatural race of giants in Irish mythology - taking inspiration from the mythical giant Rombald who is told to have lived on Ilkley Moor.

Masserella-Gill said: "The design approach was to propose a scheme that is intrinsically linked to the spirit of its place. Fomorian is of its place, part of the moors, its geology and its spirit.

"We took cues from local folklore, the surrounding rocks; ancient carvings, standing stones and escarpments that are synonymous with the landscape."

News.title: Hurricane Trudy batters Mexico’s Pacific coast with heavy rain and strong winds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Heavy rain and strong winds hit portions of Mexico’s southwestern and west-central Pacific coast early on Sunday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center reported.

A hurricane warning remains in place from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The Category 2 hurricane registered sustained winds of 100 mph (155 km/h), located 135 miles (215 kilometres) south of Cabo Corrientes and 115 miles (185 kilometres) west-southwest of Manzanillo, moving north-west at 9 mph (15 km/h).

Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi intensified into a Category 4 super typhoon as it passed Guam.

Trudy’s centre is expected to linger near the Mexican coast through Sunday evening before tracking south of the Baja California Peninsula.

Potential morning strengthening should give way to weakening later in the day. A tropical storm warning covers Las Islas Marias, though alerts east of Punta San Telmo to Lazaro Cardenas have been discontinued.

The Mexican navy has urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution, warning of high waves, torrential rain, rising rivers, flooding, and landslides in vulnerable areas.

open image in gallery A man sits along the shoreline as Hurricane Trudy advances across the Pacific Ocean off Mexico's western coast, in Boca de Apiza, Michoacan state, Mexico ( Reuters )

Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.

Trudy was expected to bring 4-8 inches (10-20 centimeters) of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches (30 centimeters) along and near the coast in Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco.

The hurricane center warned of potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas with steep terrain.

Also in the Pacific, Champi was moving away from Guam on Sunday after passing close to the island’s southern tip, with sustained winds of 150 mph (240 kph). At 1 pm Sunday local time it was 130 miles (210 kilometers) west of Guam, moving west at 16 mph (26 kph), according to the US National Weather Service.

The storm could strengthen into a Category 5 super typhoon early Monday. Guam and Rota remained under a typhoon warning, while the tropical storm warning and typhoon watch for Tinian and Saipan were canceled.

The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands both requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.

On Saturday, US President Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance is available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.

Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from FEMA.

The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

News.title: Salman Rushdie hails cockroach protests as India’s ‘most hopeful moment’ in a long time
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Acclaimed writer Sir Salman Rushdie and filmmaker Mira Nair have extended their support for India’s “cockroach” protest movement, after a police crackdown on the group’s leadership.

India has seen weeks of major street protests, first ousting the country’s education minister and then demanding the resignation of its chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter rolls.

The movement has galvanised opposition to prime minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP, with major students’ unions and opposition parties calling a series of marches that have led the authorities to lock down central Delhi.

Speaking at a fundraising dinner for the Asian American Writers’ Workshop in New York, Sir Salman called the protests India’s “most hopeful moment” in a long time.

“There is something going on in India right now. India is boiling,” said the Satanic Verses author. “And I would feel wrong not to say, maybe not the thing to say in a restaurant, to celebrate the cockroach. Young people of India have given us the most hopeful moment for a very long time.”

The gathering took place on Wednesday and included a celebration of Nair’s birthday. The filmmaker, who is also the mother of New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, described herself as a “cockroach mom” and expressed solidarity with those fighting for the country’s democracy, according to writer Amitava Kumar’s account of the event in a post on his Substack.

New York City Mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani celebrates alongside his mother Mira Nair ( AFP/Getty )

Sir Salman has spoken in the past about his concerns over “attacks on free speech and rising Hindu nationalism” in the country of his birth.

Kumar wrote that the Booker Prize winner discussed growing up in the Indian city of Mumbai, then Bombay. “Salman said when he was growing up in Bombay, the festivals were for all of us. It didn’t matter whether we were Hindus, Muslims, Sikh, Christian, Parsi. We all celebrated everything.”

Kumar wrote: “This spirit was alive in the gathering last evening but, Salman suggested, perhaps this feeling was no longer alive in that way in India any more.”

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after being detained while he was trying to participate in a march in the Indian capital.

The movement published a photo of him on X saying: “Abhijeet Dipke is a free man.”

He was released after agreeing to certain conditions, said CJP’s legal affairs chief Ratna Singh on social media, without elaborating on what they were.

Mr Dipke was produced before a special executive magistrate on Saturday afternoon, before being released.

Mr Dipke said on Instagram that he “knew going to jail was inevitable” and that he was ready to face “whatever comes my way”.

“Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country,” he said, referring to his return from the US, where he was studying for a masters degree in public relations.

Last month Sir Salman sat down with The Independent’s editor-in-chief Geordie Greig for an interview marking the launch of a new documentary on the assassination attempt that left him blind in one eye, Knife.

In it, he spoke about looking forward to the end of “brilliant liar” Donald Trump’s time as US president, saying: “I look forward to the day when there is no more Trump and every ugly thing he's built gets torn down.”

News.title: Faithful gather to welcome Pope Leo back for Sunday blessing after cancer surgery
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Catholic faithful converged on St. Peter’s Square on Sunday to welcome Pope Leo XIV back to the Vatican after surgery to remove a tumor from his lung.

Leo is delivering the traditional Angelus blessing, his first official appointment since being released from the hospital on Saturday, four days after cancer surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

He told a reporter in English that he was doing ‘’much better’’ as he drove away from Rome’s Gemelli hospital to return to the Vatican, well ahead of the weeklong hospital stay than had been initially anticipated.

“I don’t believe it, because he was just operated on the other day,” Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia, said. “It is a miracle that he recovered already.”

American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.

‘’I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,’’ Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''

Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt “very blessed” to be present for the pope’s return to his flock.

“I’m so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this,” Holland said.

Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that there are “no clinical reasons” to preclude the trip.

“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so.”

“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Margaritora said.

Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor’s molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor’s genetic characteristics.

News.title: Woman condemns ‘degrading’ and ‘disturbing’ Halloween Park experience
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A woman has condemned a “depraved” adults-only Halloween Park experience in Liverpool after she was left shocked by the sexually graphic nature of her experience.

Robyn Doughty, 33, said the optional Hellfire Club experience at Newsham Scream Park felt like a “simulation of... sexual degradation, and sexual violation.”

The tattoo artist went with a group of friends on Thursday and was asked to sign a waiver before entering the over-18s section.

But Ms Doughty has since taken to social media to call out the park, saying there should have been more warning after staff called them “s****” and made “all kinds of horrific sexual noises”.

“The whole time they’re just calling you “s****” and berating you,” she said in a video shared to TikTok.

“My friend walked out in tears and couldn’t even explain why she was horrified, and when I complained, I was told ‘oh it’s subjective’.

"Where’s the warning? Their website lists be aware of PTSD and anxiety but nowhere does it say graphically sexual.”

The scream park said its "terms and conditions, which must be agreed to before entering the attraction, outline the nature of the experience, including its adult and horror themes, physical interaction and sensory effects".

open image in gallery Robyn Doughty complained to staff after her friend was walked out in tears ( Facebook/Newsham Scream Park )

Ms Doughty told Liverpool Echo: “I don't think I fully realised the scale of it myself until all these other people started coming forward.

“I've had countless people in my DMs sharing similar stories, men and women, girlfriends and boyfriends, and the common denominator has been the same: it's degrading, humiliating and quite disturbing.

“I think it's more complicated than just a scare. It's not a fun, physical scare - it's psychological. Because it's presented in such a light-hearted setting, people aren't prepared for it. These young, impressionable kids and people who might have experienced past trauma aren't prepared for it, because it's in a light-hearted setting.”

On its website, Newsham Scream Park says it recommends the experience for adults only because of the “extreme level scare attractions designed to unsettle and terrify”.

The park transforms a derelict Victorian-era building into an immersive horror experience every year for Halloween.

“Step inside the darkness and face your fears across a series of live-action horror mazes, scare zones, and twisted theatrical experiences,” it says.

“Our scare actors will bring your nightmares to life as you navigate haunted wards, deranged experiments, and unspeakable horrors lurking around every corner. Every room tells a story. Every hallway hides a scream.”

Newsham Scream Park told the BBC the Hellfire Club was "designed to deliver an intense experience" and was optional and adults-only, with ID required for anyone under the age of 21.

"Guest welfare is a priority throughout the attraction and our terms and conditions, which much be agreed to before entering the attraction, outline the nature of the experience, including its adult and horror themes, physical interaction and sensory effects," it said. "They also highlight that some elements may cause distress, identify circumstances in which the attraction may not be suitable, and explain that guests can end their participation immediately, at any time, using the safe word provided without explanation."

The park said that guests changing their mind after reading the terms and conditions could have a refund and said it recognised the themes "will not be suitable for everyone and encourage all guests to read the information provided carefully before deciding whether to participate".

Newsham Scream Park has been contacted for further comment.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI), email jo@samaritans.org, or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch

News.title: Canada military base fire live: Multiple deaths and injuries after explosion sparks disaster in Alberta
News.content:
