World.title: Photos: Protests across France spiral into looting, blazes and clashes
World.content:
France woke up on Sunday to streets scarred by burned cars, smashed shopfronts and looted businesses after cost-of-living protests spiralled into some of the worst unrest in years.

What began as largely peaceful marches on Saturday over soaring prices and falling living standards quickly escalated, with masked youths torching vehicles, ransacking shops and attacking public buildings in cities including Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux, Lille and Strasbourg.

Paris Deputy Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said “whole streets have been devastated” as police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who hurled projectiles and set off fireworks. Authorities reported about 1,200 arrests and 150 injured police officers. It was “a miracle the toll isn’t higher,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said.

Town halls in Limoges, Marseille and Lille were targeted, while a police compound in Bordeaux and a tourist office in Lyon were vandalised. In Saint-Etienne, a 17-year-old lost his right hand after being hit by a crowd-control grenade.

The unrest follows weeks of student protests to demand more investment in education and comes six months before the presidential election. Far-right and left-wing contenders traded blame over the violence, even as President Emmanuel Macron promised that those responsible for looting and attacks on public buildings “will be prosecuted and punished”.

World.title: There is no split in MAGA
World.content:
But there is an attempt to redefine who the movement includes and what it stands for.

As the midterm elections near, we are hearing a lot about a “split” within the Make America Great Again (MAGA) coalition, which got Donald Trump elected United States president in 2024. I understand the tragedy of MAGA a little differently: not as a split, but as a refusal by the best members of that coalition to abandon the solidarity we’ve formed between us.

I had the privilege of helping bring this coalition together in 2024. It was a collection of groupings traditionally pitted against each other: social conservatives, pro-lifers, devout Christians, devout Muslims, devout Quakers, disaffected leftists, young first-time voters – all coming together behind a Republican candidacy.

Together, we made history and delivered a moral mandate based on a humane concern for the human cost of unregulated borders, thoughtless warmongering overseas and the ruling-class politicking that had allowed a Jeffrey Epstein syndicate to go unpunished while the basic dignity of the “least of our brethren” went untended.

In the campaign’s final stretch, I visited Syrian Christian churches in Pennsylvania and met Americans whose families had personally suffered the worst of what Washington’s foreign policy can do. In those communities, we talked about Gaza, peace and Trump’s promises.

This miraculous, ragtag, all-American patchwork of people who supported Trump in 2024 truly became a people when they discovered their shared belief in the mission of electing a president who would break with the Washington establishment’s inhumane policies.



Today, that coalition is remarkably intact. What is instead happening is that there is a concerted effort to redefine what MAGA is.

In the weeks following the launch of the disastrous US-Israeli war on Iran, Trump announced “I am MAGA” and insisted on including in the brand the ideology of infamous neo-cons like Mark Levin.

As a result, MAGA has now become a blunt instrument of the same war-hungry elites the original coalition aimed to depose. The brand is now on course to be destroyed this November. That, however, says nothing about the goodness and power of the movement that stood behind Trump in 2024.

Perhaps one of the central factors that is driving this process of MAGA destruction is the decision to support, fund and protect Israel at any cost as it carries out a genocide in Gaza and various other atrocities in the Middle East.

And Election Day 2026 will represent the first time the public’s moral indignation fully makes itself felt. But, bafflingly, that’s also the one matter that our most powerful politicians have made a point of doubling down on ahead of the midterms.

Just a few days ago, The New York Times reported that David Milstein, senior adviser to US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and stepson of Levin, repeatedly suppressed or rewrote embassy reporting on Israeli violence against Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. Milstein allegedly even blocked reporting about the killings of Palestinian Americans by Israeli settlers and security forces. Nevertheless, he still retains his position.

I write this as an American conservative and a Catholic. But at a time when Washington is spending America’s moral authority to shield Israel’s government from accountability while treating Palestinian lives as negotiable, both my deepest-held convictions and my patriotism require that I stand against some of the loudest self-proclaimed “patriots” and “conservative Christians”. Not because I now reject what they claim to represent, but because I still embrace it.

An April survey by Pew Research found that 57 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents aged 18 to 49 viewed Israel unfavourably. Young conservatives have watched the same harrowing footage of the Gaza genocide as everyone else. Today’s new self-proclaimed leaders of MAGA – a movement that taught the youth to distrust official narratives – cannot reasonably expect them to stop asking questions.

Especially not when there are still plenty of prominent figures who have retained their integrity and still carry the original coalition’s banner.



Trump’s former counterterrorism chief Joe Kent courageously resigned over the Iran war and publicly described the Israeli and lobbying pressure that helped bring it about. Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard bravely put on record that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and had not rebuilt its enrichment capability since the 12-day war of 2025, undercutting the “imminent nuclear threat” claim used to justify the war this year.

Former Congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene and Congressman Thomas Massie stood against the Gaza genocide and the Epstein cover-up. Trump and the donor-class backers of his newly adopted neo-con agenda pummelled them: Greene resigned, and Massie lost his primary after a multimillion-dollar campaign to unseat him.

Conservative activist Carrie Prejean Boller defended Christian opposition to Israel’s violence in Gaza and the bigoted ideology of Zionism. She paid a price, losing her seat on Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission, but proved herself a true leader in our movement.

Conservative commentators Tucker Carlson and Alex Jones similarly used their influential platforms to stand up to Trump over the Iran war and against US backing of Israeli abuses of Palestinians.

And consider the comedians and podcasters: Joe Rogan, Theo Von, Tim Dillon and others. Trump’s son Barron was credited with the brilliant idea of bringing his father’s campaign to their audiences in 2024. They graciously opened their platforms: Rogan endorsed Trump, Von interviewed him and Dillon hosted JD Vance after he became the vice presidential nominee.

Now these same voices are condemning the bloodshed and broken promises. From Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank to Iran, Trump has squandered their goodwill.

These political and cultural leaders represent a preview of the future this coalition still has ahead of it. The candidates they eventually support – or themselves, if they run – will be easily recognisable to voters. And I and millions of others will be behind them.

Browbeating the voters whose support the Trump administration betrayed will have exactly the consequences you would expect. The original MAGA coalition will destroy a Republican Party that embraces the policies the movement aimed to destroy all along. On Election Day, the coalition’s moral indignation will fully make itself felt.

Don’t be misled by talk of a “split” in our movement. When the new “MAGA” falls, it will not be due to a disintegration of our coalition. It will be because our coalition is still going strong.

And we have not yet begun to fight.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
World.content:
Relations between the two countries are dominated by policy complexes shaped by a history of hostility.

Since the start of the war, there have been several negotiation initiatives between the United States and Iran. Only one – the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad on June 18 – was concluded, but it collapsed within days.

While prevailing analyses tend to explain this failure through the details of the provisions, this article proceeds from a different premise: that the diplomatic stalemate between the two sides is shaped by a syndrome that has governed US-Iranian relations for years.

In international relations, psychological syndromes can arise as a result of deep crises that leave their mark on political consciousness and memory, potentially obstructing efforts at rapprochement and negotiation between countries.

In the case of Iran and the US, the syndrome is comprised of two complexes: the complex Washington developed as a result of the 1979 siege of the US embassy in Tehran and the complex Tehran developed as a result of historical US hostility and its withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018.

The roots of the rupture between the two countries go as far back as August 1953 when US and British intelligence agencies helped overthrow the nationalist government of Mohammad Mosaddegh after it nationalised the oil industry in 1951. Since then, a perception has become entrenched in Iranian consciousness: that Washington does not accept an independent government in Tehran and it is prepared to sabotage it if it goes against its interests.

From this perspective, Washington’s decision to host Shah Reza Pahlavi, who had just been overthrown by his people, for medical treatment in October 1979 was read in revolutionary Tehran as a prelude to a second coup.



Iranian students stormed the US embassy on November 4 that year and held 52 Americans for 444 days. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed and have not been restored to this day.

While the incident is portrayed in the Iranian narrative as a defence of the revolution, in American consciousness, it established the image of Iran as a state that does not respect international norms, whose word cannot be relied upon and whose behaviour should not be rewarded.

That is the embassy siege complex. It is not about the incident itself so much as the informal rule it produced in US decision-making: that Iran must concede first and its concession must be verified before it receives anything in return.

The Iranian complex was shaped by this history as well, but it reached its peak in May 2018 when US President Donald Trump withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) despite the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA’s) confirmation that Tehran was complying with it.

Just two weeks later, US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced 12 demands for a new deal, only four of which were related to the nuclear file. Seven of them were related to Iran’s regional behaviour in Lebanon, Palestine, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, Afghanistan and the Gulf. In other words, Washington did not merely revoke an existing agreement; it also raised the ceiling of its conditions for any future agreement.

The knot then deepened in June 2025 when the US took part in the Twelve-Day War and struck the nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at a time when a new round of indirect negotiations was scheduled in Muscat. It then reached its furthest point with Washington’s participation alongside Israel in the current war.

Accordingly, a conviction became entrenched in the Iranian consciousness that an American signature guarantees nothing, that any agreement can be overturned with a change of administration and indeed that negotiation itself may be a cover for war rather than an alternative to it.

The informal rule this has produced in Iranian decision-making is that there will be no step taken before binding guarantees and no concession before pressure is lifted.

Thus, the two complexes stand at opposite ends: The first requires Iranian action before an American quid pro quo while the second requires an American guarantee before Iranian action.

A reading of the recent negotiation initiatives shows that every US initiative bears the imprint of the embassy siege complex. The 15-point plan put forward in March demanded the dismantling of the Natanz, Isfahan and Fordow facilities; an end to uranium enrichment; the suspension of Iran’s missile programme; and the abandonment of its allies in exchange for promises to lift sanctions later.



The May draft by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner linked the release of Iran’s frozen funds to the suspension of enrichment first. The American response in September also stipulated the freezing of enrichment and the entry of inspectors throughout the negotiation period.

What remains constant in the American initiatives is that Iranian action precedes the quid pro quo and verification precedes trust.

The imprint of the JCPOA withdrawal complex in the Iranian initiatives is also a constant. The five-point response in late March demanded guarantees that war would not be repeated. The 10 points put forward in April demanded a binding UN Security Council resolution shielding any agreement from being overturned. And the 14 points in May demanded a nonaggression pledge that includes Israel.

Meanwhile, the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran last month stipulated the lifting of sanctions and the US naval blockade on Iran before the opening of the Strait of Hormuz on the sixth day and the start of nuclear negotiations on the seventh. What remains constant in the Iranian initiatives is that guarantees precede action and the lifting of pressure precedes Iranian concessions.

All these initiatives were dialogue between two complexes with each side drafting its text to protect itself from a repetition of its historical experience with the other, rather than to meet the other halfway. This may explain why the gap in substance has narrowed, but the gap in trust has not.

The Islamabad memorandum represents the exception that proves the rule as it was the closest moment to a settlement because it was formulated to reassure both sides over their core concerns. To reassure Washington, it stipulated the dilution of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium and made the lifting of sanctions and unfreezing of funds conditional on Iranian implementation.

To reassure Tehran, it provided for an end to hostilities, respect for mutual sovereignty, a mechanism to monitor implementation and UN Security Council approval of the final agreement. Ballistic missiles were also entirely absent from the text.

But this agreement did not hold. Tehran suspended its participation in the Geneva round of talks because of the absence of a ceasefire in Lebanon, which had been a consistent demand in every Iranian initiative since March. In the Iranian reading, Washington’s inability to rein in Israel confirmed that an American signature was not enough. The JCPOA withdrawal complex immediately kicked in, and the two sides returned to square one.

By late September, the dispute appeared to have shifted definitively from substance to sequencing. Informed sources indicated that it now revolves around the order of steps rather than their content and the stated goal has become a return to an enhanced version of the June memorandum.

Here the two complexes appear in their clearest form: Washington wants the Strait of Hormuz opened and enrichment frozen first because it does not trust Iran while Tehran wants the naval blockade lifted first because it does not trust the US.



A comparison between Pompeo’s 2018 conditions and the June 2026 memorandum shows that US demands have retreated from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear file and the Strait of Hormuz while Iranian demands have shifted from compensation to be paid by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties.

In other words, the substantive gap between the two sides has narrowed considerably – something that would have been unimaginable eight years ago.

However, the two complexes have not diminished; indeed, they may have deepened because of the war. Each complex feeds the other until together they have become a single syndrome, and diplomatic deadlock has turned from a passing condition into a stable structure.

Accordingly, any new formula for sequencing the steps, however precise, will remain unable to break this deadlock unless it addresses both complexes at once – something that requires a third party capable of guaranteeing both the action and the reciprocal action simultaneously.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

World.title: WNBA Finals: Gabby Williams leads Valkyries to nervy Game 1 win over Dream
World.content:
Williams scored 26 points as the Golden State Valkyries came back to take the lead at home against the Atlanta Dream.

Gabby Williams scored a game-high 26 points, including four key free throws in the final 78 seconds as the Golden State Valkyries held off the Atlanta Dream 68-64 in game one of the WNBA Finals.

Williams, runner-up to Atlanta’s Angel Reese in Defensive Player of the Year voting, has emerged as an offensive force for the Valkyries in the playoffs and carried the scoring load on a tough shooting night for the hosts, who did not have another player score in double figures on Saturday.

The French star took some time to warm up, going scoreless in the first quarter as the Valkyries got off to a tentative start in front of a raucous crowd at Chase Center.

“Once we all started having fun and the excitement got out, we started to kind of find our way,” Williams, who erupted for 16 points in the second quarter, said in an on-court interview.

“There was a lid on that basket tonight, but that’s why we rely on our defence,” she said.

Golden State trailed by one with 1 minute and 18 seconds remaining when Williams seized the rebound off a miss by Atlanta’s Allisha Gray and was fouled by Reese.

Williams made both free throws to put the Valkyries up 65-64 and added another pair of free throws to seal the win with 4.1 seconds left.

“It came down to getting stops and that’s been our bread-and-butter all ‌year,” noted Williams, whose team has allowed 335 fewer points than any other in the WNBA this season. “That’s why we harp on it so much, because we’ve built such great defensive habits.”



Gray, the Dream’s leading scorer, returned after missing two games with a hand injury and scored 19 points, but she was scoreless in the fourth quarter, when Atlanta made just two of their 19 attempts from the floor.

Reese added 14 points and 12 rebounds, and Rhyne Howard scored 12 for Atlanta.

Atlanta scored just two in an overall eight-point fourth quarter, where Gray was scoreless over the final 10 minutes and Reese scored all of her 14 points in the first half.

“I don’t think they really did anything,” Reese said. “Maybe that was just on me; I wasn’t aggressive enough with the ball and trying to get the ball and get to my spot. I’m definitely going to do a better job of that next game.”

The Valkyries will host game two of the best-of-seven series on Monday.

Both teams are chasing a first WNBA title. The Dream have come up empty in three prior trips to the Finals, most recently in 2013.

The Valkyries, who last year became the first WNBA expansion franchise to reach the playoffs in their inaugural season, are now contending for the title in their second.

World.title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as more than 1,200 arrested after protests
World.content:
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living.

At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.

In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.

Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.

Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported.

Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest.

In the French capital, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC that they were "pacifists" who were "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".

World.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
World.content:
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.

What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.

This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.

It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

World.title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
World.content:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicide

The few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood.

"This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.

The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars.

"You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.

He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.

We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.

Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.

World.title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
World.content:
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.

Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.

But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".

The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".

It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".

World.title: Several dead or injured in major fire at Canada military base
World.content:
Several people have been killed or injured as a result of a large fire near a Canadian military base in Alberta, the nation's defence minister has said.

David McGuinty did not confirm the cause or the number of casualties, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate". The Canadian military and local authorities were managing the fire, he said.

Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where the fire broke out, is one of the country's busiest military training bases.

Canadian TV network Global News reported that at least seven were killed and dozens more injured when a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise, citing unnamed military sources.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said that a "serious incident creating a major fire" had occurred, adding that his "thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected".

The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) said Royal Alexandra Hospital in Edmonton had declared a code orange, a disaster response protocol for responding to a high-casualty incident.

Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor there, told the broadcaster that the number of patients would otherwise "overwhelm" Edmonton's healthcare facilities.

"It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

After the fire erupted on Saturday, it "spread rapidly due to high winds" and tore through the fences of the base, the Municipal District of Wainwright said.

The region experienced gusts of up to 100km/h (62mph), though local officials indicated fire crews had contained the blaze.

The defence minister told reporters he "cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory".

It is unclear when the fire broke out, but the district first posted about the incident at about 17:30 local time (23:30 GMT).

Local authorities have urged residents to avoid the area and give all emergency vehicles right of way.

The mayor of the nearby town of Wainwright, Bruce Pugh, said it was a "heavy day" for his community.

"We have neighbours who are either serving or former members of the Canadian Armed Forces. We're integrated, our kids play in the same hockey teams, attend the same schools," he told CBC.

While details on the impact of the fire remain unclear, Pugh said he believed this would come to be the area's largest-ever mass casualty event.

World.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
World.content:
Donald Trump has blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.

The sanctions were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September.

But Trump issued an executive order on Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Trump's order was "an important and truly historic moment", and that the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.

Since then, Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The sanctions suspension seemed to add further fuel to the fire.

Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".

He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine â right before winter."

Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.

The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas â most significantly China and India.

It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the suspension would consist of a 60-day pause to allow for the Trump administration to analyse the impact they might have on the US and global economy.

World.title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
World.content:
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.

Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.

The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.

Protests which began in the summer have grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.

Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.

The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.

During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.

Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.

Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.

Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.

World.title: Church makes sainthood case for 'WW1 hero' priest
World.content:
A "heroic" Irish priest who was killed in World War One while trying to help injured and dying soldiers will take a step towards potential sainthood on Sunday.

Fr Willie Doyle served as a British Army chaplain during some of the bloodiest battles of the First World War, including the Somme, Messines and Passchendaele.

The Dubliner was renowned for his courage under fire, repeatedly running into No Man's Land to carry wounded troops to safety or to comfort those fatally injured.

On Sunday, the Catholic Church in Ireland will hold a special service in Mullingar Cathedral before sending thousands of documents to the Vatican to support the case for his canonisation.

World War One had been raging for more than a year when Fr Doyle volunteered to become a military chaplain to the 16th (Irish) Division of the British Army.

He served with the division for almost two years, much of that in the trenches at the Western Front, until his death at the Battle of Passchendaele on 16 August 1917.

He was killed by shellfire while going to the aid of two wounded Protestant soldiers, one of which was a young officer from Belfast - 2nd Lt Arthur Vivian Green.

Because of that, the Catholic Church in Ireland considers Fr Doyle to be an "ecumenical martyr of charity" who died ministering to soldiers of other Christian denominations.

World.title: Health workers’ strike disrupts hospital services in Katsina
World.content:
An ongoing strike by health professionals in Katsina State has disrupted services at public hospitals, leaving patients and pltheir caregivers uncertain about access to medical treatment.

The health workers embarked on a one-week warning strike following disagreements with the state government over their welfare and remuneration.

A visit to Turai Yar’Adua Maternal and Child Hospital in Katsina on Saturday revealed the impact of the industrial action, with only a few patients seen around the surgical ward.

For many families, the dispute over workers’ remuneration has heightened concerns over the health and safety of loved ones requiring urgent medical attention.

One of the affected caregivers, Aina’u Abdulmajid, said her patient was suffering from complications arising from surgery and appealed to the state government to restore normal hospital services.

“For the sake of God, we call on the government to intervene. Our patient is suffering from complications arising from surgery. Please help us and restore services,” she pleaded.

Ms Abdulmajid’s appeal reflected the predicament of families who depend on public hospitals for treatment but have found themselves caught between an unresolved labour dispute and the urgent need for medical attention.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Another caregiver, Sulaiman Mansir, said he had brought his sick child to the hospital for treatment but was confronted with the disruptions caused by the strike.

Mr Mansir expressed concern over the uncertainty surrounding his child’s treatment and urged the government to engage the striking health workers to resolve the dispute without further delay.

The industrial action has compounded the difficulties faced by families already grappling with transportation costs, medicines and other medical expenses.

Why health workers are on strike

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the strike was declared by the Assembly of Health Professionals following unresolved disagreements with the Katsina State government over workers’ remuneration and welfare.

The assembly comprises the Medical and Health Workers Union of Nigeria (MHWUN), the National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives (NANNM), and the National Union of Allied Health Professionals (NUAHP).

The assembly’s chairperson, Ibrahim Balange, said the unions issued a seven-day strike notice to the government on 7 October, but the notice expired without a satisfactory resolution of their demands.

Mr Balange explained that the dispute began in 2024, when the state government indicated plans to review the allowances of health professionals to align them with those of their counterparts in federal government service.

He said the workers subsequently raised concerns about the implementation of the minimum wage, alleging that the salary structure approved for them differed from what they were receiving.

According to him, a committee established to investigate the complaints submitted recommendations in March 2025, but the government had yet to implement them.

He said the Office of Public Service Reform later offered the workers 10 per cent of the salary difference between them and their counterparts in federal institutions.

However, the offer did not resolve the disagreement.

Government responds

Following the commencement of the strike, the state government increased its offer to 15 per cent, but the unions rejected it, maintaining that it fell short of their demands.

The Head of the State Civil Service, Masa’ud Banye, confirmed that government officials had met with representatives of the striking workers to discuss the dispute.

Mr Banye expressed optimism that the disagreement would soon be resolved and acknowledged the difficulties patients were experiencing because of the industrial action.

He said Governor Dikko Radda’s administration remained committed to effective healthcare delivery in the state.

(NAN)

World.title: SERAP sues INEC over failure to account for ‘₦126bn electoral funds’
World.content:
The Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) has filed a lawsuit against the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) “over its failure to account for over ₦126.46 billion in public funds appropriated for electoral operations but allegedly diverted, lost, mismanaged or otherwise unaccounted for.”

The funds were meant to buy ballot boxes, electoral devices and materials, sensitive materials and result sheets, vehicles and accreditation devices, and to pay for audit and consultancy services, digital archiving, and other goods and services required for the conduct and administration of elections.

According to the 2023 audited report of the Auditor-General of the Federation, published on 7 August 2026, the allegations variously covered periods between January and December 2022 and, in some cases, extended to 31 December 2023.

In the suit number FHC/ABJ/CS/2507/2026, filed last week at the Federal High Court in Abuja, SERAP is seeking “an order of mandamus to direct and compel INEC to promptly disclose detailed information on the expenditure, utilisation and disbursement of over ₦126.46 billion appropriated for electoral operations, including the procurement of election materials, equipment, and vehicles.”

SERAP is also seeking “an order of mandamus to direct and compel INEC to disclose a full financial and documentary account of the over ₦126 billion appropriated for electoral operations, including amounts released and paid, payment beneficiaries, details of contractors and their beneficial owners.”

In the suit, SERAP is arguing that: “Electoral resources are public resources. INEC must be able to account for every naira, demonstrate that it was lawfully spent and show that it served the purposes for which it was appropriated.”

SERAP is also arguing that: “These allegations are particularly disturbing given the constitutional importance of INEC and the fact that the expenditure concerns resources appropriated for the administration of Nigeria’s electoral system.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to SERAP, “With the 2027 general elections approaching, transparency and accountability in the management of these funds are essential to safeguarding public confidence in the electoral process and ensuring that resources intended to support credible elections are properly utilised.”

SERAP is arguing that, “These findings by the Auditor-General suggest a grave violation of the public trust and the provisions of the Nigerian Constitution 1999 (as amended), national anticorruption laws, and the country’s obligations under the UN Convention against Corruption.”

The lawsuit filed on behalf of SERAP by its lawyers, Kolawole Oluwadare, Kehinde Oyewumi and Andrew Nwankwo, reads in part: “Democracy requires an informed citizenry. That principle is directly relevant to public expenditure by an electoral management body: citizens are entitled to know how resources entrusted to INEC for the conduct of elections have been used.”

“According to the Auditor-General, INEC ‘irregularly paid’ over ₦112 billion [₦112,155,597,845.00] ‘for ballot boxes, electoral devices, items and materials without competitive bidding or a BPP Certificate of No Objection.’”

“The Auditor-General found ‘no evidence that the items were procured.’ The ‘contracts were awarded to companies whose competences, experience, capacities, addresses and factory locations were unknown.’ He is concerned that the money ‘may have been diverted.’ He wants the money recovered.”

“INEC also ‘paid over ₦1 billion [₦1,058,925,000.00] for Toyota Prado TXL 2021 Model without , competitive bidding, bid evaluation or a BPP Certificate of No Objection.’ The Auditor-General fears that the money ‘may have been lost’ and that the contracts ‘may have been inflated.’”

“INEC ‘paid over ₦3 billion [₦3,136,806,050.00] to four contractors for ballot guides, sensitive materials and result sheets before the contracts were awarded, with no evidence of payment.’ The Auditor-General is concerned that the money ‘may have been diverted.’ He wants the money recovered and remitted to the treasury.”

“INEC also ‘paid over ₦9 billion [₦9,245,965,502.60] for 22 contracts for similar goods and services’, with the contracts ‘split to circumvent procurement procedures and awarded on the same day.’ The Auditor-General said the money ‘may have been lost’ and that ‘the payment may have been made for items not supplied.’”

“INEC ‘paid over ₦129 million [₦129,375,000.00] to 19 accounting firms for financial audit services without evidence of utilisation or requests and expenditure by the consultants.’ The Auditor-General raised concerns that the money ‘may have been diverted.’ He wants the money recovered and remitted to the treasury.”

“INEC also ‘paid over ₦504 million [₦504,492,641.00] for accreditation devices without due procurement process. The ‘APG had expired before the security licence key was delivered and the software was valid for only four months, raising questions about economy and value for money.’ The Auditor-General also raised concerns that the money ‘may have been diverted.’”

“INEC ‘paid over ₦235 million [₦235,103,000.00] to unqualified contractors for sleeping mats and digital archiving.’ The Auditor-General identified ‘serious concerns regarding the eligibility and capacity of the contractors’, and raised concerns that the money ‘may have been lost.’ He wants the money recovered.”

“INEC should provide documentary and physical evidence that the over ₦112 billion identified as ‘irregularly paid’ was actually used to procure the electoral materials concerned and account for the present location and status of those materials.”

“Nigerians have a right to know every public act, everything that is done in the public interest, by their public institutions including INEC.”

“INEC should be directed to ensure that no electoral equipment, material or other public asset covered by the Auditor-General’s findings is disposed of, transferred, destroyed, written off or otherwise dealt with in a manner that could frustrate transparency and accountability.”

“The names of the contractors, companies, suppliers and consultants who irregularly received public funds, as well as any INEC officials or other public officials who authorised, processed, facilitated or benefited from the transactions should be widely published.”

“Nigerians have the right to know whether the contracted goods and services were actually supplied; whether payments corresponded with goods and services actually delivered; and whether contracts were deliberately split to circumvent procurement requirements.”

“SERAP notes that Section 15(5) of the Nigerian Constitution requires public institutions including INEC to abolish all corrupt practices and abuse of power. Section 13 of the Nigerian Constitution imposes clear responsibility on INEC to conform to, observe and apply the provisions of Chapter 2 of the constitution.”

“Nigeria’s obligations under the UN Convention against Corruption requires INEC to adopt preventive anti-corruption policies and transparent public procurement and public financial management.”

“Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Article 13 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights to which Nigeria is a state party protect citizens’ rights to participate in public affairs.”

No date has been fixed for the hearing of the suit.

World.title: Bangladesh battles deadly measles outbreak as investigation highlights vaccination gaps
World.content:
A measles outbreak in Bangladesh has killed 1,147 people and infected more than 202,000 others since it began in March 2026, with an investigation by Reuters linking the crisis to declining vaccination coverage, weak health data and difficulties reaching children.

The Reuters investigation, published on Saturday, found that Bangladesh’s routine measles vaccination programme faltered in 2025, with first-dose coverage falling to 90 per cent and second-dose coverage to 86 per cent.

The figures were below the 95 per cent coverage level the World Health Organisation (WHO) says is needed to prevent measles outbreaks.

The investigation was based on a review of WHO documents and interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials. Reuters also examined previously unreported documents from meetings between the Bangladeshi government, WHO and other health partners.

“Until recently, Bangladesh had been a vaccination success story,” Reuters noted. WHO and UNICEF estimated that the country achieved 96 per cent coverage for the first measles vaccine dose and 93 per cent for the second dose in 2024.

However, Reuters reports that political turmoil following 2024 protests disrupted health services.

“But that same year, protests erupted that ended 15 years of rule by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In the ensuing political turmoil, health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed, and follow-up vaccinations that usually accompany routine programmes were disrupted,” it noted.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Emergency campaign

As the outbreak worsened, Bangladesh launched an emergency vaccination campaign that reached almost 20 million children in April and May.

The government said the campaign had covered every child in the target age group of six months to five years.

However, Reuters found evidence that millions of children may have been missed. A separate routine health intervention conducted in June had a target list containing four million more children than the measles emergency campaign, despite covering the same age group.

The discrepancy raised questions about how complete the emergency campaign was and the data used to determine how many children needed vaccination.

By August, Reuters reviewed documents showing that gaps persisted. Meeting minutes described the proportion of children with confirmed measles who had not been vaccinated as virtually unchanged after the emergency campaign.

At the end of September, the government launched another campaign targeting 3.4 million children it said had previously been missed.

Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser, described Bangladesh’s experience as “a real warning to every country”, saying preventing an outbreak through vaccination was easier, cheaper and safer than responding after transmission had intensified.

Nigeria’s situation

The development comes as measles also remains a public health concern in Nigeria, where thousands of cases and more than 100 deaths were recorded in the first seven months of 2026.

According to the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), 9,308 suspected measles cases were recorded across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory between January and July.

Of these, 7,713 were confirmed, while 522 were discarded and 1,073 remained pending. The NCDC recorded 109 deaths during the period, giving a case fatality ratio of 1.41 per cent.

The burden was reported nationwide, with all 36 states and the FCT recording at least one suspected case. A total of 611 local government areas reported at least one suspected case, while measles outbreaks were recorded in 71 LGAs across 14 states.

The NCDC said children aged nine to 59 months accounted for 58.67 per cent of confirmed measles cases recorded in 2026 during the period covered by the report.

Borno recorded the most suspected cases, with 2,673, followed by Zamfara with 1,157 and Yobe with 792. The three states accounted for more than half of the suspected cases recorded during the period.

READ ALSO: US records highest measles infections in 35 years

Surveillance challenges

The NCDC has also identified surveillance and data reporting as challenges in Nigeria’s response.

Its reports have highlighted the need to harmonise surveillance and laboratory data from states and laboratories, provide timely reporting and strengthen follow-up with states experiencing outbreaks.

As of the end of July, the agency was conducting outbreak-response activities, including surveillance engagement, developing supplementary immunisation plans for measles and rubella, and testing samples through reference laboratories.

World.title: Kenya confirms four new Ebola cases, including three health workers
World.content:
Kenya has confirmed four new cases of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, including three health workers who treated the country’s first patient, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to seven.

The country’s Ministry of Health announced the new cases on Saturday, Reuters said.

The ministry said the fourth patient is a male relative of the first confirmed patient, who died after arriving in Kenya from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on 3 October.

The relative had been in quarantine since 6 October before developing symptoms and testing positive for the virus.

The four new infections represent the first known cases of local transmission in Kenya since the outbreak was detected earlier this month.

However, health authorities said there was no evidence of wider community transmission, as they had traced and quarantined nearly all identified contacts.

Health workers infected

According to the ministry, the three infected health workers are two men, aged 29 and 35, and a 32-year-old woman.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

They treated the first patient on 3 and 4 October and have been in quarantine since 9 October.

All four newly confirmed patients developed symptoms while already in quarantine and were subsequently diagnosed with the virus.

The ministry also reported that the second and third patients, whose infections were confirmed earlier, were in stable condition and responding well to supportive treatment.

Contact tracing efforts

Health authorities said they had traced and placed 128 of the 130 people identified as contacts of confirmed patients in quarantine, representing 98.5 per cent of listed contacts, exceeding the 85 per cent benchmark the ministry cited as necessary to interrupt transmission.

Contact tracing is an important part of Ebola outbreak control because it lets health workers identify people who may have been exposed to the virus, monitor them for symptoms, and isolate suspected cases before further transmission occurs.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person with symptoms, or through contaminated materials.

Health workers are particularly vulnerable when treating infected patients without adequate infection prevention and control measures.

Background

The cases in Kenya are linked to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the DRC, where the Bundibugyo virus has caused thousands of infections and deaths.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) said the DRC had recorded 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths as of 23 September.

The outbreak has raised concerns about cross-border transmission, particularly as people travel between affected areas and neighbouring countries.

The Bundibugyo virus is a distinct Ebola virus species. No vaccine or treatment has been specifically approved for this strain.

Kenyan authorities have maintained that they detected the new infections among people already under quarantine, reducing the risk of further exposure outside monitored contacts.

Nigeria’s preparedness

The development comes as Nigeria continues to monitor the regional outbreak and strengthen preparedness against possible importation of the virus.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on 7 October that the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) was reviewing the country’s preparedness after Kenya confirmed its first imported case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola.

In a statement issued on 6 October, the NCDC said the case highlighted the risk of international importation through travel and population movement, including the possibility of the virus entering Nigeria.

The agency said it was working with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Port Health Services, state governments and other partners to strengthen surveillance, early detection, laboratory diagnosis, isolation, contact tracing and infection prevention.

It also said Nigeria conducted a national Ebola preparedness simulation exercise to assess its readiness to respond to a possible case.

As of 6 October, the NCDC said Nigeria had no confirmed Ebola cases.

World.title: Gombe community gets 1MW solar power plant after 17 years off national grid
World.content:
The people of Talasse in Balanga Local Government Area of Gombe State have received a major boost in electricity supply with the commissioning of a 1-megawatt (MW) solar mini-grid project expected to benefit about 6,000 households and businesses.

At the commissioning ceremony on Saturday, the Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, urged residents to protect the newly installed electricity infrastructure against vandalism, theft and other criminal activities that could threaten its sustainability.

The minister stressed that the facility was provided for the benefit of the community and future generations, warning that its destruction or misuse could undermine the investment and deprive residents of its long-term benefits.

“These assets have been built for you, for your benefit and for the posterity of generations to come. I urge you to protect them. Do not allow vandals or other criminals to destroy what has been provided for our collective good,” he said.

He noted that reliable electricity would help local businesses operate more efficiently, improve livelihoods and create economic opportunities for young people.

Mr Tegbe commended the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), the project developer, the Gombe State Government, traditional rulers, community leaders and other stakeholders for their contributions to the project.

He said the initiative aligned with the federal government’s commitment to expanding electricity access, strengthening energy security and promoting sustainable development through renewable energy solutions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Also speaking Governor Muhammadu Yahaya, described the commissioning as a milestone in his administration’s drive to expand reliable and affordable electricity access to rural communities.

He recalled that construction began on November 6, 2025, noting that the project had been completed in less than a year.

According to him, Talasse had remained without connection to the national grid for more than 17 years, limiting economic activities and forcing residents to rely on expensive alternative energy sources.

He added that the state planned to introduce additional solar mini-grid projects with a combined capacity of 4MW in Akko, Dukku, Funakaye, and Kaltungo local government areas, while ongoing projects in Filiya and Gelengu had reached 90 per cent completion.

He said the broader rural electrification programme was expected to extend improved electricity access to 80 communities across the state.

The governor also disclosed that his administration would complement rural electrification with productive-use equipment, including rice milling machines, electric flour grinders and groundnut oil-processing machines, to promote agro-processing, reduce production costs and create employment opportunities.

He called for proper maintenance and responsible use of the facility, urging residents to protect the investment against theft, vandalism and illegal connections.

Mr Yahaya commended the federal government, the Rural Electrification Agency, the World Bank, technical partners and the Talasse community for their contributions to the project.

World.title: Poland beat Nigeria 2-1: Five takeaways as Flamingos suffer early setback at FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup
World.content:
The Flamingos of Nigeria suffered a frustrating start to their FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup Morocco 2026 campaign on Saturday, losing 2-1 to Poland in their Group B opener despite a late rally that briefly raised hopes of a comeback.

Head coach Akeem Busari’s side created opportunities to take control of the contest but were punished for defensive lapses and struggled to turn their attacking moments into goals at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat.

Wiktoria Skrzypczak converted a first-half penalty in the 33rd minute after a Football Video Assistant Referee review, before Natalia Skrok doubled Poland’s advantage in the 65th minute. Substitute Oluebube Umejiaku pulled one back for Nigeria from an impressive free-kick in the 79th minute, but the Flamingos could not find the equaliser despite pushing for a late breakthrough.

The defeat leaves Nigeria needing a strong response against Puerto Rico on Tuesday before facing defending champions Korea DPR in their final group fixture. With Korea DPR opening their campaign with a 6-0 victory over Puerto Rico, the pressure is already building on the Flamingos to get their campaign back on track.

PREMIUM TIMES takes a look at five major takeaways from Nigeria’s disappointing opening day defeat.

Defensive lapses proved costly at a crucial moment

The Flamingos entered the tournament hoping to build on their qualifying performances. Still, their opening match exposed how quickly a defensive mistake can change the direction of a World Cup contest.

Nigeria kept Poland at bay early on, with both sides searching for a breakthrough. However, the game turned in the 33rd minute when defender Ohunene Sunday was penalised for a foul inside the penalty area following a Football Video Assistant Referee review.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Skrzypczak stepped up and converted the resulting penalty, giving Poland the advantage and forcing Nigeria to chase the game.

The goal was particularly frustrating because the Flamingos had competed well enough to stay in the contest and had already created their own chances. Instead of entering the break with the possibility of building on their attacking momentum, Nigeria went into the dressing room trailing.

The defensive problems resurfaced after the interval. In the 65th minute, Poland capitalised on a poor clearance by the Nigerian defence, with Skrok finishing from Blanka Zajac’s assist to extend the lead to 2-0.

At this level, moments like these can decide a match. The Flamingos were not completely outplayed, but their inability to handle key situations decisively gave Poland the advantage they needed.

Busari will need to address those lapses before the next fixture. The Flamingos must improve their decision-making inside the penalty area, become more decisive when clearing danger and maintain concentration throughout the full 90 minutes.

Their attacking ability can still make them competitive against the remaining teams in Group B, but they cannot afford to keep giving opponents opportunities to punish avoidable mistakes.

Nigeria created chances but lacked the finishing touch

One of the biggest frustrations for the Flamingos was that they had chances to put Poland under pressure long before the game slipped away.

Nigeria showed attacking intent during the first half, with Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Queen Joseph among those who threatened the Polish goal. Adegbuyi tested goalkeeper Hanna Buchta in the 18th minute, while Joseph also went close in the 26th minute.

Mary Dunstan, Joseph and Elizabeth Adesuyi subsequently came close to finding an equaliser before half-time, but Nigeria could not convert their promising moments into goals.

That failure to capitalise on their chances became even more significant when Poland took the lead from the penalty spot.

The Flamingos entered the tournament with expectations built around their attacking potential, following an impressive run through African qualifying and strong regional performances. However, international tournaments demand greater precision, particularly against opponents who can punish mistakes at the other end.

Nigeria needed to be more clinical in front of goal. An opening goal would have changed the complexion of the match, potentially forcing Poland to abandon their preferred approach and take greater risks.

Instead, the European side grew in confidence after taking the lead. At the same time, Nigeria were left attempting to recover from a deficit that became more difficult to overcome after Skrok’s second-half strike.

The lesson for Busari’s players is clear: creating chances is only part of the job. Against Puerto Rico, the Flamingos must show greater composure in the final third and ensure that promising attacking moves produce a tangible reward.

With their qualification hopes already under pressure, Nigeria cannot afford another performance in which opportunities go begging.

The second goal exposed Nigeria’s inability to manage pressure

If the penalty left Nigeria with work to do, Poland’s second goal made the task considerably more difficult.

After the restart, the Flamingos needed to find a way back into the contest without leaving themselves vulnerable at the back. However, Skrok’s goal in the 65th minute gave Poland a two-goal cushion and placed Nigeria on the brink of defeat.

The strike followed a poor clearance from the Nigerian defence, with Zajac providing the assist. It was another costly moment in a game where the Flamingos had struggled to turn their competitive spells into meaningful progress on the scoreboard.

Conceding a second goal also changed the match’s tactical demands. Nigeria had to become more aggressive, commit additional players forward and take greater risks in pursuit of a comeback.

That created a difficult balance for Busari’s team: push for goals while avoiding further defensive problems.

The response was encouraging, but the damage had already been done. Nigeria eventually pulled one back through Umejiaku, but they left themselves too little time to recover.

The experience should teach a young team still learning to navigate the pressure of major international tournaments. When a match starts to go against them, the Flamingos must stay organised and avoid letting one setback lead to another.

The defeat does not mean Nigeria lack the quality to compete, but it highlights the need for greater composure during difficult periods. Their ability to manage those moments will be crucial in the remaining group matches.

Busari’s substitutions offered hope, with Umejiaku making an immediate impact

Despite the disappointment of the result, Nigeria’s response after the introduction of their substitutes provided one of the more encouraging aspects of the performance.

Busari made a double change in the 68th minute, bringing on Oluebube Umejiaku and Awawu Bashiru for Harmony Chidi and Mary Dunstan. Kanyinsola Yusuf and Precious Oscar subsequently entered the contest as Nigeria searched for a way back.

The changes injected fresh energy into the Flamingos’ attack, and the breakthrough came in the 79th minute.

Yusuf set up Umejiaku from an impressive free-kick to reduce the deficit to 2-1 and give Nigeria renewed belief.

The goal transformed the match’s closing stages. Poland, who had appeared comfortable after establishing a two-goal advantage, suddenly faced a Nigerian side playing with greater urgency and determination.

The Flamingos pushed forward in search of an equaliser, and their late pressure showed they could trouble Poland when they moved the ball with purpose and attacked more aggressively.

Umejiaku’s contribution was particularly encouraging. Coming off the bench to score in a World Cup opener is a significant moment for any young player, and her goal offered Nigeria a route back into a contest that had appeared to be slipping away.

However, the late rally also raises questions about how quickly Nigeria can establish that attacking intensity from the start.

Busari will have to assess whether changes to the starting approach, greater movement in the final third, or earlier substitutions can make the Flamingos more threatening before they fall behind.

The bench has shown it can make a difference. Against Puerto Rico, Nigeria will need the starting eleven to provide a stronger foundation while retaining the ability to change the game through their substitutes.

Puerto Rico clash becomes crucial as Nigeria’s margin for error shrinks

Nigeria’s immediate priority d to beat Puerto Rico on Wednesday, with the defeat to Poland putting the Flamingos under pressure in Group B.

Korea DPR’s emphatic 6-0 victory over Puerto Rico in the other group fixture means the defending champions have already made a strong statement. Poland also secured three points, leaving Nigeria and Puerto Rico without a point after the opening round.

That makes the next fixture especially important. Nigeria must approach the contest with greater urgency, but they also need to avoid letting the pressure of their opening defeat affect their decision-making.

Puerto Rico are making their debut at the tournament and endured a difficult introduction against Korea DPR. However, Nigeria cannot assume that the result against Poland guarantees an easier assignment. The Flamingos must focus on their own performance, improve their execution and take responsibility for securing the points they need.

A victory would restore confidence and give Nigeria a chance to approach their final group match against Korea DPR with renewed belief. By contrast, a loss would make their route to the knockout stage significantly harder.

The team’s attacking quality remains encouraging, as does the energy shown in the closing stages against Poland. But those positives must now translate into a more complete performance.

Nigeria have shown they can compete on the global stage, including their bronze-medal finish at the 2022 edition. Their ambitions in Morocco will not be decided by one defeat, but the response to that setback could prove decisive.

READ ALSO: Six takeaways from Nigeria vs Madagascar as Super Eagles fight back for victory

For Busari, the challenge is to turn that one-off match into a recurring problem.

The verdict: Nigeria must turn promise into results

The Flamingos’ defeat to Poland was a disappointing start. Still, it wasn’t without encouraging moments: the Flamingos created chances, showed attacking intent, and produced a late response that nearly made the closing stages more uncomfortable for their opponents.

Nevertheless, the two goals conceded exposed defensive weaknesses, and failing to convert early chances proved costly. Still, it left them chasing the contest.

The performance also showed the value of Nigeria’s bench, with the free-kick goal and the added urgency after substitutions offering a glimpse of what the team can produce when they find their rhythm.

Now, the focus shifts to Puerto Rico. Nigeria need a more disciplined defensive display, greater efficiency, and a stronger start to advance goal-scoring defence, after which they had little room for further mistakes. Their World Cup ambitions remain alive, but the next match must deliver a response, and, above all, goals in abundance, the three points they desperately need.

World.title: Akor Adams hails Venezia fans, pledges commitment under new coach
World.content:
Super Eagles forward Akor Adams has praised Venezia’s supporters for standing by the team through difficult moments. He also explained how new head coach Nicola is demanding greater intensity, discipline and collective responsibility from his players.

The Nigerian international, who joined Venezia from Sevilla during the summer, believes the fans remain an important source of motivation as the club looks to build momentum in its campaign.

Speaking at the post match press briefing about the supporters, Adams acknowledged the challenges they have endured alongside the team and promised that the players would continue to give everything on the pitch in return for their backing.

“Our fans are truly very important. They have suffered alongside us, and we need their energy. We will give our all in every match, for them too,” Adams said.

The forward’s comments underline the importance of rebuilding a strong connection between the team and its supporters, with the players determined to reward that loyalty through their performances.

Adams explains what Coach Nicola wants from Venezia

Adams also offered insight into the demands of new head coach Nicola, describing the manager as direct in his communication and clear about what he expects from the squad.

According to the Nigerian, Nicola has placed particular emphasis on increasing the intensity of Venezia’s play, while ensuring that the team works as a unit both defensively and when transitioning into attack.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Coach Nicola is very direct in the way he communicates with us.

“He asked us to work hard on the intensity of our play and gave us clear instructions, focusing on collective work in the defensive phase and during transitions to help us move into the attacking phase,” he explained.

The emphasis on collective responsibility reflects Nicola’s approach to improving the team’s overall performance, with Adams stressing that the players must understand their individual roles within the wider tactical structure.

For the Super Eagles forward, adapting to those demands will be an important part of his development as he continues to settle into life at Venezia.

Super Eagles star focused on team success and personal growth

Despite making an encouraging start to his time in Italy, Adams insists that his priority is not chasing individual targets but contributing to the team’s success and taking advantage of the opportunity to improve under his new manager.

“The most important thing today is the three points. On a personal level, I don’t set myself specific goals. I think that here in Venice I have the opportunity to learn a great deal and improve.

“Coach Nicola has come here to help us develop, so whatever he asks of me, I will do my best to deliver,” he added.

The forward has made a promising contribution since arriving from Sevilla, registering four goals and one assist in nine appearances for Venezia.

READ ALSO: Akor Adamss late goal saves Super Eagles as Nigeria levels with Russia

His performances have also been carried over to the international stage. Adams scored a stoppage-time equaliser for Nigeria in their 3-3 friendly draw against Russia on 6 October, demonstrating his ability to make an impact for the Super Eagles.

With four goals and an assist already to his name at club level, the Nigerian will now look to maintain his momentum while adapting to Nicola’s expectations.

For Adams, the objective is clear: contribute to Venezia’s results, repay the supporters’ faith and continue developing into a more complete forward under the club’s new leadership.

World.title: Serie A: Udinese coach warns Maduka Okoye after costly error
World.content:
Udinese head coach Kosta Runjaić has warned Super Eagles goalkeeper Maduka Okoye that costly mistakes could have serious consequences, following the Nigerian’s error in the defeat to Torino.

Okoye came under scrutiny after his mistake contributed to Udinese’s loss at the Stadio Olimpico Grande Torino, prompting Runjaić to address the situation ahead of Sunday’s Serie A meeting with Lecce.

The Nigerian international, who joined Udinese from Watford in the summer of 2023, has been an important figure for the Italian side. However, his latest error has placed him under pressure to respond with a more assured performance as the team prepare for their next fixture.

Speaking to Udinese’s official media, Runjaić confirmed that he had spoken firmly to the goalkeeper about the incident, stressing that players must be held accountable when their decisions affect the outcome of a match.

“A coach must use clear words with his players and I did on this occasion too,” Runjaić said.

The Udinese manager added that Okoye understood the consequences of his decision, insisting that the goalkeeper was aware of the role his mistake played in the team conceding.

“He is well aware that his decision led to us conceding a goal. You make many decisions throughout a match, and that was a bad one,” he explained.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Runjaić backs Okoye to beome one of Serie A’s best Goalkeepers

Despite his frustration with the error, Runjaić remains convinced that Okoye possesses the quality to establish himself among the finest goalkeepers in Italian football.

The Udinese coach believes the Nigerian has the ability to compete with the league’s elite, but insists that reaching that level requires consistency and the willingness to deliver his best in every match.

“If he gives it everything he’s got, Okoye is one of the five top goalkeepers in Serie A. We work a lot with him,” Runjaić said.

The manager also emphasised the importance of learning from mistakes, warning that even a single lapse in concentration or judgement can prove costly at the highest level.

According to Runjaić, Udinese have worked extensively with Okoye, and the priority now is to ensure that he makes better decisions under pressure while maintaining the confidence required to perform in goal.

“In the past two games we dominated and Maduka did not have to do much. We need to find the right balance between calm and tension. Every mistake can have major consequences, so we mustn’t make any,” he concluded.

Okoye faces opportunity to respond against Lecce

With Sunday’s encounter against Lecce approaching, Okoye will have an opportunity to put the disappointment against Torino behind him and demonstrate that he can respond positively to his coach’s criticism.

For a goalkeeper, mistakes are often magnified because they can directly influence results, leaving little room for recovery once an opponent capitalises. The challenge for Okoye will be to maintain his composure and show the consistency Runjaić believes he is capable of producing.

The coach’s comments suggest that, despite the reprimand, he has not lost faith in the Nigerian’s ability. His backing of Okoye as a potential top-five goalkeeper in Serie A reflects the confidence Udinese have in his talent.

However, that confidence comes with expectations. As the Super Eagles star prepares for the Lecce fixture, he will be eager to deliver a reassuring performance, avoid another costly error and strengthen his position as Udinese’s first-choice goalkeeper.

World.title: FRSC Ogun Sector Commander, Ogunjobi, dies after brief illness
World.content:
By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta

The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has announced the death of its Ogun State Sector Commander, Corps Commander Oludare Ogunjobi, following a brief illness.

The FRSC RS2.2 Ogun State Sector Command announced his death in a statement issued on Sunday, expressing sadness over the loss of the senior officer.

The statement, signed by the Command’s Public Relations Officer, Chief Route Commander Afolabi Odunsi, described Ogunjobi’s death as a significant loss to the Corps and the wider road safety community.

“His passing is a great loss to the Corps, his colleagues, and the entire road safety community,” the statement said.

The Command said the late sector commander would be remembered for his leadership, commitment to road safety administration and dedication to the mandate of the Corps.

It added that he contributed to efforts to promote safer roads, enhance public enlightenment, strengthen stakeholder engagement and improve compliance with traffic regulations.

According to the statement, his commitment to these areas formed an important part of his service to the FRSC and its mission to improve road safety.

The Command also extended its condolences to Ogunjobi’s family, loved ones, colleagues and associates, acknowledging the grief caused by his death.

“His demise is deeply regretted, and the Command extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones, colleagues, and associates during this difficult period,” the statement added.

The FRSC said details of the funeral arrangements would be communicated in due course.

The statement concluded with a prayer for the repose of the deceased’s soul and strength for his family, colleagues and others affected by his passing.

“May God grant his soul eternal rest and give his family, the Corps, and all those affected by his passing the strength to bear this irreparable loss,” it said.

World.title: I’ve been diabetic since 1996 – Actor Jide Kosoko
World.content:
Veteran Nollywood actor Jide Kosoko has revealed that he has been living with diabetes since 1996, saying his years of experience with the condition have helped him understand his health better.

The actor made this disclosure during a recent episode on ‘Talk to B’ Show.

“I have been diabetic since 1996; I have been managing it. I understand my health better than some doctors do. Do not misquote me. I am not saying I know how to do everything, I just do not want to die,” Kosoko said.

The veteran actor also spoke about his personal life, revealing that he had lost three wives, including the mother of his daughter, Bidemi Kosoko, who died during childbirth.

“I lost my wife during childbirth; that’s Bidemi’s mother. I have lost three wives,” he said.

Kosoko, who began his career in theatre as a child, also reflected on his longstanding contribution to the Nigerian entertainment industry.

“I started theatre at age 10, in 1964, and formed my own group in 1972. I make bold to say that I am one of the pioneers of this industry,” he said.

The actor also offered parenting advice, urging parents to treat their children equally and ensure that each child feels loved and valued.

“Treat your children equally; let them know they’re equal in your mind,” he said.

Speaking about social media, Kosoko recalled that people were initially apprehensive about the platform but noted that it had since become useful to many.

“When social media was coming, we were afraid. But now we use it to our advantage. Some use it uselessly. Must you shake your bumbum and talk about jargons before you make money?” he asked.
