World.title: Why are fewer Mexicans having children? Financial strain, security concerns and fears for the future
World.content:
Mexico’s national statistics agency, INEGI, recently released the results of the 2025 Intercensal Survey, showing that the country’s population has surpassed 130 million. The findings also reveal a striking trend: fertility rates have fallen considerably nationwide, with Mexico City recording the lowest rate, at just 0.8 children per woman.

Mexican families have changed over the decades. In earlier generations, larger families were more common, partly because of limited access to contraception and family planning services, lower levels of education among women and a more rigid division of labor. Men were generally seen as breadwinners, while women handled most household and caregiving responsibilities.

In an exploratory survey conducted by Mexico News Daily, 13 of 35 respondents said they did not want children. Participants were men and women ages 25 to 35 who were single, in relationships or married, and lived in nine cities: Mexico City, Toluca, Monterrey, Querétaro, León, Ensenada, Cancún, Guanajuato and San Miguel de Allende. They were contacted through social media and asked one open question: “Do you want to have children? Please explain your answer.” The sample is not nationally representative, but it highlights recurring concerns: insufficient income, housing, public safety, health, the climate crisis and the lack of a stable partner.

Financial strain and absent support systems

Luis, 34, lives in Querétaro with his girlfriend. He explained why he has not considered having children:

“I had a privileged upbringing. I went to private school, had enough to eat and never lacked anything. But today, I can’t provide those things for someone else, so bringing a child into the world feels unfair. There’s no guarantee of a stable future, either. My job doesn’t guarantee a steady income or the pay raises I would need to live without financial hardship. And the outlook is bleak: water shortages, housing problems, rising costs and so on.

“Another issue is that we both work, and our families live in Toluca, so we don’t have a support network to help us care for our children. We would have to rely on daycare and extracurricular activities, which would mean additional expenses. Finally, I don’t want to repeat the way I was raised. I had everything I needed materially, but not emotionally, and I’m not ready to break those patterns yet.”

Of the 22 respondents who said they wanted children or were considering having them in the future, some said they had not yet found a stable partner or wanted to become more financially secure first. Three people in this group reported health or fertility problems that had prevented them from conceiving.

Vanesa, 29, lives in San Miguel de Allende and has been married for two years.

“Yes, I want to have children, but first I would like to own a home so I can feel more secure,” she said. “I’m also afraid of global warming. I worry that by the time my child is 15, there could be a water crisis.”

Reasons behind decisions to remain child-free

The 13 respondents who did not want children cited financial pressures, insecurity in Mexico and global problems as their main reasons. Many said they did not earn enough to support a family. Others felt that conditions in the country would make it difficult to raise children in a healthy, safe environment. Wars, global warming and water shortages also influenced their decisions. A smaller number said they did not feel ready to become parents or lacked the patience or skills to care for a baby.

Milé, 34, is single and originally from Querétaro.

“I don’t think I have the skills or resources to be a mother,” she said. “Finding a man my age who wants to share that responsibility would also require me to be honest with myself and able to contribute equally. My jobs haven’t provided social security coverage, either, and I wouldn’t have the financial means to support children. I think bringing children into the world under these conditions would be selfish and irresponsible.”

Respondents who already had one or two children said that number was enough to provide a decent standard of living and, above all, give their children the attention they deserved. Some mothers said they did not want to experience pregnancy and its hormonal changes again because of the physical toll. Fathers said their incomes barely covered the cost of raising one or two children.

One respondent pointed to limited living space, describing a three-bedroom home with one room for the parents and one for each of two children. Housing constraints were another reason not to have more children. Some respondents also said that both parents needed to earn an income to support the family, making a return to paid work an economic priority for mothers.

Why parents are stopping at two children

Paul, 31, is married, has two children and lives in León. He explained why he and his wife decided not to have more:

“My wife and I decided to stop at two children, and it wasn’t a decision we took lightly. When you imagine starting a family, you often don’t think about numbers, square footage, school fees or how many chicken nuggets fit on a baking tray. You just think, ‘I want a lovely family.’ Then adulthood comes along and says, ‘Yes, that’s lovely. Now do the math.’

“That’s when we began to realize that having children involves much more than loving them with all your heart. There’s food, clothing, school, doctors, activities, vacations, birthdays, toys, transportation and all those little things that stop being little once you have children.

“We want to give our children a good life, but we also want some financial peace of mind rather than constantly calculating how to make it to the end of the month. We also believe that having two children allows us to give them time, attention and energy in a way that works for our family. We don’t want more children simply because there’s ‘room’ for them. We want to enjoy the children we have, support them, watch them grow, be present and give them the best we can within our means.”

Raising a family of four

How much money does a family of four need to live in Mexico?

The answer depends on where the family lives and its lifestyle. For this report, we focused on five of the cities where respondents lived: Mexico City, Querétaro, León, Monterrey and San Miguel de Allende.

Drawing on the National Household Income and Expenditure Survey (ENIGH), labor-market information from Data México and reference prices, Mexico News Daily estimated that a family of four living in an owner-occupied home in these cities needs between 29,500 and 48,000 Mexican pesos per month. This budget covers everyday needs such as food, clothing, public school expenses, transportation, personal hygiene products, utilities, communications and health care, while setting aside money for emergencies.

The following table breaks down expenses by category and compares costs across the five cities included in this article. Monterrey has the highest basic utility costs, while León has the lowest overall costs among the cities examined.

How do average wages compare?

Data México reports average monthly earnings in these cities, including both formal and informal employment.

The comparison reveals a gap between average earnings and the estimated budget for a family of four. Even two average incomes combined fall short of the amount needed to cover the projected expenses and save for emergencies. To make up the difference, some families seek additional income by selling products through catalogs or preparing food for sale. Others cut spending on health care, food and recreation.

Insecurity in Mexico

Safety concerns weighing on parents

Eduardo and Ana are married but have not yet decided whether to have children. They live in Metepec and regularly travel to Toluca for work.

“I don’t want children for one simple reason: insecurity,” Eduardo said. “The country gets worse every year, and more people go missing every day. If I’m already worried about the situation, I can’t imagine being responsible for a little person. I would rather avoid that worry.”

Perceptions of insecurity also emerged among respondents’ reasons for not having children. The 2026 National Survey of Victimization and Perceptions of Public Security (ENVIPE) does not measure an individual’s risk of becoming a crime victim, nor does it replace crime-rate data. It does, however, show that 74% of adults considered their state unsafe during the survey period.

The highest proportions were recorded in Estado de Mexico, at 90%; Morelos, at 88.7%; Tabasco, at 87.6%; Guanajuato, at 85.9%; and Puebla, at 83.3%. The lowest were in Coahuila, at 27.8%; Yucatán, at 35.5%; and Aguascalientes, at 41%.

Rising crime and missing persons statistics

The 2026 ENVIPE, which covers crimes committed in 2025, reported the highest estimated crime incidence rates in Mexico City, at 68,154 crimes per 100,000 inhabitants; Puebla, at 41,876; and Mexico State, at 40,915. The survey’s crime categories included theft and robbery, fraud, extortion, threats, assault, kidnapping and sexual offenses.

According to a report by the Mexican Institute for Human Rights and Democracy (IMDHD), Mexico’s national missing persons registry listed 134,257 people as missing as of May 16, 2026. That number rose to 135,048 by June 16. The report recorded 12,632 disappearances in 2024 and 12,373 in 2025, and indicated that the trend in 2026 pointed toward similarly high numbers.

As of May 16, 2026, the five states with the largest cumulative numbers of registered missing persons were Mexico State, with 14,648; Tamaulipas, with 13,787; Jalisco, with 12,765; Michoacán, with 7,782; and Nuevo León, with 7,476. Together, they accounted for 42% of the national total, according to Red Lupa’s analysis of the National Registry of Missing and Unlocated Persons (RNPDNO).

Mexico recorded 11,586 victims of intentional homicide from January through August 2026, according to figures reported by the federal Security Cabinet and the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System. Although President Claudia Sheinbaum highlighted a decline in homicides earlier in the year, safety concerns remain part of many Mexicans’ daily lives.

Motherhood as a choice

The evolution of women’s roles

Women have always worked and played an important role in society. The Industrial Revolution, which began in the mid-18th century, expanded their participation in factory work and paid employment. During World War I and World War II, their roles in industry became even more prominent as many filled jobs left by men who had gone to fight.

Over time, advances in labor rights, greater access to higher education and the availability of contraception expanded women’s opportunities and their ability to make decisions about their lives, including whether to become mothers, when to have children and how many to have.

Motherhood is now a choice, not an obligation. Women may pursue a career, raise a family or do both. For some of the mothers interviewed, returning to work was both a financial necessity and a professional choice.

Personal perspectives on motherhood and career breaks

Zayra, 32, lives in Monterrey with her husband and their two children.

“At first, I only wanted one child so I could give them the attention and care they needed for their development. But six months later, I became pregnant again,” she said. “It was a shock because I didn’t know how I would manage twice the expenses. I had my second child, but I decided to undergo sterilization so I wouldn’t have any more.

“I made that decision because I struggled badly with hormonal changes during both pregnancies, and there were concerns about preeclampsia. Having children is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you, but it’s also a lot of work and very tiring. Finances also play a role in deciding not to have another child.”

Kiev, 32, is from Querétaro, married, and has two daughters.

“Yes, I’ve thought about having one more, but I’ve practically ruled it out, mainly for financial reasons. Babies are very expensive,” she said. “On top of that, my house only has two bedrooms, and we would need to expand it sooner to live more comfortably.

“Then there’s the career break I’m taking. I wanted to look after the house and the babies myself, with the intention of returning to work once they’re a little older. Having another baby would add more years to that break.”

Rejecting social scripts and facing future challenges

Marcela, 34, lives in Querétaro with her partner and has decided not to have children.

“I don’t like children. I’ve never known how to interact with them or spend time with them, so having one seems strange to me, and I find it difficult to play with them. I don’t have a maternal instinct,” she said.

“I also don’t want to feel obligated to follow a social script of getting married and having children. I firmly believe children should be fully wanted and planned for, not something you have ‘just because’ or because it’s the next step.

“The third reason is the situation in Mexico and the world in general. The thought that having a child would mean never feeling at ease again because of the country we live in and its insecurity — especially if the child were a girl — is a major factor.

Wages, security and the environment

“There’s also the economic situation. Wages make things difficult, and building financial security keeps getting harder. Add the environmental situation, the wars happening now and tensions with the United States, and I can’t picture a bright future for a child.”

Declining fertility poses long-term challenges for Mexico. An aging population will require more health care, caregiving services and sustainable social protection systems. But the answer is not to pressure people into having more children. For those who want to start a family, the challenge is to create conditions that make raising children compatible with stable earnings, affordable housing, childcare, safety, reproductive health care and a more equitable division of caregiving responsibilities.

The interviews in this report do not represent Mexico’s entire population, but they reveal a shared tension. For many people, the question is no longer simply whether they want children, but whether they can have them without sacrificing their stability, health, careers or peace of mind.

María Ruiz is the Director of Digital Marketing at Mexico News Daily. She enjoys photographing her hometown of San Miguel de Allende in her spare time.

World.title: Spider-Man 2099 has a Día de Muertos secret in his origin story
World.content:
There may not be another superhero who is more globally renowned or imitated than Spider-Man (sorry, Superman and Batman, but you can sit this one out).

In my neighborhood’s main square, there is a man who regularly dresses up as Spider-Man and web-thwips his way into photos for a few pesos. Driving around Mexico, I’ve seen motorcyclists wearing Spider-Man-themed helmets. There’s even an official spinoff Spider-Man character, nicknamed Arácnido Jr., who hails from Mexico City and has a luchador father.

Just learned that Marvel has a Mexican Spider-Man named Arácnido Jr. who is the son of a luchador & protects Mexico City. He appeared in one of the “Spider-Verse” comics & was created by Enrique Puig & Francisco Herrera. He’s been around since 2015. Can’t believe I didn’t know 🇲🇽 https://t.co/h38pTyT9m8 — Carlos Aguilar (@Carlos_Film) August 2, 2020

It’s not just Mexicans who love El Hombre Araña, though. Right now, Spider-Man is at an all-time commercial high.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has been the most commercially successful blockbuster of the year so far. As of writing, the movie has generated more than US $923 million globally, beating out “Toy Story 5” and “The Odyssey” as the highest-grossing film of 2026, to date. In July, the movie’s star cast members even visited Mexico City to promote the film.

A futuristic webslinger with Mexican roots

Add to that a newly reinvigorated generation of Spider-Man fanatics with the children’s animated series “Spidey and His Amazing Friends” — a show that currently ranks as the third-most-watched show for kids between ages 2 and 5 (including my son, who is obsessed), with billions of streaming hours on Disney+.

Across every metric, Peter Parker is a tried-and-true hit.

But what about Marvel Comics’ other Spider-Man? The one who lives in a futuristic 2099 version of New York City (creatively renamed Nueva York) and is of Mexican Irish descent? I’m talking about Miguel O’Hara.

Created by Marvel in 1992 as part of a larger effort to refresh the brand and reconfigure its legendary characters with a larger “Marvel 2099” wave of alternate-universe storylines, O’Hara is a geneticist working for a mega-wealthy corporation, Alchemax. Rather than being bitten by a radioactive spider as the original Parker is, O’Hara is researching the by-then-archaic Spider-Man of former New York City (fourth-wall meta stuff, I know) and attempting to replicate that Spider-Man’s powers for the greedy Alchemax corporation, a private entity that happens to govern the United States through its wealth and militant force.

The unusual origin of the Day of the Dead suit

Like any true superhero origin story, O’Hara is unexpectedly turned into Spider-Man 2099 when a villainous Alchemax colleague throws O’Hara into the mutation machine that is conveniently set to the original Spider-Man’s specifications. O’Hara gets zapped. He transforms. He learns how to wield his powers and manage his personal relationships across hundreds of issues. The usual.

Here’s the unusual part, though: O’Hara — or rather, his alter ego Spider-Man 2099 — is equipped with a Day of the Dead costume rather than a traditional Spider-Man onesie.

Early on, the comics (created by Peter David and Rick Leonardi) establish that not only is O’Hara of Mexican descent, but that he took a trip down to Mexico City for a “The Jetsons”-style Day of the Dead.

There are multiple allusions to it in the opening issues of the series, with a backstory that goes something like this: A pre-superpowers O’Hara returns to his mother’s homeland south of the border (her name is Conchata, and she also appears as a character early on). There, he attends a festive Day of the Dead celebration. In this dystopian future, there is a special fabric referred to as “UMF” — or Unstable Molecule Fabric, as explained in the series — that is both indestructible and highly versatile, something O’Hara deems necessary for the rowdy Día de Muertos crowds and festivities in 2099.

Dystopian fashion and geometric design

I know all of this because I ordered a 1,384-page omnibus of “Spider-Man 2099” and have been reading it for weeks.

“Only thing I own made from UMF is this death’s head costume I brought when I went to Mexico last year for the Day of the Dead festival,” O’Hara says in issue No. 2. In the background, silhouettes of festivalgoers dressed as skeletons and demons wander as he recalls: “Festival can get pretty wild. I wanted something extra sturdy.”

The suit itself is futuristically cool, for lack of a better description, though not overly Day of the Dead-themed. It features a bright red skull-like design at the center of the chest, which extends into stripes that flare down and outward in the opposite direction, wrapping around the shoulder in a shape that loosely resembles a spider’s many legs with a geometrically balanced aesthetic. The base of the suit retains a much deeper shade of blue than the original webslinger.

In all, it retains the essence of Spider-Man’s original garb, with subtle nods to Day of the Dead aesthetics.

Reincarnation and honoring the fallen heroes

O’Hara’s suit and abilities are rounded out with razor-edged retractable talons for climbing surfaces and annihilating his foes, and spikes protruding from his forearms, which seem to be a menacing suit accessory. Though not overtly Mexican or Day of the Dead in its presentation, if you squint, you can sense minor inspirations from Mexico’s Indigenous past and geometric design work.

Simple, but striking. Creative, but balanced.

The Day of the Dead theme does, however, emerge in the storyline — with additional references to Mexico, and even an entire issue titled “Day of the Dead.” In it, O’Hara takes a trip to Mexico City, where he battles zombies who have been mass-reincarnated by Fernando Morgez, a Mexican character who had hoped to revive his late sister, Anita, but brought back more than he anticipated.

Mexico’s Day of the Dead is a series undercurrent

The idea of life and death, reincarnation and honoring the deceased is an undercurrent throughout the entire series. In the 2099 timeline, the Avengers are more myth than reality, with previously indestructible characters like Thor and Peter Parker’s Spider-Man being remembered as deceased gods who are revered and worshiped by cultish hordes of followers.

That is, the world’s heroes of yesterday have fallen, and the living must find ways to cope with that remaining void.

In that sense, the series certainly has touches of Mexico’s Day of the Dead — a remembrance of those who are no longer physically present, but perhaps offer spiritual hope and a connection to, if not preservation of, the past.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Shirley Manson’s Garbage to headline free Zócalo show next month
World.content:
Garbage in the Zócalo! And for free?

No, we’re not talking about a sanitation worker’s revolt or some weird twist to recycling and reusing household waste.

The American rock band Garbage will play a free concert in the Zócalo on Saturday, Nov. 14, the final show of their North America tour which kicked off back in September 2025.

Lead singer Shirley Manson, aka “The Godmother of Rock,” said the show will mark the close of 30 years of traditional, continuous bus-touring for the band, saying long-term heavy touring has become economically and personally unsustainable.

Shortly after the Mexico City mayor’s office jumped the gun (officials shared the announcement through the government’s official X account before deleting the post), Garbage confirmed the gig on Instagram.

“Well. The news got leaked so here we are — a little off balance and rushing to catch up,” the band wrote. “We were going to announce this show tomorrow, but someone has beaten us to it.”

Overcoming the spilled beans, Garbage — which has sold 17 million albums worldwide — declared they were enthusiastic about the invitation.

“We are so immensely proud and deeply honoured to have been invited by the Mexican Government to play in Mexico City on the 14th of November at Mexico City’s most prestigious venue – The Zócalo,” the band said.

Manson also heaped praise on the band’s Mexican fans for supporting the group since their first visit in 1996. Since then, Garbage has played in Mexico 16 times, including three shows last year (April 4 in Zapopan, Jalisco; April 6 in Monterrey and Nov. 14 in Mexico City).

“We are one of the most fortunate bands in the world to have enjoyed playing in Mexico since we first arrived on the scene but this is the absolute cherry on the top of what has been a passionate and 30 year long love affair,” the Instagram post said.

Formed in 1993 in Madison, Wisconsin, the band’s four-member line-up has remained unchanged: the Scottish lead singer Manson and American musicians Duke Erikson (guitar, bass, keyboards), Steve Marker (guitar, keyboards) and Butch Vig (drums, percussion).

With reports from El Financiero, Consequence, Chilango and Billboard

World.title: What’s On in Latin America: The Week of October 19–25, 2026
World.content:
Latin America · What’s On

Key Facts — The vote Brazil’s presidential runoff is on Sunday 25 October, between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Globo holds the final TV debate on Friday 23 October, straight after its evening news.

— The data Argentina reports its September trade balance on Monday 19 October, and Mexico publishes mid-month inflation on Thursday 22. Brazil’s mid-month inflation (IPCA-15) follows on Friday 23, according to the IBGE calendar.

— The clocks Europe moves back to winter time on Sunday 25 October, so the gap between Lisbon or London and Rio narrows from four hours to three. US clocks change on Sunday 1 November.

— On the pitch The Copa Libertadores semi-final return legs are on Wednesday 21 October (Fluminense v Palmeiras, 9:30 p.m. Brasília time, 8:30 p.m. US Eastern) and Thursday 22 (Flamengo v Estudiantes, same time).

— On stage Festival Bamba brings Juanes, Marc Anthony and Fito Páez to Santiago on 24–25 October. Fonseca plays Bogotá on Saturday 24, in a new venue.

— Prediction markets On Sunday 18 October, 4 a.m. US Eastern, Polymarket priced a Flávio Bolsonaro win in the runoff at 81.0% and Lula at 19.5%. Kalshi, regulated in the US by the CFTC, priced them at 79.0% and 20.0%.

Your Latin America week ahead for 19–25 October 2026 is built around Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October and the last television debate on Friday 23. In between come the Copa Libertadores semi-final return legs, a Colombian concert that changed venue and a Chilean festival that is new this year.

This guide was written on Sunday 18 October. Every date is checked against an official calendar, a venue or a ticketing page, and local-currency prices carry an approximate US$ conversion at US$1 = CLP 984 (EODHD close of Friday 16 October).

A Brazilian electronic voting machine. The runoff is on Sunday 25 October. (File photo.) Photo: Senado Federal, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American culture, food and life. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat to do, where to go in Rio de Janeiro › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American culture, food and life. × This week Tonight Where to eat Before you go Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

Politics you will feel on the street

Brazil votes in the presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October, one week from today. Lula, of the Workers’ Party (PT), faces Flávio Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party (PL), according to the electoral court (TSE) and Brazilian press reports.

Globo holds the final debate on Friday 23 October at its studios in Rio de Janeiro, straight after the evening news programme Jornal Nacional. The second runoff debate, hosted by Band, is today, Sunday 18 October, at 8 p.m. Brasília time, after a first debate by a media consortium on Thursday 15.

Polls are open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Brasília time across the country. Voting therefore ends earlier on the clock in the western states that sit one or two hours behind Brasília.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “US avoids pledge to accept Brazil election result” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

For US readers, the main exposure is the real (BRL). Brazilian assets often move on election news, and the real stood at about R$5.06 per US$ at the close on Friday 16 October (EODHD).

What Prediction Markets Say

Brazil runoff. On Sunday 18 October, 4 a.m. US Eastern, Polymarket priced a Flávio Bolsonaro win at 81.0% and a Lula win at 19.5%, with about US$187 million traded on the market. Kalshi, regulated in the US by the CFTC, priced them at 79.0% and 20.0% on its last trades.

Copa Libertadores. Polymarket priced Flamengo at 48.5%, Palmeiras at 40.5% and Estudiantes at 8.8% to win the title, with about US$35,000 traded. Kalshi’s last trades put Flamengo at 60% and Palmeiras at 54%, which do not add up to 100% because each club trades as a separate contract.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Deadlines and money

Argentina publishes its September trade balance on Monday 19 October at 4 p.m. Buenos Aires time (3 p.m. US Eastern), according to the INDEC calendar. The EODHD consensus is a surplus of US$2.5 billion, against US$2.19 billion before.

Argentina also receives its monthly activity index (EMAE) for August on Wednesday 21 October, according to INDEC. The EODHD calendar lists −0.9% against −1.4% before, but does not say whether that is a monthly or a yearly change.

Mexico reports August retail sales on Wednesday 21 October, according to the EODHD economic calendar. The statistics office, INEGI, publishes inflation for the first half of October on Thursday 22, with consensus at 0.3% over two weeks against 0.33% before.

Mexico then reports its August economic activity index (IGAE) on Friday 23 October, with consensus at 2.5% over twelve months against 3.4% before. That index tracks the output of the economy month by month.

Brazil reports mid-month inflation (IPCA-15) for October on Friday 23 October, according to the IBGE calendar. The EODHD consensus is 0.4% for the month and 4.6% over twelve months, against 0.7% and 4.47% before.

The central bank’s weekly Focus survey of economists comes out on Monday 19 October. It shows how private economists expect inflation, growth and the Selic (Brazil’s benchmark interest rate) to move.

Colombia reports August economic activity (the ISE index) on Monday 19 October and its August trade balance on Wednesday 21, according to the EODHD calendar. China publishes third-quarter GDP on Monday 19 at 10 a.m. Beijing time, according to the national statistics bureau, which matters for commodity exporters such as Brazil, Chile and Colombia.

No rate decision is scheduled this week at the central banks of Brazil, Chile or Colombia, according to their calendars. Chile’s central bank meets on 26–27 October, and Brazil’s Copom meets on 3–4 November.

Culture and events this week

Festival Bamba is a new two-day festival in Parque O’Higgins, Santiago, on Saturday 24 and Sunday 25 October. Juanes, Marc Anthony, Fito Páez, Carlos Vives and Bomba Estéreo are on the bill, and day passes start at CLP 79,200 (about US$80) through Ticketmaster Chile.

Fonseca plays Bogotá on Saturday 24 October at 8 p.m., his first solo concert at El Campín. The concert moved to the Vive Claro Estadio because of the state of the El Campín pitch, and tickets already bought remain valid.

Mexico City holds the Mega Procesión de Catrinas on Sunday 25 October, its 13th edition, from about 6 p.m. along the route from the Angel of Independence to the Zócalo. Entry is free, and the procession is part of the build-up to the Day of the Dead on 1–2 November.

Football. In the Copa Sudamericana semi-finals, Vasco da Gama host Boca Juniors at the Maracanã in Rio on Tuesday 20 October at 9:30 p.m. Brasília time, leading 1–0 after the first leg. Atlético Mineiro visit Montevideo City Torque in Montevideo on Wednesday 21 at 7 p.m. Brasília time, leading 3–0.

In the Libertadores, Palmeiras lead Fluminense 2–1 before the return leg in São Paulo on Wednesday 21 at 9:30 p.m. Brasília time. Flamengo host Estudiantes at the Maracanã on Thursday 22 at 9:30 p.m., after a 0–0 first leg.

Heads-ups for travellers and new arrivals

Clock change. Europe goes back to winter time on Sunday 25 October, so calls with Lisbon or London move by an hour. Brazil does not use daylight saving time, so the gap with Lisbon narrows from four hours to three.

Runoff weekend. Election day is a Sunday, so check transport and opening hours before you travel that weekend. Expect crowds and queues around polling stations in Brazil’s big cities.

Colombia. Holders of residence visas issued before 21 October 2022 must switch to the new visa types by Saturday 31 October 2026, under Resolution 9316 of 2024. Check the foreign ministry’s latest notice before you apply.

What we could not confirm. We could not confirm ticket prices for Fonseca or the football matches, or any airline strike dates for 19–23 October.

Looking ahead

The Libertadores final is on Saturday 28 November in Montevideo, and the Sudamericana final on Saturday 21 November in Barranquilla. Formula 1 returns to Mexico City on 30 October–1 November, and Chile marks a public holiday on Saturday 31 October.

Weeks like this one show a pattern: official calendars (data, debates, holidays) are firm, while markets and results stay open. The dates above are the part of the week that will not move.

More: Latin America news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Background: Brazil Elections 2026: the runoff.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Brazil runoff and the last debate? The runoff is on Sunday 25 October 2026. Globo holds the final debate on Friday 23 October, straight after Jornal Nacional. When does Brazil publish mid-month inflation? On Friday 23 October 2026, according to the IBGE calendar. The EODHD consensus is 0.4% for the month, against 0.7% before. Who plays in the Copa Libertadores semi-finals this week? Palmeiras lead Fluminense 2–1 before the return leg in São Paulo on Wednesday 21 October. Flamengo host Estudiantes at the Maracanã on Thursday 22 after a 0–0 first leg, and both matches kick off at 9:30 p.m. Brasília time. Where is Fonseca playing in Bogotá? At the Vive Claro Estadio on Saturday 24 October 2026 at 8 p.m., after the concert moved from El Campín. Tickets already bought remain valid. Do the clocks change this week? In Europe, yes: clocks go back on Sunday 25 October. Brazil has no daylight saving time, and US clocks change on Sunday 1 November.

Sources: TSE, Globo and Band reports on the runoff and the debates; INDEC, IBGE, INEGI and DANE release calendars; EODHD economic calendar for consensus and previous values and for exchange rates; Polymarket and Kalshi for prediction-market prices (18 October 2026, 4 a.m. US Eastern); Ticketmaster Chile and Chile Travel on Festival Bamba; Infobae, Vanguardia and RCN on Fonseca; Publimetro and Emprendedor on the Mega Procesión de Catrinas; Emol and CONMEBOL reports on the semi-finals; Resolution 9316 of 2024 and EY and Vialto summaries on the Colombian visa deadline; Banco Central de Chile and Copom calendars. Local-currency figures carry approximate US$ conversions at the rates cited; prices and availability move.

World.title: Key Market Events for the Week of October 19–23, 2026
World.content:
Rio Times Markets · The Week Ahead

Key Facts —Brazil CPI Friday’s IPCA mid-month print tests the disinflation path ahead of the 25 October runoff. —China GDP Monday’s growth data set the tone for commodity exporters such as Brazil, Chile and Colombia. —Mexico data Retail sales and inflation show whether the peso’s relative resilience has domestic support. —US yields Treasury yields just above 5% keep funding conditions restrictive for high-carry Latin currencies. —Argentina activity Trade and activity data measure how much the adjustment is cooling demand. —Colombia activity Monday’s economic activity reading offers an early signal on the Andean growth outlook. —Prediction markets Polymarket priced a Flávio Bolsonaro win in the 25 October Brazil runoff at 81.0% and Lula at 19.5%, and Kalshi, regulated in the US by the CFTC, at 79.0% and 20.0% (18 October, 3:59 a.m. US Eastern).

The week turns on whether global yields and China’s growth pulse let Latin American investors keep taking selective risk, with Brazil’s mid-month inflation and Mexico’s activity data as the main domestic tests. Latin American markets enter the week with U.S. 10-year yields just above 5% and Brazil’s presidential runoff on 25 October ahead. Lower Treasury yields would help, but the trade is not a uniform regional bet.

The domestic focus is back-loaded: Brazil’s IPCA mid-month CPI and Mexico’s economic activity arrive Friday, after Mexico’s retail sales and inflation earlier in the week. Argentina and Colombia add secondary prints that will be read through the dollar and commodity lens.

Three Themes for the Week

High U.S. yields remain the main external constraint on Latin American carry and duration trades. The 10-year Treasury yield closed Friday just above 5%, about 15 basis points lower on the week.

Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October keeps the real in focus. The first round on 4 October gave Flávio Bolsonaro about 47% of valid votes and Lula about 45%, according to the TSE (Brazil’s electoral court).

The Week in Context

U.S. 10-year Treasury yields closed Friday just above 5%, down about 15 basis points on the week. That still leaves funding conditions tight for high-carry Latin American currencies.

Oil near US$110 for Brent is a mixed force. It supports exporters and fiscal revenues in Brazil and Colombia, but it also reinforces higher-for-longer global rate concerns.

Spot gold traded near US$4,166 an ounce on Friday. That points to continued demand for hedges against geopolitical, fiscal and currency risk.

What Prediction Markets Say

Brazil runoff. On Sunday 18 October at 3:59 a.m. US Eastern, Polymarket priced a Flávio Bolsonaro win at 81.0% and a Lula win at 19.5%, with about US$187 million traded on the market. Kalshi, regulated in the US by the CFTC, priced them at 79.0% and 20.0%, with about 6.6 million contracts traded.

Brazil inflation. Polymarket gave 60.9% to Brazil’s 2026 annual inflation ending between 5.00% and 5.49%, and 17.5% to a reading between 5.50% and 5.99%, with about US$168,000 traded. That market is a bet on the full-year rate, not on Friday’s mid-month reading.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

The Bottom Line

Investors should treat this as a week for selective risk-taking, not a broad Latin American beta trade. Watch U.S. yields and China’s data first, then let Brazil’s Friday CPI and Mexico’s activity numbers decide whether local duration, carry or exporter equities deserve fresh capital.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most important Latin American release this week?

Brazil’s IPCA mid-month CPI on Friday, because it tests the disinflation path ahead of the 25 October presidential runoff. The release is due on Friday at 12:00 UTC, with a consensus of 0.4% against 0.7% before.

Why does China’s Monday data matter for Latin America?

China’s GDP, industrial production and retail sales shape demand expectations for commodities, which directly affects exporters such as Brazil, Chile and Colombia. Monday’s release is due at 02:00 UTC, with consensus for annual GDP growth at 4.4% against 4.3% before.

How should investors read Mexico’s data?

Retail sales, inflation and economic activity show whether the peso’s relative resilience is backed by domestic fundamentals or mainly by global positioning. Mexico publishes retail sales on Wednesday, mid-month inflation on Thursday and economic activity on Friday.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight: Dionne Warwick, Amorphis — October 18, 2026
World.content:
São Paulo · Nightlife

Tonight, Sunday 18 October 2026, São Paulo has three international acts. The Berlin Philharmonic plays the Sala São Paulo at 6:30 p.m., but that concert is sold out. Dionne Warwick brings her farewell tour to the Vibra São Paulo at 8 p.m., and the Finnish metal band Amorphis plays the Carioca Club in Pinheiros. The night is dry and cool, so a jacket is enough. All times are São Paulo time.

Tonight at a Glance — Date Sunday, 18 October 2026. All times São Paulo time (UTC-3).

— Weather Cool and dry. Open-Meteo shows 19.0°C (66°F) at 6 p.m., 15.8°C (60°F) at 8 p.m. and 15.4°C (60°F) at 11 p.m., with a rain chance of 2, 1 and 0 per cent.

— Top pick Dionne Warwick’s farewell show at the Vibra São Paulo, 8 p.m., with tickets from R$189.75 (about US$38).

— Neighborhood in focus Pinheiros, in the west of the city, where the Carioca Club hosts tonight’s Amorphis show. In the centre, the Sala São Paulo, built inside a former railway station, hosts the sold-out Berlin Philharmonic concert.

— Entry prices Dionne Warwick from R$189.75 (about US$38). Amorphis from R$250 to R$600 (about US$49 to US$119), plus fees. The Berlin Philharmonic concert is sold out. Rate used: US$1 = R$5.06 (EODHD, 16 October close).

— Safety note The centre and the Pinheiros bar streets are busy after concerts, so book a rideshare to the door and keep phones out of sight on the street.

Planning more nights? Read our São Paulo Nightlife Guide 2026, with neighborhoods, costs, safety and how the scene works.

If You Only Go to One Place Dionne Warwick at the Vibra São Paulo The soul singer behind “I Say a Little Prayer” on her “Over and Out” farewell tour, with tickets still on sale.

Tonight’s Top 3

1. Dionne Warwick, “Over and Out” farewell tour, at the Vibra São Paulo Dionne Warwick is an American soul and pop singer whose hits include “That’s What Friends Are For” and “I Say a Little Prayer”. Her farewell tour reaches São Paulo tonight. Tonight Sunday 18 October 2026, doors 6 p.m. and show 8 p.m. (tour announcement).

Genre Soul and pop standards.

Entry Tickets start at R$189.75 (about US$38) on Ticket360. We could not confirm the sectors, half-price rules or whether any tickets remain.

Address Vibra São Paulo, Avenida das Nações Unidas 17955, Santo Amaro.

Verdict The best-known name in the city tonight for English-speaking visitors. For foreigners: the repertoire is in English, and the venue is far from the centre, so book your ride home before the encore.

2. Amorphis at the Carioca Club Amorphis is a Finnish metal band touring its album “Borderland”. The Carioca Club is a long-running live-music hall in Pinheiros. Tonight Sunday 18 October 2026, doors 7 p.m. We could not confirm the start time of the show.

Genre Melodic death and progressive metal.

Entry The fourth ticket lot is on sale through Clube do Ingresso. Floor (pista) tickets cost R$250 half-price and R$500 full price (about US$49 and US$99), and balcony (camarote) tickets cost R$300 and R$600 (about US$59 and US$119). A booking fee of R$37.50 to R$90 (about US$7.40 to US$18) is added.

Address Carioca Club, Rua Cardeal Arcoverde 2899, Pinheiros.

Verdict The pick for rock and metal fans, with a loud and dedicated crowd. For foreigners: the floor is standing, while the balcony tickets cost more and are the better choice if you want a view and a seat nearby.

3. Berliner Philharmoniker, Kirill Petrenko, at the Sala São Paulo The Berlin Philharmonic plays a benefit concert for children with cancer in São Paulo, with a second concert on Monday 19 October. The programme is Brahms’s Piano Concerto No. 1 and Strauss’s “Also sprach Zarathustra”. Tonight Sunday 18 October 2026, 6:30 p.m. (Berlin Philharmonic calendar).

Genre Classical, symphonic.

Entry The concert is reported as sold out (Tribuna do Sertão, 25 September). We could not confirm any returns.

Address Sala São Paulo, Praça Júlio Prestes 16, Campos Elíseos.

Verdict The most prestigious event in town, but sold out, so treat it as a story rather than a plan. For foreigners: the hall is built inside the old Júlio Prestes railway station, and it is worth a look from outside.

Also Tonight

— Cine Joia, Liberdade No concert is listed tonight. Kneecap, the Irish hip-hop and punk trio, plays there on Friday 23 October.

— Blue Note São Paulo and Casa Natura Musical We found no confirmed 2026 listing for tonight at either venue.

Later This Week

— Monday 19 October The Berlin Philharmonic plays a second concert at the Sala São Paulo at 8 p.m. (Sala São Paulo programme).

— Friday 23 October Kneecap plays the Cine Joia, Praça Carlos Gomes 82, Liberdade (Songkick). We could not confirm the time or prices.

— Sunday 25 October Brazil holds its presidential runoff, so expect early closings and plan transport around polling hours.

The Night in Context

Tonight three international acts play in three different parts of São Paulo: a world-famous orchestra in the centre, a soul legend in the south and a metal band in the west.

The Sala São Paulo is the city’s classical landmark, built inside the former Júlio Prestes railway station, which opened in 1938, with the concert hall opening in 1999. The Carioca Club and the Vibra São Paulo draw fans who travel across the city.

That is why this guide names what we could not confirm instead of filling the gap. Venue programmes often show old dates, so we only list events whose 2026 date appears on the listing.

Brazil also votes in the presidential runoff on 25 October, one week from tonight. Election day is a Sunday, so check transport and opening hours before you travel that weekend.

World.title: ECOWAS AES Talks Open in Dakar on 17 October
World.content:
The Dakar skyline seen from Gorée Island across the bay, Senegal's capital and host city of the ECOWAS-AES talks (Photo: Fawaz.tairou, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MALI · BURKINA FASO · NIGER · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The country Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, three Sahel states with military-led governments, form the Confederation of Sahel States (AES), while Senegal hosted the talks as current ECOWAS chair.

— Why it matters Trade, free movement and counter-terrorism cooperation across West Africa depend on whether ECOWAS and the AES can agree a framework after their split.

— Why now The first formal negotiating session took place on Saturday 17 October 2026, one day after both sides held separate preparatory meetings.

— What happened Both delegations agreed to set up joint thematic working groups aiming at a framework cooperation agreement, and signed an eight-point communiqué in Dakar.

— The numbers Three AES states face the regional bloc across one table, with one session held, one expert round due on 18 October and no date yet for the next ministerial meeting.

— What it means for you US investors, aid groups and travellers with West African exposure get a first sign that the split may be managed, though no rule has changed yet.

— Still open The date and venue of the next session, the themes and members of the working groups, and the content of any framework agreement.

The ECOWAS AES talks opened in Dakar on Saturday 17 October 2026, with Senegal as host. Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger left ECOWAS on 29 January 2025, and this was their first formal negotiating session with the bloc since.

For US readers the result matters because trade routes, travel rules and counter-terrorism cooperation in West Africa depend on whether the two blocs reach terms. The delegations agreed to build joint working groups towards a framework agreement, but they set no date for the next ministerial session.

ECOWAS is the Economic Community of West African States, the regional bloc that Senegal currently chairs. The Confederation of Sahel States, known by its French initials AES and often called the Alliance of Sahel States, groups Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

What the ECOWAS AES Talks Agreed in Dakar

The two sides issued a joint communiqué after the first session of their ministerial dialogue on cooperation, signed in Dakar on 17 October 2026 by the two heads of delegation. It has eight numbered points and sets out principles and a method rather than any trade or security terms.

The parties said their relations should rest on good neighbourliness, respect for sovereignty, dignity and the well-being of West African populations. They also said they want a cooperation framework that is balanced, realistic and protects the interests of their peoples.

To get there, they agreed to create joint thematic working groups for technical exchanges, with the ultimate aim of concluding a framework cooperation agreement. The groups’ results will go to ministers before the next session, whose date and place will be set through diplomatic consultation.

The communiqué does not name the themes of the working groups. RFI reported that groups cover the free movement of goods and people, trade and the fight against terrorism, with new institutional and legal arrangements as the long-term goal.

Who Sat at the Table

Cheikh Niang, Senegal’s minister of African Integration and Foreign Affairs, led the ECOWAS delegation in the ECOWAS AES talks as chair of the bloc’s Council of Ministers. Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré, Burkina Faso’s foreign minister, led the AES side as chair of its ministerial steering committee.

The two men co-chaired the meeting, and the AES committee also includes Mali’s foreign minister Abdoulaye Diop and Niger’s Bakary Yaou Sangaré. RFI quoted Diop as saying the AES approached the talks in a spirit of openness, constructiveness and responsibility.

ECOWAS chief negotiator Lansana Kouyaté, a former prime minister of Guinea who took the post in March 2026, told RFI the aim is not to ask the AES to return. He said a return might come one day, but that nobody can tell the AES today to come back.

RFI also reported that the AES states see the talks as a way to open a page and formalise new relations, not to discuss rejoining ECOWAS. Both blocs stress that each speaks with a single voice for its member states.

What the Two Delegation Heads Said

Niang said the discussions showed “substantial convergences” on shared priorities and the legitimate aspirations of states and peoples, according to APS. He called for a gradual, pragmatic and results-oriented approach that turns stated intentions into concrete commitments.

Traoré said the talks let both sides confirm their priorities and agree the principles that should guide their relations, APS reported. He added that the AES Confederation is ready to work with ECOWAS on a new cooperation framework and wants the effects to be felt on the ground.

Niang described the Dakar meeting as a significant step that follows the Bamako consultations of 2025 and sketches the outline of a new framework for dialogue. The communiqué thanks Senegal’s president Bassirou Diomaye Faye, the current chair of ECOWAS heads of state, for hosting.

How Each Side Prepared

ECOWAS foreign ministers opened preparatory consultations in Dakar on Friday 16 October, APS reported. The AES steering committee of foreign ministers met the same day in Ouagadougou to prepare one common position, according to its own communiqué published by Malijet.

The Ivorian outlet Koaci said the AES negotiating mandate rests on three points that are not up for negotiation. These are the sovereignty of the Confederation’s states, the consolidation of the AES itself and the protection of its populations’ interests.

The committee’s communiqué says the Ouagadougou meeting followed the Bamako consultations of 22 May 2025 and a confederal task-force meeting on 14 October. The Dakar communiqué likewise refers back to the ECOWAS and AES consultations held in Bamako on 22 May 2025.

RFI dates the three states’ announcement of their withdrawal from ECOWAS to 28 January 2024, and ECOWAS says their exit took effect on 29 January 2025. Our earlier coverage tracked the split in Three Sahel Juntas Open Their Own Parliament as the ECOWAS Split Deepens and the confederation’s own assembly in The Sahel Juntas Open a Parliament in Niamey.

Separately, customs experts from Togo and the three AES states drafted a joint tariff plan in Ouagadougou. We covered it in Togo and 3 Sahel States Draft Tariff Plan, and the Dakar communiqué does not mention it.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors, aid groups and travellers with exposure to West Africa follow the ECOWAS AES talks because they will shape trade and travel rules between coastal and landlocked states. The working groups on trade and free movement that RFI named cover the issues closest to commerce.

Counter-terrorism is also on the agenda, in a region where security conditions feed into travel advice and company risk assessments. Nothing agreed on Saturday changes a rule today, so existing travel and business conditions stand.

What Is Not Known

The date and place of the next ministerial session of the ECOWAS AES talks were left open and will be set after diplomatic consultations. The communiqué does not list the working-group themes, their members or a deadline for a framework agreement.

Technical talks between experts were due to continue on Sunday 18 October, RFI reported, and we have not seen their outcome. It is also unclear what a framework agreement would cover, since no draft text has been seen.

The sources reviewed do not say whether ECOWAS would accept separate terms for the three states, or whether the AES would ever consider rejoining. Both sides described the aim as a new cooperation framework, not a return.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did ECOWAS and the AES agree in Dakar?

They agreed on 17 October 2026 to set up joint thematic working groups to prepare a framework cooperation agreement. Results will go to ministers before the next session.

Who led the delegations?

Cheikh Niang, Senegal’s foreign minister, led ECOWAS, and Burkina Faso’s foreign minister Karamoko Jean-Marie Traoré led the AES. They co-chaired the meeting.

Are Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger rejoining ECOWAS?

No, neither side presented the talks as a return. The AES says it wants to formalise new relations, and ECOWAS’s chief negotiator said nobody can tell the AES to come back today.

When is the next meeting?

The date and place have not been set and will be fixed after diplomatic consultation. Expert-level technical talks were due to continue on Sunday 18 October.

Why does this matter to US readers?

Trade routes, travel rules and counter-terrorism cooperation in West Africa depend on how the two blocs work together. Nothing has changed in practice yet, because the Dakar session only created working groups.

World.title: Benin Growth at 7% Among Fastest in Africa
World.content:
Freight trucks and containers in the Zongo district of Cotonou, Benin (Photo: Adoscam, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

BENIN · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Benin is a West African coastal state whose Port of Cotonou is its main gateway for trade.

— Why it matters Growth of 7% a year is far above the regional pace, and a small, fast-growing economy draws investor and trade attention.

— Why now The IMF published its October forecasts this week, and Benin appears fifth in the sub-Saharan ranking that outlets circulated on 16 and 17 October 2026.

— What happened The IMF forecasts Benin growth of 7% in 2026, after 8.1% in 2025, against 4.5% for sub-Saharan Africa as a whole.

— The numbers The IMF sees 6.8% growth in 2027, inflation of 0.8% in 2026 and an economy of about US$27.4 billion.

— What it means for you US investors and importers see one of the few West African economies growing faster than 6%, with a moderate debt risk.

— Still open Whether Benin holds 7%, how much of the forecast the port and industrial zone deliver, and how the fifth place is shared with Niger.

Benin growth is forecast at 7% in 2026, which puts the country fifth among the fastest-growing economies in sub-Saharan Africa on the IMF’s October figures, La Nouvelle Tribune reported on Saturday 17 October 2026. The Fund expects the region as a whole to grow 4.5%, so Benin is expanding more than one and a half times as fast.

For US readers the ranking shows where growth is concentrated in West Africa, which matters to investors in African debt and to firms that ship through the Port of Cotonou. It is a forecast rather than a result, and the IMF’s own public database shows Benin sharing fifth place with Niger at 7.0%.

Benin’s 2025 expansion was covered in our earlier report Benin Economy Grew 8.1% in 2025 on Port and Factory Work. The IMF now also puts 2025 growth at 8.1%, up from the 7.5% it projected in February.

How Benin Growth Compares Across Africa

In the IMF’s public database, opened on 18 October, South Sudan leads at 10.5% for 2026, followed by Ethiopia at 9.2%, Rwanda at 7.4% and Guinea at 7.2%. Benin comes next at 7.0%, level with Niger, which matches the order that La Nouvelle Tribune and Africa Manager published.

South Sudan’s figure follows a database entry of 41.4% growth for 2025 after a 28.1% contraction in 2024, which Africa Manager describes as a base effect. The ranking says nothing about how large or stable each economy is.

Looking ahead, the IMF sees Ethiopia easing to 7.8% in 2027, Rwanda to 7.2% and Niger to 6.5%, while Guinea rises to 7.8%. Benin is forecast to slow only slightly, to 6.8%, which keeps it above the 4.7% forecast for the region in 2027.

Among Benin’s four land neighbours, only Niger matches it, with Togo at 5.0%, Burkina Faso at 4.4% and Nigeria at 4.2%. Other well-known markets are forecast at 6.0% in Côte d’Ivoire, 5.7% in Ghana, 4.5% in Kenya and 1.0% in South Africa.

What Is Behind Benin Growth

La Nouvelle Tribune credits the modernisation of the Port of Cotonou, farm progress, industrial development, including the Glô-Djigbé industrial zone, and trade. It also cites seed-cotton output of 647,290 tonnes in the 2025-2026 season.

The paper does not say how much each factor adds, and the sources reviewed give no sector breakdown of the IMF forecast. Our explainer Benin Explained: Wadagni’s New Era, the Cotonou Port Boom and the Jihadist North sets out the port and security background.

On 25 February 2026 the IMF Executive Board completed the seventh review of Benin’s Extended Fund Facility and Extended Credit Facility arrangements and the fourth review of its resilience programme. That released about US$118 million, and the Fund said the risk of debt distress remained moderate.

Prices, Debt and the Size of the Economy

The IMF database sees inflation of 0.8% in 2026, down from 1.1% in 2025, rising to 2.0% in 2027. Low inflation leaves households more purchasing power, though forecasts of this kind can change quickly when fuel and food prices move.

Public debt is forecast at 58.1% of output in 2026, down from 59.3% in 2025 and 60.5% in 2024, and the current account deficit at 5.6%. Both are watched by lenders, and neither is unusual for a fast-growing frontier economy.

The same database puts Benin’s 2026 output at about US$27.4 billion, or about US$1,799 per person. Fast growth from a small base lifts incomes only slowly, and it is still a modest economy next to Ethiopia, at about US$127.1 billion.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors in African bonds and funds can read the ranking as a sign of where the IMF sees the strongest momentum in French-speaking West Africa. They should note that Benin’s growth rests heavily on one port, which our report Benin’s Port of Cotonou Turns to Burkina Faso After 52% Cargo Jump examines.

Importers and shippers dealing with Cotonou face a growing local market and busier port lines, although the sources reviewed do not quantify either. Our report Benin Plans 14.7% Budget Rise to US$8.1 Billion shows how the government plans to spend as growth continues.

What Is Not Known

The IMF’s own World Economic Outlook report text could not be opened for this article, so the figures rest on its public database, checked on 18 October, and on three outlets that quote it. The release date of 13 October comes from Africa Manager alone.

It is not known how much of the 7% forecast the port, cotton and the industrial zone will deliver, or whether the 2026 outcome will match the forecast. The sources also do not show how the IMF treats northern security risks in its Benin projection.

The ranking depends on one-decimal rounding, so Benin’s fifth place is shared with Niger and could shift in later releases. The same database shows Sudan at 7.0%, but the outlets leave it out of their sub-Saharan lists and the sources reviewed do not state how the IMF groups it.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where does Benin rank for growth in sub-Saharan Africa?

On the IMF’s October forecasts, Benin ranks fifth in 2026 at 7.0%, behind South Sudan, Ethiopia, Rwanda and Guinea. Niger is also forecast at 7.0%, so the place is shared.

What growth does the IMF forecast for Benin?

The Fund forecasts 7.0% for 2026 and 6.8% for 2027, after 8.1% in 2025. The regional average is 4.5% for 2026.

Why is Benin growing so fast?

La Nouvelle Tribune credits the Port of Cotonou, farming, industry and trade. The sources reviewed do not give a sector breakdown of the IMF forecast.

How big is the Benin economy?

The IMF database puts it at about US$27.4 billion in 2026, or about US$1,799 per person. That is small next to Ethiopia, at about US$127.1 billion.

What does it mean for US readers?

It points investors and importers to a fast-growing West African market with low inflation and a moderate debt risk. It remains a forecast, and a small economy can swing quickly.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook database, Benin, opened 18 October 2026; La Nouvelle Tribune, 17 October 2026; Kaweru Infos, 15 October 2026; Africa Manager, 16 October 2026; IMF press release 26/63, 25 February 2026.

World.title: Kenya GDP Growth Is 5.1% Despite Oil Shock
World.content:
Aerial view of the Nairobi Expressway and industrial areas in Nairobi, Kenya, file photo, 2025 (Photo: Bahnfrend, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

KENYA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The country Kenya is a major East African economy and a tea, coffee and tourism exporter whose official growth figures come from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics.

— Why it matters Growth held above 5% while oil prices were far higher than a year earlier, which bears on investors in Kenyan debt, the shilling and East African trade.

— Why now The statistics bureau published its second-quarter 2026 national accounts on Friday 16 October 2026, three months after the first-quarter report.

— What happened Kenya’s economy grew 5.1% in the quarter to June, up from 4.9% in the same quarter of 2025 but below the 5.3% of the first quarter.

— The numbers Transport and storage grew 4.4%, accommodation and food 7.4% and agriculture 3.5%, while average crude oil rose to US$104.45 a barrel from US$67.44.

— What it means for you US investors in Kenya, travellers and importers of Kenyan tea and coffee see an economy absorbing an energy shock, with living costs still rising.

— Still open Whether the second half of 2026 holds near 5%, and how far dearer fuel and weaker rains reach food prices and household budgets.

Kenya GDP growth came in at 5.1% in the second quarter of 2026, the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics said on Friday 16 October 2026. The result matters to US investors holding Kenyan debt or shilling assets, because oil prices jumped during the period.

Average crude oil cost US$104.45 a barrel in the quarter, against US$67.44 a year earlier, and the bureau also pointed to an early end to the long rains. Even so, the economy grew faster than the 4.9% recorded in the second quarter of 2025.

We covered the run-up in Kenya’s GDP Growth Faces a 5 Percent Test. That piece set the first-quarter pace of 5.3% as the benchmark, and the new figure lands slightly below it.

What the Kenya GDP Growth Figure Shows

The bureau put real growth at 5.1% for April to June 2026, compared with 4.9% in the same period of 2025. Business Daily, the Nairobi business paper, said the economy “shrugged off” the Iran war and below-average rainfall.

The first-quarter figure was 5.3%, published by the same bureau on Friday 10 July 2026, so the pace eased by 0.2 points. The latest reading is also higher than the 4.9% a year earlier, so growth is slower than the previous quarter but faster than last year.

The bureau described the quarter as marked by disruption and uncertainty in global energy markets and by the early end of the long rains. Capital FM, a Nairobi broadcaster, reported the same headline figure and the same oil price comparison.

Business Daily put average consumer inflation in the quarter at 6.23%, up from 3.89% a year earlier, driven by food and transport prices. The Central Bank of Kenya kept its policy rate at 8.75% on 7 October 2026, according to its website.

Transport, Services and Power Led the Quarter

Transportation and storage grew 4.4%, up from 3.3% a year earlier, helped by more activity in land, rail and water transport. Accommodation and food services grew 7.4%, although that is slower than the 12.8% recorded in the second quarter of 2025.

Electricity and water supply grew 7.7%, information and communication 7.2% and financial and insurance activities 6.1%. Construction grew 6.0%, down from 7.3% a year earlier, even as production of galvanised sheets rose 19.7% to 92,424 tonnes.

Business Today, a Kenyan business outlet that quotes the bureau’s report directly, said wind power generation rose 13.5% to 469.8 million kWh. Thermal generation fell 16.3% to 288.4 million kWh, and total electricity sales rose 15.0%.

Manufacturing grew 2.2%, up from 1.3% a year earlier, according to Business Daily. That is a modest gain, but it shows factory output improving despite dearer fuel.

Weak Rains Slowed Agriculture

Agriculture, forestry and fishing grew 3.5%, down from 4.0% a year earlier, as the March to May long rains ended early in May. The bureau said the early end cut expected crop production at a critical stage of crop development.

Agriculture is Kenya’s largest employer, and Business Daily said it accounts for more than a fifth of GDP. A weaker farm sector matters because food makes up about a third of the consumer price basket, the paper added.

Some crops still did well. Tea output rose 11.1% to 162,600 tonnes from 146,300 tonnes, and coffee exports rose 10.0% to 22,046.4 tonnes.

Vegetable exports rose to 16,025.9 tonnes from 13,326.8 tonnes, and cut flower exports edged up to 33,105.8 tonnes from 32,953.9 tonnes. Fruit exports fell 5.8% to 76,084 tonnes, and milk taken in by processors fell 3.1% to 263.6 million litres, according to Business Today.

Oil Prices Hit Fuel Costs

The bureau put the average crude oil price at US$104.45 a barrel in the quarter, up from US$67.44 a year earlier. Business Daily dated the Iran war to US and Israeli strikes on Iran from 28 February, and linked it to the energy-price shock.

The average retail price of light diesel rose 32% to Sh217.8 a litre (about US$1.68) from Sh165.1 (about US$1.27) a year earlier, Business Daily said. Conversions use the Central Bank of Kenya’s rate of Sh129.81 to US$1, posted on 15 October 2026.

Higher fuel prices feed into transport and distribution costs, Business Daily noted, and weaker farm output adds pressure on food supplies. That squeezes household buying power and raises operating costs for firms, even while output grows.

Our earlier report Kenya Lawmakers Vote to Keep Fuel Tax at 8% covers one policy lever on fuel prices. The new national accounts show why that debate matters for households.

What It Means for You

For US investors, a 5.1% quarter suggests Kenya’s economy kept growing through an energy shock, which is a point in favour of Kenyan debt and shilling assets. The slower pace than the first quarter, and average inflation above 6%, keep the picture from being one-sided.

Travellers will see tourism-related services still growing, with accommodation and food up 7.4%, although more slowly than last year. Kenyan tea output and coffee exports both rose in the quarter, which is a measure of volume and not of price.

Our guides Who Runs Kenya’s Economy, the Key Players in 2026 and Kenya Economy Estimate Hits US$151 Billion give the wider picture. Our overview Kenya in 2026: Political Issues, Economy and the 2027 Vote covers the politics behind the economy.

What Is Not Known

The bureau’s own Second Quarter 2026 report could not be opened from our systems, because its website did not load. The figures rest on Business Daily, Capital FM and Business Today, which quote the report and agree on the headline numbers.

The outlets differ on cement, with Business Daily giving an 11.1% rise to 2.69 million tonnes and Business Today a 10.5% rise to 2.73 million tonnes. We have not used either figure beyond this note.

It is not known whether the second half of 2026 will hold near 5%, or how far the energy shock and weak rains will reach food prices. It is also not known whether the bureau will revise the quarter in later releases.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Kenya’s GDP growth in the second quarter of 2026?

The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics said the economy grew 5.1% in the second quarter, up from 4.9% a year earlier. The first quarter had grown 5.3%.

Which sectors drove Kenya GDP growth?

Transport and storage grew 4.4%, accommodation and food services 7.4%, and electricity and water supply 7.7%. Information, finance and construction also grew between 6.0% and 7.2%.

How did higher oil prices affect Kenya?

Average crude oil rose to US$104.45 a barrel from US$67.44, and Business Daily said retail diesel rose 32%. The economy still grew, but living costs and transport costs rose.

Why did agriculture grow more slowly?

Agriculture grew 3.5%, down from 4.0%, after the March to May long rains ended early in May. Tea and coffee output still rose.

What does the result mean for US readers?

It shows Kenya’s economy absorbing an energy shock, which matters to holders of Kenyan debt and to travellers. Inflation and weaker farm output remain risks.

Sources: Business Daily, 16 October 2026; Capital FM, 16 October 2026; Business Today, 17 October 2026; Kenyans.co.ke, 10 July 2026; Central Bank of Kenya; Kenya National Bureau of Statistics.

World.title: Ghana BRICS Bid Draws 5 Demands From APC
World.content:
The Independence Arch at Independence Square in Accra (Photo: Kwameghana, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

GHANA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The country Ghana is a West African democracy and a major exporter of gold and cocoa, governed by President John Dramani Mahama from the capital Accra.

— Why it matters BRICS is an 11-member bloc of emerging economies, and US President Donald Trump has threatened an extra tariff on countries that align with its “anti-American policies”.

— Why now On Saturday 17 October 2026 a party leader urged Mahama to take the plan to Parliament, and the Foreign Minister defended it the same day on television.

— What happened Hassan Ayariga, leader of the All People’s Congress, set out five demands, joining the parliamentary Minority’s call of 8 October for an urgent briefing.

— What it means for you Nothing changes yet for US exporters, investors or visitors, but any tariff risk would depend on how Washington reads Ghana’s steps.

— Still open Whether a BRICS partnership needs a parliamentary vote, whether partner status is a step towards full membership, and when Parliament next sits.

The Ghana BRICS bid met fresh demands for parliamentary scrutiny on Saturday 17 October 2026, when All People’s Congress (APC) leader Hassan Ayariga asked President John Dramani Mahama to put the plan before Parliament. Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa defended the bid the same day on JoyNews.

For US readers the stakes are trade and diplomacy, because Trump has threatened an extra 10% tariff on any country aligning with the “anti-American policies” of BRICS. The Ghana BRICS bid therefore lands in a wider debate about how an African government balances Washington and the bloc.

Cabinet approved the application on Tuesday 6 October, as we covered in Ghana Cabinet Approves BRICS Bid: What It Means for US Ties. The new element is an argument inside Ghana about who decides on the Ghana BRICS bid.

Where the Ghana BRICS Bid Stands

Ablakwa announced the Cabinet decision at a joint briefing in Accra with India’s External Affairs Minister Jaishankar. He welcomed Ghana’s interest but said any expansion needs collective consideration by current BRICS members.

The wording has shifted since then. Ablakwa told TV3 on Saturday 10 October that Ghana would seek BRICS partner-country status rather than full membership, and Mahama spoke on Friday 16 October of a decision “to apply for partnership with the BRICS countries”.

Partner countries take part in the bloc’s work without being full members, and Citi Newsroom lists Malaysia, Nigeria, Uganda and Vietnam in that category. MyJoyOnline wrote on 12 October that Ablakwa called partner status a first step towards full membership, but on Newsfile on 17 October he said the government seeks partner status rather than full membership.
