But Uber says the model works because the three companies share a common goal of bringing autonomous taxis to more markets.

“You have Verne, which is an incredible local company in Zagreb, with fleet expertise and vehicle operations and then you Pony.ai, which has world-class AV technology, and you have Uber which helps bring that all together in terms of the mobility platform, rider experience,” said Duvnjak.

“So, it’s really everyone’s bringing the best of what they do coming together.”

Verne, the European partner in this venture, was co-founded by Mate Rimac and is named after the sci-fi writer Jules Verne. It has been working on robotaxis since 2019 and launched its own service in April.

Verne acts as the local service operator and fleet owner, managing the day-to-day operations of the robotaxi service. It also serves as the regulatory lead, talking to local, regional and national authorities to secure legal approval for autonomous vehicles on the road in these areas.

Annie Duvnjak, Global Head of Autonomous Mobility Operations at Uber, presents the partnership to journalists. Source: Uber.

This is perhaps the biggest obstacle facing the partnership. Europe’s patchwork legal framework governing driverless cars has left the continent lagging far behind the US and China, where robotaxis have operated commercially for several years.

The partnership with Uber gives Verne the opportunity to scale up its operation by offering its services through the app and bring them to other cities across Europe as the roll-out expands.

“This is an important milestone not only for Verne, but also for Croatia. A service pioneered here in Zagreb is now available through the world’s largest mobility platform. The experience we are gaining every day in Zagreb will help us bring Verne to other European cities,” said Marko Pejković, the CEO of Verne.

In June 2024, the Croatian company unveiled its own autonomous two-seater concept car aimed at business travellers.

“We want people to be impressed when you arrive in one of these vehicles,” said Pejković.

It is a long, sleek vehicle with enough room for the seats to recline fully while driving. A huge dashboard screen entertains and informs passengers during their ride.

Despite its more luxurious appearance, the company says rides will not come at a premium, because removing the driver cuts costs significantly.

“We are introducing a completely new vision for the vehicle interior, one designed not as a concept for the distant future, but as something that can work in real service. It will help people use their time in a way that is more productive, more enjoyable, and more relaxing,” said Pejković.

The company plans to roll out the vehicle in future but, for now, uses the BAIC Arcfox.

A driving school for AI agents

The third partner in this venture is Chinese AI firm Pony.ai, which provides the artificial intelligence technology that drives the vehicles.

The company also brings a lot of experience in the sector. Pony.ai says it was the first autonomous vehicle company to secure a taxi licence in China, and it is one of the few companies globally operating fully driverless commercial vehicles.

In Zagreb, the Arcfox vehicles are equipped with Pony.ai’s Gen-7 autonomous driving system, its latest level 4 autonomous driving kit.

The kit includes 34 individual sensors. Among them are nine LiDAR sensors, 14 cameras and four millimetre-wave radars, as well as four microphones, two water sensors and one collision sensor. Together they give the vehicle considerable awareness of its surroundings and enough redundancy to reduce the chance of accidents.

Pony.ai Virtual Driver controls the autonomous vehicle. Source: Uber.

Driving the car is the Pony.ai Virtual Driver, which treats the vehicle like a physical AI agent. But before an AI agent can hit the road, it must first drive in a virtual environment.

“It’s like a virtual training ground, that shows the AI how to drive. It’s like how humans learn to drive is how the AI drivers learn to drive in that environment. Then, after it graduates the ‘virtual driving school’, the AI drivers take control, so we don’t rely on any remote control,” said Dr Ludi Wang, director of global communications at Pony.ai.

Next steps

Uber announced this week that the partnership’s next city will be Manchester, in the UK. Tests are already under way in the city, and Uber says a service like the one in Zagreb will follow in the coming months.

In total, Uber is considering more than 30 cities and has schemes at various stages in London, Madrid, Munich and Zurich.

“And we hope to expand this model to other cities as well. So we’ve announced Manchester, where we’ll be coming next with this partnership, and so, more to come from there,” said Duvnjak.

But could Brussels be next?

“We’re actually talking to Brussels, we’re talking to 30 cities and Brussels is one of those cities. But we don’t want to roll out tests in a city if we don’t see it as an option in the future to fully roll out a driverless service as the end goal. But Brussels is definitely on the map,” said Pejković.

World.title: Leisure out of reach for one in eight people in the EU: Where is the problem biggest?
World.content:
About 46 million people in the EU miss out on regular leisure activities because they cannot afford them, according to Eurostat. In Greece, more than one in four people face this barrier — the highest share in the bloc.

 

The figures reveal wide differences across Europe, even between countries with similar income levels.

Several studies link social and leisure participation to better mental well-being and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety. Eurostat also highlights the role leisure and social interactions can play in improving quality of life.

So, where are costs most likely to prevent people from taking part, and how much does income explain the gap?

In 2025, the share of people who couldn't afford to participate regularly in a leisure activity ranged from 3.9% in Croatia to 27.3% in Greece, compared with an EU average of 12.1%, according to Eurostat.

Figures cover people aged 16 and over. With about 381 million people in this age group in 2025, this means around 46 million people in the EU faced this financial barrier.

This share was also above 15% in Romania (23.3%), Lithuania (17.9%), Latvia (16.2%), North Macedonia (15.9%) and Hungary (15.8%).

France and Spain are above the EU average

More than 13% of people in France (13.9%) and Spain (13.4%) also reported that cost prevented them from taking part regularly in leisure activities. Switzerland (13%) was also above the EU average.

Germany (11.7%) was just below the EU average. In Italy, regular leisure activities were out of reach for 10.7% of people because of the cost.

Czechia (4.1%), Luxembourg (5.4%), Norway (5.7%) and Slovakia (5.7%) were also close to Croatia (3.9%) at the lower end.

The share was also higher than in Croatia in the Nordic EU countries: Denmark (10.4%), Sweden (9.7%) and Finland (7.9%).

Elsewhere, it stood at 6.7% in the Netherlands, 8.7% in Turkey and Portugal, 9.2% in Ireland and 9.7% in Belgium.

Leisure activities are less affordable for women

Except for Malta, where the difference was slight at 0.1 percentage point, leisure activities were less affordable for women than men. In the EU, the share was 13% among women, compared with 11.1% among men.

The gender gap was particularly large in several countries: 5.1 percentage points (pp) in Lithuania, 4.7 pp in Romania, 3.9 pp in Denmark and 3.7 pp in France.

Is income linked to leisure affordability?

Analysis by Euronews Business covering 33 European countries shows that income plays a role, but it does not tell the whole story. There is a moderate link between median income and the share of people who miss out on regular leisure activities because of the cost. Income data come from Eurostat and show median equivalised income in purchasing power standards (PPS).

Income accounts for less than a fifth of the variation between countries. Czechia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had almost identical median incomes, all between 17,097 and 17,190 PPS. Yet only 4.1% of people in Czechia couldn't afford to take part regularly in a leisure activity, compared with 10.7% in Estonia, 16.2% in Latvia and 17.9% in Lithuania.

The same pattern appeared among wealthier countries. France and Cyprus had virtually the same median income, at 23,792 and 23,782 PPS, respectively. But the share of people facing this financial barrier was more than twice as high in France (13.9%) as in Cyprus (6.3%).

Greece had the highest rate at 27.3%, with a median income of 13,612 PPS. Turkey (8.7%) and Serbia (9.9%) had lower incomes but much lower rates. Croatia, Czechia and Slovakia had some of the lowest rates despite incomes below the EU median of 22,638 PPS.

The role of inequality within countries

Across the EU, people below the poverty line were more than three times as likely to miss out on regular leisure activities as those above it, with 29% unable to afford them.

While inequality within countries may play a role, Euronews Business analysis finds only a weak link between income inequality and leisure affordability, which is not statistically significant.

The analysis uses Eurostat’s Gini coefficient, a measure of how unevenly income is distributed.

How people answer the survey may affect the results

How people answer the survey matters. A Eurostat working paper by Anne-Catherine Guio and colleagues found that “poor people may report that they do not want things, simply because they cannot afford them”. They found that leisure was the item most often not seen as a necessity.

What is a leisure activity?

According to Eurostat, leisure activities include sport, cinema and concerts, among others, and should take place outside the home. These activities involve spending money on entrance fees or travel, such as for swimming; on equipment, such as a bicycle; or on participation in organised activities, such as football club fees.

World.title: ‘Every sunny surface’ is being put to work. Europeans transforming their homes with solar driveways
World.content:
Europeans are transforming their driveways and patios into mini solar farms, bringing the continent closer to a “cheaper, more secure” energy system.

 

The war on Iran and subsequent stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route that usually carries around one-fifth of global oil supplies, has sent oil and gas prices soaring.

Solar has stepped in to help cushion the fossil fuel price shock, saving the EU €40 billion in avoided gas imports since the conflict began – according to the latest analysis from Solar Power Europe. But electricity and gas bills across the continent remain high – which experts say has spurred households to “take control” of their own energy.

In Germany, renewable energy firm Enpal BV saw inquiries for solar panels rise by 30 per cent following the first weeks of the US-Israel war against Iran. Over in the UK, energy firm EON witnessed interest in solar spike by 23 per cent between 23 February and 1 March, before surging a further 63 per cent between 2 and 8 March.

And it isn’t just rooftops that are harnessing the power of sunlight, as more and more companies get creative with the ways in which solar panels can be integrated into the home.

Europe’s driveways get a solar makeover

PLATIO is one of a number of start-ups selling solar panels specifically designed for decking and patios after unveiling their first prototypes in 2016.

Now covering 13 countries across Europe, the firm aims to replace paving stones and asphalt in urban spaces, parks and homes with solar technology.

In 2018, PLATIO placed a nine-metre-square installation on the driveway of a family house in Kecsmét, Hungary. The 1.7 kWp system can theoretically generate enough electricity to power base loads such as a fridge and fridge-freezer, as well as LED lighting and small kitchen appliances like a blender or slow cooker.

In 2021, the company installed solar paving in the courtyard of a six-flat apartment building near Frankfurt, Germany. Due to the larger size, this 6.64 kWp system is more than enough to cover the annual electricity needs of a typical three bedroom home if it performs at maximum generation.

SolarPave, based in the UK, also specialises in transforming outdoor spaces with sustainable energy solutions. On its website, the company has three already finished projects in the Yorkshire region, including a residential solar driveway and a residential balcony floor.

How do solar driveways and patios work?

Companies like PLATIO use a toughened, anti-slip glass to protect the solar panels – meaning you can walk across it or even park your car on it.

Cleaning the panels to remove any dirt will help maximise the amount of energy the panels can create, but PLATIO says the performance loss from dusty panels is as little as three per cent depending on the specific installation.

A public pathway in the Netherlands made out of solar panels. PLATIO

Of course, solar panels fixed horizontally on the floor opposed to angled on a rooftop will generate less electricity. This is because they miss the sun’s direct rays for most of the day, while accumulated dirt reduces their efficiency.

However, depending on their location, they may still be able to generate enough electricity to help lower your energy bills.

It is therefore difficult to say exactly how many years such a system would take to pay back.

‘Every sunny surface’ is being put to work

“People are choosing solar because it puts them back in control,” Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council, tells Euronews Earth.

“After years of volatile energy bills, households in Europe and across the world want to take energy into their own hands and solar is one of the most affordable ways to do that.”

While traditional rooftop solar panels may remain the back-bone of home-grown solar, not everybody has a suitable roof.

For example, heavily shaded roofs may generate little energy – increasing the payback time and making installation unfeasible. Roofs made from materials like thatch are also unsuitable for traditional solar panels.

“As prices have fallen and designs have become more versatile – driveways, patios, fences and car parks are becoming part of the picture,” Dunlop says.

“Every sunny surface we put to work brings Europe closer to an energy system that is cheaper, more secure and owned by the people it serves.”

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.

World.title: Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
World.content:
Vietnam has signed a deal with four non-EU members that covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, and sustainable development, among other areas.

Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.

The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.

Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made upNorway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).

The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.

How does the deal benefit Vietnam?

The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.

Is Vietnam set to replace China as the world's factory? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports ​to ‌Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% ‌to be tariff-free within seven ‌years, ​the Norwegian government said in a statement.

According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.

Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.

Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.

It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

World.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
World.content:
Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

How Starlink enables communications

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis , the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

There are around 50,000 Starlink terminals in Ukraine Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

The role of Starlink in drone warfare

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

What throttling Starlink would mean

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

More than just satellite internet

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Strategic dependence

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

Starlink terminals enable mobile internet connection on the battlefield for the operation of drones Image: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
World.content:
Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.

The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.

What happened in the Czech Senate elections?

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.

The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.

Babis called the result "catastrophic."

"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.

That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.

Czech journalists warn of dangers of public media reform To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.

Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

World.title: India: CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention
World.content:
Two other prominent CJP leaders are set to be released on Sunday. India has seen huge rallies calling on the country's top election official to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India.

The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.

The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."

"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.

In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way."

"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."

What are the protests about?

All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening.

Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.

Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.

The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned.

The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP



Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy".

BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.

Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."

"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.

India: Protesters jailed amid election row To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar.

Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.

The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released.

"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.

World.title: India news: Kolkata stampede dampens Durga Puja festivities
World.content:
10/17/2026 October 17, 2026 CJP's Dipke arrested after detention — reports

The 'Cockroach' movement has called Dipke's detention a 'kidnapping' Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Founder Abhijeet Dipke has been arrested, following his detention on Friday when he stepped out to participate in a rally he had called in New Delhi, media reports said.

Dipke was arrested to ‌prevent a ⁠breach ⁠of the peace and will be taken before a Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) court later today, news agencies ANI and PTI reported.

CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh also said that Dipke had been arrested, adding that he would appear before the SEM court in central Delhi's Mandir Marg at 12 p.m. (630 UTC).

Singh claimed that Dipke's lawyers had not met him.

The 'Cockroach' movement said early on Saturday that they did not know where their founder had been detained, calling his detention a "kidnapping."

"Until now, neither his parents nor his lawyers and not the CJP team have been given any updates about his location," the CJP said on X, as it published a video of CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde asking about Dipke's whereabouts.

Dipke was detained publicly on Friday as he left the house in Jhandewalan where he was staying to take part in CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' (Wave the tricolor) protest rally in Connaught Place.

Videos of his detention showed the CJP founder being told by a police official that he was being placed under "preventive detention" before he was taken to a police car.

Dipke was seen displaying India's flag as police and media personnel surrounded him. Some supporters were seen trying to block the police vehicle from driving away with Dipke.

Just hours earlier, a group of Delhi Police officials had visited the 31-year-old at the Jhandewalan residence and served him a notice barring the Friday protest.

The Delhi Police had previously reiterated that Section 163 of India's criminal procedure law, which prohibits any form of assembly or protest, was in force in the Connaught Place area.

"The manner in which he was picked up from right outside his residence, no information about his whereabouts, and the fact that even his lawyers have been unable to meet him raise serious concerns about due process and fundamental rights," Singh wrote on X.

Even after Dipke's detention, hundreds of protesters turned up in Connaught Place defying the heavy security deployment. The protesters were seen waving the Indian national flag as part of the CJP's 'Tricolor' rally. According to police, some 150 protesters were detained during the demonstrations.

The fresh protests came after CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to a five-day detention in jail on Wednesday for alleged violation of prohibitory orders and breach of a peace bond after they attempted a demonstration. They too were carrying the Indian tricolor and the flag has since been at the center of CJP's campaign.

The Indian flag "belongs to the 1.3 billion people of this country and not the Delhi police. We will wave it where we want!" the movement has said.

Dipke, Das and Ranka were earlier detained on October 10 from a plane as they arrived in the capital for a protest march calling for the resignation of India's Chief Election Commionser Gyanesh Kumar over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

They were released after nearly 24 hours.

World.title: Canada: Major fire reported at military base in Alberta
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta. He did not provide details on the cause of the fire.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday said a "serious incident" sparked a major fire at a military base in Alberta.

"A serious incident creating a major fire has occurred at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta," Carney said in a post on X.

He added that the federal government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities.



Defense Minister David McGuinty later confirmed that there have been "fatalities and injuries" as a result of the incident on the base.



Located about 180 kilometers (112 miles) southeast of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, Canadian Forces Base Wainwright is one of the country's busiest military training bases.

What else do we know about the major fire in Alberta?

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire was spreading rapidly due to high winds.

"The fire south of Wainwright crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed ... Emergency crews remain focused on protecting life safety, homes, and other structures," it said.



Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire "significant and tragic" and said many military personnel are affected.

"We are learning of a significant and tragic fire at CFB Wainwright today that is affecting many of our brave military personnel," Smith said in a post on social media.

The incident occurred just days before people in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote in the October 19 referendum on whether the province wants to begin the process of separating from the rest of Canada.

World.title: 'No Kings' rallies push early voting ahead of US midterm elections
World.content:
Organizers of the "No Kings" protests, known for their anti-Trump sentiment, are urging Americans to vote early in the November 3 midterm elections, as Republicans face tough races to retain control of Congress.

Protesters gathered across the United States for the latest "No Kings" demonstrations as Americans begin casting ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," Saturday's event aimed to fire up Americans to vote early in the midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, rather than protest against President Donald Trump and his administration.

"It's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard," organizers said in a statement.

Most areas of the United States allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.

There were more than 3,000 'No Kings' events planned across the US Image: Daniel Heuer/REUTERS

Trump opposes mail-in voting

Trump repeatedly criticized mail-in voting and sought to restrict the practice ahead of the midterms. He regularly votes by mail-in ballot, arguing that his job makes him an exception to his criticism of the practice.

The US president blamed election fraud, without providing evidence, for his defeat in the 2020 presidential election against Democrat Joe Biden.

Various surveys have concluded that restricting mail-in ballots could benefit Republicans, as Democratic voters disproportionately use the system to cast their ballots.

Opponents fear that the Trump administration may try to interfere with the midterm results, particularly if Republicans lose the majority.

Opinion polls suggest Democrats are poised to regain control of the House ​of Representatives, while the Senate remains too close to call.

World.title: Ilhan Omar: The US Democrat targeted by Donald Trump
World.content:
Donald Trump has described her as "garbage" and a "criminal" who does nothing but "bitch." Congress member Ilhan Omar has long been the target of angry verbal attacks from the US president. But why her?

"Ilhan Omar, whatever the hell her name is, with the little – with the little turban, I love her. She comes in, does nothing but bitch."

"Ilhan Omar is garbage. She's garbage. Her friends are garbage. […] These aren't people that work. These aren't people that say, let's go. Come on, let's make this place great. These are people that do nothing but complain."

"She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other. And she comes into our country, and she says, 'I have a constitutional right.' She's telling us about the constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet."

These are just three of Donald Trump's many attacks on US Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar. Few people have been targeted as ferociously by the US president. But why has Trump singled her out for such hostility?

Who is Ilhan Omar?

Ilhan Abdullahi Omar, 44, was born in Mogadishu, the capital of Somalia. She fled the civil war in the country while still a child, and spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya. She finally came with her family to the US in 1995, at the age of 12, and became a US citizen in 2000. She joined the Democratic Party, and made a career as a politician on the party's left wing. Since January 2019, she has served as representative for the state of Minnesota and one of the first two Muslim women to enter the US Congress.

Ilhan Omar is a practising Muslim who wears a hijab, and Congress altered a 180-year-old rule for her that prohibited head coverings in the chamber of the House of Representatives. Politically and socially, Omar champions progressive values, and often makes a connection between her faith and her commitment to social justice, human rights, and the protection of minorities.

Omar campaigns on issues such as universal health insurance, increasing the minimum wage, climate protection, and the cancellation of student debt. She is also one of Donald Trump's most prominent and outspoken critics, repeatedly accusing him of racism and systematically fomenting hatred against minorities, immigrants, and Muslims. She has frequently condemned raids by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which she describes as a "militarized campaign of fear." She has also accused the president of corruption in office.

Minneapolis, the capital of Minnesota, is home to the largest Somali community in the United States Image: Jessie Wardarski/AP Photo/picture alliance

Criticism of Israel and accusations of antisemitism

Young, outspoken, female, Muslim, and a left-wing Democrat – politically, Ilhan Omar is almost the polar opposite of the 80-year-old Republican Trump. But she is also a controversial figure within her own party.

Omar is one of the fiercest critics of Israel in US politics, and has repeatedly called Washington's support for the country into question. She has been accused of antisemitism, and of supporting the movement BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions), which encourages people to boycott Israeli businesses. Omar has defended BDS as a legitimate form of non-violent protest and freedom of expression. In 2019, she even introduced a resolution in the US Congress that aimed to strengthen the right of Americans to boycott, with a view to countering laws that restrict what the BDS movement can do.

In early 2023, Republicans removed her from the House Foreign Affairs Committee over a number of controversial tweets, including a comment she made in 2021 that seemed to equate the actions of the US and Israel with those of the Taliban in Afghanistan, and the Palestinian group Hamas. The latter is classified as a terrorist organization by the US and many other countries around the world.

Accusations of embezzlement and immigration fraud

Her critics also tried to link Omar to a corruption scandal in her home state of Minnesota. During the COVID-19 pandemic, around $250 million (€220 million) were misappropriated from a government-funded food program for children. Omar had previously called for the rules of the program to be eased.

Many of those convicted were from the state's Somali community, something that political opponents, including Trump, seized on to claim Omar was involved. No law enforcement authorities have ever accused her of any wrongdoing.

The most recent accusation against Omar concerns her immigration to the US. For years, her opponents have claimed that she made false statements during the procedure, even alleging that she entered into a fraudulent marriage with her biological brother to help him secure a US visa. On October 12, federal officials ordered a search of Omar's home, investigating allegations that Omar's father lied about her age on her immigration application.

Officers from the Department of Homeland Security raided the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on October 12, 2026 Image: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

Controversial house search

Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations, describing them as part of a "campaign of political intimidation" and "an attempt to target political enemies." Several leading Democratic politicians have come to her defense, accusing the Trump administration of weaponizing the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security against its political opponents.

Former immigration officials told the Reuters news agency that it is extremely unusual for a house search to be conducted as part of such an investigation, as the government should already have all the relevant immigration documents.

Many see a raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress over a formality from 26 years ago as excessive, and have been especially critical of the timing of the raid, just three weeks before the Congressional elections in which Omar is standing for re-election.

The long-standing, unwritten "60-Day Rule" holds that authorities do not take any public action against political candidates in the two months before an election, so as not to influence the outcome. Critics see the fact that this practice has been ignored in Omar's case as amounting to election interference.

'Timing wildly suspicious' — Unpacking the search of Ilhan Omar's home To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other Muslim politicians also targeted

With the midterm electionslooming, Trump is battling with plummeting approval ratings, and Omar is not the only Muslim politician the president has been attacking. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate in the Senate election in Michigan, is another.

At a rally last Saturday in Tennessee, Trump said of El-Sayed: "I call him Mohammed. Somebody said, 'His name isn't Mohammed, it's Abdul.' I said, 'To me, it's Mohammed.' I'm the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he's Mohammed, and he's a radical jihadist."

Abdul El-Sayed is the Democratic Party's candidate to represent the state of Michigan in the US Senate Image: Emily Elconin/Getty Images/AFP

There is no intelligence whatsoever to suggest that El-Sayed has any extremist connections. The 41-year-old epidemiologist was born and brought up in Michigan. He went to university there, then won a Rhodes scholarship to Oxford, where he gained a doctorate in public health. For many years, he was the health director of the city of Detroit. Like Omar, he too belongs to the progressive left wing of the US Democratic Party.

During the election campaign, El-Sayed has repeatedly emphasized that he is not the one responsible for the rise in food prices, the expensive rents, and other political grievances. He has placed the blame squarely on what he describes as the failed policies of the administration in Washington.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Francia prende fuego al macronismo
World.content:
El segundo mandato del presidente, desconectado de la sociedad, tiene aún por delante seis largos meses en los que el país debe aprobar un presupuesto y buscar respuestas al imparable ascenso de la ultraderecha

Francia salió a la calle el 17 de octubre de 2026 y, entre manifestaciones, incendios y pillajes, certificó la muerte del macronismo. Lo hizo con violencia, como suele hacerlo. Rabia, cólera y también miedo hacia el futuro. Y lo que constató mientras destrozaba comercios e incendiaba Ayuntamientos y comisarías fue la defunción de una idea política que quería instaurar una centralidad ideológica radical y contener el auge de los extremos. En lugar de eso, fueron nueve años en los que se vaciaron los servicios públicos, se multiplicó la deuda (pasó del 98% del PIB al 119% actual) y los polos ideológicos en el Parlamento engulleron el debate público hasta ser hoy las dos fuerzas políticas —la izquierdista La Francia Insumisa (LFI) y el ultraderechista Reagrupamiento Nacional (RN)— con más posibilidades de llegar a la segunda vuelta en las elecciones de la próxima primavera.

El sábado se encontraron en las calles y las rotondas de Francia todos aquellos que desde hace mucho temen por la llegada del fin de mes y los que, además, lo hacen por la del fin del mundo. O, al menos, el mundo en el que vivieron sus padres.

Macron, que pocas horas antes de la anunciada protesta se fue a ver el concierto de Céline Dion con su esposa, llegó al poder cuando tenía 39 años. Era joven, listo y arrogante. Ni de izquierdas ni de derechas, anunciaba la construcción de su relato político. Había que introducir fluidez en la economía y flexibilidad en el mercado laboral. Macron conocía ese mundo, venía de la banca. Entendía el dinero. Pero se había criado en el Partido Socialista y era también consciente de la necesidad de preservar ciertos equilibrios, impartir justicia social, coser las fracturas identitarias. Engrasar el ascensor social que impulsaba la educación pública. Pero nada de eso ocurrió.

Abdul Saboor (REUTERS) Manifestantes saquean una oficina de turismo durante una protesta contra el aumento del coste de la vida y en apoyo a las reivindicaciones estudiantiles, en Lyon. Jack Taylor (REUTERS) Un manifestante se enfrenta a agentes de policía durante una marcha cerca de la Plaza de la República de París. Carl Court (Getty Images)

Francia está más fracturada que nunca y la extrema derecha, que el macronismo pretendía marginar, se encuentra a las puertas del Elíseo por primera vez desde la II Guerra Mundial: los sondeos le dan un 35% de intención de voto en la primera vuelta de los comicios. “Es el final de un reinado con una gran descomposición. Hay ecos del 1968, cuando también se llegaba al final del gaullismo. La protesta de los estudiantes es un movimiento inesperado que el Gobierno vio venir, pero no pudo imaginar la magnitud. Además, otro aspecto peligroso para Macron es que no hay dinero en la caja. Y eso rompe la regla de oro de una crisis social: pagar”, explica el periodista y biógrafo del presidente de la República, François-Xavier Bourmaud.

El jefe del Estado prometió revertir una sociedad gobernada y diseñada por y para boomers, la generación nacida entre 1946 y 1964. Lo tenía todo. En las últimas elecciones presidenciales obtuvo el voto mayoritario de la generación entre 25 y 34 años. Solo cinco años después, los treintañeros le desprecian, según los sondeos de Ipsos-BVA, y se inclinan por cualquier otra opción política. En las elecciones legislativas de 2024, menos de uno de cada diez votantes jóvenes apoyó a un candidato del bloque presidencial.

Macron siempre se rodeó de jóvenes colaboradores. Pero no le sirvió para entenderles. En junio de 2025, al margen de una cumbre del G-7, confesó al escritor Emmanuel Carrère que “nunca ha sido adolescente” y que no le “gustan” ni “comprende” a los adolescentes. La “Francia de Macron”, como la definen en las protestas de los estudiantes, ha dado la espalda a los jóvenes. La edad media de consumo televisivo en el país (France 2 y France 3) es de 60 años. El relato publicitario de los grandes segmentos de consumo no es para ellos: la edad a la que uno puede permitirse un coche nuevo son 55 años. El sábado, nueve de cada diez detenidos por los altercados eran menores de edad.

El deterioro de las cuentas públicas, la desaceleración del crecimiento y el aumento del desempleo han dejado obsoleto ese ideal, hasta el punto de reavivar un conflicto generacional. Pocos candidatos se atreven a defender abiertamente los intereses de los jóvenes, que se abstienen de votar en una medida ampliamente superior que las personas mayores.

Un manifestante lanza un bote de gas lacrimógeno durante los disturbios en Nantes, este sábado. Stephane Mahe (REUTERS)

Las protestas ya no alcanzan solo el problema de las pensiones ni llegan de la parte alta generacional, obsesión de sus dos mandatos. Hoy, eso es lo inquietante, no hay un interlocutor. El primer ministro, Sébastien Lecornu, no sabe si sobrevivirá al debate presupuestario de las próximas semanas. El presidente de la República apenas se ha referido al conflicto estos días y, a seis meses de ser relevado, es ya una figura de escasa autoridad. “Esta es la crisis final del macronismo”, insiste Bourmaud. “El movimiento de los estudiantes ya resuena como el de los chalecos amarillos en el primer mandato. Pero es todavía más sorprendente que se produzca meses antes de una elección presidencial, cuando nunca ocurren estos fenómenos. Las protestas suelen llegar después de una reforma o unos meses después de unas elecciones a causa de alguna desilusión. Los periodos antes de unas elecciones suelen ser tranquilos”.

El Ejecutivo sabe que no podrá satisfacer sus demandas económicas. El paisaje de fondo banaliza este tipo de esfuerzos. El Banco de Francia ha rebajado su previsión de crecimiento para 2026 hasta una horquilla entre el 0,4% y el 0,5%, muy por debajo del 1% que manejaba a finales de 2025, y elevó su pronóstico de inflación hasta el 2,5% para este año, casi un punto por encima de lo calculado meses atrás. La propia entidad admite que ese menor crecimiento, combinado con el encarecimiento de la deuda, empujará el déficit público al 5,2% del PIB en 2026, frente al 5,1% de 2025. Un cóctel que eleva la deuda pública hasta el 119,8% del PIB.

El politólogo Pascal Perrinau cree que Francia atraviesa “una crisis de confianza política”. “La desilusión en el sistema político es enorme. El presidente bate récords de impopularidad, el primer ministro no logra aprobar el presupuesto. Los franceses tienen la impresión de que no pueden esperar nada de la política y que el sistema está completamente gripado. Los jóvenes son los portavoces de un malestar y una reivindicación que también comparten con los padres. Y anuncia una campaña presidencial que oscilará entre la indiferencia y el apoyo a los partidos de protesta: el Reagrupamiento Nacional y La Francia Insumisa”, advierte.

La izquierda radical de LFI, liderada por el vehemente Jean-Luc Mélenchon, es la única capaz de entrar en las manifestaciones y canalizar políticamente la rabia de los estudiantes (tiene un 40% de intención de voto entre los menores de 35 años). Y la ultraderecha del RN, de Marine Le Pen, aparece como la formación capaz de restablecer el orden y la ley. “Macron prometió que esa idea de no ser ni de derecha ni de izquierda marginalizaría al RN. Pero la ultraderecha no ha estado nunca tan fuerte como hoy. Estamos objetivamente en un momento de fin de reinado. El presidente está al final de su mandato, no puede presentarse y el macronismo afronta su destino: ser un paréntesis en la historia”, insiste Perrineau.

Policías se protegen tras sus escudos durante las protesta en Nantes, este sábado. Stephane Mahe (REUTERS)

El problema va mucho más allá. La violencia y la sensación de caos se han apoderado de las calles. Las escenas de pillaje, ultraviolencia y sabotaje del sábado han dado la vuelta al mundo. Unos 300 estudiantes de secundaria han resultado heridos, junto con 150 miembros del personal educativo y 900 integrantes de las fuerzas del orden desde el inicio del movimiento. Este balance humano va acompañado de 9.000 detenciones policiales, de las cuales el 85% corresponden a menores de edad, y de una treintena de investigaciones encomendadas a la Inspección General de la Policía Nacional (IGPN), el organismo encargado de indagar en posibles irregularidades policiales.

Manuel Valls, exprimer ministro y exministro del Interior durante el mandato de François Hollande, cree que el Estado es ahora “muy débil”. “Nunca los manifestantes, la calle, habían tenido la sensación de enfrentarse a un Estado y un poder político tan frágil. Tan incapaz de plantar cara y buscar soluciones”, señala. “El vacío de poder es tremendo y advierte, con todos los síntomas, como una policía en crisis, el papel de LFI y los chalecos amarillos, que el Titanic se hunde. La situación favorece a las dos fuerzas de los extremos: el RN y LFI”, explica Valls al teléfono.

Los problemas de estabilidad se agravaron con la inesperada disolución de la Asamblea Nacional que decretó Macron en junio de 2024. El presidente de la República, en una jugada política que nadie entendió y que todos sus asesores le desaconsejaron, logró justo lo contrario de lo que se proponía y sembró el caos parlamentario. “Macron además de no dar un sentido a su segunda legislatura, destrozó lo poco que quedaba. Cuando fui primer ministro tuve una crisis en el Partido Socialista, cero crecimiento, a Europa presionando en el presupuesto y terrorismo… Pero nunca tuve la impresión de perder el control del camión. Si destruyes el legado gaullista, que es la estabilidad, creas una confusión enorme. Soy muy pesimista. Creo que estos seis meses se harán muy largos”, advierte Valls.

World.title: Información genética para una medicación más segura y eficiente
World.content:
Con una simple muestra de saliva, la farmacogenética permite el análisis de decenas de genes y cientos de fármacos de uso habitual y revela por qué un simple analgésico quita el dolor a una persona y a otra le produce una reacción adversa

Según estima la Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios, entre el 3% y el 6,5% de la población tiene una variante genética que provoca que su hígado transforme la codeína (un compuesto presente en medicamentos o soluciones tan frecuentes como las pastillas para la tos) en morfina. Este proceso, que se produce a gran velocidad incluso si la dosis administrada es normal, puede desembocar en una sobredosis accidental, que en algunos casos termina en el fallecimiento del paciente.

El ejemplo lo pone Javier Suela, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid). Él mismo pertenece a este pequeño grupo poblacional de riesgo: “Hay mucha evidencia acumulada de la toxicidad de ciertos medicamentos en ciertos pacientes. Estas reacciones adversas van desde un brote cutáneo hasta la muerte en casos extremos, como este mismo de la codeína”, explica.

Suela trabaja para reducir esa peligrosidad al mínimo. En el laboratorio que dirige, desde el pasado mayo, se extrae el perfil genético de quien lo solicite para “determinar si tiene un componente genético, una proteína, que produce que determinados fármacos se procesen de una forma que no es habitual”, sintetiza.

El perfil genético, en tres pasos 1 Recepción de las muestras e identificación de cada paciente El paciente lleva una muestra genética (basta la saliva, por ejemplo) en un tubo. Este tubo va a una primera máquina que realiza una preanalítica y transforma las muestras en placas que identifican a cada persona: en la posición A1 está la muestra de un paciente concreto y en la B1, otro, y así sucesivamente. 2 Procesado del material genético El material genético de la placa, que contiene muestras de hasta 96 pacientes, se prepara y depura (se corta, se colorea...) en otra máquina para el análisis final. Lo que se obtiene, tras cuatro horas de refinado, es la placa definitiva (en la imagen) que se usará para extraer el perfil genético. 3 Obtención del perfil genético La placa, con el material genético ya refinado, se introduce en un escáner que analiza cada celda, que contiene más de un millón de variables (cada una asociada a un genotipo) que procesar. Cuando este escáner finaliza se obtiene el perfil genético del paciente, el resultado final del proceso.

Esta disciplina se conoce como farmacogenética y en Sanitas está disponible para todos sus asegurados bajo el nombre de Mi Farmagen. “Un ser humano puede metabolizar todos los fármacos, pero en función de ciertas variables genéticas los metaboliza a distintas velocidades; entonces el medicamento puede funcionar demasiado bien o demasiado mal. Esto es lo que da lugar a reacciones adversas o reacciones inexistentes, es decir, cuando el fármaco no funciona”, detalla.

29 genes y 125 fármacos analizados

Mi Farmagen analiza hasta 29 genes y más de 125 fármacos de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las reacciones a cada uno de estos medicamentos. Y siempre es útil, tanto si se obtiene antes o después de la prescripción, ya que “permite ajustar la medicación sin perder efectividad, pero evitando posibles efectos adversos y aumentando la seguridad”, incide Suela.

Hay casos en los que un cambio anticipado de medicación puede salvar la vida del paciente, pero también situaciones más cotidianas en las que esta información es de mucha utilidad. Así lo explica Andrea Azcárate, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid): “Es el ejemplo de un paciente con colesterol alto al que le sienta mal un tipo de estatina, que es el tratamiento habitual para esta patología. Para corroborarlo, se le hace la prueba farmacogenética. A partir de ahí, probablemente escojamos otro tipo de estatina que vaya a tolerar mejor”. Sin embargo, cada caso, en opinión de Azcárate, no es blanco o negro: “Lo que el análisis nos da es una predisposición de respuesta, una información probabilística que nos permite individualizar el tratamiento”, puntualiza.

0:00 ANDREA AZCÁRATE, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid)

Azcárate y Suela inciden, precisamente, en la importancia de la interpretación facultativa de esta información, que por sí sola vale poco. “Es fundamental la interpretación y el ajuste, algo que siempre se ha hecho: la medicación, en función de las características clínicas del paciente, las casuísticas y las edades, se individualiza”. Y eso mismo se hará a partir de ahora, subraya: “Ajustaremos caso a caso, pero con más información. Es una herramienta más, muy buena y útil, pero hay que tener prudencia a la hora de incorporarla”.

En esa misma línea se expresa Suela: “El informe son páginas de metabolización, nada más. No vale de nada sin facultativo detrás que las interprete. Y, sobre todo, hay que combinar toda la información: igual tienes un paciente del que el análisis dice que el fármaco le va a sentar muy bien, pero esa misma persona tiene unas condiciones físicas complicadas o es un paciente polimedicado, en el que es fundamental medir las interacciones entre fármacos”. Es una cuestión de personalización, como dicta la tendencia actual en la medicina, pero con un conocimiento más preciso.

Así funciona Mi Farmagen Mi Farmagen analiza cómo las variantes genéticas influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos.
