The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two. The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history. Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war. At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine. On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population. Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk. On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there. Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026 Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″. Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”. “Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.” “True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery. At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers. Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”. “This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.” Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026 The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children. Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war. In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations. The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries. The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026 However, tensions over historical issues reemerged this year, when President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres. That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. However, the two sides subsequently made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026 Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project. PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant. However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis. The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year. Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation. According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule. The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026 Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts. The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Everything you need to know one year ahead of Poland’s parliamentary elections
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Daniel Tilles Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called. Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign. When will the election take place? Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023. Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible). It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term. How does voting work? The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list). The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat. How is a government formed? A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm. After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence. If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm. Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister. That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023 If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government. If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called. Who is likely to form the next government? At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture. According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%. Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%. If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition. It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun. However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside. The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law. There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government. PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult. All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation. What about the Senate? The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset. It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO). In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026 The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies. In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition. To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023. What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest. What role will Nawrocki play in all of this? Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work. Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition. During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right. But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together. In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections. Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition. What issues are likely to feature in the campaign? A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer. Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump. On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland. President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026 Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland. While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign. The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims. Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024. The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025 The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues. As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy. The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation. World.title: Kraków’s new mayor withdraws patronage of LGBT+ equality march
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march. Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall. His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city. Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK — Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026 Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people. In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”. However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did. "I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024 The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”. “I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.” Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments. Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch). During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed. When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would. However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków. In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union. The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries. Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue. Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46). The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026 In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”. Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”. World.title: Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs. “The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation. In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year. Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8 — Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026 Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks. While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast. Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028. Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw. Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia. The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus. Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe. The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland. In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab. Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology. On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea. World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: Prague Expands Tram Network With Five Projects Underway
World.content:
Prague is expanding its tram network, with five projects now under construction across the capital.

Two new projects began in October 2026, extending the network from Malovanka to Strahov and from Libuš to Nové Dvory.

Work is also progressing on the tram line across Wenceslas Square, where the tracks have been connected between Vinohradská Street and the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.



The projects aim to improve public transport connections to developing residential areas and strengthen links with other transport services, including the future Metro Line D.

New tram line to connect Malovanka with Strahov

Construction of the new tram line from Malovanka to Strahov began on October 5, following preparatory work. The tracks will run along Vaníčkova Street, starting at Bělohorská Street and continuing toward Strahov Stadium.

The Malovanka stop will also be modified and moved to a position before the intersection, allowing it to serve trams heading toward Strahov.

The existing Stadion Strahov stop, currently used for passengers to disembark, will be renamed Strahov.

Tram extension to Nové Dvory will complement Metro Line D

Construction of the second new line, extending the tram network from Modřany through Libuš to Nové Dvory, began on October 7, 2026.

The extension will introduce two stops, Přírodní and Nové Dvory. At Nové Dvory, the line will end in a loop using Durychova, Libušská and Chýnovská streets.

The new connection is being developed alongside plans for Metro Line D and the wider expansion of the surrounding residential area. It will provide a direct tram connection to central Prague, including the Palackého náměstí area, with a future connection toward Smíchov also planned.

The extension will change operations on tram line 17. Once the project is completed, the temporary dead-end terminus in Libuš will be removed, allowing single-ended trams to return to longer routes. A second tram line is also planned for the new tracks after Metro Line D opens.

Hodkovičky gains a new tram stop

The new Hodkovičky stop, located between Belárie and Černý kůň, is another addition to Prague’s tram infrastructure in the south of the city.

The stop is intended to improve access to public transport for residents of the growing residential developments nearby. Further housing construction is also expected in Nové Dvory, where the planned tram extension will provide additional transport capacity.

Tram tracks connected across Wenceslas Square

Work on restoring tram services across Wenceslas Square is also progressing. In early autumn, construction crews connected the tracks running from Vinohradská Street, past the National Museum, across the square and toward the junction of Jindřišská and Vodičkova streets.

The track infrastructure in this section is complete. Remaining work includes finishing the surrounding surfaces and installing overhead power lines.

Once these works are finished, the new line will restore tram services across Wenceslas Square, strengthening public transport connections in central Prague.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets 2026 Start in November – Dates and Locations
World.content:
Prague’s Christmas markets will return in November 2026, with the first stalls opening at Náměstí Míru on November 20.

The main markets in Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will follow on November 28, bringing traditional Czech food, handmade decorations and a program of seasonal performances to the city center.

Náměstí Republiky follows on November 25, and Tylovo náměstí opens on November 26.



The main markets at Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square begin on November 28 and continue until January 6, 2027. The other markets close on Christmas Eve, December 24.

Here are the opening dates and hours for the main locations.

– náměstí Míru — November 20 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– náměstí Republiky — November 25 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

– Tylovo náměsti — November 26 to December 24, 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

– Old Town Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

– Wenceslas Square — November 28 to January 6, 2027, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Smaller Christmas Markets Across Prague

Several markets open before the main city-center venues and offer alternatives for visitors who want to explore different neighborhoods.

Further options include the market at Anděl and Lesser Town Christmas on Kampa Island.

náměstí Jiřího z Poděbrad will host farmers’ markets during Advent, with a design market joining them every Sunday during the season. These events offer opportunities to browse locally made products and find gifts beyond the usual Christmas-market stalls.

World.title: Modeselektor to Open Spectaculare Festival at Prague’s ROXY
World.content:
Berlin electronic duo Modeselektor will open the 14th edition of Spectaculare on 3 March 2027, bringing their live show to ROXY alongside new music from their latest album, MDSLKTR

Gernot Bronsert and Sebastian Szary will perform a set combining techno, electro, hip-hop and bass music, accompanied by visual projections and lighting.

The concert comes shortly after the release of MDSLKTR, an album that revisits the sound and influences that have shaped the duo’s nearly three-decade career.



The record follows Classics Vol. 01, a project that revisited material from their early albums Hello Mom! and Happy Birthday! and drew on years of studio recordings and unfinished ideas.

With MDSLKTR, Modeselektor return to the sounds that first defined their music, drawing on Berlin rave culture, techno, electro, IDM and hip-hop while continuing to move between genres.

Since emerging from Berlin’s underground electronic scene, the duo have built an international following through their studio albums, live performances and collaborations with artists including Radiohead frontman Thom Yorke, Tommy Cash, Flohio and Blixa Bargeld.

They also formed Moderat with producer Apparat and run the independent record label Monkeytown Records.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Spectaculare (@spectaculare_music)

Berlin-based multi-instrumentalist Philipp Johann Thimm will open the evening. A longtime collaborator of Apparat, Thimm has worked across electronic and acoustic music as well as audiovisual projects. His work on Apparat’s album *LP5* contributed to a Grammy-nominated project, while his solo work explores the meeting point between electronic composition and live instrumentation.

World.title: Prague’s Día de Muertos Festival Returns to Holešovice on November 5th
World.content:
Prague’s Holešovice Market will host the fifth annual Día de Muertos festival on November 5, bringing Mexican food, live music, traditional decorations and family activities.

The event, organized in cooperation with Jarritos and Nuevo Progreso, will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. Halls 13 and 11 will host a Mexican market and a carnival for children.

Visitors can arrive throughout the day, with the food stalls opening at lunchtime.



The selection will include Mexican and South American specialties, tortillas, grilled dishes and Jarritos soft drinks. A special beer brewed by Falcon brewery for the occasion will also be available.

The food zone will remain open until 10 p.m., giving visitors time to sample different dishes and explore the festival’s other attractions.

One of the main attractions will be a traditional ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, prepared by the Mexican Embassy. Decorated with photographs, flowers, candles and personal objects, the altar will introduce visitors to the traditions behind the holiday.

Día de Muertos is dedicated to remembering deceased family members and loved ones.

In Mexican tradition, the holiday celebrates their continuing place in family life and the belief that their spirits return to visit the living. Its customs differ from Halloween, combining remembrance with food, music, flowers and colorful decorations.

Hall 11 will become the PEDRO Kids’ Zone from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m., with a program designed for children and families.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Holešovická tržnice (@holesovickatrznice)

Activities will include dance workshops, Mexican music, crafts, stories about the holiday and a game in which children throw balls at illuminated skulls. Visitors will also have the opportunity to meet a Xoloitzcuintle, the Mexican hairless dog traditionally associated with guiding souls to the afterlife.

Costumes are welcome, and the organizers have divided the program into six one-hour sessions beginning at 1 p.m., 2 p.m., 3 p.m., 4 p.m., 5 p.m. and 6 p.m.

Admission costs CZK 100 per person for adults and children aged three and older. Tickets are available through GoOut and at the venue, subject to availability. Each ticket covers one hour of activities, after which visitors can explore the rest of the festival.

The program will also feature mariachi musicians, stilt walkers, colorful masks and costumes, and a festival parade. DJs will provide music throughout the day, while a screening of the animated film Coco will offer another introduction to Mexican traditions surrounding death and remembrance.

World.title: Danish-Japanese Chain Sticks’n’Sushi to Open First Prague Restaurant
World.content:
Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Czech restaurant in central Prague on Wednesday, November 4, introducing its combination of Japanese cuisine and Danish design to the local dining scene.



The restaurant will occupy a site on Jungmannovo náměstí in Prague 1. Ahead of the official opening, guests will be able to sample the menu at half price from November 1 to 3.

Those interested in attending the preview must register online. Registered guests will then receive a link to book a table for one of the available dates.

The menu combines sushi, sashimi and salads with kushiyaki, Japanese-style grilled skewers. The restaurant will also offer set menus intended for sharing, making them suitable for groups.

Among the dishes are Beef Tataki, served with miso aïoli, truffle ponzu and crispy Jerusalem artichoke, and the Temaki Setto, which allows diners to assemble their own hand rolls with ingredients including lobster, Wagyu tartare and avocado.

Another addition is the Ebi Sando, a sandwich featuring crispy shrimp, truffle and miso aïoli. The Sticks Setto features skewers of Japanese Wagyu beef, Iberian pork, shrimp and miso-marinated black cod, served on a hot stone at the table.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sticks’n’Sushi Czech Republic (@sticksnsushi_cz)

The drinks list includes sake, Japanese teas, cocktails and premium spirits. The restaurant will also serve a Japanese rice lager brewed for the chain by Danish brewery Mikkeller.

Zbyněk Pokorný, chief executive of Sushi Group s.r.o., which is bringing the concept to the Czech market, said the opening followed nearly two years of preparation.

“We believe that the combination of Japanese quality, Danish hospitality, and a strong focus on the overall guest experience is a perfect fit for Prague,” Pokorný said. He added that the company was looking forward to welcoming its first guests.

Reservations can be made through the company’s Czech website.

About Sticks’n’Sushi

Founded in Copenhagen in 1994, Sticks’n’Sushi was established by brothers Jens and Kim Rahbek, who have Danish and Japanese roots, and Thor Andersen. The first restaurant opened in a basement space in the Danish capital.

The business has since expanded into an international restaurant group, with locations in Denmark, Germany and the United Kingdom. Its interiors draw on Japanese and Danish influences, with individual restaurants featuring their own design elements within the brand’s overall concept.

World.title: Using private health insurance with direct billing in Budapest
World.content:
International private health insurance can be reassuring until you actually need to use it outside your home country. For foreigners living in Budapest, business travelers, and tourists, one of the first practical questions when arranging private medical care is: Will I have to pay the bill myself?

Collaborative content

The answer depends on both the insurance policy and the healthcare provider. In some cases, direct billing to health insurance in Budapest allows the clinic and insurer to handle eligible medical costs between them. Instead of paying the full amount upfront and submitting a claim later, you may only need to deal with costs that are not covered by your policy.

Direct billing can considerably simplify getting medical care abroad. However, international private health insurance or travel insurance doesn’t automatically mean you can use direct billing. In other cases, you will need to pay out of pocket and submit a reimbursement claim later.

How can you use your private health insurance at a clinic in Budapest?

There are two common ways to use private health insurance for medical treatment in Budapest, Hungary.

With the traditional reimbursement model, the patient pays for the treatment in Budapest and receives an invoice and supporting documents from the clinic. You then submit these to the insurance company, which reimburses eligible expenses according to the policy terms.

Direct billing simplifies reimbursement: the healthcare provider submits the required claim information directly to the insurer, which then pays for covered services, if the arrangement is available.

Direct billing to health insurance can remove a significant administrative burden for an international patient already navigating an unfamiliar healthcare system and language in Hungary.

Can direct billing to insurance be processed with travel insurance?

Travelers visiting Budapest may also use direct billing, but under special conditions. Coverage usually applies to eligible illnesses or injuries that occur or begin while you are outside your home country and within the policy’s validity period. The clinic may require a guarantee of payment from the patient before billing the insurance company directly.

For this reason, travelers should contact their insurer or ask the clinic to check the arrangement before assuming the insurer will settle the visit directly.

When direct billing is unavailable, the usual alternative is to pay upfront and request reimbursement afterward. Keeping the invoice, medical documentation and any forms requested by the insurer is therefore important.

Check your insurance policy before choosing a clinic in Budapest

When you need medical care unexpectedly, insurance administration is unlikely to be a priority. Spending a few minutes checking your policy details before booking a visit can make the process much easier.

Geographical coverage: Check whether your insurance covers treatment in Budapest, Hungary.

Check whether your insurance covers treatment in Budapest, Hungary. Direct billing: Check whether the healthcare provider you plan to visit can bill your insurer directly, or whether you need to pay upfront and claim reimbursement.

Check whether the healthcare provider you plan to visit can bill your insurer directly, or whether you need to pay upfront and claim reimbursement. Specific treatment coverage: Confirm that your consultation, examination, or treatment is covered, and whether a referral is needed to see a specialist.

There may be additional conditions. Some insurers require pre-authorization before particular medical services. You may also need a referral before seeing a specialist, even if the clinic doesn’t require one. The clinic may ask for a guarantee of payment (GOP), which confirms the insurer will cover eligible costs.

Also, check your deductible or co-payment rate or amount, and be aware of any exclusions. Direct billing only changes how the clinic settles eligible costs; it does not expand your insurance policy’s coverage.

Have your insurance card ready, as you may need to show it at your first appointment. The policy information can also help the clinic verify the necessary details before booking.

Checklist for direct billing to health insurance: things to do before booking an appointment Source: FirstMed Budapest

Remember that direct billing is not the same as receiving treatment free of charge. Any deductible, co-payment, or excluded service remains the patient’s responsibility. If the insurance company ultimately refuses a claim, the patient may also be responsible for the medical costs.

Having your insurance card and your insurer’s contact information readily available can help you quickly determine your options in an unexpected situation.

How direct billing to health insurance works at a private clinic in Budapest

Direct billing procedures vary between private healthcare providers in Budapest and insurance companies, but the process usually begins before the appointment.

At FirstMed, an English-speaking private clinic in Budapest, patients provide their insurance information when arranging their first visit so the clinic can check whether direct billing can be organized. FirstMed works with more than 130 private health insurance providers, although arrangements may sometimes also be possible with insurers outside its existing network, explains Ilana Varga, FirstMed’s insurance manager.

The patient brings their insurance card to the first visit and completes the required payment guarantee documentation. Depending on the insurer, a claim form may also need to be signed. Once direct billing is confirmed, the clinic handles the relevant claim documents and payment arrangements with the insurer.

If direct billing cannot be arranged, the alternative is generally to pay for the treatment and submit a reimbursement claim yourself. In this situation, international patients should ask whether the healthcare provider can issue invoices and supporting documents in English and in a format suitable for their insurer.

Understanding your insurance policy is key

Private health insurance can make accessing medical care in Budapest easier, particularly for international residents and visitors who prefer English-speaking healthcare. But the practical experience depends heavily on knowing how the individual policy works.

Checking direct billing eligibility, coverage limits, referrals, pre-authorization requirements and out-of-pocket costs before an appointment can help avoid unexpected bills and unnecessary paperwork.

Frequently asked questions about using private health insurance in Budapest

Do I always have to pay first when visiting a private doctor in Budapest? No. If your insurance policy allows direct billing and the healthcare provider can arrange it with your insurer, they may settle eligible costs directly. Otherwise, you will generally need to pay the clinic and claim reimbursement afterward. Does having international health insurance guarantee direct billing? No. Direct billing depends on your individual policy terms and the arrangements between your insurer and the healthcare provider. It is best to confirm this before treatment whenever possible. What if the Budapest clinic does not normally work with my insurer? It is worth asking before assuming that direct billing is unavailable. In some cases, an insurer may issue a guarantee of payment that lets the clinic arrange direct settlement even without an established relationship. If that isn’t possible, your policy may still cover reimbursement after payment. Can tourists use travel insurance for direct billing at a private clinic? Sometimes. The policy must allow direct billing, and the insurer may need to provide a guarantee of payment. Coverage also depends on the circumstances of the illness or injury and the policy’s terms and validity period. What documents should I ask for if I need to claim reimbursement? Ask your healthcare provider for an invoice and any medical or claim documentation your insurer requires. Foreigners staying in Budapest may also want to confirm in advance that these documents can be provided in English and in a format their insurance company accepts.

For a more detailed explanation of the process and how FirstMed handles it, read the full guide to direct billing to health insurance in Budapest.

Remember, insurance coverage and direct billing eligibility depend on the terms and conditions of the individual insurance policy. Confirm your coverage and any authorization requirements with your insurer.

World.title: Hungary needs an AI workforce plan before anxiety becomes resistance
World.content:
Artificial intelligence no longer feels like a distant policy discussion. It is beginning to shape how companies hire, train, automate and reorganise work. The latest IMF message from Bangkok adds urgency to this trend: AI investment is supporting growth, but it is also likely to disrupt labour markets.

Written by A.S. Alhebsi / Abdulla Saeed Alhebsi – Author and Researcher specializing in Security, Heritage, Risk Management, and Control Room Operations

That should matter in Hungary, where the economy depends heavily on manufacturing, supplier networks and a workforce expected to adapt quickly to changing industrial demand. If AI enters these sectors without a credible workforce plan, productivity gains could arrive alongside deeper uncertainty.

The UAE’s recent emphasis on digital skills and secure digital public infrastructure is relevant because it highlights a simple but often neglected truth. Technological transition is not managed by software alone. It is managed by institutions that prepare people for new expectations before anxiety hardens into resistance.

Hungary’s risk is not necessarily immediate job collapse. It is a slower erosion of confidence. Workers may wonder whether routine administrative, planning or support roles still offer a future. Younger employees may worry that entry-level opportunities will shrink. Employers may underestimate how much clarity people need when job design begins to change.

If you missed it – Exclusive interview: What is business education for in the age of AI?

This matters because labour-market transition is partly psychological. Employees who feel ignored or kept in the dark are less likely to embrace new systems. Public debate then turns suspicious, even when some technologies could genuinely improve competitiveness.

Hungary therefore needs a practical AI workforce plan.

That means identifying which sectors face the earliest task disruption, aligning retraining with actual job redesign, and ensuring that employers treat communication as part of implementation. Vocational systems and universities should not merely discuss AI; they should translate it into applicable competencies.

There is also a broader regional dimension. Central European economies compete for investment partly on the basis of skills and reliability. Countries that manage the human side of AI better may become more attractive places to build higher-value operations. Those that neglect it may discover that social unease becomes an economic cost.

The best AI strategy is not the loudest. It is the one that keeps productivity rising while preserving public confidence that the future of work has not been written without the people who still need work.

As we wrote earlier, Hungary passed its first Artificial intelligence law

World.title: Micro Budapest: a free website turns 40 of Kolodko’s mini statues into a treasure hunt
World.content:
A new website invites locals and visitors to track down 40 of the tiny, mostly bronze figures that sculptor Mihály Kolodko has placed around Budapest.

Searching is part of the fun. Each entry on Micro Budapest therefore gives only an approximate address, enough to bring you to the right place and leave the figure for you to discover. If you still cannot find it, help is one tap away: the exact GPS coordinates open the spot in OpenStreetMap.

Visitors can browse by district or by theme, from “Hungarian Childhood” and “Politics & History” to “Curious & Touching”, open a map of the 40 selected figures, and use “My Location” to see which one is nearest. Micro Budapest is free to use and available in Hungarian, English, German, French, Greek, Italian and Spanish.

Every location was checked on the spot rather than copied from existing lists. The site also offers a background story for each statue. Kolodko rarely explains his works himself, so these stories are Micro Budapest’s own: independently researched from newspaper articles and Hungarian sources, and the team’s view of what each figure means, not an official explanation.

Photo: Kolodko Art / Facebook Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH Photo: DNH

Most of the statues appear unannounced, and they can be stolen, moved or altered at any time. A news section reports new figures and losses, and three statues are currently marked as missing on the map. The site asks visitors to report anything they notice.

Micro Budapest is a curated selection, not a complete list, and has no connection to the artist.

Website: microbudapest.com
