World.title: Rayalaseema landscape: Preserving the past, securing the future
World.content:
Across the Rayalaseema region of Andhra Pradesh, fragments of a historically-rich landscape stand amid rocky hills, river valleys, and expanding settlements. Forts that once guarded strategic routes, temples that drew generations of devotees, and monuments bearing the imprint of successive dynasties offer vivid glimpses into the region’s political, cultural, and religious history. Today, however, these sites face severe pressure from quarrying, road construction, and unregulated tourism.

Geologists aptly describe this landscape as a library of deep time, preserving natural events spanning billions of years. Much of Rayalaseema lies within the Cuddapah Basin and the ancient Dharwar craton—one of India’s oldest crustal blocks. Its basement rocks formed more than 2.5 billion years ago during the Precambrian era. Over centuries, sediments accumulated, volcanoes erupted, and layers were buried, folded, and eventually exposed again.

This ancient foundation stands in stark contrast to the young, restless Himalayas, which were born from the collision of tectonic plates and remain seismically active.

Prof. U. Suresh from the Department of Geology at Sri Venkateswara University, Tirupati, explains this profound difference: “The southern heartland of Andhra Pradesh is the weathered, unyielding skeleton of an ancient Earth. Safely sitting on the Dharwar Craton and the Cuddapah Basin, this region was formed 2.5 billion years ago. While the Himalayas strive restlessly toward the sky, Rayalaseema rests in profound structural calm.”

For those who know where to look, this ancient stillness is hidden in plain sight. Along the ghat road up to Tirumala, that mysterious calm is written in stone. Exposed on a steep, dusty road cut that thousands of pilgrims pass without a second glance lies the Eparchaean Unconformity—one of the world’s most significant geological boundaries. Here, light layers of 1.5-billion-year-old Nagari quartzite rest directly on dark, 2.5-billion-year-old Archaean granite. Between them, nearly 800 to 1,000 million years of Earth’s history have vanished. It is a billion-year gap where older rocks were uplifted, eroded to a plain, and buried again.

Further south, the Nagari Hills dominate Chittoor and Tirupati. Their flat-topped profiles are classic mesas—ultra-hard quartzite on ancient granite bases. Formed 1.5 billion years ago, these peaks were strategic lookout posts during the British Raj and the two World Wars. Today they are spiritual sentinels. The sharpest is Nagari Nose, standing at 2,805 feet and visible within a radius of 70 kilometres.

“Devout families from hundreds of villages surrounding the Nagari hills and neighbouring Tamil Nadu revere the peak and perform pujas atop it on every full moon day,” says Ramanuja Chalapathi, a former government schoolteacher and social activist in Nagari.

Now, mining activity is slowly climbing toward the peak, threatening Nagari Nose and other geological wonders—Three-Rocks-Mound (Moodu Ralla Banda) and Bheemuni Palada rock, he says. “Once a ridge is cut, its original structure can never be restored.”

Similar damage was reported at Nemaligundulu on the Tirupati–Madanapalle highway. Rare breccia and sheared quartzite recording dynamic fault movements from over 1.5 to 1.9 billion years ago were blasted for road material during widening. “When road widening was underway a few years ago, we submitted a memorandum to the officials and senior politicians to preserve Nemaligundlu rocks and divert the road, but no one really cared. An influential political leader even got angry at us, rejecting the geological wonders as mere stones and chips,” said a geology scholar, requesting anonymity.

Another site of interest is Moghili Ghat in Chittoor, which is approximately three billion years old. Prehistoric layers and ancient outcrops were flattened for a highway, illustrating how rapidly modern machinery can obliterate eons of history. “After the destruction of Moghili Ghat, the human–elephant conflict escalated at the tri-state junction. The natural migratory path has been ruthlessly disturbed. Although an elevated express corridor was constructed, the damage is already done,” says a senior forest officer in Chittoor.

In Nandyal, geology and devotion coexist at Yaganti. The historic Uma Maheswara Swamy temple sits among rugged hills with natural cavities. The rocks belong to the Kurnool Group, particularly the tough Banaganapalli quartzite. Quartzite forms when quartz-rich sandstone is deeply buried, compacted, and cemented into an exceptionally hard rock that resists weathering. Joints widen, creating steep escarpments and hollows that characterise Yaganti. Yet uncontrolled construction, drilling, litter, and visitor pressure threaten the fragile structure.

Another site that reflects a different chapter is Belum Caves near Kolimigundla. Unlike exposed cliffs, Belum preserves a subterranean landscape carved by acidic groundwater upon limestone over millions of years. The system was developed in the Narji Limestone of the Kurnool Group. Belum is India’s longest natural cave system. In June 2025, the Geological Survey of India designated it a protected geo-heritage site.

First explored by Robert Bruce Foote in the nineteenth century and later surveyed by a German team in the 1980s, its chambers, Thousand Hoods, Meditation Hall, and Patalaganga amaze visitors. “Unregulated groundwater extraction or artificial illumination altering the cave’s thermal balance can cause irreversible damage to delicate speleothems that took a billion years to form,” says a senior official of the Department of Archaeology.

These ancient geological foundations also gave the region an acidic, iron-rich, and fast-draining soil that most flora cannot tolerate. Yet, nature adapted, transforming Rayalaseema into an evolutionary refuge. The Red Sanders tree, for instance, grows exclusively in the rugged, rocky hills of Kadapa, Tirupati, Chittoor, and Nellore, drawing on the soil’s high mineral content to develop its prized, deep-crimson heartwood.

This harsh terrain also fosters rare, highly specialised fauna. The Golden Gecko, a species of lizard, is restricted to the rocky ravines and quartzite caves of the Seshachalam Hills. Deep within the Siddavaratam range of Kadapa district, the critically endangered, nocturnal Jerdon’s Courser depends entirely on the specific gravelly soil formed by 1.4-billion-year-old rocks. Meanwhile, the elusive Slender Loris finds shelter in the scrub forests draping the boulder-strewn quartzite hills of Sri Venkateswara National Park.

The same Precambrian forces that folded this bedrock also gave birth to the region’s waterfalls. Plunging 270 feet inside SV National Park, Talakona Falls cascades over stepped benches of 1.4-billion-year-old quartzite. At the foot of the Tirumala hills, Kapilatheertham plunges over granitic gneiss and quartzite along an ancient fault line where the hills uplifted over a billion years ago. Kailasakona and Ubbalamadugu (Tada) Falls flow through narrow gorges carved into 1.9-billion-year-old Nagari quartzite—landscapes sculpted long before the arrival of plant life on Earth.

The ultimate testament to this stands at Silathoranam in the Tirumala hills. This striking natural arch, measuring 25 feet wide and 10 feet high, was sculpted from 1.5-billion-year-old quartzite by centuries of wind and rain. Now enclosed within a protective garden by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams, Silathoranam demonstrates how cultural reverence can safeguard irreplaceable natural heritage.

Preserving these geological structures remains a key concern. Geologists believe that one way to strengthen the protection of these structures is by securing UNESCO Global Geopark status for several of these geological wonders. “Such recognition would establish strictly regulated tourist zones, protect the historical integrity of nearby forts, and introduce heritage education tours. It can transform these sites from simple tourist spots into protected world-class geological models,” says Prof. T. Madhu, Head, Geology, Sri Venkateswara University, Tirupati.

“Rayalaseema’s rocks have preserved chapters of Earth’s history that no modern engineering project can recreate once destroyed. Protecting them is not a choice between development and conservation. It is an opportunity to make development more intelligent, tourism more meaningful, and scientific knowledge more accessible,” he adds.

Dr. Peta Srinivasulu Reddy, retired professor of Telugu Studies at SV University and a popular writer of several books on Tirupati and Tirumala, says, “From the mysterious Eparchaean Unconformity to the natural formations of Sleeping Balaji, Standing Garuda, Shiva Linga, and Elephant Trunk in Tirumala hills, the wonders are undeniable. Deepest inheritance lies hidden beneath rugged hills, within caves, and along ancient valleys. Recognising it is the first step. Preserving naturally follows.”

World.title: Deforestation in Brazil's Amazon falls to all-time low
World.content:
Deforestation in Brazil's Amazon rainforest declined to the ​lowest level on record in the 12 months through ⁠July, according to data released by Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday (October 16, 2026).

Some 3,335 square kilometres (1,287.65 square miles) of Amazon jungle were destroyed ‌in the 12 months through July, an all-time low in the historical series that goes back to ‌1988. It was a fall of about 42% from ‌the ⁠preceding period.

The previous lowest level for Brazil's Amazon ⁠deforestation was reached in 2011-2012, when 4,571 square kilometres were destroyed. In the mid-90s, the figure had reached a record high of nearly 30,000 square kilometres ​destroyed a year.

The data ‌released on Friday (October 16, 2026), which is produced yearly by Inpe's PRODES satellite monitoring program, is measured from August to July as there is less cloud cover in the middle of ‌the year to obscure deforestation on satellite images.

"The figures ​released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do ⁠Clima, adding they show the world that "with political will, it is possible to curb deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions."

President Luiz Inacio ‌Lula da Silva took office in 2023 pledging to end deforestation by 2030, after it soared to its highest in 15 years during the administration of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Mr. Lula will face Mr. Bolsonaro's eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, in a presidential election runoff on October 25, after the younger Mr. Bolsonaro performed ‌better than expected in the first round.

The senator pledged in his manifesto ​to strengthen environmental oversight in the Amazon, prioritizing areas under the greatest pressure from deforestation and wildfires. ⁠He said law enforcement would focus on organized crime rather than on extractive ⁠workers and small farmers.

In Brazil's Cerrado savanna, deforestation fell about 24% in the period, to some 5,517 ‌square kilometres, also the lowest on record in a series going back to 2001, Inpe data showed.

World.title: Kumaraswamy cannot tolerate a Dalit like me making political progress: Priyank Kharge
World.content:
Home Minister Priyank Kharge on Sunday (October 18, 2026) accused Union Minister and Janata Dal (Secular) leader H.D. Kumaraswamy of being unable to tolerate the political and social progress of Dalits.

Reacting sharply to Mr. Kumaraswamy’s remarks targeting him, Mr. Kharge said his attire and ability to speak English appeared to have become sources of irritation for the JD(S) leader.

“If my wearing a suit is intolerable to Mr. Kumaraswamy, I will get 10 suits stitched and wear them. If my speaking English is intolerable to him, I will continue speaking English. He can become a film producer and a real estate businessman. However, he cannot tolerate a Dalit like me making political progress,” Mr. Kharge said at a press conference in Kalaburagi.

Responding to Mr. Kumaraswamy’s padayatra, Mr. Kharge alleged that the former Chief Minister had never undertaken such marches in the public interest.

“Let him undertake padayatras and remain healthy. Let him release the evidence relating to the alleged sting operation targeting former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah. Let the people know who was behind it. The needle of suspicion is pointing towards him, which is why he is doing all this,” he said.

Mr. Kharge alleged that Mr. Kumaraswamy had never undertaken a padayatra for farmers or women, nor had he raised issues concerning Karnataka before the Union government. He accused the JD(S) leader of undertaking such activities solely for personal interests.

“A person who has lied to his own family several times and later apologised in the Assembly cannot tell the truth to the people,” he said.

When asked about Mr. Kumaraswamy’s allegation that JD(S) activists were being targeted in the investigation into the alleged sting operation involving Mr. Siddaramaiah, Mr. Kharge said the police could not be expected to halt their investigation merely because the suspects were JD(S) activists.

“Should the police refrain from issuing notices and summoning suspects for questioning just because they are JD(S) activists? Mr. Kumaraswamy insists that the police should investigate the matter. But when they begin the investigation, he accuses them of targeting his party activists. The police conduct their investigation impartially and do not function according to the way Mr. Kumaraswamy wants them to,” Mr. Kharge said.

Reacting to Mr. Kumaraswamy’s objection to Mr. Kharge and his father, AICC president Mallikarjun Kharge, contesting elections from constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes, the Home Minister questioned whether society was mature enough to elect Dalit candidates from general constituencies.

“President Droupadi Murmu was not allowed into a temple because she was a tribal woman. A purification ritual was conducted at a place in Uttarakhand after Congress president and Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge, a Dalit leader, addressed a public meeting. This is the mindset of our society which forces Dalits to contest elections from the constituencies reserved for them,” he said.

MLC Jagadev Guttedar, GESCOM chairman Praveen Patil Harwal, District Congress Committee president Kiran Deshmukh and other Congress leaders were present.

World.title: Karnataka brings government employees’ services under Sakala Act; hefty fines for delays and malicious complaints
World.content:
In a major administrative reform, the State government has issued a notification bringing a wide array of personnel and service-related requests of government employees under the ambit of the Karnataka Sakala Services Act, 2011. Concurrently, under the Karnataka Sakala Services (Amendment) Act, 2026, the government has revised financial penalties for defaulting officials as well as citizens filing frivolous or malicious grievances.

Following recommendations from the seventh report of the Administrative Reforms Commission-2, time-bound delivery of internal staff services has been extended across all field-level departments and organisations. The notification issued by Harsha Gupta, Principal Secretary of the Praja Seva Department, stated that strict timelines have been fixed to ensure public service delivery is transparent, efficient, and accountable.

Prescribed timelines for civil services

Under the notification, the disbursement of salary and issuance of salary certificates must be completed within three working days, while Form-16 issuance is set at five working days. A seven-working-day deadline applies to higher study permissions, festival advances, permission to draw first salary, and the routing of applications for KGID, GIS, and GPF. Sanctioning leave, charge allowances, and issuing No Objection Certificates (NOC) for passports must be settled within 10 working days.

A 15-working-day limit has been stipulated for processing time-bound pay advancements, annual increments, Last Pay Certificates (LPC), leave salary, vehicle and house construction advances, foreign trip permissions, and copies of service books. A 30-working-day timeline applies to medical reimbursement claims, forwarding pension and gratuity proposals to the Accountant General (AG), General Provident Fund (GPF) advances, Travelling Allowance (TA) sanctions, property or vehicle transaction approvals, probation declarations, and senior pay scale sanctions. The longest timeline of 90 working days has been allocated for compassionate appointments, pay arrears, and disability allowances.

Nodal officers from newly included departments must submit designated officer lists to the Sakala Mission within 15 days, while a uniform 35-working-day limit has been set for competent authorities to dispose of first and second appeals under the Act, the notification stated.

Revised penalties for officials and citizens

Under the amended provisions, officials who fail to deliver services or dispose of appeals within the stipulated timeframe will face financial penalties deducted directly from their salaries and awarded as compensation to the applicant. The penalty slab begins at ₹20 per day for the first one to five days of delay (capped at ₹100) and scales up to ₹100 per day for delays between 21 and 25 days, with a maximum cumulative penalty of ₹1,500. Additionally, for deficient service or wrongful rejection of applications without valid grounds, a penalty of up to ₹1,500 will be recovered from the responsible officer, according to the notification.

To curb misuse of the grievance mechanism, the amendment empowers authorities to penalise citizens who file false or malicious complaints intended to harass or intimidate government personnel. If an inquiry confirms a complaint was filed with ulterior motives, the applicant will be fined ₹1,500 per application, with repeat offenses attracting an additional fine of ₹1,500 per instance, recoverable as arrears of land revenue.

World.title: Laddu prasadam in high demand at Vijayawada’s Indrakeeladri during Dasara Navaratri
World.content:
Officials of the Sri Durga Malleswara Swamy Varla Devasthanam on Indrakeeladri in Vijayawada have sold about 4.5 lakh laddu prasadams in just two days.

Laddu is one of the prasadams in good demand during the Dasara Navaratri Utsavams. The temple authorities are also selling ‘pulihora’, ‘chakkara pongali’ and other prasadams to devotees.

“Laddu prasadam is prepared with ghee and dry fruits, and is having good taste. We purchased about 15 laddus for distributing the same to our family members and neighbours,” a devotee, Shiva Narayana of Chintalapudi, said.

Temple officials said about 2.5 lakh laddus were sold on Friday (October 16, 2026), Moola Nakshatram day, the birth star of Goddess Saraswati Devi.

“On Saturday (October 17, 2026), nearly 2 lakh laddu prasadams have been sold on the seventh day of the Navarathri Utsavams,” a temple official told The Hindu.

A heavy rush was seen at the laddu ATM, which was launched recently. The Endowments Department has also arranged prasadam-selling counters at different locations in and around Indrakeeladri.

“We are getting laddu prasadam in just a few seconds after paying the amount online in the ATM. Each devotee can take two laddus,” a devotee, Srivalli of Kondapalli, said.

A heavy rush was seen at the prasadam counters. Devotees were asking for ‘chakkara pongali’, ‘pulihora’ and ‘laddu prasadam’, the temple staff said.

World.title: 8 India-sponsored terrorists killed in Quetta, Khuzdar, Nushki districts: ISPR
World.content:
Security forces have killed eight “India-sponsored” terrorists during three intelligence-based operations conducted in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Sunday.

The IBOs took place on Oct 17 (Saturday) on the “reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxy Fitna al Hindustan”, the military’s media affairs wing said in its press release.

The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan.

In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists’ attempt to establish a roadblock to disrupt local traffic was “intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five India-sponsored terrorists”.

Separately, during a sanitisation operation in Nushki district, security forces busted a terrorist hideout and “after an intense fire exchange, two India-sponsored terrorists were sent to hell”. Weapons and ammunition were also recovered, ISPR added.

In another IBO in Khuzdar, a terrorist hideout was “engaged by security forces through prompt offensive action”, killing one terrorist. ISPR said a large quantity of explosives (490 kilogrammes) was also recovered.

Sanitisation operations were being conducted to eliminate any other terrorist found in the area, according to the statement.

ISPR reaffirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign under Vision ‘Azm-i-Istehkam’ (as approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”.

President Asif Ali Zardari, in a statement, paid tribute to the security forces for eliminating eight terrorists.

He also commended their professional capabilities for thwarting the attempt to disrupt traffic in Quetta, as well as their actions in Nushki and Khuzdar.

“Conspiracies of the terrorists’ foreign patrons and their local facilitators will be foiled,” President Zardari declared.

Intensified operations

Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, prompting security forces to intensify counterterrorism operations.

On the night of Oct 12/13, security forces busted a terrorist hideout and killed five terrorists during an IBO in Washuk, ISPR said.

Days later, Balochistan government officials said that six terrorists affiliated with the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), two would-be female suicide bombers, and two commanders of a banned organisation had been arrested during IBOs across the province.

They said around 90 arrested terrorists were being held at a centre where investigations and legal proceedings were under way.

Earlier this month, five terrorists were eliminated in Balochistan’s Mastung district, state media reported.

The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August, according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). As per the report, Balochistan was declared the province “most affected” by terrorism.

World.title: Saudi-led coalition says 2 pilots killed in helicopter crash near Yemen
World.content:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Sunday said two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed near the Yemen border, after the group claimed it shot the aircraft down.

The coalition blamed a “technical malfunction” for the incident, which inflicted its first military fatalities since the long-running conflict with the Houthis reignited in July.

The incident comes a week after strikes by the Houthis killed 13 people at Riyadh’s international airport, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

“An AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter belonging to the Ministry of National Guard crashed inside Saudi territory in Najran Region due to a technical malfunction,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said, according to the official Saudi Press Agency.

“The accident resulted in the martyrdom of its aircrew, consisting of two officers.”

Late on Saturday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the group had “downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy” in the same area.

After an uneasy, four-year truce, Yemen’s conflict has surged back to life and intensified when the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea, oil facilities and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.

The Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government has launched repeated air raids on Houthi territory.

The coalition said overnight that it intercepted two drones in the Riyadh area and a third over the oil-rich Eastern Province. Saudi authorities had earlier issued a threat alert in the capital.

Two ballistic missiles “launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Khamis Mushait” were intercepted in the kingdom’s south, the coalition added.

On Saturday, the Houthis reported that Saudi strikes killed 12 people in Yemen, including three children.

The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz.

On Sunday, Egypt’s parliament will hold an emergency session after President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi asked lawmakers to authorise support to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks.

Sisi said he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it. “I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said on Saturday. “We are speaking only about defence.”

World.title: First Pakistani astronaut to undertake space mission from China on Nov 25: Ahsan Iqbal
World.content:
Pakistan’s first astronaut will undertake a space mission from a Chinese space centre on November 25, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday.

The minister made the announcement while addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week in Narowal, held in collaboration with the Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco), the planning ministry said in a statement.

According to the handout, the planning minister also said the country was aiming to achieve a lunar landing by 2035, expressing hope that Pakistan’s cooperation with China would help it “reach new heights in space exploration”.

In his address at the ceremony, the planning minister highlighted the importance of space technology in agriculture, communications, climate monitoring, education and national security.

Iqbal stressed that scientific research and space exploration were essential for technological advancement, the ministry’s statement said.

He further noted that Muslim scholars had once made significant contributions to astronomy and scientific discovery, calling for renewed efforts to restore Pakistan’s leadership in knowledge and research.

The astronaut will be one of the two — pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khur­ram Daud— China selected in April this year as candidates for its manned space programme and who have been undergoing intensive training in Beijing.

China has not said which of the two will fly or when, but speaking to Reuters last month, Amer Gilani, who oversees human spaceflight cooperation at Suparco, said a final astronaut selection decision was expected in mid-to-late October.

According to another Suparco official quoted by Reuters, once in space, the chosen pilot will carry the title of “payload specialist”, which is astronaut-speak for someone whose job in orbit is running Pakis­tan’s science experiments rather than flying the ship.

The astronaut will fly aboard a Chinese-built spacecraft, launched from a Chinese site, trained by Chinese instructors and communicating in Mandarin in orbit.

World.title: One in three adults in Pakistan lives with psychological disorder: study
World.content:
KARACHI: Pakistan’s first nationally representative mental health survey has shown that nearly one in three adults is living with a diagnosable mental and behavioural disorder, highlighting a major public health challenge affecting millions of people across the country.

The findings come from the largest and most comprehensive mental health study ever conducted in Pakistan, say researchers representing the Pakistan Psychiatric Society (PPS).

The five-year research is published in the British Medical Journal.

The survey was led by Professor Raza-ur-Rahman from Hamdard University, Karachi, in collaboration with Brighton and Sussex Medical School UK, University of South Florida, US, and psychiatric institutions across Pakistan.

Experts term findings of first national mental health survey ‘most reliable’

Nearly 18,000 adults from all four provinces participated in the 2018-2022 study, providing the first nationally representative picture of mental health in the country.

Key findings

The study found that 32 per cent of adults were currently living with mental and behavioural disorders, while 38 per cent had experienced a disorder during their lifetime.

One in five adults met criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). More than one in 10 adults had depression, whereas six per cent reported suicidal thoughts in the previous month.

Researchers also identified significant social inequalities in mental health. Higher rates of mental disorders were found among older adults, individuals with lower levels of education and income, unemployed people, and those who were widowed, divorced or separated.

Mental health problems were associated with substantial impairment in family life, social relationships and the ability to work.

“This survey provides the evidence needed to develop effective mental health policies and services in Pakistan. It identifies who is most at risk, where support is most needed, and the scale of the unmet need for care,” said lead investigator Prof Raza-ur-Rahman, currently heading the department of psychiatry at HU.

According to him, the researchers used international standard tools to carry out the survey and the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics identified the areas for survey and provided the sample size.

He hoped that it would contribute to reducing stigma and improving access to diagnosis and treatment for millions of people.

“For the first time, policymakers, healthcare planners and researchers now have reliable national data that can be used to strengthen mental health services, allocate resources more effectively and develop evidence-based programmes across the country,” he added.

The study represents a major milestone for mental health research in Pakistan and demonstrates the country’s growing capacity to undertake large-scale, internationally recognised public health research.

Prof Anjum Memon, Chair in Epidemiology and Public Health Medicine at Brighton and Sussex Medical School (UK) and the senior co-author of the study, said: “This is a landmark moment for mental health research in Pakistan. For decades, policymakers have had to rely on fragmented local studies or international estimates. We now have robust national evidence showing, for the first time, the true scale of mental and behavioural disorders across the country.”

These findings provide an invaluable evidence base for policymakers, clinicians and healthcare planners, not only in Pakistan but also in other low- and middle-income countries facing similar challenges, he added.

Mental health, researchers say, is increasingly recognised as an essential component of national health and economic development and they recommend greater integration of mental health services into primary healthcare, increased investment in community-based support systems, enhanced training for frontline health workers and sustained national efforts to reduce the stigma surrounding mental illness.

“Pakistan currently faces major challenges in the provision of mental healthcare, including limited specialist services and a shortage of trained mental health professionals. The survey findings will help inform future policy development, service planning, workforce training and community-based support programmes,” said President of PPS Prof Wajid Akhundzada.

Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026

World.title: Saad Baig handed debut as Sri Lanka win toss, bowl first in ODI tri-series opener against Pakistan
World.content:
Wicket-keeper-batter Saad Baig was handed his Pakistan debut as Sri Lanka won the toss and opted to bowl first in the One-day International tri-series opener against the hosts at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Sunday.

Former under-19 captain Saad has stayed in and out of Pakistan contention over the last couple of years especially after hitting 1000 runs in the 2025-26 season of the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy — the countries premier first-class competition.

The left-hander is picked over fellow wicket-keeper Ghazi Ghori, who had his ODI and Test debuts earlier this year.

Meanwhile, all-rounder Shadab Khan and spinner Sufyan Moqim were ruled out of the first match due to illness, the Pakistan Cricket Board said.

“Both the players are receiving treatment under the supervision of team’s medical staff,” read an update by the PCB.

“Their progress will be monitored and they will be considered for selection in the upcoming matches owing to their recovery.”

The tri-series marks the commencement of Pakistan’s final phase of preparation for next year’s 50-over World Cup, with the side looking to end its nine-year International Cricket Council trophy drought.

Under Shaheen, Pakistan’s ODI side has spent the past year rebuilding, winning all their home series in the process.

Those assignments were played on slower surfaces, with spin-friendly pitches used most recently during the series against Australia in May and June.

The conditions for the tri-series, however, are expected to offer a different challenge, with pitches being prepared to better resemble those in South Africa.

The surfaces appeared greener during Pakistan’s recent T20I series against Sri Lanka, and Shaheen confirmed that there had been a deliberate effort to encourage lateral movement and bounce.

“Over the course of the last four one-day series, we have tried to build this team, since our focus is on [next year’s] World Cup and how we can prepare for it,” he said. “Henceforth we have also tried to prepare the wickets accordingly.”

Fellow senior pros Fakhar Zaman and Naseem Shah have also spoken over the past week on how the World Cup will remain on the back of the minds of the Pakistan players.

“We know it’s been quite a while since we’ve won a major tournament,” Fakhar had said.

“We’ve reached finals and played in semi-finals, too.

“But, obviously, the happiness you feel as a nation when you win a trophy is something you don’t get simply by reaching finals or semi-finals, no matter how many you play.

“We’ve sat down and discussed this at length, and many of the players are taking it very seriously. God willing, we’ll give it our best, and we hope for Allah’s help as well. We’ll make every effort to bring this trophy back to Pakistan.”

Teams:

PAKISTAN: Saim Ayub, Fakhar Zaman, Babar Azam, Saad Baig (wicket-keeper), Hasan Nawaz, Salman Ali Agha, Arafat Minhas, Faheem Ashraf 9 Shaheen Shah Afridi (captain), Haris Rauf, Naseem Shah

SRI LANKA: Avishka Fernando, Kamindu Mendis, Kusal Mendis (captain/wicket-keeper), Pavan Rathnayake, Sahan Arachchige, Janith Liyanage, Dasun Shanaka, Sachindu Colombage, Eshan Malinga, Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka

World.title: 'Serious incident' at Canada base causes deaths, sparks fire: govt
World.content:
Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said late on Saturday there were “fatalities and injuries” following an incident at a military base in western Canada.

“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” identified as Wainwright in Alberta, McGuinty said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney had posted to X earlier on Saturday that “a serious incident creating a major fire” had occurred at the base.

Neither offered details on the number of casualties or the nature of the incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

“We will have more to say in the coming hours and days,” McGuinty said.

CFB Wainwright is one of the busiest Army bases in Canada.

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, about 200 km northwest of the base, told public broadcaster CBC that Wainwright’s health-care facilities were “completely overwhelmed” by the number of patients requiring care.

“It is more patients than any of us want to count right now,” Warren Thirsk said. “It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.”

The Municipal District of Wainwright posted on social media that the fire had “spread rapidly due to high winds.”

It said later on Saturday that the blaze was “being held at this time,” though firefighting crews would continue to monitor the area.

Carney said the government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities.

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said on X.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on a future poll on whether Alberta wants independence from Canada. Alberta’s office responsible for overseeing provincial elections said the advance voting station in Wainwright had closed.

World.title: Digging in Karachi for Red Line damages gas pipeline, disrupts supply
World.content:
KARACHI: Gas supply to several areas of the metropolis was suspended during lunch hours on Saturday after a high-pressure pipeline was damaged during excavation work for the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Red Line on University Road, adding to the miseries of residents in the affected areas.

The disruption affected Gulshan-i-Iqbal, areas around Mazar-i-Quaid, parts of Garden, Saddar, Burns Road and several other localities.

A spokesperson for the Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) said that the high-pressure pipeline near the Gulshan-i-Iqbal telephone exchange on University Road was damaged at around 1pm during BRT construction activity.

She said teams immediately reached the site and started repair work, which was completed by 5pm. “After completion of the work, gas supply was restored,” she said.

Residents in the affected areas said the sudden suspension caused considerable inconvenience, particularly during cooking hours.

Several households reported disruption in preparing afternoon meals, while commercial eateries and roadside hotels in Saddar and Garden saw a rush of customers as many people had no option but to dine out or take food home for their families.

Domestic consumers complained that low pressure persisted even after the announced restoration time.

Many families said they had to arrange food from nearby restaurants. “We had guests at home and the gas suddenly disappeared. We had to order biryani from a nearby hotel, which cost us extra besides causing embarrassment,” said Rozina Adnan, a resident of Saddar.

Another resident from Garden said his wife could not cook and they had to bring food from a restaurant for the children.

Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026

World.title: Out-of-control truck kills 13 at religious festival in India's Madhya Pradesh
World.content:
A speeding truck in India killed 13 people when it ploughed into a crowd at a Hindu festival, officials said on Sunday, with President Droupadi Murmu describing the deaths as “heartbreaking”.

The heavily loaded truck reportedly lost control in the early hours of Sunday and hit devotees gathered at a temple in Gwalior, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh.

The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency cited hospital officials as saying 13 people had died.

“I express my deepest condolences to the bereaved families and pray for the swift recovery of those injured,” Murmu said on social media.

The Indian Vice President C.P. Radhakrishnan expressed sorrow at the loss of life.

“Deeply saddened by the tragic loss of lives in the accident involving devotees in Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh. My heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families. I wish a speedy recovery to all those injured,” he wrote in a post on X.

The incident comes a day after at least 17 people were killed and two dozen more injured on Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that was likely caused by sudden rainfall during a Hindu religious gathering, officials said.

India, with 1.4 billion people, recorded more than 183,000 road traffic deaths in 2025, or over 500 a day, according to the roads ministry.

Many are linked to inadequate road infrastructure, ill-maintained vehicles and exhausted drivers, according to official data.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
