However, obtaining IDP status and applying for state-provided housing are two different things. A child’s IDP status does not automatically mean that the state must provide them with housing.

When allocating housing, the state considers people born before 1 January 2023. Those who were minors on that date count as members of their family when the authorities allocate housing to their parents or other adult relatives. In other words, the state takes children into account when determining the size and other parameters of the family’s accommodation, but they cannot claim a separate flat once they reach adulthood.

As a rule, the state’s obligation to provide housing does not extend to children born on or after 1 January 2023. There is one exception: if an IDP parent or parents die before receiving housing, the child becomes entitled to the accommodation that the state would have provided to their parent or parents.

Why is the programme facing criticism?

One of the main criticisms concerns property prices. Critics question whether families forced to leave their homes can afford to buy another property with the proposed payment, particularly if they have no savings.

The Social Justice Center has issued a statement on the financial compensation scheme for displaced people. The organisation warns that the initiative could leave families without housing or savings facing homelessness and social exclusion.

The Social Justice Center points out that the government has not explained how it calculated the 10,000-lari payment. It also remains unclear whether the authorities based the figure on any property market research. The organisation further stresses that even several tens of thousands of lari — the amount a large family might receive — may not be enough.

The organisation is also seeking clarification on whether families must use the money specifically to buy a home, and what support, if any, they can expect if they cannot afford one.

This question is particularly important because the official order defines the compensation as a form of “long-term resettlement”, implying that the payment comes in exchange for housing. The organisation is urging the authorities to explain the programme’s legal consequences in advance and guarantee continued support for families.

How many families are still waiting for housing?

According to the Public Defender’s report, Georgia had 300,492 internally displaced people and 97,280 displaced families at the end of 2025. Of these, 45,160 families had yet to receive long-term housing. Georgia

In 2025, various programmes resettled 4,636 families. The report continues to highlight delays in construction, insufficient funding for temporary rental accommodation and safety concerns over some residential buildings.

“You can buy a sofa for 10,000 lari, but not a flat”

“You can buy a sofa for 10,000 lari, but not a flat,” Koka Markelia, 26, tells JAMnews. His parents were displaced from Abkhazia.

Koka works as a programmer. He finished school in Zugdidi but could not find a job there, so he stayed in Tbilisi. He has been renting a flat with his parents for more than ten years.

He wants to get married and move out on his own. He says he has a stable job, but under the current rules, the bank will not approve a mortgage.

Everyone in the family works, although his parents are self-employed: his mother works as a nanny, and his father is a mechanic. Only Koka has an official income, so the bank will not grant the family a loan. He says 10,000 lari would not even cover the deposit required for a mortgage. As a result, he will not receive the compensation.

“How much do we pay in rent? If they had offered us a flat with a mortgage, we would already have our own home. What am I supposed to do with these 10,000 lari? What can I buy with that money? I would take it and spend it on little things because I could not do anything meaningful with it. So it is better not to accept the money; otherwise, I would lose the prospect of getting a flat one day,” Koka says.

We checked two popular property websites but could not find a house for 10,000 lari, either in Tbilisi or in the regions.

In Koka Markelia’s home town of Zugdidi, for example, we found just one house listed for 10,000 lari — and it is due for demolition. Even if the Markelia family pooled all its money, it could not buy a house in Zugdidi for 30,000 lari.

“We cannot even buy a house in Zugdidi for that amount. And even if we could, how would we move there? Would we find work? If I worked as a nanny there, I would earn less than a third of what I make now,” says Koka’s mother, Irma.

The government’s initiative has sparked sarcastic jokes online.

“I’m sitting here wondering whether to buy two flats with these 10,000 lari or compete with Coca-Cola,” Gela Khasaia, an activist displaced from Abkhazia who also rents a flat in Tbilisi, wrote on Facebook.

Why is resettlement taking decades?

The government laid the foundations for its long-term housing policy in a national strategy approved in 2007. In 2009, it also adopted an action plan to implement the strategy.

The process got off to a painful start, marked by serious disputes and human rights violations. A 2011 study by Amnesty International documented cases of forced evictions from temporary accommodation in Tbilisi, a lack of proper consultation with residents and difficulties finding sources of income after relocation.

At the time, the authorities offered people displaced from Abkhazia who lived in Tbilisi housing in other regions, prompting widespread protests. The main challenge of relocating to the regions was the loss of income and familiar social networks. Although families received renovated flats, they often found themselves in areas with few job opportunities and limited access to basic services.

Under the Georgian Dream government, the resettlement process has continued through several schemes: providing flats in newly built or renovated buildings, purchasing private houses and formally transferring ownership of homes that displaced people already occupy. According to the Public Defender’s report, 4,636 families received long-term housing in 2025, compared with 2,022 in 2024. Nevertheless, 45,160 families were still waiting for housing at the end of 2025.

The process continues to face construction delays and inadequate housing conditions. The Public Defender’s 2025 report notes that the 300-lari allowance for temporary rent does not cover displaced people’s needs. Concerns also remain over the safety of some buildings that the authorities have already transferred to families.

Georgia’s housing programme for displaced people

World.title: Russia seeks to retain Armenian railway concession as Yerevan avoids confrontation
World.content:
Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

“Armenia is not fixated on taking the concession away from Russia. The issue is ensuring that the railway operates to an adequate standard,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in response to a question about whether the authorities might strip South Caucasus Railway of its rights to operate Armenia’s railway network.

Since 2008, South Caucasus Railway has operated Armenia’s railways under a concession agreement. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession runs for 30 years. Since the Russian company took over, freight traffic has halved, some routes have ceased operating, and the company has yet to deliver on its mandatory investment commitments.

Pashinyan said Western companies were ready to invest, but they saw the existing Russian concession as an obstacle. Russia, meanwhile, considers further investment “economically unviable”.

“We say: fine, if it is economically unviable, then sell or transfer the concession rights to those who consider it viable. Alternatively, we will find ways to solve our problems ourselves,” the prime minister told journalists.

Pashinyan also said he had agreed with Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov to set up a joint working group. The group will have three months to answer all the Armenian government’s questions, including whether the Russian side is willing to invest in developing Armenia’s railway network. Yerevan will decide on its next steps only after that.

The prime minister believes the scale of any potential Russian investment could put an end to all “political debate”. In particular, he was referring to concerns that Western countries might refuse to use a railway network under Russian control.

“If Russia, for example, says, ‘I will invest $3 billion’, that means it has no concerns that the countries we mentioned might choose alternative routes. It would mean Russia is confident that these countries will use these railway lines and that its investment will pay off,” he stressed.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan told JAMnews that Yerevan’s concerns had political rather than economic or investment-related roots from the outset.

For some time, people have been saying that international partners are unwilling to use a railway network under a Russian concession. This, in turn, prevents Armenia from becoming a transit country. Meliksetyan believes Armenia has “made concessions” compared with its original position.

“By deciding to set up a working group, Armenia is trying to postpone the serious and painful consequences that could follow if Russia decides to use its leverage,” he said.

The political analyst recalled that Moscow had hinted at a possible increase in gas prices and was already applying economic pressure by banning Armenian exports.

In the expert’s view, the creation of an Armenian-Russian working group effectively turns the concession dispute into a “negotiation process”.

“Three months from now, another issue could emerge and take a further three months to discuss. The problem would remain unresolved, but this approach would help avoid further deterioration in relations with Russia,” he said.

Pashinyan: “We have no problem with the Russian concession”

The prime minister recalled discussions with the Russian side in April 2026. At the time, Russian partners said investment in Armenia’s railways was economically unviable and that investment from other countries would be unacceptable.

“During the blockade, we might have said, ‘Fine, we’ll manage somehow.’ But now, as the region opens up, we cannot accept leaving our railway in its current condition. It needs investment, and we are talking about substantial sums,” he said.

Pashinyan stressed that investment was essential if Armenia’s railway network was to compete with the Kars–Dilucu line that Turkey is building. At the same time, he noted that competition might not even become an issue, given the expected growth in freight traffic across the region.

Speaking about his talks with Belozerov, Pashinyan said he had made it clear to his Russian counterpart that Armenia did not object to Russian management under the concession agreement. However, Yerevan expected the railway to become competitive.

“Our analysis of how to achieve this goal shows that a change in the concession management model would be a rational approach, particularly by involving third countries in the process,” the prime minister said.

He added that Russian partners could put forward their own proposals if they knew how to resolve the issue.

Moscow has yet to offer any concrete solutions. However, Russian partners assured Armenia that sanctions would not obstruct railway operations.

Nikol Pashinyan outlined the strategic priorities that the Armenian government expects to address now that the region anticipates the reopening of all borders:

Reopening the Ijevan–Hrazdan railway section;

Building a facility in Akhurik to change wheelsets, as Turkish railways use a different track gauge;

Connecting the Ijevan–Hrazdan railway line to the Vanadzor–Gyumri line.

“We understand that this is an extremely difficult task, both in terms of investment and from a technical and organisational perspective. But we cannot simply say, ‘You know, there are difficulties, so we will not pursue this.’ We will approach our friends in the most friendly manner possible, but these issues must be resolved,” he stressed.

What Armenia’s prime minister and the head of Russian Railways discussed

The previous day, Pashinyan received a delegation led by Russian Railways CEO Oleg Belozerov.

According to the Armenian prime minister’s office, Pashinyan stressed that his government aims to integrate Armenia’s railway network with those of neighbouring countries. The meeting covered:

Opportunities arising from regional developments;

Measures to improve the competitiveness of Armenia’s railways and integrate them into international transport routes;

Railway reconstruction projects, particularly the Gyumri–Akhurik–Turkish border line and the Yeraskh–Nakhchivan line, as well as the opportunities these projects would create;

Infrastructure development carried out by South Caucasus Railway under the concession agreement;

Management efficiency, existing problems and possible solutions.

Comment

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Russia proposed setting up an Armenian-Russian working group on the railway issue to delay the process and buy time.

In his view, Russia intends to maintain its presence in Armenia’s railway network. He explains that Moscow wants to take advantage of the expected reopening of regional transport links and secure a political role in the process.

“This matters to Russia economically, in terms of its image and in terms of its geopolitical presence in Armenia. Moscow does not want to lose a very important lever of influence as the region’s transport links reopen.”

Meliksetyan believes the Armenian authorities are trying to act constructively and avoid escalating tensions with Russia. In this context, he recalled the “instruments of blackmail” that Russia openly uses.

At the same time, the political analyst does not rule out the possibility of Russian investment in Armenia’s railways.

“The scale of this investment would not pose a significant problem for Russia. We are talking about just tens of millions of dollars. Even amid Russia’s current crisis, that is a very small sum. Its daily military spending runs into billions of dollars.”

According to Meliksetyan, three months of work by the Armenian working group are unlikely to persuade Russia to relinquish the concession.

“Formal decisions or partial amendments to the concession agreement in Armenia’s favour are possible. However, this is a political issue. In the near future, I do not see a political solution that would not lead to a further deterioration in Armenian-Russian relations.”

Russia seeks to keep Armenia railway concession

World.title: Fidan says ‘everything is fine’ in Baku, but relations remain strained
World.content:
Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

Turkey’s Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan arrived in Baku on the evening of 14 October. The official reason for his visit was the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA), where Fidan represented Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. However, the visit came amid worsening relations between the two countries in recent weeks, putting every detail under close scrutiny.

Azerbaijan’s Youth and Sports Minister Farid Gayibov greeted Fidan at Heydar Aliyev International Airport. The decision to assign him to welcome the Turkish foreign minister prompted mixed reactions on social media in both Azerbaijan and Turkey. On 15 October, Fidan met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Later that day, during the summit, he left the hall along with representatives of several other delegations when Israeli President Isaac Herzog began his speech.

After his meeting with Aliyev, Fidan said relations between the two countries remained strong and unbreakable. However, his remarks also acknowledged that disagreements existed between Baku and Ankara.

One of the main factors behind the deterioration in relations has been the de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools. JAMnews examined the issue in detail in an earlier article. This time, however, the focus is on a different question:

What is happening in relations between Baku and Ankara, and how serious is the growing chill between them?

Fidan’s message: “There are disagreements, but…”

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan at a dinner hosted by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Baku to mark the seventh CICA summit. Photo: president.az

Speaking to journalists in Baku, Fidan said relations between the two countries had stood the test of wars and crises, while their leaders shared an “unbreakable friendship and brotherhood”. He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had given him special instructions before the trip.

At the same time, the minister openly acknowledged that the two countries might hold different positions on certain issues. Fidan stressed that neither side should allow these disagreements to damage their strategic relationship:

“We are a people with an ancient history. We must resolve our problems as befits a people with such a past: by sitting down at the negotiating table and discussing them in a civilised manner.”

The minister also said the two sides should not turn their differences into a propaganda tool on social media. He said his conversation with Aliyev had followed this approach, with the Turkish side hearing the Azerbaijani president’s position and his assessment of the situation.

Fidan did not explicitly mention the hijab issue, Israel or Aliyev’s speech on 2 October. However, his references to “our problems”, “differences in approach” and the “use of disagreements” suggest that Ankara acknowledges the existence of tensions but prefers to address them through diplomatic channels rather than in public.

Meanwhile, photographs from the visit attracted the most attention on social media. Some users analysed Fidan’s body language, noting that he appeared relaxed both at the airport and during his meeting with the president, as though relations between the two countries faced no problems. Although such assessments are subjective, they show how closely the public watches every gesture by representatives of Baku and Ankara.

However, the most notable moment of the visit came during Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech. At the summit in Baku, Fidan refused to listen to Herzog and left the hall. Just a month earlier, the decision by an Azerbaijani representative to remain in the hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech at the UN General Assembly had drawn sharp criticism in Turkey.

What triggered the tensions?

A series of events over the past three weeks has heightened tensions between Baku and Ankara:

23 September — Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”.

— Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Erdoğan described bans on headscarves in schools in “some countries” as an infringement of women’s rights. During the same session, Azerbaijan’s representative remained in the hall while Netanyahu delivered a speech in which he called Erdoğan a “tyrant”. 2 October — Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews).

— Speaking at a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Aliyev said, without naming anyone in particular, that everyone should “know their place” and that nobody had the right to interfere in the Azerbaijani people’s way of life. He stressed that Azerbaijan had achieved its military victories without foreign patronage and had bought weapons with its own money (JAMnews). 9–12 October — Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews).

— Azerbaijani schools began inspections during which officials barred female pupils and teachers wearing hijabs from attending classes. The measures sparked protests and led to the detention of 37 people (JAMnews). 12 October — Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement.

— Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral called on Azerbaijan to “correct this mistake” as soon as possible. Leyla Şahin Usta, deputy chair of the parliamentary group of the Justice and Development Party (AKP), made a similar statement. 13 October — YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan).

— YAP’s press service criticised Saral and AKP MPs, naming them individually. Its statement called on the AKP to abandon its “harmful policy” and also referred to “hegemonic ambitions” (Yeni Azerbaijan). 14–15 October — Fidan arrived in Baku and met Aliyev.

Against this backdrop, AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik limited his response to saying that the two countries’ leaders shared a “genuinely brotherly relationship”.

Why relations are cooling: Israel, Russia and claims to the role of “big brother”

All the experts JAMnews interviewed before Fidan’s visit believe the hijab issue represents just one manifestation of deeper problems in relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey.

“The need to choose between two rivals”

Araz Aliyev | Photo: Third Republic Platform

Politician Araz Aliyev, one of the founders of the Third Republic Platform, told JAMnews that he linked the current tensions to Azerbaijan’s foreign policy.

In his view, Baku has begun to see itself as “a major geopolitical player”. However, unlike the US or China, Azerbaijan lacks the capacity to maintain close relations with two rival states at the same time:

“Over the next ten years, Turkey and Israel will be the two main rivals in the Middle East. At the same time, Azerbaijan is a strategic ally of both countries. When Netanyahu speaks, the Turkish delegation leaves the hall, while the Azerbaijani delegation cannot do the same, even if it wants to. Israel also invests in Azerbaijan and supports it. Naturally, this causes resentment in Turkey.”

Araz Aliyev notes that Azerbaijan first felt the negative consequences of its “multi-vector policy” after it backed Pakistan in its confrontation with India. According to the politician, India blocked Azerbaijan’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, while trade between the two countries — worth as much as $2 billion — suffered a setback.

Aliyev identifies Russia as a second factor. In his view, Baku has been pursuing closer relations with Moscow since August. He sees the resolution of disagreements over the crash of an AZAL aircraft as one sign of this rapprochement. Historically, he notes, closer ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have gone hand in hand with a degree of distancing from Turkey.

Araz Aliyev also links these changes to the domestic political situation in the US. In his view, Baku’s foreign policy strategy, which has largely relied on Donald Trump’s administration, could come under threat if Republicans lose the US midterm elections in November. The politician believes concerns about this scenario are pushing the Azerbaijani authorities to seek alternative foreign policy partners.

“I don’t depend on you”

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu | Photo: Grand National Assembly of Turkey

Ömer Faruk Gergerlioğlu, a member of Turkey’s parliament representing Kocaeli province and the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), told JAMnews that he sees Aliyev’s 2 October speech as a rejection of Turkey’s claim to the role of “big brother”.

“Turkey has always seen itself as the big brother of Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan. Aliyev, however, disagrees. His message is: I don’t depend on you; I need you only as much as you need me. We have mutual interests, but ours is not a relationship between an older and a younger brother.”

In the MP’s view, Baku sees cooperation with Israel as a “lifeline” that helps it preserve its authoritarian system of government, and it has no intention of making concessions on this issue.

Gergerlioğlu also points to what he sees as contradictions in Erdoğan’s position. The Turkish president sharply criticises Israel but turns a blind eye to oil shipments from the Turkish port of Ceyhan to Israel. The oil reaches the port through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The MP claims he has repeatedly presented the government with documentary evidence of these shipments.

“If tensions between Turkey and Israel escalate, I think Aliyev will openly side with Israel. For him, the principle of ‘one nation, two states’ takes a back seat. He views the world primarily through the lens of preserving his own power.”

Against this backdrop, Fidan’s decision to walk out rather than listen to Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s speech in Baku takes on particular significance. This time, Ankara demonstrated its differences with Azerbaijan over Israel directly in the Azerbaijani capital.

Growing discontent in Turkish society

Джавид Ага | Фото: личный архив

Journalist and analyst Javid Agha notes that discontent with Azerbaijan in Turkish society extends beyond the hijab issue.

According to him, Turkish businesspeople have complained for years about the difficulties of doing business in Azerbaijan, demands for unofficial payments by tax authorities and deliberate delays affecting lorries at the Georgian-Azerbaijani border.

“Turkish society has accumulated numerous grievances against Azerbaijan. However, people have only begun expressing them more openly and actively since the summer. Previously, Erdoğan’s inner circle kept this discontent in check through groups it funded, which fell silent at the president’s first signal. Now I see posts supporting protests in Azerbaijan on Instagram, TikTok and even platforms where I would never have imagined seeing such things before.”

The hijab factor: a sensitive issue for Turkey

The de facto ban on wearing the hijab in Azerbaijani schools has provoked a particularly strong reaction in Turkey. According to Gergerlioğlu, bans on headscarves remained one of the most hotly debated issues in Turkish society from the 1980s until the 2010s. Today, even voters who support the secular Republican People’s Party (CHP) consider the issue “a thing of the past”.

“Footage showing girls in headscarves being turned away from school brings back painful memories for Turkish society. Supporters of the ban argued that without it, Turkey would become a state governed by Sharia law. But the ban was lifted, and Turkey still did not become a Sharia state.”

The MP also clashed with Azerbaijani lawmakers over the issue. He said that during an online meeting of the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), he criticised the ban. Azerbaijani MP Hikmet Mammadov then claimed that no such ban existed in the country and accused him of lying. However, according to Gergerlioğlu, a lawmaker from Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), who attended the meeting, chose to remain silent.

Araz Aliyev believes Ankara’s reaction was inevitable. In his view, under Erdoğan, Turkey presents itself as a defender of “moderate Islam” and Muslims, while religious voters form one of the ruling party’s main support bases. “In this situation, Baku’s decision could not go unanswered,” he says.

Javid Agha, meanwhile, points out that Leyla Şahin Usta was among those whom Azerbaijan’s ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) criticised in its statement. In the late 1990s, a headscarf ban prevented her from continuing her studies in Istanbul. Şahin Usta later lost her case against Turkey at the European Court of Human Rights and completed her education in Vienna.

“These bans did not stop her. Today, she is among those who govern Turkey. The authors of the statement should at least have familiarised themselves with her biography,” Agha says.

Sheikh-ul-Islam: “Consultations could have taken place, but they did not”

Allahshukur Pashazade, chairman of the Caucasus Muslims Board, has also commented on the situation. In an interview with Real TV, he acknowledged that the authorities had not consulted the religious organisation he heads before making the decision:

“I deeply regret that consultations could have taken place on this issue in advance, but they did not.”

At the same time, Pashazade supported the government’s position. He said the school uniform regulations do not mention the word “hijab” and that the country has no ban on wearing it. Children can study in hijabs at madrasas, he added, “but a different decision was taken regarding state schools”.

The Sheikh-ul-Islam stressed that “religion is separate from the state, and school is separate from religion”. He also accused certain “internal and external forces” of politicising the issue and trying to turn citizens against the state.

Araz Aliyev sees Pashazade’s statement as evidence that the authorities made the decision hastily:

“If the decision had been carefully considered and prepared over many years, the authorities should have consulted someone. It appears they made the decision in haste.”

For more on the legal aspects of the hijab ban, protests at schools and detentions, see JAMnews’ earlier report.

How will relations develop?

None of the experts interviewed expects Azerbaijan and Turkey to break off their alliance. However, they all believe the chill between the two countries will persist for some time.

Araz Aliyev believes the tensions will remain at the political level and gradually ease:

“Turkey needs Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan needs Turkey even more in terms of national security, the economy and defence. Companies close to the leadership in both countries may face pressure from one another, but I do not believe their alliance will be threatened. After some time, we will hear declarations of brotherhood again.”

He notes that the two countries have weathered similar crises in the past. In particular, tensions in the late 2000s, when Turkey and Armenia were discussing protocols to normalise relations, led to Turkish flags being taken down in Baku. Aliyev believes the summit of the Organisation of Turkic States, which is expected to take place in Turkey at the end of the month, could indicate the direction in which relations between Baku and Ankara will develop.

Gergerlioğlu also does not expect Erdoğan to distance himself from Baku solely over the hijab issue. He says Ankara places much greater importance on revenue from the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, Turkey’s ambition to play a leading role in the “Turkic world” and the support of its nationalist-conservative electorate.

“Behind closed doors, they will probably say politely: ‘Wouldn’t it have been better not to introduce such a ban?’ However, if Aliyev begins openly supporting Israel, Turkey will also start signalling its discontent with the relationship more openly.”

The MP also points to declining electoral support for the ruling party. He claims that some voters dissatisfied with the AKP’s “two-faced” policy towards Israel backed the New Welfare Party in the last election. In his view, the hijab issue could deepen this discontent further.

Javid Agha reaches a similar conclusion. He believes that no matter how often Erdoğan repeats the slogan “one nation, two states”, he will have to take into account the views of the religious-conservative electorate that forms the foundation of his political support and adjust his position accordingly.

Fidan’s statements in Baku also offer insight into this diplomatic strategy. Ankara does not deny that problems exist, but seeks to move discussions about them out of the public arena and into closed-door diplomatic channels. So far, however, there are no signs that Baku intends to make concessions either on the hijab issue or on its relations with Israel.

Strained relations between Turkey and Azerbaijan

World.title: Azerbaijan marks October 18 - Day of Restoration of Independence
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 18. Today, Azerbaijan celebrates the Day of Restoration of Independence.

The Supreme Council of the Republic of Azerbaijan adopted the Constitutional Act "On State Independence of the Republic of Azerbaijan" on October 18, 1991.

The Constitutional Act contained a reference to the Declaration of Independence of May 28, 1918 and the declaration of the Supreme Council of the Republic of Azerbaijan "On the restoration of state independence of the Republic of Azerbaijan" of August 30, 1991, and it was established that the Republic of Azerbaijan is the successor of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic.

The Azerbaijani people created an independent republic at the beginning of the last century, and in 1991 the Republic of Azerbaijan restored its independence as the successor to the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic.

In May 1992, the Milli Majlis approved the National Anthem of the Republic of Azerbaijan (music by Uzeyir Hajibeyli, lyrics by Ahmed Javad), and soon after that, the State Emblem, on the shield of which, against the background of the colors of the State Flag, there is an image of an eight-pointed star with tongues of flame in the center.

A new law "On Independence Day" was adopted at the plenary session of the Azerbaijani Parliament on October 15, 2021. On the same day, President Ilham Aliyev approved the law "On Independence Day".

With the approval of the law, October 18 - State Independence Day was renamed to Day of Restoration of Independence.

The Day of Restoration of Independence is a working day that is celebrated annually as a holiday.

World.title: Fatalities as 'serious incident' causes fire at Canadian military base
World.content:
People have been killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, according to Canada's defence minister, while the media is reporting that large numbers were being transported to hospitals.

Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.

It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180km north-west, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing treatment.

Doctors called the disaster a "one in every 15- to 25-year event". (AP: John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News.

" It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster. "

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate."

He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information soon.

The RCMP said officers were called shortly after 4pm on Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation.

Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts of up to 100 kilometres an hour.

Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. (Reuters: Camden Scott/Canadian Forces)

The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11pm, the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held, and that property and critical infrastructure were protected.

There was no evacuation order for residents.

Mr McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.

"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," Mr McGuinty said.

"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days."

He said armed forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved.

"This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation," he said

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.

It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Mr Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Mr Poilievre said.

Canadian province's breakaway push Alberta's separatist movement is exposing deep fractures inside one of the world's most stable federations and shares striking similarities with WA's historical secession attempts.

He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.

Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early on Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

AP

World.title: Two teenagers arrested after fight involving dozens of youth at Glenelg
World.content:
Two teenage boys have been arrested following an alleged fight at Mosely Square in Glenelg, after reports of a disturbance involving a large group of youths.

SA Police said they were called to the beach after 3:50pm on Sunday.

"Two youths who were fighting each other were arrested at the scene and charged with disorderly behaviour," police said in a statement.

Police said a nearby patrol was on scene about four minutes after the initial call was made for police assistance.

"No police officers were injured during the incident," police said.

"Police are actively patrolling all coastal areas in the metropolitan area.

" Police would like to advise the public that there is no tolerance of bad behaviour by members of the public and police will be taking a proactive approach and taking positive action against those who behave in a disorderly manner in public. "

Patrols responded to reports of a disturbance at Glenelg Beach on Sunday. (Supplied)

Police said dozens of youth witnesses gathered to watch the fight, officers dispersed the crowd and are patrolling the area.

It comes more than two weeks after police said they were investigating several public brawls that occurred at Glenelg and Henley Beach.

Police said they would examine the "level of organisation" of the fights after numerous social media videos emerged online.

Several videos posted of the September brawls showed people in separate fights on the Glenelg shore and at Henley Square, watched on by hundreds of young people.

Other clips showed large groups of youths running across roads in front of traffic.

Earlier this month, police launched Operation Jericho which will focus on addressing anti-social behaviour, criminal activity and road safety issues throughout the warmer months.

The operation will run until April 2027.

The two teenagers will appear in court a later date.

Police are urging anyone who witnesses disorderly behaviour to call the Police Assistance Line on 131444.

World.title: Kangaroos flick switch to kill off Bombers' resistance
World.content:
Ash Riddell has starred through the midfield and Tahlia Randall kicked three goals as North Melbourne unleashed a second-half masterclass to thrash Essendon by 52 points at Windy Hill.

Essendon led by seven points at quarter time and was still within striking distance at the main break, with North Melbourne holding a 29-20 lead after two terms.

But the reigning AFLW premiers flexed their muscles, scoring eight goals to two in the second half to win 12.13 (85) to 5.3 (33).

Riddell was prolific with 32 disposals, six clearances and two goal assists.

Jasmine Garner (27 disposals, two goals) and Eilish Sheerin (25 disposals, one goal) were also influential.

Madison Prespakis battled valiantly for Essendon on the way to 32 disposals, Bonnie Toogood kicked two goals from 18 possessions, while Stephanie Wales (23 hit-outs, 13 disposals, four clearances) was important in the ruck.

The Kangaroos (9-1 win-loss record) will snare the minor premiership if they win their remaining two matches against Adelaide and Richmond.

The Bombers (1-9) are among three one-win teams vying to avoid the wooden spoon.

Earlier at Windy Hill, Chloe Molloy and Cynthia Hamilton unleashed an early goal barrage to lead Sydney to a 51-point victory over Collingwood.

Molloy and Hamilton had three goals apiece by the opening minute of the second term against Collingwood, before forward-turned-ruck Taylor Smith chipped in with three of her own, as Sydney cruised to a 12.8 (80) to 4.5 (29) triumph.

The result kept seventh-placed Sydney (7-3) in the hunt for a home final with two rounds remaining.

Giants stun Hawks

Hawthorn's finals hopes are on thin ice after its forward Aine McDonagh missed a snap with just 18 seconds remaining as GWS pulled off an upset one-point win at Sydney's Henson Park.

The Hawks (5-5) slipped to ninth after falling 7.13 (55) to 7.12 (54) to the 15th-placed Giants (2-8).

Tilly Lucas-Rodd (left) enjoyed the Giants' win in their milestone match. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

They trailed by eight points with 2 minutes remaining before Jacqueline Dupuy took the ball out of the ruck and snapped truly to make it a two-point game.

With just 25 seconds remaining, McDonagh took a mark in the pocket, giving her the chance to clinch victory.

McDonagh played on but sent her snap wide, allowing GWS to hang on for a rare victory in what marked the perfect way to celebrate Tilly Lucy-Rodd's 100-match milestone.

AAP

World.title: Teenage boy rescued from Brisbane stormwater drain
World.content:
Firefighters have rescued a teenager from the "maze" of stormwater drains under Brisbane.

Emergency services received reports that the boy was caught in the underground waterway system in the Kangaroo Point area about 2pm on Sunday.

Five firefighting crews were involved in the rescue effort. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

It took five firefighting crews about half an hour to find the boy, who was with his brother. The other boy did not need to be rescued.

Queensland Fire Department station officer Clint Pilon said he was found about 20 metres from the entrance of a stormwater drain and fire crews were able to bring him to safety on an inflatable rescue boat in a "pretty smooth" rescue.

Emergency services after the successful rescue. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

He said the teenager was uninjured and did not need to be taken to hospital.

Mr Pilon said that "playing in stormwater drains" was never a good idea, particularly after a bit of rain.

"The stormwater drains venture ... all over the city. It's like a little maze and they exit throughout the whole river," he explained.

He described the rescue as a positive outcome.

World.title: Live: Diamonds fall short against Silver Ferns in Constellation Cup opener
World.content:
A penalty shot for the Silver Ferns sees them out by six goals at the final whistle. That's their 11th consecutive victory against the Diamonds on home soil.

The Diamonds will be proud of the way they fought back to win the fourth quarter 17-11. Especially with goal aggregate back to determine the winner of this series. That could make all the difference at the end of game four in who lifts the trophy.

But make no mistake, this was an absolute spanking for much of the match. The Australian coaching staff will really need to go back to the drawing board. Whether Kate Moloney is back and fit to play might help the decision making. But if she isn't they'll have to ask some serious questions about captain Watson. Has she done enough to hold onto her starting spot? Probably not based on this game alone. Price deserves to start at centre in our opinion. The Kiwis were so unbelievably fit and fast and Australia needs midcourters that can match that pace.

There also seems to be a reluctance from the Diamonds staff to shift Horjus into goal attack. During the Super Netball season what makes her so lethal as a WA / GA swing is when she has the opportunity to push into the circle in the back half of games. Maybe Marinkovich worrie about her height against the long-limbed Silver Ferns defenders? But she manages to hold her own just fine in the domestic competition. At 172cm tall she is 12cm shorter than captain Burger and 20cm shorter than Jackson. It is an option they haven't properly explored yet and Horjus is a game winner.

Lastly, Donnell Wallam hasn't had a proper run for the Diamonds in years. She has the X-factor and brings something different than Garbin and Koenen. Could her extra height (193cm) and unpredictability be the difference Australia needs?

World.title: Two people in custody after protest at offshore Woodside gas platform
World.content:
Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside gas platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations.

An Australian Border Force (ABF) spokesperson said they were working with federal and state agencies to respond to the situation after activists occupied the rig overnight and disrupted the gas giant's operations.

Images shared by environmental advocacy group Greenpeace Australia Pacific show its activists scaling a Woodside gas platform and hanging a banner in protest of the company's planned gas project at Scott Reef.

Greenpeace said four protesters travelled to the platform early Saturday morning, and two of them set up "temporary hanging tents" to occupy the platform for "as long as possible".

On Sunday afternoon Greenpeace said two of its activists had been taken into police custody.

Protesters scaled a gas platform operated by Woodside. (Supplied: Greenpeace)

"Special police forces landed a helicopter on the [platform] at around 11:30am AWST," Greenpeace said.

"The activists safely removed themselves from their equipment before being taken into police custody around 1pm."

Woodside confirmed the protest had disrupted operations at the rig, which forms part of the company's $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project.

"Pre-commissioning activities at Scarborough have been paused as part of routine procedures following the unauthorised access," a spokesperson said.

Scott Reef is Australia's largest standalone oceanic reef and a refuge for thousands of aquatic creatures and shorebirds — Woodside's plans have been heavily contested by environmental groups opposed to gas developments in the area.

Woodside's Browse gas project plans to tap into Australia's largest undeveloped offshore gas reserve, and is estimated to cost about $48.7 billion according to a Deloitte analysis.

A banner unfurled by protesters at a Woodside gas platform. (Supplied: Greenpeace)

Woodside said Greenpeace's activists had "deliberately and unlawfully" accessed the floating production unit and had "not only endangered their own safety, but that of Woodside staff".

"Greenpeace's actions have triggered a significant, potentially costly and entirely avoidable response, requiring Western Australian resources to be mobilised to manage the safety, security and operational consequences of their actions," a Woodside spokesperson said.

" The activists' conduct is not peaceful. It is dangerous, reckless and illegal. "

Greenpeace Australia Pacific CEO David Ritter said the activists involved in the latest demonstration were "highly trained and experienced", and said care was "always taken in the health, safety and welfare of all involved".

He said environmental groups had been scaling up their activism in response to Woodside's planned Browse project.

"Greenpeace and other community organisations have been building up their activities matching that rise in community concern," Mr Ritter told the ABC.

"There is no question that our activities are increasing to match this reckless threat of Woodside."

'Reckless behaviour': Minister

Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King said the activists had broken several laws, and described the protest as "reckless behaviour in the extreme".

Madeleine King says the behaviour of the protesters was "reckless". (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"Putting so many lives at risk all for a 20-second TikTok ... we expect the authorities once they've done their proper processes to throw the book at them," Ms King said.

WA Greens fossil fuels and climate change spokesperson Sophie McNeill rejected Ms King's comments.

"The real selfish ones putting lives at risk is Woodside — not these Greenpeace activists — as the fossil fuel giant recklessly opens massive new gas projects in the middle of a worsening and increasingly deadly climate crisis," she said.

World.title: Violence forces lockdown, early closure of Perth agricultural show
World.content:
Fighting between groups of youths forced a long-running Perth agricultural show into lockdown and an eventual early closure on Saturday evening.

The Kelmscott Agricultural Show is a family event that has been running for more than 100 years, and features rides, showbags, log-chopping events and livestock exhibitions.

Police were called to the show on Saturday afternoon as dozens of youths tried to enter the venue at Rushton Park on River Road in Kelmscott.

Kelmscott Agricultural Society president Daryl Dawes said fights between youths inside the showgrounds escalated throughout the day, before culminating in between 50 and 70 juveniles trying to enter the venue.

He said the show went into lockdown about 5pm on Saturday.

"Over the day we had some issues with youth coming in and causing fights on the grounds and it sort of escalated and grew and grew," Mr Dawes said.

Daryl Dawes says the trouble is "disappointing" and it is the first time in his eight years with the society the event has been locked down. (ABC News)

"We ejected people that were causing disruptions in the show and it built up, out on River Road it just got worse and worse so unfortunately we had to go into a lockdown.

" All of our gates got shut … physically padlocked shut until we had a police presence to deal with what was going on outside. "

Mr Dawes described the trouble as "disappointing", saying that it was the first time in his eight years as president of the society that the event had gone into lockdown.

Mr Dawes said some of the juveniles were walking between the show's River Road entrance and it's Orlando Street entrance, looking for weak points and cutting fences and cable ties to try and gain entry.

The Kelmscott Agricultural Show went into lockdown about 5pm on Saturday. (Facebook: Kelmscott Agricultural Show)

"Our security team did a great job ... anyone that got in was very quickly ejected," he said.

Mr Dawes said the crowd dispersed quickly after police arrived.

Police said they received reports of a large group of juveniles causing a disturbance at the show just after 4pm.

A police spokesperson said no charges had been laid, but one juvenile received a caution for disorderly behaviour.

World.title: ‘I couldn’t account for it’: Sue Neill-Fraser opens up on lies to police after partner vanished
World.content:

A Tasmanian grandmother convicted after a high-profile murder trial of killing her partner on their yacht has spoken for the first time, revealing why she lied to police about her whereabouts on the day he died and how she now fears for her life as she attempts to clear her name. In her first interview since being convicted and serving 13 years in jail, Sue Neill-Fraser has told 60 Minutes she maintains her innocence and fears for her safety for speaking out about the 2009 death of her partner, Bob Chappell, in Hobart. “There are huge vested interests in keeping this quiet,” Neill-Fraser tells 60 Minutes. Sue Neill-Fraser speaks publicly for the first time since a gag order imposed as part of her parole conditions was lifted. 60 Minutes Fearful for her safety, Neill-Fraser says she wants it known she’s “not depressed” and if she was to die in suspicious circumstances, no one should believe it was self-harm. The unlikely murderer Sue Neill-Fraser is a softly spoken and extremely articulate lady, with kind but tired eyes. She’s also one of Tasmania’s most notorious, cold-blooded killers.



At 72, she’s strikingly beautiful, although she insists her face is weathered from her years working in paddocks with horses. When Neill-Fraser talks about her grandchildren over a cup of tea, it’s almost impossible to reconcile the person in front of you with the violent murder she was convicted of committing. “I’ve never physically harmed anybody, ever,” Neill-Fraser says in the exclusive interview. Sue Neill-Fraser and Bob Chappell had been a couple for nearly 20 years before he was killed. 60 Minutes It’s the first time she’s spoken publicly since leaving jail in 2022, and Neill-Fraser admits she’s nervous about finally telling her version of events. But she’s determined to explain herself. Because four years into her parole, Neill-Fraser says she feels far from free. “Sitting with a wrongful conviction is like having an infected thorn in your mind,” she says quietly.



“Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine that I could be convicted in Australia if I hadn’t done anything.” Body overboard It was Australia Day 2009, and Neill-Fraser and Chappell, her partner of nearly 20 years, were pottering about the 53-foot yacht they’d bought months earlier with plans to spend their retirement sailing. The Four Winds was moored at Hobart’s Sandy Bay, and Chappell was fiddling with the electrical wiring when Neill-Fraser decided to head back to land, to the home they shared. Chappell planned to spend the night onboard, as he regularly did, and Neill-Fraser says their last words, down in the boat’s saloon, were the sort of idle chit-chat you’d expect between long-term partners. “He said, ‘yep, all right, bye!’ And that was it,” Neill-Fraser says. According to Tasmania Police, Neill-Fraser picked up a large wrench, bashed Chappell to death, and winched his body up two sets of stairs to the deck before manoeuvring him over the edge of the vessel into an inflatable dinghy below.



She then dumped his body somewhere in the Derwent River. “I can’t make it real, even now,” Neill-Fraser says. Released from prison, Sue Neill-Fraser says she will fight to clear her name. 60 Minutes “I don’t understand how you would get somebody up two flights of stairs … I have a slipped disc that I’ve had for about 35 years, and I would’ve had trouble lifting anything over about 10 or 12 kilos.” The police case was circumstantial; Chappell’s body nor a weapon were ever found. But there were signs of foul play; the Four Winds was found sinking and sabotaged the following morning and Chappell’s blood was splattered about the saloon. In the absence of witnesses or suspects, police quickly narrowed in on Neill-Fraser. As the victim’s partner and the last person to see him alive, she was the obvious culprit.



Investigators claim she stood to inherit Chappell’s assets and was motivated by money. Neill-Fraser disputes this, and while usually private about finances, wants to set the record straight. “When Bob went missing, I had over $80,000 in cash in a bank account,” she says. Bob Chappell was last seen onboard his yacht Four Winds. 60 Minutes “I paid for my half of the yacht outright. I had two rental properties and a farm. I didn’t need money.” But she did nothing to dispel police suspicions. In fact, in the days following Chappell’s disappearance, Neill-Fraser gave authorities every reason to believe she had something to hide.

Jake Stringer is expected to do a medical at St Kilda on Monday as the club moves towards signing the goalkicker as a delisted free agent. The 32-year-old kicked 48 goals for the Giants in 2026 from 93 shots at goal but was delisted at the end of the season as the club looked to reset for its next generation to emerge. He started at the Western Bulldogs, moved to Essendon and played two seasons for GWS. Now Jake Stringer looks bound for St Kilda. Getty Known to commentators as “The Package”, Stringer would add much needed firepower to the Saints, who finished 11th in 2026 without the services of injured spearhead Max King and with Liam Ryan their leading goalkicker with 33 goals. Stringer, who played in the Western Bulldogs 2016 premiership was recruited by Saints’ recruiting manager Simon Dalrymple in the 2012 national draft alongside Jack Macrae. He would join Macrae at the Saints if they decide to sign him.



Stringer is a proven goalkicker, with 440 goals to his name from 250 matches at three clubs – the Western Bulldogs, Essendon and the Giants for the past two seasons. Two industry sources, who preferred to remain anonymous when discussing contract matters, said the Saints were moving towards securing Stringer. The strong-bodied forward said late in the season, as he prepared for his final game as a Giant, that he was comfortable with the club’s decision not to renew his contract. He admitted the timing was right for him, as he wanted to spend more time with his daughters in Melbourne, and for the club, which was looking to develop a new crop of young forwards. But he was adamant he was still capable of performing well at the top level. “I definitely feel like I have quite a few years left,” he said.



He is one of several delisted players attracting interest from new clubs. Essendon’s Elijah Tsatas, Richmond’s Samson Ryan and Carlton’s Zach Williams are also on the radar of clubs after the completion of the AFL trade period last week. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes After a big trade period last season when they recruited Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Liam Ryan and Sam Flanders, the Saints were much quieter last week. They brought in Sam Marshall from the Brisbane Lions and sent Rowan Marshall to Geelong. The Saints now have picks 10 and 16 in this year’s national draft and are hoping for previous top-10 picks Tobie Travaglia and Alix Tauru to become regular senior players in 2027. The next delisted free agency period opens in the first week of November. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘What’s the next Cochlear implant?’ Melbourne Uni’s bold plan for renewed optimism
World.content:
Exclusive NationalMelbourne Assembly ‘What’s the next Cochlear implant?’ Melbourne Uni’s bold plan for renewed optimism Jackson Graham October 18, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Melbourne should avoid trying to be “17 different things” and double down on its strengths as it looks to create a renewed sense of optimism and ambition focusing on finite resources, says the University of Melbourne’s new vice chancellor. Professor Carolyn Evans, who started in the top job at the university this month, will make one of her first public appearances at The Age’s Melbourne Assembly on Monday. University of Melbourne vice chancellor Carolyn Evans says Melbourne needs to double down on health, sports and culture, and innovation. Wayne Taylor Her vision for Melbourne and for the state’s oldest university is one and the same: to build on existing global advantages in health and wellbeing, and sport and culture, and build a pipeline of innovation as the employment landscape changes.



“There’s going to be limited resource in coming years, limited resource financially, but limited resource in terms of time, energy and effort for people,” Evans said. “That doesn’t mean we should never do anything else, but we should be capable of building on a couple of areas that we are already globally renowned in.” Loading “We will not necessarily be able to rely on the service industry jobs that have been the overwhelming majority of employment in this city to date. “To really try to say, we’re not just trying to get by, we’re not just trying to be liveable, we’re actually trying to become a city which has a global reputation for being outstanding … That can’t be at 17 different things for a city of Melbourne’s size; that’s got to be a couple of things.”



Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum presented in partnership with the University of Melbourne, will bring together industry leaders, key decision makers and the community to help shape the city’s future. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly The Parkville biomedical precinct surrounding the university is widely recognised as among the best in the world, but leaders in the precinct say that matching equivalent hubs such as in Boston or London would require securing greater capital and more collaboration. Evans points to the planned Australian Institute for Infectious Diseases, which could position the city as a world leader in the next pandemic or epidemic, as the kind of “big, ambitious play” born from university, philanthropic and government investment that she believes is reinforcing Melbourne’s strengths. “That’s the sort of thing that I think we can be doing more of into the future.”



The university is also focused on how its surrounding precinct can produce the next generation of innovations, including by raising its ambitions to have the university’s intellectual property translate into 20 start-ups a year by 2030, and 30 to 40 by 2035. “When people around the world think of Melbourne they need to think that was a place that invented a cure for this, or that was a place that was the home for this amazing company, as they did for a while,” Evans said. “What’s the Cochlear implant of the next 10 years?” In sport and culture, Evans sees a need for cross-disciplinary research to explore and fine tune how these sectors support health and wellbeing in the city. If international students were capped at 25 per cent of university intake, there could be thousands of job losses, Evans warned. Luis Enrique Ascui “Melbourne is very strong in the cultural precinct, and it’s helping to train the performers of the next generation, the artists, and those who think about culture,” she said. “But with both culture and performance and sport, we can bring a level of research and science and integration.”



Evans spent nearly two decades at the university in several senior roles before moving to south-east Queensland as vice chancellor of Griffith University in 2019. She will measure her success by whether she can form deeper partnerships between the University of Melbourne, the city and the nation. Related Article University International student cuts risk ‘very significant hole’, universities warn “I’d like to see start-ups that have had their birth here on campus becoming successful businesses, but maybe still being based in or near the university,” Evans said. “I’d like to see our research partners joining in ever closer collaboration with us. I’d like to see our fine arts students in the art galleries.” Cuts to international students



However, the ambitions of universities face a looming threat from duelling policies to reduce Australia’s intake of international students. The federal government has pledged to curb overall migration by cutting net migration – including by reducing visas for family members of students – while the Coalition intends to reduce the share of international students in higher education to below 25 per cent of total enrolments. Evans, also chair of Universities Australia, said the impact would be severe: “If we were to face the sorts of cuts that some of the political parties are suggesting, it would mean thousands of jobs would be lost at the University of Melbourne alone. If you went to 25 per cent being a requirement across the country in each individual university, I see tens of thousands of jobs being lost. “It won’t just be jobs in our sector; a lot of people rely on universities as anchor institutions. If you look around Melbourne University, small business owners in cafes and hospitality. All sorts of areas absolutely rely on those students,” she said.



If international students were capped at 25 per cent, Evans said, the university would do everything it could to work with industry and philanthropists “to try and remain ambitious and world leading”. An increase in public funding for universities might also be needed, she said. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Inside Melbourne universities’ plans to future-proof degrees and jobs “But it would be a lot harder. We would have to be more focused on where we can really pursue great outcomes.” The university recorded an operating deficit of $124 million in 2025 – higher than the $99 million in 2024 and the fourth consecutive operating deficit. “We would really love political parties of all stripes to look to make those challenges easier, rather than continuing to make them harder,” Evans said.



Degrees of change In the background of these economic headwinds is change to education. At the University of Melbourne, the rise of artificial intelligence has forced the use of assessments such as oral tests and timed exams to ensure students are not offloading their thinking to AI. “Of course every one of our students will have to graduate with AI skills,” Evans said. “But I think we’ll also need to think about in a world where AI can do many of the tasks that graduates would have done, how important are other skills going to be?” Evans said there remained strong commitment to the fundamentals of the Melbourne Model, which since 2008 has seen students undertake a broad undergraduate degree before a discipline specific or professional graduate degree, but she believes the university needs to make sure it remains fit for the modern day.



“I don’t think [there will be changes] in terms of its fundamental architecture,” she said. “But I certainly am a strong believer in deep partnerships with employers, with industry, with government, to help make sure that those degrees are informed by the needs of the workplace.” Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne Assembly Fix it up or knock it down? How a hidden velodrome is holding back John Cain Arena Still, Evans said she is a supporter of students receiving a broad education. “If they become too narrow, and too industry focused, I think that actually will give neither student nor future industries the service that they should have.” She is cautious not to claim to have all the answers weeks into her new role, and is keen to model curiosity and openness to students and staff. As a legal scholar with a research interest in academic freedom and free speech, she is keenly aware of the threat of partisanship and polarisation around the world. “It has increasingly painted people into a corner of simple solutions, and a sense that if you disagree with somebody that person is not only wrong but also bad,” Evans said.



Next year, the university’s law school will roll out work to help students engage in civil debate. “I think we need to find ways of reiterating values that include curiosity, which should be a core academic value. Curiosity more than certainty, and asking open and interesting questions,” Evans said. “We need to see that in the classroom, and we need to see that in our public debate.” Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: There’s snow business: Veteran Santa buckles up for another Christmas
World.content:
NationalVictoriaChristmas There’s snow business: Veteran Santa buckles up for another Christmas Carolyn Webb October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. It’s a sunny day outside, but inside a hall in Melbourne’s south-east, 50 Santas are listening intently to a once-a-year seminar. In a few weeks, they will don red and white suits, perfect jolly laughs and reign from velvet thrones at shopping centres across Victoria. Jolly good fellows: Teacher Bruce Eagle holds court at a Santa education session last week. Eddie Jim Last Thursday, at Springvale Reserve Hall, there was a sackful of stuff to learn. Such as how to interact with your elves. How to banter with cheeky teenagers.



What to say if a child asks for a dog for Christmas (answer: handball that query to Mum and Dad). And the eternal question: how to tame cranky toddlers. Back to school: at 31, Sam Hargreaves (right) was one of the youngest Santas in class last week. Eddie Jim Instructor Bruce Eagle, looking fresh from the North Pole with an affable manner, white beard and glasses, has the room spellbound. Speak gently, he counsels. Get down to the child’s level. Read a book and invite them to share it. Give them a high five if they brighten up.



He shrugs. “Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t.” If anyone is qualified to teach How to Be Santa, it’s Eagle, 75. Bruce Eagle started as a shopping centre Santa at Eastland, aged 16, in 1967. Eddie Jim He debuted as Santa at Eastland shopping centre, weeks after it opened, in 1967, at age 16, and has played it at shopping centres and events for most Christmas seasons since. Eagle will be one of four Santas at Eastland this Christmas, from November 7 until December 24.



In 1967, there was no training. Just an interview, a contract and a borrowed Santa suit. Eagle’s friends went fruit picking on the summer holidays but for him, that work was too hard. Trying on the role: A student receiving his Santa suit at the seminar in Springvale on Thursday. Eddie Jim “My mum saw an  for Santas, and she said, ‘You could do that’,” he says. Playing Santa was like going to a fancy dress party and was indoors – albeit with no air-conditioning.



He still loves the job, which he even does at his Croydon retirement village’s Christmas concert. Related Article Religion Highway to heaven: Melbourne teens gather to venerate relics of ‘influencer’ saint “It’s so much fun,” he says. “You’re a different person, you’re in character, and part of a merry scene.” “The joy is passing on the joy to others.” Last week, Eagle taught 100 Santas in three seminars run by the agency Scene to Believe.



Sam Hargreaves was among the youngest students, at age 31, but this is a refresher class for him. Hargreaves is preparing for his seventh season as Santa, this year on weekends at Casey Central shopping centre in Narre Warren South. Hargreaves works full-time for a computer retailer but also acts in Gilbert and Sullivan light operas and does stand-up comedy. He says Santa is the most rewarding performing genre because of the interaction with people and imaginative play aspects.



“I love the joy that it brings to the families,” Hargreaves says. Retired sales executive Guy Bassett, 66, will be a newbie as a retail centre Santa, at Bayside Shopping Centre in Frankston, but has played the part occasionally, at social events and hotels. Bassett’s inspiration is his Uncle Ken, who would immerse himself in the character at parties. Bassett aims to be a slow and easygoing Santa. “I’ll be that big happy chap in the corner with the glasses halfway down his nose,” he said. World.title: From galas to art shows: The real cost of being a private school parent
World.content:
NationalNSWPrivate schools From galas to art shows: The real cost of being a private school parent Christopher Harris October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As students across Sydney celebrate the end of year 12, a parade of thanks-giving masses, valedictory dinners and final parent catch-ups has been under way over the past month at the city’s private schools. This year, Kincoppal invited parents for canapes on the terrace overlooking the harbour. Tickets were $130 per parent and $75 for graduates. Student attendance was compulsory. The school said ticket pricing reflects the costs associated with delivering the event. While it was small change compared to the $45,000 parents pay for year 12, it was another comparatively small but extra cost of private school not disclaimed on the sticker price. While some families are in a position to donate, others will find it a bit of a stretch. Aresna Villanueva There are 20 NSW schools charging more than $45,000 annually for year 12, but the real cost goes beyond fees. Some private schools advise parents to set aside $2000 to buy the entire uniform, while the prevailing rule of thumb is to budget for fee rises of 5 per cent per year. Then there’s the capital levy, the costs of camps and excursions, application fee, enrolment acceptance fee, extra fees for music lessons and sport.



But there is also another shadow economy that a first-time parent might not be aware: giving days, fundraising events and a busy social calendar all geared towards extracting more cash. Schools have also published legal contract templates, so alumni can bequeath houses, share portfolios or art collections upon their death. At Kincoppal, the parents and friends association’s latest financial report in 2024 reveals it generated $3000 from the welcome cocktail party and the country weekend made a small $1125 surplus. The Mother’s Day raffle made $15,000, while Father’s Day generated $12,000. The association donated $146,354 to the school in 2024, comprising a $120,000 contribution to replace the staff and students’ bus and $26,354 to build and install the barbecue area on Fernon Fields. Related Article Private schools One $50,000 private school just revealed next year’s fees. Here’s how much lunch costs Next door, Kambala’s parent association raised $123,610 in net income that same year from the canteen alone, donating a total of $125,000 to the school to fund teacher training scholarships, a junior school playground and a lecture theatre upgrade, financial records show. At north shore girls school Monte Sant’ Angelo Mercy College, parents spent $9119 on advertising and marketing, $20,000 on raffle prizes and $300,000 on event costs in 2025. Parents donated $50,000 to the school that year.



Wenona’s parent association managed much more. Revenue included $21,000 from the sale of second-hand uniforms and $418,000 from the gala before posting a total operating profit of $217,000. The association made a donation of $266,000 to the Wenona Foundation in 2025. At the King’s School preparatory school, the fathers’ association generated $16,000 in revenue from the art show and $74,000 in canteen sales, while the trivia night brought in $54,000, financial records from 2025 show. Minus expenses, the association managed a $131,629 operating surplus. Last month at SCEGGS’ Festival on Forbes, raffle tickets for $150 each offered parents the chance to win a 50 per cent discount on their daughter’s fees in 2027. SCEGGS in Darlinghurst. Louise Kennerley At most schools, the real money spinners have become simply known as “giving” days.



Related Article Private schools Revealed: The Sydney schools where most families earn $500,000-plus Newington’s giving day this year raised $250,432, to raise funds for means-tested scholarships. It aims to fund means-tested scholarships for 100 children by 2040. Monte raised $133,786 this year for its bursary fund to provide hardship assistance, while SCECGS Redlands in Cremorne raised $500,000 for both the expansion of its high country campus and scholarships in 2024. Barker’s inaugural giving day last year raised $762,808 to provide scholarships for Indigenous and refugee students. Ravenswood’s giving day raised $466,550 for scholarships and the building fund and masterplan this year. Regent Consulting’s Carly Landa, who assists parents secure a spot in Sydney’s schools, said most parents were aware of the potential for fee rises and extra costs. “Some schools have more expenses than others. There can also be a donation culture as well. The schools tend to expect if you’re able to send your child to that private school, you have some money,” she said.



She said while some families were in a position to donate, that was not everyone at a private school. “There are definitely families for whom just getting in and paying the fees is a stretch, it takes a lot of their resources. It can be daunting,” she said. All the parent fundraising events coupled with giving days generate substantial revenue for private schools. What constitutes “other private sources” contributes up to a quarter of some private schools’ total income. At Abbotsleigh, it was 25 per cent ($17 million); at Sydney Grammar it was 18 per cent ($19 million) and for Shore, it was 15 per cent ($13 million) in 2024 – the latest year for which public data is available.
