World.title: Trying to find a job is now as toxic as dating apps. I want a career, not a booty call
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceJob hunting Opinion Trying to find a job is now as toxic as dating apps. I want a career, not a booty call Amy Fallon Journalist October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm

October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Last week, I sat next to my phone at the end of a long day and waited for it to ring. The caller was 15 minutes late. I had the same anxious feeling that I’d had when I’d dealt with men off dating apps. They weren’t going to call. I’d been stood up. This time, I wasn’t waiting around for a guy. I was waiting for a recruitment manager to see if I’d get a job. Scheduling last-minute phone interviews makes it much easier to stand up job applicants. Studio Romantic Welcome to 2026, when, sadly, the toxic behaviour from apps such as Tinder has crept into the hiring process, to the detriment of desperate jobseekers. I don’t have an official name for this new practice, which I’ve encountered twice in the past month while applying for part-time roles. But this is what’s happened: potential employers have long-listed me for interviews at very short notice, even though (unbeknown to yours truly) they already had enough candidates. Then they have cancelled the meetings abruptly, saying they’d found someone else.



Related Article Opinion

Jobs Friends my age are being cut out of the workplace even though they’re brilliant at avoiding brain rot Annie Lawson Contributor In dating language, it could be called a “booty call” (a short-notice message to hook up), “flaking” or “bailing” (what it says on the tin). But probably the most apt term from modern dating parlance is “benching” (keeping someone as a back-up while other options are explored). Most recently, I received a text message from a hiring manager one morning in which she asked me to have a chat with her at 4.30pm the same day. “Sure thing,” I texted back, before making some quick notes and getting my head into interview mode. By the time 4.45pm came around, I hadn’t heard from her. I knew something was up, and pretty soon I received a text telling me that she’d just finished interviewing for the day and had found a suitable candidate, so we wouldn’t need to chat. I never even spoke to her on the phone. She was a human – I think – but I might as well have been communicating with an AI bot. And she had been texting me, a real person, albeit an easily disposable one, I was now discovering.



To say that I was flabbergasted to be “benched” so casually via SMS for a job is an understatement. Yes, Gen Zs are taking iced coffees into interviews. But with this behaviour, I can imagine they’re consuming something stronger outside work hours. Then we have “ghosting”, as it’s known, a practice now so common that there are jokes about it in the Halloween lead-up on professional networking site LinkedIn. Not good jokes, mind. It is LinkedIn, after all. There is at least some good news on this front, though, and it comes from the land known for its nice manners that has also given us the gift that is leader Mark Carney. A law came into force this year in Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, banning “ghosting” in the hiring process. Under an amendment to Ontario’s Employment Standards Act, employers with 25 or more staff must notify candidates within 45 days of their final interview whether they have been successful in landing the job or not. Employers who fail to respond can be fined up to about $100,000. In Australia, we wait to see if employers will be forced to give up the ghost, a move that would surely take some power away from companies and hand it back to workers. Human resources executive Jessica Ciccozzi has noted that in today’s world of social media shaming and corporate brand risk, employers would do well to improve transparency and accountability.



Related Article Opinion

Australian culture Margot Robbie and I started out with ‘bogan’ accents. I’ve still got mine Amy Fallon Journalist “Candidates are already demanding better communication,” she writes, adding that “silence can damage brand credibility in ways that are difficult to repair”. Until the hot mess that is the current hiring system can be sorted out, it’s perhaps best to look at it with a silver-lining approach. I am thankful that, just as I’ve dodged bullets in the past when it comes to matters of the heart, I’ve dodged some in my working life, too. Amy Fallon is a journalist and media consultant. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘I’m afraid of civil war’: The voters travelling from Australia to vote against Netanyahu
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘I’m afraid of civil war’: The voters travelling from Australia to vote against Netanyahu Matthew Knott October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tel Aviv: With a little over a week remaining until election day in Israel, the streets of Tel Aviv are humming with hope and fear. In this bastion of progressive Zionism, there is hope that maybe, just maybe, Israelis will reject Benjamin Netanyahu on October 27. But there is also fear that the great survivor of Israeli politics will somehow find a way to overcome the odds and cling to power yet again. The latest polls show the pro- and anti-Netanyahu party blocs evenly matched, heightening expectations of a tight result. Australian-Israeli voters such as Nirit Eylon have spent at least $2000 on plane tickets to travel around the world to cast a ballot, reflecting their view that this is one of the most important elections of their lifetimes. The long journey is necessary because Israel does not allow any pre-poll or absentee voting: you must be physically present in the country on election day to participate (unless you are a diplomat or member of the military stationed overseas). Benjamin Netanyahu, already Israel’s longest serving prime minister, is running for another term in office. Bloomberg Eylon, a former professional swimming coach, emigrated from Israel in 2006 after falling in love with Australia during a work visit. She has not participated in an Israeli election since she moved, but is travelling from her home in Melbourne to Tel Aviv to vote this year.



“I feel like we have reached a critical turning point,” says Eylon, president of Hatikvah Australia, a left-wing Jewish association that participates in the World Zionist Congress. She says it is time for Netanyahu, who was first elected prime minister in 1996 and has been in power for most of the past two decades, to be sent into retirement, and for his far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich to be kicked out of government. Nirit Eylon is travelling from Australia to vote in the Israeli elections. Justin McManus “We can’t let someone like Bibi stay in power because we know that when people stay in power for too long, they become corrupted,” she says, using Netanyahu’s nickname. “This government is not only affecting what’s happening in Israel. It’s affecting Israelis overseas, Jewish people overseas. If we want to go back to normality, part of it is to get Israel back on track.” For the first time since moving to Australia, Eylon knows of many Israelis returning to the country to vote. The America-Israel Democracy Coalition estimates that around 53,000 of the 600,000 Israelis living abroad will fly in for election day — more than usual.



One of them is Sydney tech entrepreneur Ayal Steiner, 50, who is travelling to vote in his first Israel election since moving to Australia 18 years ago. “This is an election for the soul of the country,” says Steiner, who was born in the northern Israeli city of Haifa. The expat vote could add up to almost two seats in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament — no small thing if the result is closely divided. Elections have led to several deadlocks in the past few years; there were five elections between 2019 and the most recent in 2022. Like Eylon, Steiner believes this election will have ramifications not just for Israel but the world. The Australian Jewish community has suffered a surge in antisemitism since the October 7 attacks of 2023 and the devastating war in Gaza, which has seen Israel accused of genocide at the International Court of Justice. Even as the Israeli-Palestinian conflict continued without resolution, Steiner says Israel’s global brand was associated with its success at advanced technology and innovation. No longer. “Since October 7, being Israeli has become a radioactive term,” he says. “Some people hide their identity now, but I don’t. Being Israeli is part of my origin story, part of who I am.” A Pew research poll released in June found that 79 per cent of Australians have an unfavourable view of Israel, making them among the most critical in the world.



After three years of the most right-wing government in Israel’s history, Steiner hopes the next government will turn down the temperature. “I am not foolish enough to think there is any chance of peace in the near future, but I want to nudge the country to the centre rather than the right,” he says. Related Article World elections Israel is having its most important elections in history. How do they work? He is weighing up which opposition leader has the best chance of defeating Netanyahu; he is most likely to vote for either former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot or former prime minister Naftali Bennett. “They don’t have delusions of expansion, but they are hardliners on security needs and that’s the sort of neighbourhood we are in.” While some voters may travel from Australia to Israel to support Netanyahu or his coalition partners, the consensus in the Jewish community is that the vast majority want a change of government. Netanyahu certainly thinks the influx of expats will hurt him: his Likud party unsuccessfully sued to block the America-Israel Democracy Coalition’s Fly & Vote initiative, which is running charter flights to help Israelis travel from overseas to vote. The leftward tilt of the diaspora contrasts to Israeli society itself, which has become more conservative, religious and hawkish in recent decades. The clash between these two visions of Israel was visible when activist influencers supporting Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir showed up at an anti-government rally in Tel Aviv on Saturday night, aiming to goad their opponents into arguments they could upload to generate social media engagement.



Esther Takac, a psychologist and filmmaker from Melbourne, has travelled to Israel with husband Robert to vote in her first election since 1992, when Labor’s Yitzhak Rabin was pursuing peace with the Palestinians. She plans to vote for the left-wing Democrats – the only mainstream Jewish party advocating a two-state solution. “We want to get this extremist government out, we want to get Netanyahu out,” she says. “We feel this government is taking Israel into a totally wrong direction, making it more nationalistic, militaristic, religious. This government is betraying the values that Israel was founded on.” Psychologist and filmmaker Esther Takac says Israel needs a change from Benjamin Netanyahu. Eamon Gallagher Takac laments that, since October 7, Australians’ views of Israel have been shaped largely by footage of the Israeli military pummelling Gaza, settler violence in the West Bank and Ben-Gvir taunting detained pro-Palestinian activists.



“There’s a whole other nuanced, more humane, more complex side of Israeli society that I think is important for people to see,” she says. Her most recent documentaries have explored Israel’s anti-government protest movement and the personal toll of the conflict on Israelis and Palestinians. The past few years, she says, have been a “pretty awful” time to be Jewish in Australia. She was doxxed and “called a baby-killing Zionist with my tentacles all over the ABC” when religious program Compass screened a shortened version of her documentary The Narrow Bridge, which profiles Israeli and Palestinian peace advocates. “The doxxers put up screenshots and encouraged people to ring my private practice number and leave abusive messages,” she says. Even though she is travelling from Australia to vote, Nirit Eylon says she is worried the elections won’t take place at all. Like many Netanyahu critics, she fears he will use a pretext, like renewed military strikes on Iran, to postpone a vote and remain in power. “To be honest, I’m very concerned by what will come the day after,” she adds. “The chances of civil war are very high.” Takac too feels a strange mix of foreboding and optimism. “I’m concerned about violence and intimidation because Netanyahu is absolutely terrified of losing power,” she says. “I’m feeling hopeful that there’ll be a change, but I’m worried about it. It’s not in the bag at all.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘I couldn’t account for it’: Sue Neill-Fraser opens up on lies to police after partner vanished
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Tasmanian grandmother convicted after a high-profile murder trial of killing her partner on their yacht has spoken for the first time, revealing why she lied to police about her whereabouts on the day he died and how she now fears for her life as she attempts to clear her name. In her first interview since being convicted and serving 13 years in jail, Sue Neill-Fraser has told 60 Minutes she maintains her innocence and fears for her safety for speaking out about the 2009 death of her partner, Bob Chappell, in Hobart. “There are huge vested interests in keeping this quiet,” Neill-Fraser tells 60 Minutes. Sue Neill-Fraser speaks publicly for the first time since a gag order imposed as part of her parole conditions was lifted. 60 Minutes Fearful for her safety, Neill-Fraser says she wants it known she’s “not depressed” and if she was to die in suspicious circumstances, no one should believe it was self-harm. The unlikely murderer Sue Neill-Fraser is a softly spoken and extremely articulate lady, with kind but tired eyes. She’s also one of Tasmania’s most notorious, cold-blooded killers.



At 72, she’s strikingly beautiful, although she insists her face is weathered from her years working in paddocks with horses. When Neill-Fraser talks about her grandchildren over a cup of tea, it’s almost impossible to reconcile the person in front of you with the violent murder she was convicted of committing. “I’ve never physically harmed anybody, ever,” Neill-Fraser says in the exclusive interview. Sue Neill-Fraser and Bob Chappell had been a couple for nearly 20 years before he was killed. 60 Minutes It’s the first time she’s spoken publicly since leaving jail in 2022, and Neill-Fraser admits she’s nervous about finally telling her version of events. But she’s determined to explain herself. Because four years into her parole, Neill-Fraser says she feels far from free. “Sitting with a wrongful conviction is like having an infected thorn in your mind,” she says quietly.



“Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine that I could be convicted in Australia if I hadn’t done anything.” Body overboard It was Australia Day 2009, and Neill-Fraser and Chappell, her partner of nearly 20 years, were pottering about the 53-foot yacht they’d bought months earlier with plans to spend their retirement sailing. The Four Winds was moored at Hobart’s Sandy Bay, and Chappell was fiddling with the electrical wiring when Neill-Fraser decided to head back to land, to the home they shared. Chappell planned to spend the night onboard, as he regularly did, and Neill-Fraser says their last words, down in the boat’s saloon, were the sort of idle chit-chat you’d expect between long-term partners. “He said, ‘yep, all right, bye!’ And that was it,” Neill-Fraser says. According to Tasmania Police, Neill-Fraser picked up a large wrench, bashed Chappell to death, and winched his body up two sets of stairs to the deck before manoeuvring him over the edge of the vessel into an inflatable dinghy below.



She then dumped his body somewhere in the Derwent River. “I can’t make it real, even now,” Neill-Fraser says. Released from prison, Sue Neill-Fraser says she will fight to clear her name. 60 Minutes “I don’t understand how you would get somebody up two flights of stairs … I have a slipped disc that I’ve had for about 35 years, and I would’ve had trouble lifting anything over about 10 or 12 kilos.” The police case was circumstantial; Chappell’s body nor a weapon were ever found. But there were signs of foul play; the Four Winds was found sinking and sabotaged the following morning and Chappell’s blood was splattered about the saloon. In the absence of witnesses or suspects, police quickly narrowed in on Neill-Fraser. As the victim’s partner and the last person to see him alive, she was the obvious culprit.



Investigators claim she stood to inherit Chappell’s assets and was motivated by money. Neill-Fraser disputes this, and while usually private about finances, wants to set the record straight. “When Bob went missing, I had over $80,000 in cash in a bank account,” she says. Bob Chappell was last seen onboard his yacht Four Winds. 60 Minutes “I paid for my half of the yacht outright. I had two rental properties and a farm. I didn’t need money.” But she did nothing to dispel police suspicions. In fact, in the days following Chappell’s disappearance, Neill-Fraser gave authorities every reason to believe she had something to hide.

World.title: Package deal: St Kilda moves in on Jake Stringer
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Package deal: St Kilda moves in on Jake Stringer Peter Ryan October 18, 2026 — 8:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Jake Stringer is expected to do a medical at St Kilda on Monday as the club moves towards signing the goalkicker as a delisted free agent. The 32-year-old kicked 48 goals for the Giants in 2026 from 93 shots at goal but was delisted at the end of the season as the club looked to reset for its next generation to emerge. He started at the Western Bulldogs, moved to Essendon and played two seasons for GWS. Now Jake Stringer looks bound for St Kilda. Getty Known to commentators as “The Package”, Stringer would add much needed firepower to the Saints, who finished 11th in 2026 without the services of injured spearhead Max King and with Liam Ryan their leading goalkicker with 33 goals. Stringer, who played in the Western Bulldogs 2016 premiership was recruited by Saints’ recruiting manager Simon Dalrymple in the 2012 national draft alongside Jack Macrae. He would join Macrae at the Saints if they decide to sign him.



Stringer is a proven goalkicker, with 440 goals to his name from 250 matches at three clubs – the Western Bulldogs, Essendon and the Giants for the past two seasons. Two industry sources, who preferred to remain anonymous when discussing contract matters, said the Saints were moving towards securing Stringer. The strong-bodied forward said late in the season, as he prepared for his final game as a Giant, that he was comfortable with the club’s decision not to renew his contract. He admitted the timing was right for him, as he wanted to spend more time with his daughters in Melbourne, and for the club, which was looking to develop a new crop of young forwards. But he was adamant he was still capable of performing well at the top level. “I definitely feel like I have quite a few years left,” he said.



He is one of several delisted players attracting interest from new clubs. Essendon’s Elijah Tsatas, Richmond’s Samson Ryan and Carlton’s Zach Williams are also on the radar of clubs after the completion of the AFL trade period last week. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes After a big trade period last season when they recruited Tom De Koning, Jack Silvagni, Liam Ryan and Sam Flanders, the Saints were much quieter last week. They brought in Sam Marshall from the Brisbane Lions and sent Rowan Marshall to Geelong. The Saints now have picks 10 and 16 in this year’s national draft and are hoping for previous top-10 picks Tobie Travaglia and Alix Tauru to become regular senior players in 2027. The next delisted free agency period opens in the first week of November. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Barbarians at the gate? Time to write a letter
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Barbarians at the gate? Time to write a letter October 18, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Illustration by Badiucao To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. CIVIL SOCIETY Hugh Riminton’s “My view from the news chair: the worst of the mob is coming for us” (17/10) provides a crystal clear overview of the changes in power and influence, and how the shift has gradually occurred in recent times.

The article should be used in schools for its documentation of the first part of this century.

Our access to social media to vent and absorb anger has been easy. However, as the article points out, the unscrupulous monetising of rage bait is the disease affecting today’s social cohesion, and instead of providing a remedy, it is poisoning society which is seemingly helpless to resist this gradual process.

Now we have to work consistently at bringing a huge dose of positivity and good feelings as an antidote.

Judith Hudson, Elwood Common ground hard to find

As a member of the ‘We The People’ conglomerate made up of millions of ordinary Australians, and one who still enjoys the correspondence of the Letters pages in our legacy media, I heartily endorse Hugh Riminton’s sentiments. Sadly.

My concern is the death of expertise.

We have a group of generalists running the country, masquerading as knowledgeable in their portfolios, but plainly either incompetent, lazy or both. Experts are marginalised, and their good sense ignored as the country flounders and common ground is increasingly hard to find.

No wonder we are getting angrier as we see our social issues build into fragmentation where noise is what matters, not reason, and where clickbait importunes an ugly consensus.

Grievance is real and amplified by algorithms.

My answer to this is to stay away from X and to express myself in a letter which, at least, has the benefit of some thought, rather than the virulent rantings that appear to colonise digital platforms.

It might be old school, but there is still a level of civility to be found here in these pages which reflect some of the wider WTP conversation.

Ann Rennie, Surrey Hills



Opposition lurches towards extremes

The new Digital Duty of Care bill sounds very sensible to me, and your chief political correspondent, Peter Hartcher, outlines why it is world leading (″⁣Liberals in full sponsorship cycle″⁣ 17/10). He also lists several adjustments the government has made to appease the Coalition.

So why are they still opposing it, unless just trying to score petty points? They entirely misattribute ″⁣sock puppet″⁣ testing to political censorship – stoking libertarians who believe it their unalienable right to say anything even if untrue, downright obscene or socially divisive.

Meanwhile, the mental health of children and our social cohesion are at risk from the ravages of social media and its diabolical algorithms.

And why is shadow treasurer Tim Wilson decrying the free trade agreement we’ve finally and painstakingly negotiated with the European Union over many, many years (including under Coalition governments)?

There will always be the odd unhappy farmer or manufacturer, here or in Europe, but we need to nail it now for the overwhelming common good, especially in a global trade environment disrupted by Trump and his whimsical tariffs.

The Liberals and Nationals should pick their battles and not obstruct reform beneficial to the huge majority of Australians. How about they focus on some decent policies of their own to make themselves relevant and electable? They are taking the term ″⁣opposition″⁣ to extremes, which is not healthy for our democracy.

Caroline Leslie, Hawthorn Big tech Faustian pact

Peter Hartcher’s summary of our vulnerability to the harms the web has brought us (“A washing machine has more safeguards than the web”, 17/10) tells only part of the story of the Faustian pact we have made with American “big tech”. It is not only in social media that the US tech giants hold us in their greedy grip.

In its persecution of the International Criminal Court, the US government has, among many sanctions, banned American companies from providing technical and digital services to the court. In a world dominated

by AI giants, this is a terrifyingly big stick.

Australia long ago surrendered our entertainment to the United States, then our social media, which has Americanised our news and gifted such cultural “treasures” as the “manosphere”.

If we object, will they turn off Microsoft, Google etc? Such a move would cripple our private and public industries.

Our vulnerability and reliance on foreign technology is a sovereign risk as great as our defence vulnerabilities, requiring the same attention and finances to rapidly become independent.

Michael Langford, Flinders THE FORUM One Nation cartoon

One Nation has mocked Jacqui Lambie in their latest cartoon for being honest regarding her symptoms and raising awareness of a common women’s health condition that affects thousands of women every year.

Was similar ridicule directed at Barnaby Joyce when he had prostate surgery last year? No.

Another personal attack on women’s health by a political party who should know better.

It’s exhausting.

Shelley Durance, Beaumaris Treaty must stay

Re ″⁣Targeting treaty″⁣ (18/10): One hopes Jess Wilson reads this article and reflects deeply on the importance that the Treaty must not be repealed should the Liberals win the Victorian election.

The Treaty has been a long overdue process acknowledging a pathway for the rights of our First Nations People in Victoria in determining ″⁣not only the gift of recognition, legitimacy, and absolving the moral stain″⁣ of history, but the way forward for reconciliation and dignity.

Judith Morrison, Nunawading



Excise state governments

Your correspondent (Letters, 18/10) has the right idea in eliminating state and territory governments and thus raising the status of local governments.

Currently, we aren’t a united country, we have different rules

on a number of key matters affecting everyday life in the name of state rights.

Think of the savings by eliminating state governments, however, no politician is likely to vote to eliminate their job.

Howard Brownscombe, Brighton East Over-representation

Your correspondent’s argument has merit (Letters, 18/10). Why do we need separate states and territories? A centralised federal government alongside competent local councils should be more than adequate. We are a small population over-represented politically, and streamlining the government makes perfect fiscal sense.

Maree Harrison, Nerrina States are ‘laboratories’

I cannot agree with your correspondent’s call to abolish the states (Letters, 18/10). The fact that rules and regulations differ between states is actually a strength of our current

federal system.

As former US Supreme Court judge, Louis Brandeis, once argued, federalism means that states can serve as ″⁣laboratories″⁣ in which new social and economic policies can be tested. If a policy is successful at the state level, then it can be applied federally. If it fails, then its failure will not affect the rest of the country.

More broadly, federalism also provides an important check

on the power of Canberra to impose its will on different regions that have different needs from

each other.

Instead of abolishing the states, which would centralise governing power in the federal government, our political system should operate on the principle of subsidiarity.

The Commonwealth government should perform only those functions which cannot be more effectively performed by state or local governments.

Nikhil Dhanabal, Clyde North Make Melbourne bigger

The Melbourne Assembly sponsored by The Age and the University of Melbourne will no doubt contribute to Melbourne’s standing as the ″⁣world’s most talkative city″⁣, but will it be silent on the need for metropolitan governance?

There have been multiple attempts at governing Melbourne dating from the Melbourne Metropolitan Board of Works to the Melbourne Planning Authority and Metropolitan Partnerships. But all have been undone by successive state governments.

Why do we not have a ″⁣Greater Melbourne Council″⁣ like other governed metropolitan regions such as New York, London, Paris, Vienna, Vancouver and Toronto?

The metropolitan issues that we grapple with and often seem insurmountable include transport infrastructure, affordable and social housing, employment, open space and nature-based solutions, responses to climate change impacts and renewable energy.

We can no longer rely on a patchwork of 32 metropolitan cities to meet the challenges

we face.

We need a Greater Melbourne Council that will future-proof metropolitan Melbourne and give meaning to Melbourne as the “world’s most liveable (metropolitan) city”!

Martin Brennan, Carlton Real estate reserve prices

The Real Estate Institute of Victoria says it welcomes and supports improved transparency in real estate auction sales, yet it opposed the introduction of the new auction rules designed to stamp out the trickery of underquoting.

The REIV is now obfuscating the implementation of the new rules by saying that notwithstanding the requirement to have a published reserve price seven days before an auction, that vendors do not have to sell if bidding reaches or exceeds that reserve price.

Technically, this is correct – misleading and deceptive conduct legalisation does not apply to private individuals, and in Victoria, a sale isn’t binding until contracts have been signed by both the vendors and purchasers.

However, consumer legalisation and misleading and deceptive conduct rules do apply to estate agents who engage “in trade or commerce” by managing the

sale process on behalf of their vendor clients.

If an estate agency or their auctioneer works in alliance with their vendor to abuse a published reserve price, they will not only be corrupting the auction system and their trustworthiness, but will also be subject to the misleading and deceptive conduct provisions of consumer law and liable to severe penalties.

John Keating, auctioneer, Woodend



War stories

Your correspondent (Letters, 17/10) urges Pauline Hanson’s ″⁣Crusaders″⁣ to brush up on history. Apart from military skills, Muslim leader Saladin is judged by many historians as the better man than Christian icon, Richard the Lionheart, who is praised for his generosity, mercy and willingness to negotiate.

For example, the Crusaders conducted a large-scale massacre in Jerusalem after capturing the city in 1099 – an atrocity that Saladin declined to repeat on retaking Jerusalem.

Further, on their journeys east from Europe, Crusaders indiscriminately slaughtered many Christians, capturing and sacking Constantinople, a major Christian city in 1204.

Norman Huon, Port Melbourne Racing tragedy

Punters can move onto the next race with another bet, television executives will erase the vision, owners will say their horses are well treated, stewards will say the horse was humanely euthanised. But no one can erase the memory of Ohope Wins’ life ending in agony behind a plastic screen in front of a boozed-up crowd.

Simon Williamson, West Footscray John Cain Arena fix

Re “Fix it up or knock it down? How a hidden velodrome is holding back John Cain Arena” (18/10): Having run a place in a wheel-race circa 1992/3 at the then Northcote velodrome (now DISC), John Cain as premier was asked to give out prizes. When Cain came to me, I bravely asked him when Victoria was likely to get an indoor board track facility, similar to what I’d raced on in Ghent Belgium in 1984.

He looked rather perturbed by my unexpected brazenness, shaking his head while taking a step backwards. Ironically, the velodrome in Melbourne Park now has his name emblazoned on it.

The original outdoor board track at Olympic Park was knocked down for a greyhound track in 1962; John Cain Arena could also be facing demolition.

I and many others may unfortunately never get to ride it.

Anthony Barnes, Kinglake City vibe is high

I was dining in the city and saw the great New Orleans brass band from Melbourne’s Jazz Festival marching through the city and the vibe was amazing.

We have a lot to celebrate here in Melbourne. Let’s not take our safety and security for granted

in this amazing city.

Mel Smith, Brighton AI or HI?

Julia Baird’s article, “What my dad Bruce taught me” (18/10), raises interesting insights regarding the possible effects of the continuing rise of AI.

HI (human intelligence) engages the human mind to question and pay attention to human detail. It connects with the human spirit. Will AI be the answer to this?

Will our young people become our future philosophers, poets or people who can think outside the box if all answers are influenced

by AI?

Christine Baker, Rosanna



AND ANOTHER THING Victoria

Re: “Labor pledges $30 weekly toll cap to undercut Coalition pitch” (18/10): Yet another bribe from a government mired in debt with no plan to get out of it. This is no way to win my vote, Mr Carroll.

Ivan Glynn, Vermont Why do we not insist and mandate that data centres be constructed close to sewage treatment plants and force them to treat and recycle the water they need to operate

the centres?

Malcolm Fraser, Oakleigh South



United States

Your correspondent (Letters, 18/10) asks when gun laws in the United States will change. I came to the conclusion that the answer is never, when even after the tragedy at the school in Sandy Hook in 2012 where 20 children and six adults died, then-president Barack Obama could not bring about a change in gun culture.

Norma Togneri, Ivanhoe So I guess one Zacharia equals half a Scaramucci.

Mary Gilevitis, Kew Sport

Racing: The sport where participants are killed and the audience keeps boozing.

Susan Scalise, Ascot Vale If it’s good enough for the Matildas soccer team to accept government (taxpayer) funding, surely they can bring themselves to sing the national anthem before the game? Not good enough girls!

Helen Leach, Bendigo Grape season

Re your correspondent’s letter ″⁣Sour Grapes″⁣ (18/10): the simple message is to know when fresh fruit and vegetables are in season. Buy Australian grapes from late summer through to autumn, when they are cheap, plentiful and at peak quality.

Sandra Fordyce-Voorham, Black Rock



Fascinating letter about grapes. It’s sometimes hard the way supermarkets play around with prices, but with grapes it’s easy. If they cost twice as much as you expect, then they are from the United States. We leave them on the shelf, awaiting the Australian grapes to come on sale when they are in season.

World.title: ‘What’s the next Cochlear implant?’ Melbourne Uni’s bold plan for renewed optimism
World.content:
Exclusive NationalMelbourne Assembly ‘What’s the next Cochlear implant?’ Melbourne Uni’s bold plan for renewed optimism Jackson Graham October 18, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Melbourne should avoid trying to be “17 different things” and double down on its strengths as it looks to create a renewed sense of optimism and ambition focusing on finite resources, says the University of Melbourne’s new vice chancellor. Professor Carolyn Evans, who started in the top job at the university this month, will make one of her first public appearances at The Age’s Melbourne Assembly on Monday. University of Melbourne vice chancellor Carolyn Evans says Melbourne needs to double down on health, sports and culture, and innovation. Wayne Taylor Her vision for Melbourne and for the state’s oldest university is one and the same: to build on existing global advantages in health and wellbeing, and sport and culture, and build a pipeline of innovation as the employment landscape changes.



“There’s going to be limited resource in coming years, limited resource financially, but limited resource in terms of time, energy and effort for people,” Evans said. “That doesn’t mean we should never do anything else, but we should be capable of building on a couple of areas that we are already globally renowned in.” Loading “We will not necessarily be able to rely on the service industry jobs that have been the overwhelming majority of employment in this city to date. “To really try to say, we’re not just trying to get by, we’re not just trying to be liveable, we’re actually trying to become a city which has a global reputation for being outstanding … That can’t be at 17 different things for a city of Melbourne’s size; that’s got to be a couple of things.”



Melbourne Assembly, a civic forum presented in partnership with the University of Melbourne, will bring together industry leaders, key decision makers and the community to help shape the city’s future. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly The Parkville biomedical precinct surrounding the university is widely recognised as among the best in the world, but leaders in the precinct say that matching equivalent hubs such as in Boston or London would require securing greater capital and more collaboration. Evans points to the planned Australian Institute for Infectious Diseases, which could position the city as a world leader in the next pandemic or epidemic, as the kind of “big, ambitious play” born from university, philanthropic and government investment that she believes is reinforcing Melbourne’s strengths. “That’s the sort of thing that I think we can be doing more of into the future.”



The university is also focused on how its surrounding precinct can produce the next generation of innovations, including by raising its ambitions to have the university’s intellectual property translate into 20 start-ups a year by 2030, and 30 to 40 by 2035. “When people around the world think of Melbourne they need to think that was a place that invented a cure for this, or that was a place that was the home for this amazing company, as they did for a while,” Evans said. “What’s the Cochlear implant of the next 10 years?” In sport and culture, Evans sees a need for cross-disciplinary research to explore and fine tune how these sectors support health and wellbeing in the city. If international students were capped at 25 per cent of university intake, there could be thousands of job losses, Evans warned. Luis Enrique Ascui “Melbourne is very strong in the cultural precinct, and it’s helping to train the performers of the next generation, the artists, and those who think about culture,” she said. “But with both culture and performance and sport, we can bring a level of research and science and integration.”



Evans spent nearly two decades at the university in several senior roles before moving to south-east Queensland as vice chancellor of Griffith University in 2019. She will measure her success by whether she can form deeper partnerships between the University of Melbourne, the city and the nation. Related Article University International student cuts risk ‘very significant hole’, universities warn “I’d like to see start-ups that have had their birth here on campus becoming successful businesses, but maybe still being based in or near the university,” Evans said. “I’d like to see our research partners joining in ever closer collaboration with us. I’d like to see our fine arts students in the art galleries.” Cuts to international students



However, the ambitions of universities face a looming threat from duelling policies to reduce Australia’s intake of international students. The federal government has pledged to curb overall migration by cutting net migration – including by reducing visas for family members of students – while the Coalition intends to reduce the share of international students in higher education to below 25 per cent of total enrolments. Evans, also chair of Universities Australia, said the impact would be severe: “If we were to face the sorts of cuts that some of the political parties are suggesting, it would mean thousands of jobs would be lost at the University of Melbourne alone. If you went to 25 per cent being a requirement across the country in each individual university, I see tens of thousands of jobs being lost. “It won’t just be jobs in our sector; a lot of people rely on universities as anchor institutions. If you look around Melbourne University, small business owners in cafes and hospitality. All sorts of areas absolutely rely on those students,” she said.



If international students were capped at 25 per cent, Evans said, the university would do everything it could to work with industry and philanthropists “to try and remain ambitious and world leading”. An increase in public funding for universities might also be needed, she said. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Inside Melbourne universities’ plans to future-proof degrees and jobs “But it would be a lot harder. We would have to be more focused on where we can really pursue great outcomes.” The university recorded an operating deficit of $124 million in 2025 – higher than the $99 million in 2024 and the fourth consecutive operating deficit. “We would really love political parties of all stripes to look to make those challenges easier, rather than continuing to make them harder,” Evans said.



Degrees of change In the background of these economic headwinds is change to education. At the University of Melbourne, the rise of artificial intelligence has forced the use of assessments such as oral tests and timed exams to ensure students are not offloading their thinking to AI. “Of course every one of our students will have to graduate with AI skills,” Evans said. “But I think we’ll also need to think about in a world where AI can do many of the tasks that graduates would have done, how important are other skills going to be?” Evans said there remained strong commitment to the fundamentals of the Melbourne Model, which since 2008 has seen students undertake a broad undergraduate degree before a discipline specific or professional graduate degree, but she believes the university needs to make sure it remains fit for the modern day.



“I don’t think [there will be changes] in terms of its fundamental architecture,” she said. “But I certainly am a strong believer in deep partnerships with employers, with industry, with government, to help make sure that those degrees are informed by the needs of the workplace.” Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne Assembly Fix it up or knock it down? How a hidden velodrome is holding back John Cain Arena Still, Evans said she is a supporter of students receiving a broad education. “If they become too narrow, and too industry focused, I think that actually will give neither student nor future industries the service that they should have.” She is cautious not to claim to have all the answers weeks into her new role, and is keen to model curiosity and openness to students and staff. As a legal scholar with a research interest in academic freedom and free speech, she is keenly aware of the threat of partisanship and polarisation around the world. “It has increasingly painted people into a corner of simple solutions, and a sense that if you disagree with somebody that person is not only wrong but also bad,” Evans said.



Next year, the university’s law school will roll out work to help students engage in civil debate. “I think we need to find ways of reiterating values that include curiosity, which should be a core academic value. Curiosity more than certainty, and asking open and interesting questions,” Evans said. “We need to see that in the classroom, and we need to see that in our public debate.” Melbourne Assembly will be held from October 19 to October 21. More information is available on the Melbourne Assembly website. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: There’s snow business: Veteran Santa buckles up for another Christmas
World.content:
NationalVictoriaChristmas There’s snow business: Veteran Santa buckles up for another Christmas Carolyn Webb October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. It’s a sunny day outside, but inside a hall in Melbourne’s south-east, 50 Santas are listening intently to a once-a-year seminar. In a few weeks, they will don red and white suits, perfect jolly laughs and reign from velvet thrones at shopping centres across Victoria. Jolly good fellows: Teacher Bruce Eagle holds court at a Santa education session last week. Eddie Jim Last Thursday, at Springvale Reserve Hall, there was a sackful of stuff to learn. Such as how to interact with your elves. How to banter with cheeky teenagers.



What to say if a child asks for a dog for Christmas (answer: handball that query to Mum and Dad). And the eternal question: how to tame cranky toddlers. Back to school: at 31, Sam Hargreaves (right) was one of the youngest Santas in class last week. Eddie Jim Instructor Bruce Eagle, looking fresh from the North Pole with an affable manner, white beard and glasses, has the room spellbound. Speak gently, he counsels. Get down to the child’s level. Read a book and invite them to share it. Give them a high five if they brighten up.



He shrugs. “Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t.” If anyone is qualified to teach How to Be Santa, it’s Eagle, 75. Bruce Eagle started as a shopping centre Santa at Eastland, aged 16, in 1967. Eddie Jim He debuted as Santa at Eastland shopping centre, weeks after it opened, in 1967, at age 16, and has played it at shopping centres and events for most Christmas seasons since. Eagle will be one of four Santas at Eastland this Christmas, from November 7 until December 24.



In 1967, there was no training. Just an interview, a contract and a borrowed Santa suit. Eagle’s friends went fruit picking on the summer holidays but for him, that work was too hard. Trying on the role: A student receiving his Santa suit at the seminar in Springvale on Thursday. Eddie Jim “My mum saw an  for Santas, and she said, ‘You could do that’,” he says. Playing Santa was like going to a fancy dress party and was indoors – albeit with no air-conditioning.



He still loves the job, which he even does at his Croydon retirement village’s Christmas concert. Related Article Religion Highway to heaven: Melbourne teens gather to venerate relics of ‘influencer’ saint “It’s so much fun,” he says. “You’re a different person, you’re in character, and part of a merry scene.” “The joy is passing on the joy to others.” Last week, Eagle taught 100 Santas in three seminars run by the agency Scene to Believe.



Sam Hargreaves was among the youngest students, at age 31, but this is a refresher class for him. Hargreaves is preparing for his seventh season as Santa, this year on weekends at Casey Central shopping centre in Narre Warren South. Hargreaves works full-time for a computer retailer but also acts in Gilbert and Sullivan light operas and does stand-up comedy. He says Santa is the most rewarding performing genre because of the interaction with people and imaginative play aspects.



“I love the joy that it brings to the families,” Hargreaves says. Retired sales executive Guy Bassett, 66, will be a newbie as a retail centre Santa, at Bayside Shopping Centre in Frankston, but has played the part occasionally, at social events and hotels. Bassett’s inspiration is his Uncle Ken, who would immerse himself in the character at parties. Bassett aims to be a slow and easygoing Santa. “I’ll be that big happy chap in the corner with the glasses halfway down his nose,” he said. World.title: From galas to art shows: The real cost of being a private school parent
World.content:
NationalNSWPrivate schools From galas to art shows: The real cost of being a private school parent Christopher Harris October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As students across Sydney celebrate the end of year 12, a parade of thanks-giving masses, valedictory dinners and final parent catch-ups has been under way over the past month at the city’s private schools. This year, Kincoppal invited parents for canapes on the terrace overlooking the harbour. Tickets were $130 per parent and $75 for graduates. Student attendance was compulsory. The school said ticket pricing reflects the costs associated with delivering the event. While it was small change compared to the $45,000 parents pay for year 12, it was another comparatively small but extra cost of private school not disclaimed on the sticker price. While some families are in a position to donate, others will find it a bit of a stretch. Aresna Villanueva There are 20 NSW schools charging more than $45,000 annually for year 12, but the real cost goes beyond fees. Some private schools advise parents to set aside $2000 to buy the entire uniform, while the prevailing rule of thumb is to budget for fee rises of 5 per cent per year. Then there’s the capital levy, the costs of camps and excursions, application fee, enrolment acceptance fee, extra fees for music lessons and sport.



But there is also another shadow economy that a first-time parent might not be aware: giving days, fundraising events and a busy social calendar all geared towards extracting more cash. Schools have also published legal contract templates, so alumni can bequeath houses, share portfolios or art collections upon their death. At Kincoppal, the parents and friends association’s latest financial report in 2024 reveals it generated $3000 from the welcome cocktail party and the country weekend made a small $1125 surplus. The Mother’s Day raffle made $15,000, while Father’s Day generated $12,000. The association donated $146,354 to the school in 2024, comprising a $120,000 contribution to replace the staff and students’ bus and $26,354 to build and install the barbecue area on Fernon Fields. Related Article Private schools One $50,000 private school just revealed next year’s fees. Here’s how much lunch costs Next door, Kambala’s parent association raised $123,610 in net income that same year from the canteen alone, donating a total of $125,000 to the school to fund teacher training scholarships, a junior school playground and a lecture theatre upgrade, financial records show. At north shore girls school Monte Sant’ Angelo Mercy College, parents spent $9119 on advertising and marketing, $20,000 on raffle prizes and $300,000 on event costs in 2025. Parents donated $50,000 to the school that year.



Wenona’s parent association managed much more. Revenue included $21,000 from the sale of second-hand uniforms and $418,000 from the gala before posting a total operating profit of $217,000. The association made a donation of $266,000 to the Wenona Foundation in 2025. At the King’s School preparatory school, the fathers’ association generated $16,000 in revenue from the art show and $74,000 in canteen sales, while the trivia night brought in $54,000, financial records from 2025 show. Minus expenses, the association managed a $131,629 operating surplus. Last month at SCEGGS’ Festival on Forbes, raffle tickets for $150 each offered parents the chance to win a 50 per cent discount on their daughter’s fees in 2027. SCEGGS in Darlinghurst. Louise Kennerley At most schools, the real money spinners have become simply known as “giving” days.



Related Article Private schools Revealed: The Sydney schools where most families earn $500,000-plus Newington’s giving day this year raised $250,432, to raise funds for means-tested scholarships. It aims to fund means-tested scholarships for 100 children by 2040. Monte raised $133,786 this year for its bursary fund to provide hardship assistance, while SCECGS Redlands in Cremorne raised $500,000 for both the expansion of its high country campus and scholarships in 2024. Barker’s inaugural giving day last year raised $762,808 to provide scholarships for Indigenous and refugee students. Ravenswood’s giving day raised $466,550 for scholarships and the building fund and masterplan this year. Regent Consulting’s Carly Landa, who assists parents secure a spot in Sydney’s schools, said most parents were aware of the potential for fee rises and extra costs. “Some schools have more expenses than others. There can also be a donation culture as well. The schools tend to expect if you’re able to send your child to that private school, you have some money,” she said.



She said while some families were in a position to donate, that was not everyone at a private school. “There are definitely families for whom just getting in and paying the fees is a stretch, it takes a lot of their resources. It can be daunting,” she said. All the parent fundraising events coupled with giving days generate substantial revenue for private schools. What constitutes “other private sources” contributes up to a quarter of some private schools’ total income. At Abbotsleigh, it was 25 per cent ($17 million); at Sydney Grammar it was 18 per cent ($19 million) and for Shore, it was 15 per cent ($13 million) in 2024 – the latest year for which public data is available. World.title: Trying to find a job is now as toxic as dating apps. I want a career, not a booty call
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceJob hunting Opinion Trying to find a job is now as toxic as dating apps. I want a career, not a booty call Amy Fallon Journalist October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm

October 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Last week, I sat next to my phone at the end of a long day and waited for it to ring. The caller was 15 minutes late. I had the same anxious feeling that I’d had when I’d dealt with men off dating apps. They weren’t going to call. I’d been stood up. This time, I wasn’t waiting around for a guy. I was waiting for a recruitment manager to see if I’d get a job. Scheduling last-minute phone interviews makes it much easier to stand up job applicants. Studio Romantic Welcome to 2026, when, sadly, the toxic behaviour from apps such as Tinder has crept into the hiring process, to the detriment of desperate jobseekers. I don’t have an official name for this new practice, which I’ve encountered twice in the past month while applying for part-time roles. But this is what’s happened: potential employers have long-listed me for interviews at very short notice, even though (unbeknown to yours truly) they already had enough candidates. Then they have cancelled the meetings abruptly, saying they’d found someone else.



Related Article Opinion

Jobs Friends my age are being cut out of the workplace even though they’re brilliant at avoiding brain rot Annie Lawson Contributor In dating language, it could be called a “booty call” (a short-notice message to hook up), “flaking” or “bailing” (what it says on the tin). But probably the most apt term from modern dating parlance is “benching” (keeping someone as a back-up while other options are explored). Most recently, I received a text message from a hiring manager one morning in which she asked me to have a chat with her at 4.30pm the same day. “Sure thing,” I texted back, before making some quick notes and getting my head into interview mode. By the time 4.45pm came around, I hadn’t heard from her. I knew something was up, and pretty soon I received a text telling me that she’d just finished interviewing for the day and had found a suitable candidate, so we wouldn’t need to chat. I never even spoke to her on the phone. She was a human – I think – but I might as well have been communicating with an AI bot. And she had been texting me, a real person, albeit an easily disposable one, I was now discovering.



To say that I was flabbergasted to be “benched” so casually via SMS for a job is an understatement. Yes, Gen Zs are taking iced coffees into interviews. But with this behaviour, I can imagine they’re consuming something stronger outside work hours. Then we have “ghosting”, as it’s known, a practice now so common that there are jokes about it in the Halloween lead-up on professional networking site LinkedIn. Not good jokes, mind. It is LinkedIn, after all. There is at least some good news on this front, though, and it comes from the land known for its nice manners that has also given us the gift that is leader Mark Carney. A law came into force this year in Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, banning “ghosting” in the hiring process. Under an amendment to Ontario’s Employment Standards Act, employers with 25 or more staff must notify candidates within 45 days of their final interview whether they have been successful in landing the job or not. Employers who fail to respond can be fined up to about $100,000. In Australia, we wait to see if employers will be forced to give up the ghost, a move that would surely take some power away from companies and hand it back to workers. Human resources executive Jessica Ciccozzi has noted that in today’s world of social media shaming and corporate brand risk, employers would do well to improve transparency and accountability.



Related Article Opinion

Australian culture Margot Robbie and I started out with ‘bogan’ accents. I’ve still got mine Amy Fallon Journalist “Candidates are already demanding better communication,” she writes, adding that “silence can damage brand credibility in ways that are difficult to repair”. Until the hot mess that is the current hiring system can be sorted out, it’s perhaps best to look at it with a silver-lining approach. I am thankful that, just as I’ve dodged bullets in the past when it comes to matters of the heart, I’ve dodged some in my working life, too. Amy Fallon is a journalist and media consultant.
