World.title: A whirlwind of education change
World.content:
Erica Stanford has had more impact on the school system than any education minister in decades.

In less than three years, she has overseen the rewrite of every school curriculum, dug a grave for the NCEA qualification and mandated the structured literacy approach to teaching children to read in every primary school.

Stanford has effectively seized control of teachers' standards, excised school boards' Treaty of Waitangi obligations and increased learning support funding - and that's not even half of it.

There is also banning cellphones from classrooms, mandating an hour a day of reading, writing and maths, and accelerating the school building programme.

On top of that, there's the work of Associate Education Minister David Seymour and Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds.

Between them, they've re-introduced charter schools, slashed the cost of free school lunches, brought a tougher approach to school attendance, dismantled mega-tertiary institute Te Pūkenga and moved the year of fees-free study from the first year of study to the final year.

The government now finds itself in a position of unprecedented control over the various levers that influence the school system, but has it strengthened the education system, as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon claimed earlier this year?

Stanford told RNZ there were early signs of improvement in maths, writing and five-year-olds' ability to read.

Anecdotally, there was certainly talk of improvement, especially in maths and early reading, but evidence was sketchy at a nationally measurable level.

The strongest proof came this week, with the New Zealand Council for Educational Research's analysis of the past 15 years of results from Progressive Achievement Tests (PATs). It showed maths and reading skills improved in the past couple of years, and at a reasonbly sharp rate this year.

The study also showed that, for maths and reading vocabulary, the improvement began before this government's tenure, and it did not attribute the improvements to any particular cause.

Other studies - the Curriculum Insights study of children in Years 3, 6, and 8, and the OECD's PISA tests for 15-year-olds - showed, for the most part, statistically insigificant changes.

The main area of improvement in schools that might have been influenced by the government was attendance. Last term, 64 percent of children attended regularly - the best term 2 result since 2020 and a bounceback from post-Covid lows.

Meanwhile, 19 percent of school-leavers last year had no formal qualification - one of the worst figures of the NCEA era, and likely driven by must-pass online reading, writing and maths tests introduced by the previous government.

Expecting clearly measurable changes to children's achievement from the government's actions is unfair - principals and teachers told RNZ it was too early to expect to see change.

They said schools were still coming to grips with the first of the new curriculums and many teachers continued to do things their way, until they were ready to change. Rather, this term of government has been about laying foundations.

Primary schools have worked with a new English curriculum since the start of 2025, although many shifted or started to shift to the structured literacy approach for teaching children to read under the previous government.

They've also got a new and more-difficult maths curriculum backed up by free workbooks, which is expected to bring measurable improvements in primary school maths achievement.

The remaining Y0-10 curriculums have been rewritten, with a focus on knowledge and clear progressions from year to year, for introduction next year and in 2029.

The final senior secondary curriculums are yet to drop, but the drafts are out and the government has sketched the broad outline of the qualification that will replace NCEA from 2028-2030 - exams in every subject, no mixing-and-matching of different subjects and new vocational subjects developed with industry.

Learning support funding has increased, but teachers don't believe last year's boost of $747m over four years has been as "seismic" as the minister declared at the time. The government initially raised spending by six percent and, by 2028/29, the learning support envelope will total $1.67 billion, 14 percent more than the 2024/25 starting point.

Special schools are being expanded for the first time in years and charter schools are back, with 19 open and more due to start next year.

For the most part, the charters appear to be boutique schools, but with more of a focus on neurodiverse and other disenfranchised learners than last time the model was tried. The exception is Aotearoa Infinite Academy - the online school on track to become one of the biggest.

The government has shifted control of teachers' professional standards and standards for initial teacher education to the Education Ministry.

Early childhood education regulations have been rewritten and the funding system is under review.

Independent polytechnics have been re-established as mega institute Te Pūkenga is dismantled - a change helpfully cushioned by a surge in domestic enrolments and the return of valuable foreign students.

That's a lot of change and it doesn't cover everything this government has done. In many cases, the foundations have appeared shaky.

The primary school maths curriculum was changed late in 2025, even though schools had already been using the supposedly final version for nearly an entire year.

Teachers have told RNZ that structured literacy helps more children learn the basics of reading, but some also warn that it comes at a cost to comprehension and enjoyment of reading.

Draft curriculums were condemned by subject experts and teachers as overcrowded and containing errors.

The shift to mass-provided school lunches was dogged by complaints.

Criticism has been a big feature of the government's reforms - it has not brought the school and early childhood sectors with it, and there have been remarkable levels of opposition.

Nearly every regional principals association in the country and subject associations spoke out against what they saw as badly drafted new curriculums.

More than half the country's schools publicly declared their opposition to the sudden removal of their Treaty of Waitangi obligations. Others told RNZ they shared the sentiment, but did not speak out, because they did not want to appear "political".

Nearly every education peak body opposed the government's takeover of teachers' registration and the Teaching Council standards body.

Much of the school sector's response can be characterised as backing some or even much of what the government is doing, "but not like that".

The government would have more support without culture-war moves like reducing the importance of the Treaty, omitting climate change from the curriculum in Years 0-10, only to reinstate it (sort of), and ditching the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum.

There might also be more support, if peak bodies felt they had more or even some input into the government's plans. Subject associations told RNZ their members contributed to curriculum work, but could see no evidence of their input in resulting drafts.

In early childhood, many in the sector fear the current funding review will recommend watering down or removing incentives to employ fully qualified registered teachers, and decoupling their pay rates from those of school and kindergarten teachers.

Early-years teachers aren't the only ones worried about ECE. An experienced school principal warned the government's education ambitions would fail without more attention to quality in ECE.

"If you nail ECE the rest will fall into place," they said.

Despite the lack of widespread and strong support, teachers and principals spoken to by RNZ do not want to abandon the changes altogether, if the election brings a change of government.

They say the sector has been through too much turmoil and it would be better to continue with modifications than to switch horses altogether at this late stage.

They made an exception for the deletion of boards' Treaty of Waitangi obligations, arguing they were the cornerstone of equity in schools and must be restored, and the Teaching Council changes.

The Labour Party has clearly heard the same message - its policy would freeze the NCEA reforms and any curriculums that have not yet been introduced, and check with the sector how they want to proceed.

Education Minister Erica Stanford told RNZ the government had to move fast to raise achievement and close equity gaps.

"There is no time to waste when around 60,000 children start school every year," she said. "The work is not finished, but the early signs show why this government has been so relentlessly focused on evidence, implementation and getting support into classrooms quickly.

"We have made enormous change in three years, but these reforms now need time to embed and deliver their full impact. We cannot afford to put that progress at risk."

The past three years have left the school sector poised for consolidation of reforms that will lead to an unprecedented standardisation of what is taught, when it is taught, and how it is taught.

World.title: Recap: Rugby League World Cup: Fiji v Cook Islands
World.content:
The Fiji Bati have started their Rugby League World Cup with a strong win, 40-12 over the Cook Islands.

The Bati scored seven tries to the Aitu's two.

The Fiji Bati sung 'This is my Prayer' (Oqo na noqu masu) in response to Cook Islands' pre-game challenge and went on to a powerful win in the teams' pool clash in Newcastle.

Cook Islands, led by captain KL Iro, laid down the challenge after the national anthems, walking up to the Bati team as they lined up at halfway.

Api Korosau led Fiji Bati in singing their response at halfway.

On the field they managed to rake up seven tries, with Solomone Saukuru finishing with two.

It took the Bati just six minutes to get over the Cook Islands' line and score the first points of the game, with Solomone Saukuru powering over at the left corner, following a flat pass from Kurt Donoghoe.

Playmaker Brandon Wakeham slotted the ball in between the uprights to send the Fijians into the lead with six points.

Then it was Waqa Blake who beat the drifting Cook Islands' defensive line on the right, before a Wakeham bomb saw forward Jacob Saifiti climb high, collect the ball and reached over the line to plant the ball down for his try in the 29th minute.

Taane Milne and Caleb Navale got their names also on the scoresheet, as Fiji led 28-0 at halftime.

Cook Islands had their moments too in the first half, with Esan Masters directing their play.

He also pinned the Fijians on their tryline with two long restarts that forced the Bati to kick off their line twice in the first half.

Mason Teague, Makahesi Makatoa, Delahia Wigmore, Reuben Porter, and Pride Petterson-Robati tried their best to win territory and create chances against the Fijians.

But the Fiji Bati defense stood their ground and responded with their own attacks.

Safiti, Navale, Milne, Kitione Kautoga, Blake, Sunia Turuva and captain Koroisau kept the Bati running forward.

Kitione Kautoga got the Bati on the board again as the second spell started, going over nine minutes after the restart.

However, Cook Islands managed to get some good momentum in the second half and got two tries over Fiji's line.

Maui Winitana-Patelesio and Davvy Moale got two tries for the Cooks midway through the second half.

Winitana-Patelesio sidestepped his way to the tryline to score in front. He converted his own try, closing the gap to 34-6.

Six minutes later Moale ran on to a short pass to crash over. Patelesio converted, with the Cook Islands closing the gap to 34-12.

But with 10 minutes to go 21-year-old Saukuru went over for his second try when he ran on to a short pass from Donoghoe, with the Bati taking control again on the scoreboard. Wakeham pushed Fiji to 40-12 with his additional two points.

Cook Islands made a late push, playing deep in the Fiji Bati red zone but just could not get any more points.

Fiji skipper Koroisau said they knew Cook Islands would be tough and it was a good win as they kicked off their campaign in the pool of death, Pool A.

"We knew what we had to do today and we did that," he said.

"It was a great effort by the boys.

"We executed in that first half and it was a great win and pretty proud of how the boys turned up."

Koroisau said their next clash against world champs Australia will be a tougher match but they will go out to do their best.

"They are at the top of the food chain for a reason and we will go out there and put everything on the field."

Cook Islands captain KL Iro said Fiji was the better team on the day.

"Feels so good to see the fans come out to support us, we are sorry we can't put on a better performance for you guys," he said.

"Fiji were the better team today. They came out harder than we did, unfortunately that's how rugby league is sometimes.

"Very thankful to the family and aways proud to put this jersey on."

World.title: Aitutaki braces for Tropical Cyclone Wati
World.content:
The Aitutaki Island Council has activated its emergency operations centre as Tropical Cyclone Wati approaches.

Wati, a category 2 system, is moving southeast towards the Southern Cook Islands, with conditions expected to deteriorate over the coming days.

The Cook Islands Meteorological Service said Tropical Cyclone Wati is gradually moving south to southeast at around 16 km/h and is about 290km north of Palmerston at 2pm today local time with max sustained winds of upto 91 km/h close to its centre, with gust reaching 130 km/h.

Its forecast for Aitutaki and Ngaputoru (Mauke, Mitiaro and Atiu) is:

Fresh to strong winds of 35-55 km/h, with gusts up to 80 km/h.

Winds are expected to strengthen to damaging gale force from Sunday, averaging around 95 km/h, with gusts up to 130 km/h.

Cloudy periods with showers, increasing to periods of rain, heavy at times with squally thunderstorms from tomorrow.

Rough seas with moderate to heavy swells. High to very high seas are expected from Sunday morning.

For the Northern Cook Islands, the Meteorological Service has issued its final special weather bulletin for the group.

Emergency Management Cook Islands Director, John Strickland told RNZ Pacific its monitoring Wati as it moves towards Aitutaki.

He said Aitutaki island is very much set and prepared.

"Aitutaki is under the management of the island council which is the Mayor, his council, and an executive officer for the Government.

They ave now activated their own emergency operation centre and are ready for anything that might hit them probably tomorrow morning or maybe tonight," he said.

Schools have been organised on the island, and a maintenance team, police, the water authority, Red Cross and other supporting agencies are on stand-by for Wati.

Strickland said its predicted that Wati will go between the islands of Mauke, Mitiaro and Atiu.

Ready for Wati

The Cook Islands Meteorological Service's Nathan Tism said it was fortunate that they spotted the tropical depression before it turned into a tropical cyclone.

"A lot of warnings were sent out to everyone before the system intensified, and because it was up in the north tracking towards the south where no islands in its pathway, we were quite fortunate with that," he said.

The system is forecast to leave the Exclusive Economic Zone of the Cook Islands in the next three days.

World.title: Police officer pleads guilty to dishonestly accessing database, reckless driving
World.content:
A police officer was so keen to impress his brother-in-law that he used a police database to find sensitive information about the man's ex-partner, and took him on an unofficial ride-along, activating the siren and reaching speeds of up to 146km/h.

This week the police officer, who cannot be named for legal reasons, pleaded guilty to representative charges of dishonestly accessing a computer system and reckless driving.

NZME understands he is still employed by New Zealand Police but has been stood down.

In the summary of facts, the police said the constable wanted to show his brother-in-law he had access to privileged information "increasing his importance, influence and credibility".

According to the summary, the police officer used the Police National Intelligence Application database multiple times for non-police business.

The database holds a broad range of sensitive material, including private personal information, incident and intelligence reports and car registration details.

In 2024, he used the database on his phone to look up information on his brother-in-law's ex-partner, such as the names of her current and past boyfriends and family members.

He then shared that knowledge with his brother-in-law.

But that wasn't the first time he accessed the database for personal use, using it multiple times the year before when buying and selling cars.

He checked a car he had sold had been changed to the name of the new buyer and to see if two cars he was looking at buying were of interest to police.

While looking at a third car with his brother-in-law, he looked it up on the database on his phone, in front of the seller and, finding the seller was not the registered owner, challenged him on whether the sale was legit.

The police officer activated the siren and reached speeds of up to 146km/h during the unofficial ride-along. RNZ/ Marika Khabazi

An unofficial ride-along

Early one morning last year, the constable was given a marked patrol car to attend court.

About 1pm, he stopped off at home in the car and asked his brother-in-law if he wanted to go for a drive.

As they drove in a residential area, in a speed limit of 50km/h, he turned on the red and blue flashing lights and siren and accelerated, reaching speeds of up to about 146km/h.

He drove through a street with roadworks at about 101km/h then through a semi-rural 80km/h area at around 135km/h.

He then again got up to 141km/h in a 60km/h area with his emergency lights and sirens still going, overtaking traffic that pulled over for him.

During this time, he crossed to the other side of the road ahead of oncoming traffic.

As he passed another police car, he briefly slowed down and turned off his lights and siren before turning left and accelerating away to 122km/h with his siren blaring, speeding past a primary school and overtaking more cars that pulled over for him.

This took less than an hour, and the police officer dropped off his brother and returned the car to the police station.

His brother-in-law took videos of the police officer driving and laughing.

When spoken to by police the officer declined to comment.

He pleaded guilty to the two representative charges this week, and is set to be sentenced in February.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: High school students urged to get vaccinated to prevent measles disrupting exams
World.content:
High school students are being urged to ensure they are fully vaccinated against measles, to help prevent an outbreak like the one that disrupted exams and end of year celebrations at multiple schools last year.

Last November measles cases were reported among students from Wellington College, Wellington Girls' College and Auckland Grammar, with some unvaccinated students asked to stay home.

Nikki Turner, the Immunisation Advisory Centre's principal medical adviser, said students sitting NCEA exams should ensure they are fully vaccinated against measles as overseas outbreaks increase the risk of the virus being brought into New Zealand.

She said there were increasing numbers of outbreaks around the world, leading to sporadic cases of measles popping up in New Zealand.

"Many young people may be unsure of their vaccination history, but it is safe and recommended to be vaccinated if there is any doubt," Turner said.

She said measles can have serious complications.

"It can do anything from killing you, to cause inflammation of the brain and brain damage, a whole lot of other consequences.

"The other problem with measles is if you catch it but get through it it actually affects your immune system, so for many months afterwards you are prone to other infectious disease as well. It is a very nasty virus."

World.title: Election 2026: Everything that happened on the campaign trail today
World.content:
It has been another busy Sunday on the campaign trail, with politicians spread out across the motu making policy announcements and meeting supporters as election day draws closer.

There have been significant announcements from National and Labour regarding children's screentime and justice, but the minor parties also had plenty to say.

Here's everything you need to know about what happened on the campaign trail on Sunday, 18 October.

NZ First leader Winston Peters speaks in Christchurch on Sunday, 18 October. RNZ/Keiller MacDuff

NZ First commits to 12-month commuter rail trial in Canterbury

New Zealand First says it will commit to a 12-month trial of commuter rail in Canterbury, as well as bringing back the Southerner Train that connected Christchurch with Dunedin and Invercargill, if re-elected.

Winston Peters said the party's ambition was to get passengers from Rolleston to central Christchurch in around 20 minutes by train, instead of spending up to 50 minutes on the road.

He said travelling from Rangiora into Christchurch by train would be faster than driving too. Currently, the KiwiRail train that covers that stretch of track takes about 30 minutes to get from Addington in Christchurch to Rangiora.

It would give Cantabrians a real alternative to sitting in traffic every morning and every evening, he said.

Labour announces its screens policy on Sunday. RNZ/Baz Macdonald

Labour pledges $7m to get kids off screens

Labour wants to get kids off screens and "back to being kids" by making after-school activities more affordable, setting "healthier" boundaries in schools and providing better support for parents when it comes to online safety for children.

At a cost of $7 million per year, Labour would invest in programmes that offer grants to help children take part in sport and recreation, and in community groups running after-school sport and activities for kids.

Labour Leader Chris Hipkins says too much of childhood is being spent on screens, while sport, hobbies and other after-school activities are out of reach for too many families.

The Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick speaks to media on Sunday. Nick Monro/RNZ

Opposition parties raise concerns over what they say is voter suppression

Opposition parties are raising concerns over what they call voter suppression by the government, as the enrolment deadline draws near.

Recent figures from the Electoral Commission show that as of the 15 October only 65.5 percent of 18-24 year olds are enrolled to vote.

It also comes as RNZ revealed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon picked a "challenging" election date, despite the Electoral Commission favouring two other options.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was "very concerned" about enrolments, particularly about youth enrolments, as well as people being moved onto the dormant role.

The Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick was also "incredibly concerned about this government's moves to actively suppress voting in this country".

Paul Goldsmith says too many children die at the hands of those who should be protecting them. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

National would remove right to silence in cases of child murder

National says it will take away a person's right to silence when a child is murdered if the party is re-elected.

Justice spokesperson Paul Goldsmith announced on Sunday morning that the party would make it a Crimes Act offence not to disclose information to police when a person has been present at the location where a child under 12 has been killed.

It would carry a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison.

"Too many children in New Zealand die at the hands of, or with the knowledge of, people who should be protecting them. The right to silence should not be abused to the extent that these horrific crimes go unpunished," Goldsmith said.

ACT leader David Seymour campaigns on Sunday. Lauren Crimp/RNZ Political Reporter

ACT pledges $400 million to get more doctors

The ACT Party plans to keep more general practitioners in New Zealand and attract more from overseas with a $400 million funding boost.

Announcing the policy on Sunday morning, ACT'S Tāmaki candidate James Christmas says the money would increase the supply of appointments by keeping the doctors NZ already has, rather than subsidising demand.

"That means a parent can get a sick child seen more quickly, that means the cough that won't go away or the lump that you're concerned about can get checked early before it becomes serious. And it means that we keep more people out of our emergency departments, where they don't need to be."

World.title: One person killed in avalanche on Mount Dixon
World.content:
The body of a man who died following an avalanche in the Aoraki Mount Cook National Park this morning has been recovered.

Police say the man became trapped in an avalanche on Mount Dixon.

Emergency services were called just after 10am, and Search and Rescue was activated.

World.title: Recap: New Zealand Kiwi Ferns v Fiji Bulikula - women's Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
The Kiwi Ferns have been given a huge fright in their Rugby League World Cup opener, before beating Fiji 18-12 in Newcastle.

The courageous Fiji Bulikula, playing in their maiden World Cup, refused to be overawed.

With the score 10-12 at the break, Fiji held their lead until 18 minutes in the second half when the Ferns drew level with a penalty from former Jillaroo Zahara Temara.

She booted over another to give them a 14-12 lead with five minutes remaining.

Leianne Tufuga scored the try that sealed Fiji's fate, scoring in the corner after a superb chip kick from Raecene McGregor with two minutes to go.

Stacey Waaka scored both New Zealand's tries in the first half, benefiting firstly from a long pass from Apii Nicholls for the first effort and then a beautiful delayed pass from centre Mele Hufanga for the second.

In between those efforts Losana Lutu scored for Fiji, followed by Sienna Laing, who kicked ahead and scored after a grubber from Lutu.

The Kiwi Ferns did most of the attacking in the second half but it took them an age before they finally broke the Fijian resistance.

World.title: Animal welfare group calls for accountability after latest racing death
World.content:
Animal welfare campaigners have called for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths after Ohope Wins was put down following a fall in the Caulfield Cup.

The Chris Waller-trained Ohope Wins was in the finishing straight of the 2,400m Group One race when it was brought down by last year's winner, Half Yours, which had fallen at the 300m mark.

Half Yours got up and ran riderless down the straight, while Ohope Wins was assessed by vets as it lay on the track and was euthanased.

Half Yours received lacerations and abrasions after falling in the Caulfield Cup, but got up and ran to the finish rider-less. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours's rider Mark Zahra and Ohope Wins's jockey Jye McNeil were taken to hospital for observation.

Racing Victoria confirmed Zahra was released on Saturday night, and McNeil would be released on Sunday, with both jockeys escaping serious injury.

Racing Victoria stewards will hold an inquiry into the incident, although a time has not been set for this to happen.

Ohope Wins euthanased after Caulfield Cup fall A Racing Victoria track veterinarian euthanases New Zealand mare Ohope Wins after a shocking fall in the Caulfield Cup that included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

The Coalition for the Protection of Horses campaign director Elio Celotto said at least 160 horses have been killed as a result of injuries sustained in racing across Australia this year.

"When a horse falls their legs are very delicately poised when they hit the turf," Mr Celotto said speaking to ABC's News Breakfast.

"They're a half a tonne horse and all they need to do is fall slightly off and it can result in damage to their bones and that is why we see so many horses killed on our race tracks."

He said the racing industry was responsible for deaths on race tracks.

"The racing industry has got a lot to answer for. They say they are open and transparent, they are anything but," he said.

"They really need to be made accountable for the thousands [over the years], not just the horse that was killed yesterday, but all the horses that are killed around Australia simply to make money and for the pleasure of punters. It's simply not acceptable."

Top racing trainer Peter Moody defended the industry, saying that safety improvements had been brought in since a series of deaths in the Melbourne Cup beginning more than a decade ago.

Moody told ABC Radio Brisbane there were less incidents in major races following the changes, including what he called "stringent protocols" horses go through before they are allowed to race by authorities.

Most of the deaths in the Melbourne Cup were standalone incidents, where horses broke down while running rather than colliding with or falling over other horses.

Racing Victoria requires all international horses coming for major races to have one CT scan of the distal (lower) limbs to identify possible bone damage before travel. They then must have a standing CT scan before every start in the Spring Racing Carnival.

There have been no further deaths in the Melbourne Cup since the introduction of scanning requirements.

Mandatory scans for Melbourne Cup runners A diagnostic scan on racehorse Anthony Van Dyck may have picked up on the potential for more serious injuries before his ill-fated run in the Melbourne Cup, a review finds.

Moody described the incident at Caulfield as "very sad and very disappointing".

Moody was asked if there was any way such incidents could be avoided when big fields of horses were running around.

"Whether there were some misjudgements, some horses rolled around in the race, it got tight, one horse (Half Yours) stumbled and dislodged the rider, and then the second horse unfortunately got tangled in that horse and fell also," he said.

"It's just one of those unfortunate accidents. No-one sets out for that to happen. Everyone wants to see the horses and the riders come home safely.

"The love and care and attention [given] to these animals is second to none.

"Unfortunately in all walks of life, whether it's horse racing, a football match, walking across the road to catch a bus and accidents do happen."

World.title: 'Outstanding' Tonga puts England on the brink of World Cup elimination
World.content:
Coach Kristian Woolf says Tonga showed off its new-found "depth and quality" in marching past England at the Rugby League World Cup.

The result left the English at risk of missing the semifinals for the first time.

With His Majesty King Tupou VI and Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala among the sellout 18,302 crowd in Perth on Saturday night, Tonga controlled the game when it counted, for a 30-12 win.

"We got more and more confident. What I liked the most was the way we defended; we put ourselves under pressure a couple of times, but our defence was outstanding," Woolf said after the game.

"You could see how much the game meant to us, and we showed that in our effort, and it's something that will carry us through the tournament."

The Mate Ma'a got better as the game went on, powering away from the world number three side to seal a victory which puts them in the box seat to reach the semifinals.

Kangaroos halfback's World Cup over Mitchell Moses will play no further part in Australia's Rugby League World Cup campaign after suffering a calf injury.

A first-half try to Stefano Utoikamanu set up a 10-0 lead at the break. But an early score from AJ Brimson was quickly countered, with two tries to Haumole Olakau'atu and one from Tolutau Koula asTonga ran away with the game.

A try to Dominic Young with under 20 minutes to go was only a consolation for England.

"We've done some special things with the Tonga team, but we're still quite new to beating tier-one nations, and England are that – they're a very strong team. We knew they would come out and be physical, and challenge us in different ways," Woolf said.

"It's a continuation of a journey that we're on. If you look at some of the young guys and some of the guys who are a little bit more experienced now, the experience they've got over the last three or four years has been outstanding.

"It's put us in a really good position. They're getting better and better. We've got depth and quality, and we can go and do something with it now."

Team Tonga took their bows to the big crowd in Perth after wrapping up a vital win over England. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The defeat is a huge blow to England's chances.

England (or previously Great Britain) has never failed to reach the final four at a Rugby League World Cup.

This result leaves Brian McDermott's team likely to fall short, given the format of the competition.

The team was playing for the first time since losing to Australia in Leeds in November last year.

"It was a really good contest, and when it wasn't a contest, that was probably more to do with us in the errors that we made," McDermott said.

"They're a big team, strong team, and they've got some tremendous players in there. And I thought we we stuck toe-to-toe with them for nearly all the game."

England has to beat France on October 24 and Papua New Guinea on October 30 and hope other results and scores go their way, as they try to finish in the top two of the combined six-team Pool B and C.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

With Samoa opening its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, it leaves England needing to post massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Renshaw to stay at number five as Aussies delay naming Test side
World.content:
Matt Renshaw is set to remain at number five for the second Test against South Africa, as Australia waits on the opening day's weather to name the team.

Captain Pat Cummins confirmed on Saturday he expected Renshaw to again bat in the middle order after his match-winning heroics in Durban.

That all but ensures Nic Maddinson will stay in the side and open with Travis Head, after scores of 0 and 48 on his shock Test recall last week.

Renshaw's scores of 190 and 82 came after he'd originally been recalled as an opener in Australia's previous Test against Bangladesh, the position where he has batted for most his career.

Test win silences critics Australia started the first Test against South Africa on the back foot, but its 214-run victory has silenced any critics of the selection strategy.

"After what Renners did last week, I presume he'll stay at number five," Cummins said on the eve of the Gqeberha Test.

"What he deserved even more credit for is that we'd asked him to do a different role, and he just said straight away, 'Yep, no worries, whatever the team needs.'

"So many positives in addition to the runs he scored last week. He was a delight, and really helped me and [Nathan] Lyon get through those partnerships."

Cummins also confirmed Cameron Green remained sidelined with an abdominal strain, while Josh Inglis was close to being declared fit.

Josh Inglis is unlikely to return despite recovering from a fractured finger.

Even if Inglis is cleared to play following his fractured finger, it is unlikely he will be able to force his way into Australia's side.

Rain is expected across the opening two days in Gqeberha, with the prospect that both sides will be able to factor that into their XIs should the toss be delayed.

That could potentially reduce the need for spin and provide the option of a fourth quick in Scott Boland, with extra grass also left on the St George's Park wicket.

Depending on the weather in Gqeberha, Scott Boland could get one of his rare chances to break into the Australian side. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor, file photo)

But Cummins gave every indication that Lyon would remain as a key part of the attack.

"We always look at all options," Cummins said when asked if it was conceivable that they could go in without a specialist spinner.

"We love playing with Nath. We saw last week, a couple of key wickets in the first innings.

"And even the control he gives. It makes the rest of us fast bowlers be able to function around him."

AAP

World.title: Is New Zealand holding back women's Test cricket?
World.content:
For years fans and players have been crying out for more women's Test cricket.

Yet by the time Australia's women next don the whites at Headingley to kickstart the 2027 Ashes, 15 months will have passed since their last red-ball match.

Much of this comes down to the team's limited opposition. Just four of the top-ranked women's teams have cricket boards willing to commit to Tests.

Australia, England, India and South Africa have been pushing forward the past five years.

They've played 13 Tests since 2021, either as a standalone or part of a multi-format series, a significant improvement on the five years prior when two Tests were played worldwide.

Both of these fell in the 2017 and 2019 Ashes. The biennial contest has safeguarded tradition for England and Australia at a time when governing bodies have been hell-bent on growing the women's game through the shorter formats.

Australia and England play one Test as part of each multi-format Women's Ashes series. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

In fact, the Ashes points-based system used to determine the better side across three T20Is, three ODIs and a single Test, has widely been suggested by administrators and players as the best way to increase women's Tests overall. Enticing those on the fence to give it a go.

Tacking on a four-day Test match to a tour that already features six white-ball fixtures sounds like a no-brainer.

Unfortunately, two countries have knocked back that idea this year.

Australia missed out on a chance to face the West Indies in a Test for the first time in 50 years in March when their plans to play a multi-format series in the Caribbean fell through.

Then New Zealand declined to play a Test against Australia later in the year.

The three T20Is and three ODIs scheduled between the trans-Tasman rivals were originally supposed to run through February and March, but when the ICC's inaugural Champions Trophy shifted on the calendar, the tour had to be split.

Instead the three T20Is will now be played at North Sydney Oval, starting Sunday, while the ODIs will still be played at the end of the summer.

The White Ferns are currently in Australia to play three T20 internationals. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

As close neighbours, the White Ferns would be ideal opponents for regular Test match cricket. Both in proximity and habit, the sides already meet most seasons for the Rose Bowl series.

Sadly, New Zealand Cricket doesn't share that view.

Despite being one of the first three nations to play women's Test cricket in the 1930s, it now refuses to play the longest version of the game.

Limited overs prioritised

The summer of 1934–35 saw the birth of women's Test cricket, when Australia and New Zealand hosted England on its first overseas tour.

Now, the White Ferns haven't played a Test since 2004.

After the governance of the men's and women's sides of the game were amalgamated, the frequency of Tests for the White Ferns gradually decreased and have now been non-existent for 22 years.

It also appears New Zealand Cricket is unwilling to budge on the matter, as per their previous statement in the media:

"The limited-overs formats have proven to be very effective in terms of attracting and retaining young players, which is a significant factor in the health of the women's game here. "In time, this will provide a bigger base from which talented players will emerge to ultimately play for the White Ferns. "Focusing on formats which include ICC global events, such as World Cups, is our preference for now."

ABC Sport requested a fresh response and more clarification but did not hear back.

That means retiring Kiwi legends Sophie Devine, Suzie Bates and Lea Tahuhu never got to experience red-ball cricket internationally.

At the end of the T20 World Cup the trio retired.

The New Zealanders warmed up for their T20Is in Australia with a clash against the Governor-General's XI. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Various Australian players told ABC Sport it was an "atrocity" and a "real shame" that after 15 to 20 years of service the trio weren't offered the opportunity.

"Those girls are absolute icons and to think that they've never played a Test match and never will, knowing that they want to, that's tricky," Australia captain Sophie Molineux said.

"Hopefully one day we can play another Test against New Zealand, that would be really special."

"It's a tragedy that they won't get a baggy black cap," Beth Mooney said.

"I feel really sorry for them," Ellyse Perry added.

"They've had amazing, decorated international careers and never got to experience it."

Equal pay to blame

In 2022, New Zealand Cricket was heralded for a groundbreaking pay deal that granted men and women equal match fees.

From then on, when representing their country, both sets of athletes would be paid $NZ4,000 ($3,245) per ODI and $NZ2,500 per T20I.

Although this five-year agreement, due to expire next year, was a positive step in the recognition of female cricketers, it seems to have put the final nail in the coffin for Tests. Requiring a fee of $NZ10,250 per player, it pushed the dream further out of reach.

Especially in light of New Zealand Cricket's latest budget update, which predicted a $NZ7.3 million deficit for the past financial year.

New chief executive Geoff Allott started in the role in July and has indicated the organisation will need "to be prudent" as it looks to get back on track and "ensure long-term sustainability" of the game.

Tahuhu, Devine and Bates made history as New Zealand won its first T20 World Cup in 2024. (AP: Altaf Qadri)

White Ferns head coach Ben Sawyer recently finished up a four-year tenure where he took the team to its maiden Women's T20 World Cup victory in 2024 and a bronze medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games.

Speaking with ABC Sport, Sawyer highlighted the financial burden and the recent news that the England and Wales Cricket Board is considering footing the bill for its April Test match against the West Indies in order to ensure their 2027 multi-format series goes ahead.

"The reality is that it's a very expensive venture because of the equal match payments in New Zealand, and the cost is a huge part of it," Sawyer said.

"I'm assuming that's over $NZ150,000 in match payments and there are other priorities for them.

"Their domestic structure isn't full-time, and so it's my opinion that they think that money could be better used elsewhere."

Sawyer has previously held a range of coaching roles in women's cricket — as an Australian assistant, the head coach of the Sydney Sixers and the head coach of the Birmingham Phoenix.

Ben Sawyer has held several high-profile coaching roles in women's cricket. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He explained that New Zealand's top players are only contracted from October to March for eight hours per week. They train individually in the off-season and with teammates in-season at night after work.

When Sawyer first took on the White Ferns job, he recommended the national sporting body copy England's county system and gradually build their numbers the same way; starting with two to three professionals in each county, before eventually signing five to seven and then making the entire team full-time.

Since then, he hasn't seen any progress in this regard.

"I've always respected the vision that Cricket Australia have for five to 10 years down the track and the money they're willing to invest; that's what makes them the best in the world," he said.

If New Zealand Cricket was to change its mind and green-light a women's Test, Sawyer believes it'd be better to play someone with a lower ranking and a similar part-time domestic structure.

"They'd need a good lead in, and I wouldn't necessarily want to play Australia first.

"Maybe that's where two countries like New Zealand and Sri Lanka get together and say let's play one.

"I've got no doubt it'd be tough and hard the first time, but it's the only way to get better."

This article was written for the ABC Cricket Magazine, available online, or in local newsagents from November.

World.title: Meet the first hijab-wearing non-verbal wheelchair basketballer
World.content:
It was the speed and adrenaline that first attracted Reema El Qassem to wheelchair basketball.

After two years in the game, she is regarded as one of the best up and coming players in the Women's National Wheelchair Basketball League.

Not only extremely talented, El Qassem is the first non-verbal and hijab-wearing player on the court, challenging the notion of who belongs in the game.

"I feel the most alive and the most able when I'm playing sport," El Qassem told ABC Sport.

"For those moments, I'm not thinking about my disability; I'm just an athlete."

Reema El Qassem plays for the Sydney Uni Lions in the National Wheelchair Basketball League. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

El Qassem's journey has been a difficult one; she acquired her disability, Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), in 2023.

The condition affects how the brain and nervous system function, leading to a variety of neurological symptoms, including walking and speech difficulties, cognitive issues, and chronic fatigue.

After spending 320 days in hospital and taking eight months to adjust to life as a wheelchair user, sport was the pathway to normality for El Qassem.

"When the doctors told me I would be going home in a wheelchair, I remember thinking, that's OK, I'll just play wheelchair basketball," the 35-year-old said.

"Finding sport again after acquiring my disability felt like finding a part of myself that I had lost."

It's been a meteoric rise in the sport for El Qassem, who plays for the Sydney Uni Lions, with the team making it to both the 2025 and 2026 national league play-offs.

Paralympian Hannah Dodd is coach of the Sydney Uni Lions and a mentor for Reema El Qassem. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

In recent years the women's game has been actively rebuilding across the country, adding three new teams to the national league in 2025.

Sydney Uni Lions player and coach Hannah Dodd believes this growth is what has supported the development of players like El Qassem.

"She's naturally got a really good push on her, and she's got naturally some good speed on her, so we've just been teaching her how to control it and how to use it successfully," Dodd said.

"It's just teaching her the patience and the finesse of things."

It's not just the team that is teaching El Qassem; in bringing her disability and faith to the court, she is showing the league that anyone can play.

Muslim women face additional barriers

Muslim women can face many barriers in sport, such as uniforms that don't meet modesty needs, discrimination and inflexibility around religious and cultural practices.

Reema El Qassem's community, including her four daughters, often turn up to support her at national league games. (Supplied: Wheelchair Sports NSW/ACT)

This has made El Qassem's journey into wheelchair basketball even more remarkable as the first ever player to wear a hijab on the court.

Marta Myhill, from Wheelchair Sports NSW, said El Qassem was helping those around her learn about her culture and faith.

"In her bringing her culture, wearing her hijab, there's not a problem with that at all," Myhill said.

"Everybody within the wheelchair basketball community has embraced her."

From her teammates reminding her it was time to pray, as well as notifying officials and players that they can't shake her hand, the support has almost bought El Qassem to tears.

"Growing up, I spent a lot of time trying to shrink myself and be subtle because I was always scared to draw attention," she said.

"To be so outwardly me as a Muslim woman and feel safe and welcome to practise my faith is something I don't take for granted."

Another key part of El Qassem's life is being a single mother to four daughters, some of whom also have additional needs.

Balancing her sport, faith and family can be a challenge.

The single mother of four daughters wants to show what is possible for other Muslim and non-verbal women in sport. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"There is always that guilt when I leave them, when I fly interstate, or when I come home from sport and I'm too tired for them," El Qassem said.

"There were so many times when I considered leaving the sport completely because I felt like I was being a bad mum for choosing myself."

As a mother, it has been important for El Qassem to show her children what people with disabilities are capable of.

Loading Instagram content

They have become her biggest supporters, with El Qassem taking them to cheer her on at national league games.

"It [wheelchair basketball] gives them an environment where they can admire other people, appreciate what they have, and understand that life isn't over because someone has a disability or because something difficult has happened to them," El Qassem said.

"Now they see the person, they see the athleticism, the speed, the talent, the strength, and the determination, and for me, that is such a beautiful thing for them to experience."

Non-verbal El Qassem team's 'loudest player'

Naturally very expressive, El Qassem relies on body language and facial expressions, alongside her phone app, to communicate with her team on and off the court.

So much so, last season she won the Uni Lions team award for the loudest player.

But the technology on her phone can be fiddly to use and doesn't quite cut through the ambient sounds during a game.

Generally, Reema El Qassem uses a phone app to communicate, but this doesn't work when on the court during a game. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"I can't call out that a pick is coming, call for help, or yell out to my teammates that I'm open," she said.

"Those are all things I would normally be communicating on court.

"I'm starting to see and understand the game as a whole, rather than just my own role and that has made me much more aware of the impact of being non-verbal."

Embracing the challenge with gusto, the Sydney Uni Lions have trialled different tools to help El Qassem communicate with her teammates, including talking buttons.

Unfortunately, these were not loud enough for game days when fans were cheering from the sidelines.

They are also contemplating trialling an air horn of some kind, which she could bump with the side of her leg, but the search for an effective solution is ongoing.

"Having a player like Reema has obviously been a new experience for all of us and a new way to figure out how to play a very verbal sport, non-verbally," Dodd said.

"A lot of the time we'll pair [Reema] up our most experienced pointers, to help her navigate, so she has someone that will talk to her constantly."

The Sydney Uni Lions wheelchair basketball team has been working with Reema El Qassem to figure out a way for her to communicate on court. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

Despite occasionally feeling frustrated having to rely on her team this way, El Qassem appreciates the community and friendship she has found with the Lions.

Being in a safe and supported environment has enabled her to focus on developing her potential and set her sights on representing Australia one day.

Getting classified to play at an international level, however, has proven her biggest barrier in the sport yet.

The role of classification is to make Para sport as equal and fair as possible for all athletes, but in recent years there have been some changes that have affected newer athletes like El Qassem.

Unfortunately, her impairment, FND, doesn't fit within eligibility requirements for the sport.

Reema El Qassem dreams one day of playing for Australia in wheelchair basketball, but faces an uphill battle to be classified. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"The problem isn't that the disability isn't real, it's that the current classification system isn't designed around [it]," El Qassem said.

Unable to be classified for international competition means that El Qassem is limited to playing within the national and local league seasons.

"There is not a lot of competition available for us in Australia; even our national league only runs for three months of the year," Dodd said.

"[It's] trying to get game time for the developing players, in a space where they're comfortable and where they are going to succeed and not get frightened or stressed."

Representation and belonging key: El Qassem

While El Qassem may be locked out of international competition, it's her cheerleaders at home that make the game worth it, including retired Paralympic wheelchair basketballer Gerry Hewson.

Reema El Qassem is working with retired Paralympian Gerry Hewson to improve her skills. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

El Qassem has brought Hewson on for one-on-one training with the focus on building her skills, with Hewson taking her through her drills each week.

Hewson says her determination is unbelievable.

"She's on a big learning curve at the moment," he said.

"For me as a coach it's just kind of building her self-belief that she can play at a national league level and that's what I'm trying to help her out to do."

And while the dream of representing Australia one day is still there, for El Qassem it is the community she has created and the pathways she is carving out for athletes like her that keep her in the sport.

Reema El Qassem wants to see more Muslim and non-verbal women participating in sport. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"For Muslim women living with disabilities, I think representation and belonging are particularly important, and we deserve to see ourselves in sport too," she said.

"I also love how sports bring people together. It doesn't matter what your race, ethnicity, background or mobility is, everyone has a place, and everyone belongs."

World.title: Wallaroos not content with simply being 'better versions' of themselves
World.content:
Among Siokapesi Palu Sekona's many impressive qualities as Wallaroos captain is her uncompromising approach.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

As such, it does not come as a shock to learn she feels the Wallaroos still have much room for improvement following their dominant 56-12 win over Scotland in this afternoon's Global XV Series Test.

The eight-tries-to-two victory did not represent a complete performance in Palu Sekona's eyes, which should serve as music to the ears of Wallaroos supporters.

Why?

It shows the Wallaroos are setting the highest possible standards for themselves.

"We still know there is room for improvement and we definitely know what to do to clean that up," Palu Sekona said.

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona put in a solid shift on both sides of the ball. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Wallaroos defeated Scotland 30-10 three weeks ago in Edinburgh during their three-Test swing through Great Britain and France as part of the Global XV Series.

The victory snapped a six-match losing streak but left Wallaroos players and coaches dissatisfied.

It was a sign of the Wallaroos' quickly developing harder edge, which Palu Sekona wants carried through to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

"We knew we could put together a better performance," she said.

"Ultimately results and scores are what people look at. But if we want to break down our rugby, there are so many things to clean up.

"From discipline, to our ruck, to the accuracy of our set-piece. There are things we can continue to work on."

Wallaroos set bar high

The Wallaroos, ranked seventh in the world, are starting from behind scratch when compared to teams such as England and New Zealand.

Both enjoy the benefit of being full-time programs, with their respective governing bodies making a wise move to invest in the women's game.

The Wallaroos are still semi-professional, but a shift to full-time status — as part of an integrated program alongside the women's sevens squad — is in progress.

There is no doubt the Wallaroos' rate of improvement will be accelerated once they go full-time in the lead-up to the World Cup, which Australia will host.

"We don't want to only be the better versions of ourselves," Palu Sekona said.

" We want to be the best in the world. "

Winger Amelia Whitaker scored a double in the Wallaroos' victory. (Getty Images/Corbis: Steve Christo)

The Wallaroos' makeshift coaching team, under the leadership of Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh, has had a positive influence on the playing group.

Sione Fukofuka will take over as head coach next year and work alongside Walsh, who enjoyed tremendous success in charge of the Australian women's sevens squad.

Like Palu Sekona, Walsh was not completely satisfied with the Wallaroos' display against Scotland.

But he saw enough to know they are heading in the right direction.

"I think it was another step forward, for sure," Walsh said.

The Wallaroos will complete their 2026 Test season when they meet Scotland in Canberra on Friday night.

World.title: World Cup heartbreak for Kangaroos half as Tonga notches first win over England
World.content:
Mitchell Moses will miss the remainder of the Rugby League World Cup, after being ruled out of the Kangaroos' title defence with a lower leg injury that continues his representative misery.

The Parramatta playmaker suffered the injury during Australia's 24-22 win over New Zealand in the tournament opener on Thursday night in Sydney.

He attempted to play on but eventually left the field less than two minutes into the second half.

Meanwhile, England's hopes of reaching the World Cup semi-finals are already on life support after suffering a 30-12 loss to world No.5 Tonga in their blockbuster showdown in Perth.

Moses was injured during the Kangaroos' World Cup opener against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Matt King)

While initially believed to be a calf issue or a hairline fracture, scans following the match revealed Moses had suffered an unspecified "high-grade muscle tear", meaning his World Cup campaign is over.

It's a blow to the Kangaroos, who are already missing Nathan Cleary with a serious leg injury, with Moses the Kangaroos' strongest last-tackle kicker.

Moses switched allegiance to play for Australia at this tournament after captaining Lebanon at the 2022 World Cup.

In Perth, Tonga produced a defensive masterclass in its four-tries-to-two victory over England.

The result put Tonga in the box seat to reach the semis, with games against Lebanon and Samoa to round out the group stage.

England's World Cup campaign is already on life support after Tonga's statement win in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

In contrast, world No.3 England have been left on the brink of elimination — even if it wins its remaining two games against France and PNG.

Under the confusing group stage system employed for the World Cup, only two teams from across pools B and C will progress to the last four.

If England finish on the same number of wins as Tonga, then Tonga will go through given they won Saturday's head-to-head battle.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

Samoa opened its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, leaving England needing to post some massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

Stefano Utoikamanu opened the scoring in the 24th minute when he found a hole in England's defence to stroll over untouched.

A pair of Isaiya Katoa penalty goals extended the margin to 10 points by half-time, with England left to rue a series of fumbles and near misses.

England started the second half full of steam, resulting in a team-lifting try to AJ Brimson in the 46th minute.

But in a game where hard work was king, it was a slice of fortune that ended up giving Tonga a vital edge with Haumole Olakau'atu scoring the first of his two tries after he soccered the ball into an opponent's arm and then gathered the bouncing rebound.

And when Tuimoala Lolohea's neat dribble found Tolutau Koula in the corner to make it 22-6 in the 58th minute, it was as good as game over.

The win was a powerful statement from Tonga, whose only previous taste of international success against England came in 2019 when they beat Great Britain.

In Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea's men's side earned a gritty 42-18 win over Lebanon hours after the country's women's team had dispatched France 58-4.

Veteran Rhyse Martin began his farewell tournament in style, scoring a try and going perfect from seven conversions against a dogged Lebanon outfit.

His try with nine minutes left on the clock finished off the Cedars, who were fading in humid conditions.

But Lebanon never stopped trying, with fullback Jacob Kiraz (207 metres) and winger Tony Frances (292 metres) constant threats in attack, while Wests Tigers stalwart Alex Twal led the defence with 48 tackles.

Winger Naomi Kelly crossed four times in the women's game as the Orchids ran in 12 tries to one.

England ended the day's women's action in comprehensive fashion against Wales, with Connie Boyd and Anna Davies both scoring hat-tricks in the 70-6 rout in Perth.

AAP/ABC

World.title: 'Terrible to watch': Ohope Wins euthanased after fall in Caulfield Cup
World.content:
New Zealand mare Ohope Wins has been euthanased after a fall in the Caulfield Cup that also included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

With about 200 metres to go in the 2,400m race, which was won by Gavin Bedggood's Kingswood, Half Yours was in the middle of the pack when there appeared to be contact with Kings Valley.

Half Yours went down hard, sending jockey Mark Zahra into the turf, with Ohope Wins also coming down after Jye McNeil was unable to avoid the fallen McEvoy Racing product.

Racing Victoria Stewards later confirmed Ohope Wins, from Chris Waller Racing, was euthanased by the on-course veterinarian.

Jye McNeil on Ohope Wins in the mounting yard before the Caulfield Cup. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"The mare was unable to be saved due to the nature of the injury sustained," a Racing Victoria (RV) statement read.

"RV extends its condolences to Yulong, the owners of Ohope Wins, her trainer Chris Waller and their stable staff who cared for the horse and are deeply saddened by their loss."

Yulong and Waller released a statement, saying "few words can express our current emotions".

"Ohope Wins was a true star of the turf, but to the people who looked after her everyday, she was so much more," the statement read.

"She was brave. She was kind. She was full of character, but more importantly, she was loved.

Ohope Wins won the Oaks at Randwick in April. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

"Our hearts go out to all involved throughout her career, especially those who cared for her on a daily basis."

Half Yours, the defending Caulfield Cup victor, got up and eventually crossed the finish line without a jockey.

The stewards said Half Yours would undergo a "thorough veterinary examination" after falling in "a racing incident", which would be subject to an inquiry.

Half Yours got up and crossed the line without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours returned to his stall, while stewards said Zahra and McNeil were both "conscious and alert" and transported to hospital for further assessment.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said after the race that Half Yours had suffered some abrasions but looked OK, all things considered.

"That was terrible to watch," McEvoy said.

"The horse, he's got a couple of lacerations, he seems bright, he seems composed in himself.

"He's got a laceration under his arm, he's got a laceration on a hind leg. They look superficial."

The final race of the day at Caulfield was delayed.

Tech.title: TikTok bans Musk documentary account
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, was informed Friday afternoon that a “permanent suspension” was imminent. Bleecker Street has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase.

Last month, YouTube, Meta, X, and TikTok all faced backlash for rejecting ads for the film. YouTube and Google quickly reversed course, calling it an “error.” However, TikTok and X have refused to change their stance, and neither platform has allowed paid s for the film.

Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.”

The irony. Screenshot: The Hollywood Reporter

Tech.title: Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Earlier this year, Mercedes’ AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower. Well, now meet its beefier cousin, the 2028 Mercedes-AMG GT SUV, an equally powerful, ultra-fast-charging electric people-hauler.

The AMG GT SUV (say that five times fast) marks the first time in the performance brand’s 59-year history that it has developed a full-size SUV entirely in-house from the ground up. Scheduled to hit the US next summer, the new EV is built on Merc’s high-performance AMG.EA architecture to combine sports-car handling with full-size SUV suburban practicality.

It will be available in three trims — GT 53, GT 55, and the flagship GT 63 — with the top model delivering 1,153hp via the same three axial flux motors powering the four-door coupe. That beats the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric with Launch Control, which is sure to make for some awkward run-ins around Stuttgart.

Previous Next

















1 / 10

Thanks to an 800-volt architecture, the SUV supports blistering-fast charging speeds up to 710kW on the 128kWh battery (GT 63 / GT 55) and 600kW on the 106kWh battery (GT 53). Drivers can charge 10–80 percent in 12 minutes or gain up to 450km (around 280 miles) of WLTP range in just 10 minutes. The 128kWh battery trims will have an estimated max range of 435 miles.

That battery, by the way? It utilizes F1-inspired technology with specialized NCMA cathodes, silicon-containing anodes, and cylindrical cells. An electrically nonconductive oil flows directly around each individual cell for uniform thermal management, enabling continuous high-power delivery and long battery life. Mercedes has quietly been on the vanguard of battery technology for a while now, with the AMG GT SUV just the latest example. The 710kW charging speed, in particular, could give Mercedes another edge over Porsche’s 320kW speeds.

For a full-size SUV, the AMG GT sounds like it could handle like a vehicle half its size. Mercedes-AMG replaced the traditional mechanical roll bars with a newly developed suspension that uses active hydraulic elements to eliminate pitch and roll during acceleration, heavy braking, and cornering. Combined with three-stage air springs and standard six-degree active rear-axle steering, it purports to balance track precision with long-distance comfort.

But just because it’s a beefy lad doesn’t mean it’ll tip the scales. The AMG GT 63 SUV weighs in at 5,941lbs, making it slightly lighter than the Lotus Eletre R (6,007lbs) and Lucid Gravity (6,100lbs), and nearly identical to the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric (5,960lbs).

Previous Next















1 / 9

Silence is golden — except to a performance brand’s EV engineering team. That means piping in recorded sounds of real AMGs — in this case, the legendary AMG V8 and six-cylinder engines — to preserve the “emotional” AMG identity. Mercedes is proud that it’s using real engine sounds over synthetic EV tones, though some may disagree. The system even simulates mechanical gear shifts with paddle controls, offers adjustable sound profiles, and integrates physical seat vibrations — so you can still feel like there’s a real engine under that hood instead of a 78-liter frunk. The so-called AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program is offered as standard across all three trims of the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV.

Inside, you’ll find the MB.OS platform on your 14-inch display, with an army of AI agents from ChatGPT, Microsoft, and Google at your disposal to boss around. Use them to set navigation, discover random locations, do web searches, tell bad jokes, or whatever else people use AI for in their cars. Merc’s own onboard AI system can handle the physical stuff, like adjusting HVAC, changing drive modes, or fiddling with the lighting — all through voice commands.

Previous Next 1 / 1

Beyond voice and navigation, the AMG GT SUV applies AI to high-performance track driving through something called the Predictive Performance Manager. Mercedes says the PPM uses track-mapping data to dynamically throttle or boost electric motor output depending on topography, conserving battery energy on downhill or technical winding sections so full power is available on steep inclines and long straights. That could also mean faster, more consistent overall lap times by eliminating battery overheating and power throttling during track driving — something an AMG lover would likely appreciate.

Mercedes didn’t release the official pricing yet, though we can expect something closer to its official launch.

Tech.title: Elon Musk settles lawsuits over $1 million voter giveaway
Tech.content:
In 2024, Elon Musk promised to give away $1 million a day to a randomly selected registered voter in a swing state. That prompted legal challenges, raised questions about its legality, and drew lawsuits from two Arizona residents claiming the lottery was a fraud. Musk has now agreed to settle the two lawsuits filed in Austin, Texas, though the details of the settlement have not been made public.

That directly contradicted Musk’s claim that the drawings were random. The plaintiffs say they never would have signed the petition required to enter the giveaway if they had known it wasn’t random. They accused Musk and America PAC of using it as a ploy to obtain user data and said the petition “places no limitations on America PAC’s use of or sale of the personal data it collects, nor does it provide any additional information about the planned use of data.”

Tech.title: Meta removes language that may have allowed it to scrape news sites
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page:

… Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.

Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an attempt to give Meta the right to use content scraped from sites to train its AI products for free and supersede blocking instructions in a site’s robots.txt file.

Andy Stone, Meta’s vice president of communications, and spokesperson Daniel Roberts pushed back, saying that “There is no change to how Meta uses web crawlers; any suggestion to the contrary is false.” Today’s update to its terms and a new statement go further, removing the controversial language entirely. Roberts said in a follow-up statement to The Verge this morning:

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”
