Tech.title: These 12 Automatic Cat Feeders Were the Best We Tested in 2026
Tech.content:
Compare Our Picks

Others Tested

Photograph: Molly Higgins

Oneisall 2-in-1 Automatic Cat Feeder and Water Dispenser for $60: Generally, I'm a fan of all the Oneisall pet products I've tested. While they aren't the most technologically advanced, they are always reliable and affordable. This model is relatively simple. To set up, you'll need to attach the bowl supports and dishwasher-safe stainless-steel bowls, fill the water and kibble compartments, and plug in. This model runs on corded power but also has an optional 4 AA batteries in case of a power outage. There is no connected app. You'll just set the clock and adjust meal settings, and you can schedule one to six meals per day with adjustable portions, from one to 10 portion sizes. I don't love having food and water so close, since cats prefer them separate to prevent cross-contamination in the wild. I always recommend automatic pet fountains instead for a fresh source of water, but if you don't have a lot of space, are on a budget, and need a temporary solution for getting fresh water to your kitty while you're out of town, the gravity-fed water system helps keep water relatively fresh (plus, the translucent tank makes it easier to check water levels). I'd recommend this basic option if you're on a budget and need a temporary solution for when you're out of the house (and don't mind not having a connected app).

Photograph: Molly Higgins

Closer Pets C200 2-Meal Automatic Pet Feeder for $50: This automatic feeder is super simple, which is both its weakness and its strength. It’s essentially two shallow plastic containers with stainless-steel inserts (both dishwasher-safe) and tamper-resistant lids that lock and automatically open using an old-school egg-style timer that runs on an AA battery rather than electricity. Although the container has an ice pack to keep the wet food cool, after one night it lost virtually all of its coolness. There’s a lid-link clip attachment, a small piece of plastic that links the lids to ensure they open at the same time, which is super helpful for owners of two cats like me. I wish the timer were electric so I could program it to the exact time I want it to open, rather than guesstimating the timing on the little marks. However, this is a simple solution to help make sure both my cats are given wet food without me having to wake up at the crack of dawn.

Photograph: Molly Higgins

Oneisall Cordless WiFi Automatic Cat Feeder for $53: I had high hopes for this cordless feeder, which boasts a rechargeable battery with a 100-day life and an integrated app, but it's just too unreliable. Through the app, you can program up to 10 daily meals (in 1-12 portions each), monitor pets' eating habits, and customize meal calls. Unlike other apps, you can't choose portion size; instead, you have to multiply the number of servings. The app gave me constant problems and would often disconnect from the feeder and be unable to reconnect to WiFi. Luckily, I was able to program meals via the screen and buttons, but it would've been much nicer if the app had worked reliably.

Do Not Recommend

Courtesy of Amazon

Catit Pixi Smart 6-Meal Feeder for $86: Like others on this list, the Catit Pixi wet and dry feeder uses ice packs to keep wet food fresh and rotates meals among six compartments on a set schedule. The schedule can be programmed via the app or adjusted on the feeder itself. At this price point, the app shouldn’t be this limited and glitchy. The schedule is available in military time only, and the app is extremely limited—you can only set the meal schedule for the same day. When I wanted to do only two to three meals a day spread over two days, I had to reschedule the meals for every new day. The feeder didn't keep it cold enough to spread the meals out, and the wet food was not at a safe eating temperature. At this price point, just get the Petlibro Polar wet feeder.

Catit Pixi Smart Cat Feeder for $112: Kibble is stored in the feeder’s body, but it lacks a window to visually check food levels. The meal-planning calendar shows only a week at a time, and although it should repeat daily based on the schedule, I found that some days had no schedule despite setting one up. The Pixi also doesn’t tell you how much food was dispensed; it just refers to it as a “portion”—I manually measured and found the portion was less than a tablespoon of kibble. After using it continuously for more than a month, I found it was extremely glitchy and almost never reliably stuck to the programmed schedule, sometimes skipping meals altogether. This feeder is potentially dangerous, and I'd caution pet parents against relying on it.

Closer Pets C500 for $77: This automatic wet and dry feeder can schedule up to four pre-portioned meals (and one meal given manually) and opens them on a timer using three AA batteries (sold separately). The user sets the four times they want the bowls, which have ice packs underneath, to rotate. The bowls are quite deep and narrow, and they aren’t super easy for cats to reach, which could cause whisker fatigue. Although there are two relatively large ice packs, when I checked on the feeder after a night’s sleep, the packs weren’t very cold. This may be OK for kibble, but wet food was kept at unsafe temperatures, and my cats couldn't reach all of the food.

Tech.title: HTC Made Smart Glasses That Are Way More Private
Tech.content:
You can’t really talk about smart glasses without bringing up Meta. HTC, the company behind 2010-era virtual reality headsets and a failed smartphone business, seems quite eager to tackle that comparison directly.

In September, HTC started selling its $499 Vive Eagle smart glasses in the US. The Eagles have lots of the same features as other glasses on the market—cameras for capturing photos and video, speakers in the frames for music playback and calls, an embedded AI agent you can ask questions of and even get recipes from by taking pictures of stuff in your fridge.

But HTC also wants to steer clear of the ongoing debate about privacy in camera-equipped smart glasses. Meta has been dogged by controversy for its smart glasses, with people worried about the company’s interest in enabling face-recognition features, and calling the people who wear them creepy. HTC is aware of that discourse and thinks it is completely possible to make smart glasses that aren’t a privacy nightmare.

“It's not just about protecting the consumer, but it's also about protecting people around the consumer,” Dan McDowell, HTC Vive’s head of enterprise sales, tells WIRED. “People can usher in, I think, what are really tremendous experiences with a new layer of confidence and protection.”

I’ve been wandering around with the glasses for a couple of weeks, and so far they meet my expectations for what smart glasses have become. They protect my eyes from the sun. They snap good photos and videos. You can record and transcribe voice notes. The music playback has decent sound quality. (I’ll always prefer a solid pair of headphones if I’m actually trying to listen to music, but the speakers work just fine.) They come in two styles—one with square Wayfarer-esque lenses and the other more rounded.

Tech.title: Don’t Let a Crypto Inheritance Get Stuck on the Blockchain
Tech.content:
If someone you know has cryptocurrency that you might inherit, let me just say ahoy matey! I hope your pirate spirit is alive and your treasure-hunting skills sharp, because that's what it might take to get those assets. And if you're the one holding crypto, know that if you do nothing, it's very possible those funds will die with you.

In the US, cryptocurrency is considered a digital asset rather than money in terms of probate and estate law. With money and physical assets, you can sign a beneficiary form and create an estate plan or write a last will and testament naming who should get what when you die. With digital assets, however, the law says we should not assume that a deceased person wanted their private materials—everything from emails to photos—given to another person unless they explicitly said so. This puts cryptocurrency, as a digital asset, in an awkward position.

The options for arranging a transfer of cryptocurrency upon one's death or incapacitation breaks down by one big division: whether the crypto is held by a custodian or in a noncustodial crypto wallet.

Two Types of Wallets

A custodian or custodial wallet means a third party, such as a bank or a cryptocurrency marketplace, holds and manages the assets for you. Typically, transferring assets after death is much easier with a custodian, especially if it's a bank.

Noncustodial wallets eliminate the middleman and let a person hold their assets directly. For crypto enthusiasts whose interest in digital currency is driven by a distaste for the traditional banking system, then using a noncustodial wallet is kind of the whole point.

Noncustodial wallets can be software or hardware-based. It can even be a piece of paper with the instructions and passwords for accessing the cryptocurrency on it. (I use "password" here and throughout to refer to any string of letters, numbers, and characters needed to gain access to someone’s cryptocurrency.) Whatever kind of noncustodial wallet you choose, passing on your assets will require a DIY solution.

Pros and Cons of a Custodial Wallet

When you use a third-party custodian to hold your cryptocurrency, you can choose one that has a beneficiary process in place.

Charles Schwab and Chase are just two examples of large, well-known financial institutions that offer crypto services and have experience transferring assets after death. Schwab, for example, houses its cryptocurrency services within brokerage accounts. Signing a beneficiary form for a brokerage account applies to the crypto account as well. One and done.

Another benefit of using a bank is that at least three entities know you have an account: the bank, the government, and the credit reporting bureaus. Avenues exist for finding the banked money of deceased people. With a noncustodial wallet, this is not at all the case.

Tech.title: Voicemod’s New Phone Gadget Changes Your ‘Sonic Identity’ for Mobile Games and Streaming
Tech.content:
For years, Voicemod has given people a way to change their voices online, which they’ve done for any number of benign reasons — for game players with feminine-pitched voices to avoid harassment, for those with damaged vocal cords to simulate their former voices, for anonymity or even just for fun. Now the company has a new product to bring its voice-changing tech on the go in a physical device that magnetically clips on the back of phones.

The Voicemod Key Pocket, available to preorder now for $130, is a small soundboard about the size of a magnetic battery and serves as a controller interface for the company’s voice-changing apps. The half-dozen buttons on the back of the device can be used to switch between voices or audio effects while streaming or playing games, while the wheel adjusts volume of the projected voice.

The Key Pocket works in tandem with the Voicemod app, but all voice processing is done locally and in real time separate from games and streaming apps in order to maximize privacy as well as performance, according to a Voicemod statement. The Voicemod app provides access to over 200 original voices made by the company, over 76,000 voices made by the service’s community and over 800,000 sounds and memes made by users.

More from CNET

The Key Pocket is a versatile gizmo, with an LED wheel at the top-left corner for toggling voices and checking sound setup, while programmable trigger buttons enable swapping between voices and soundboard playback. The device supports wired and Bluetooth wireless headsets, has USB passthrough charging and clips securely to the back of phones with MagSafe-compatible magnets.

Beyond phones, the Key Pocket works on tablets and consoles, including PS4 and PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2 and the Meta Quest 2, 3 and 3S headsets. It can plug into USB-C, wired 3.5mm ports or connect via Bluetooth.

There are plenty of reasons folks might want to change their voice, from goofing off with friends to avoiding harassment when gaming online — a sad reality for gamers with feminine voices. It’s also an accessibility boon for people who have health conditions or other circumstances leading them to want to change their vocal timbre and pitch.

These days, changing voices can be cause for concern, especially with artificial-intelligence scams spoofing the voices of loved ones to extort money. But when I sat down at Mobile World Congress 2026 earlier this year to chat with Voicemod’s Daniel Pearson, vice president of marketing, and Alex Bordanova, chief product and technology officer, they explained how it aligned with the ethos of the company. The Key Pocket is the result of years of Voicemod’s work to support the idea that one’s online voice is as much an expression of identity as their visual look.

“Everyone has their digital visual appearance where they tweak their cosmetics and skins, but when it comes to voice, it’s kind of been left out, right? It’s this missing half of digital identity,” said Pearson.

As voice-changing tech makes its way into Fortnite, Arc Raiders, Marvel Rivals and other spaces for online third spaces, people are opening up to the idea that their personal expression isn’t just limited to how they’re seen, but also how they’re heard — or as Pearson calls it, their “sonic identity.”

Voicemod

When voice becomes a way to express identity

In our earlier chat, Pearson and Bordanova laid out what Voicemod meant to its community, with the latter describing one memorable story from last October’s TwitchCon 2025. A woman approached him explaining that she was a streamer who lost her voice for about six months but was able to make up for it with Voicemod’s tech.

“She used an AI voice, because that was enough to turn something audible out of just very nuanced sounds that she could project,” Bordanova said.

It spurred discussion about ways the Voicemod team might preserve the community’s voices — a vault, say, to future-proof their voices in the event that health or injury might limit their speaking.

The Voicemod creators don’t just see its tech as just to alter voices for fun or privacy — they see it as an expression machine, one that reflects who you are online. That comes in the form of a voice tweaked to a desired pitch and timbre, but also more abstract communication, like a soundboard. Yes, the signature toy of radio shock jocks from yesteryear is an aspect of expression, too, especially among a community where sounds take on specific meanings.

“It’s giving you the capacity to react and expand by giving extra context that you and your friends understand, but the normies don’t,” said Pearson.

Voicemod’s team has been encouraged by the increasing availability of voice-changing tech in games. Around a year ago, Arc Raiders launched its voice changer in beta but only offered ten voices at launch, and Voicemod offered their own tech to expand those options.

“[Gamers] are social beings, they don’t want to have the default skin. They want to have their own skin customized,” Pearson said. “If the game just gives you 5-10 skins, you’re gonna want the next one, you want to differentiate yourself.”

The company’s Voicelab enables further voice tweaking with fun effects. One could, if they wanted, change their voice to sound like they were wearing a helmet in a cave inside a volcano — wacky but evocative sonic context placing the person in a specific space and circumstance. It enhances expression and storytelling and uses AI to do it. But not the AI you’re thinking of.

AI has been at the heart of Voicemod — but not generative AI

There’s no denying that technological advancement has enabled voice generation, but Voicemod came long before that. It was founded 14 years ago, using digital sound processing to alter voices, launching first on an iPhone 3GS, Bordanova explained.

What their tech enabled that traditional DSP could not is changing the timbre of the voice — its tone, color and personality. Using math, Voicemod’s tech could change a vocal signal in ways that would simulate changing the human organs that naturally shape one’s voice, like elongating or shrinking the vocal cords or altering the width of your throat or nose.

More traditional AI powered Voicemod’s older methods of voice changing, which improved thanks to technological developments. The company’s advantage was to be one of the first to invest heavily in AI’s use in voice changing, Bordanova said.

“There was something unique, something very special, that would evolve us from being a voice changer to having fun with friends online, into giving real utility for a 24/7 use case,” Bordanova said.

What he clarifies is that Voicemod’s tech isn’t based on generative AI, unlike the tech behind voice processing tricks like Google’s live translation. Instead, their language models are around 20 megabytes in weight, and take about a week to train. Unlike the immense large language models used in generative AI, Voicemod’s are small enough to fully download on phones and other client-side devices. They can be consulted immediately on device for 42 millisecond latency, rather than need to go to the cloud.

That doesn’t mean they’ll never use LLMs — but the use case they’re envisioning is as a glorified assistant helping people find the right toggles and settings to get the voice they want from existing choices.

“You can type, I want the voice of SpongeBob and the LLM would pick the right effect and parameters and just create the voice for us,” Bordanova said.

Voicemod

Expression on the go, through your phone to your digital life

Back in March at MWC 2026, I chatted with Bordanova and Pearson when they brought out a prototype for the Key Pocket, the follow-up to the company’s earlier Voicemod Key, a dongle device that aimed to help change voices for console play. Even in its cruder form, the Key Pocket felt special.

As even the prototype was MagSafe compatible, I clipped it to the back of my own iPhone 15 Pro Max. Even if the device wasn’t far enough along to be usable with software, I could still simulate how it would feel in action with my phone rotated sideways, as if I had it active while gaming. The row of buttons rested below my fingers, easy to press if I wanted to tweak my voice or trigger vocal or sound effects. The volume wheel was nice and accessible. If I was streaming or chatting with my friends, the Key Pocket would be a nice accessory to have.

While a lot of gaming happens at home on PC and console, mobile gaming is a huge sector. The Key Pocket is a neat tool for gamers who either play on the go or who opt to play on phones for other reasons — possibly because they can’t afford pricey bigger platforms, which have only gotten more expensive since the RAM shortage. Odds are good that the phone in many gamers’ pockets can play the games they want, and the Key Pocket could help with their so-called sonic identity.

Voicemod’s goal goes beyond the Key Pocket to eventually integrate their tech at a system level, so that anyone booting up a computer or phone could use the tens of thousands of voices created by the Voicemod community (along with the filters and sound effects) to modify their aural appearance anywhere on the device.

“The last frontier is to get rid of the hardware,” Bordanova said.

Expanding Voicemod’s tech across a device’s software and apps would broaden its appeal — imagine not just customizing your voice in games and voice chats with friends, but work Zooms and other calls. Having the same options and interface available everywhere you could use your voice would open up possibilities for folks who’ve never thought about tweaking their voices.

But any mobile gamer will tell you that external controls make a world of difference compared to on-screen digital buttons. Integrating voice tech into the back end of devices is good, but having the Key Pocket soundboard at the touch of your fingers is a far more tactile and responsive set of controls. For streamers and presenters on the go who rely on exact timing, the Key Pocket is a neat solution. Sometimes all you need is an attractively designed gadget to expose folks to new tech possibilities — and in this case, the potential to express themselves online in a way they may not have considered before.

Tech.title: Texas Says It’s Fixed a Glitch That Delayed Nearly 600,000 Voter Registrations
Tech.content:
Like in many states, Texans can register to vote or update their registration when renewing their driver’s license or getting a new one.

But the state of Texas has blamed a software glitch related to this system for more than half a million voter registration delays. The extensive backlog of voting registration applications, which reportedly began to accumulate a year ago, is now the subject of a lawsuit filed by a pair of voter advocacy groups: the League of Women Voters Texas and MOVE Texas Civic Fund. The state says it has already fixed the issue and filed the applications.

The suit characterizes the delay as part of a pattern of voter suppression that has disenfranchised voters in Texas. Filed in Bexar County, Texas, the lawsuit names Texas Secretary of State Robert S. Howden and his office, as well as the Department of Public Safety and its director Freeman F. Martin.

More from CNET

Meanwhile, the office of the Texas Secretary of State told media this week that the delayed applications were filed to voters’ home districts and that the problem has been fixed. As a safeguard, a spokesperson for the secretary of state said anyone still affected by the problem will be able to file a provisional ballot. But according to a report from The Texas Tribune, county officials have found another system error has caused issues with another 15,000 registrations over the last month.

Now, counties are scrambling to fix those issues ahead of the start of early voting in the state on Oct. 19 for a high-profile midterm election season that has put the state in the national spotlight. Chris McGinn, executive director of the Texas Association of County Election Officials, told the Tribune, “Just when most counties were seeing the light at the end of the tunnel, another unexpected backlog is being dropped on county voter registrars.”

Representatives from the secretary of state and DPS office did not immediately return a request for comment.

Heated election season, unanswered questions

The state has not given details on what kind of technical problem caused the voter registration backlog in the first place. At first, it was attributed to a “computer glitch,” but subsequent reports have the secretary of state’s office describing it as a programming error arriving in a software update to the DPS driver’s license online portal.

The registration problems come five years after voting groups won a suit against the state that forced it to comply with the National Voter Registration Act, which guarantees the right to register to vote while updating a driver’s license online.

The new suit claims the registration delays are a violation of those safeguards.

Texas has for years been a reliably red state, but polls put several Republican candidates up for election this year behind Democratic challengers, most notably a US Senate race between Attorney General Ken Paxton and State Representative James Talarico.

That race in particular has become so hotly contested that the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, has spent nearly $160 million to back Republican candidates in the state. The vast amount of money spent on the Texas races and the unpredictability of the outcomes is drawing more scrutiny to potential voter suppression in the state.

Tech.title: Disneyland and Disney World: New Lands, Rides and Areas in 2026 and Beyond
Tech.content:
After finally wrapping up its yearlong 70th anniversary celebrations, Disneyland is looking ahead to the future. Disney is building three new rides at its California parks and revealed new details about them during its D23 Fan Convention in August.

And over at Walt Disney World in Florida, four new lands are being constructed, themed around villains, Pixar characters and more.

Here’s everything you need to know about what’s coming to Disneyland and Disney World, from offerings arriving at the end of this year to those planned beyond 2026.

Avengers Campus is doubling in size, with two new rides

Concept art of the Avengers Infinity Defense attraction coming to California Adventure. Disney

Avengers Campus already has two rides: Spider-Man Web Slingers and Guardians of the Galaxy. Soon, this will double as Disney builds two more Marvel attractions at California Adventure.

The first new ride, Infinity Defense, saw Disney Imagineers “invent some new” tricks, said executive creative director at Walt Disney Imagineering Brent Strong at D23. “It’s going to feel like you’re hurtling through worlds.” In Avengers Infinity Defense, you’ll assemble alongside the Avengers to battle King Thanos in a multiverse-spanning adventure featuring Ms. Marvel, Hawkeye, Captain America, Thor and Iron Man.

In the second ride, Stark Flight Lab, you’ll help test Tony Stark’s latest tech. It’ll star Captain America, Iron Man and Captain Marvel, who will see you go through flight instruction as you train like an Avenger.

Both rides are opening in 2028. The route between Cars Land, and Avengers Campus will be reopening very soon.

Villains Land at Disney World

Concept art for the new Villains Land. Disney

Disney’s first villains-themed area will celebrate all the classic baddies from Disney films, and it’s coming to the Magic Kingdom at Disney World in Florida. The entrance to Villains Land will have a “broken, twisted wishing well,” said president and chief creative officer of Walt Disney Imagineering Bruce Vaughn at D23.

The land will have two attractions: a roller coaster that takes guests through Maleficent’s fortress; and a dark boat ride through the other side of the glass of the magic mirror.

Imagineers have drawn design inspiration from architecture in Paris and Barcelona — including Antoni Gaudí’s buildings in the latter — to design Villains Land.

Villains Land, first teased during D23 2022, will be located on the other side of Big Thunder Mountain at the top left edge of the current Magic Kingdom map, extending towards the Haunted Mansion.

Monstropolis is coming to Hollywood Studios in 2027

Concept art of the Monsters, Inc. suspender coaster. Disney/Pixar

Replacing the old Muppets area of Hollywood Studios is Monstropolis — home of the Monsters, Inc. movies, shorts and Disney Plus streaming series. It will feature Disney’s first suspended roller coaster inside the city’s laugh/scream factory. The coaster will lift you 40 feet in the air in 4 seconds when you board, before it shoots you through the doors.

There will also be a new signature show hosted by Mike and Sulley, with concept art featuring characters from Monsters University; an Elite Scarers Club; the Scareporium store; and Harryhausen’s restaurant, featuring an animatronic octopus sushi chef.

With MuppetVision 3D closing last year to make way for Monstropolis, the Muppets characters were moved to the Rock ‘n’ Roller Coaster. That overlay didn’t take long to complete — Rock ‘n’ Roller Coaster Starring Aerosmith closed after its last day of operation on March 1, and the Muppets-themed version opened on May 26.

CNET’s Bridget Carey toured the Monsters area while it was under construction. You can watch her full video about the new land below.

First peek at Piston Peak

A miniature model of Piston Peak. Corinne Reichert/CNET

The Rivers of America and Tom Sawyer Island at Disney World’s Magic Kingdom have been closed and removed from the online map, as Disney works to construct a new land themed after Pixar’s Cars movies. Cars Land, which was added to Disney’s California Adventure back in 2012, remains extremely popular in the west, so it was only a matter of time before it was added to the eastern outpost.

In an expansion of Frontierland — which also includes Tiana’s Bayou Adventure and Big Thunder Mountain Railroad — Route 66 will draw inspiration from the Rocky Mountains and the “American Frontier and its national parks.”

There will be two attractions:

Miss Fritter’s Daredevil Spin-Along will feature a huge, school bus-sized animatronic of the character from Cars 3, who is hosting a demolition derby for guests to ride.

Cars Ridge Run Rally is a rally car race ride, where you’ll be competing for the fastest ride in the wilderness. The cars will travel along a bouncy track that travels over the mountains, through the geysers and into a sprint finish.

While construction has begun and Disney even showed off a full-scale miniature of Piston Peak at D23 in August, showing exactly how the land and rides will look, we don’t expect Piston Peak to open until at least 2027 or 2028.

A Coco ride is coming to California Adventure

Concept art for the new Coco ride. Disney/Pixar

Construction is well underway at California Adventure on a new dark ride themed to the beloved Pixar movie Coco and populated with Audio-Animatronics. Imagineers are working with Pixar to ensure the ride fits with both the original film and the newly announced Coco 2, which will follow Miguel as a teenager.

The Coco ride will be located near Pixar Pier and Paradise Gardens in an area currently used primarily as backstage space for cast members. Its story takes place a year after the first movie, as Miguel looks back on his journey inside a new museum dedicated to Héctor Rivera. You’ll travel by boat through Miguel’s memories and into the land of the dead.

Tropical Americas Land at Animal Kingdom

Concept art of Tropical Americas. Disney

Animal Kingdom’s DinoLand USA area is no more, with the area on the Disney World map now a blank sea of grass as Disney slowly builds out the new Tropical Americas Land.

Construction began in fall 2024, with TriceraTop Spin and the midway area closing in January 2025. The Dinosaur ride remained open until February 2026, when it closed to be transformed into Indiana Jones and the Myth of the Jade Serpent. The attraction’s storyline is set in the 1950s inside an ancient Maya temple protected by a giant mythical creature. You’ll be sucked through a portal into the underworld.

The Pueblo Esperanza area will be themed to resemble a South American village, with an Encanto-themed attraction called Antonio’s Fiesta de Encanto. The ride vehicles will resemble furniture from Casita and take you upstairs into Antonio’s room, which transforms into a rainforest after he receives his magical gift. More than 50 animals will appear throughout the attraction.

Tropical Americas is slated to open in 2027 and will also include a huge quick-service dining location, a fountain and a carousel. El Carrusel de los Animalitos will feature 22 unique, hand-carved animals from across the Disney universe, including Pua the pig from Moana, Nigel the pelican from Finding Nemo, the capybara from Encanto and Eeyore from Winnie the Pooh.

Hand-carved animals for the Tropical Americas carousel. Corinne Reichert/CNET

Soarin’ Across America, coast to coast

At Disney’s California Adventure and Disney World’s Epcot, the Soarin’ Around the World attraction got a US-themed makeover this summer, and I got a first look on its opening day in Anaheim. Soarin’ Across America is part of Disney’s celebration of America’s 250th anniversary.

It features the sights, sounds and smells of American landmarks, including the Statue of Liberty and the New York City skyline, the New England coastline, the Washington Monument, the Louisiana bayou, the Grand Canyon, Mount Rushmore and even the launch of Artemis II.

The launch of the recent Artemis II mission around the moon is the first sight you see on Soarin’ Across America. Corinne Reichert/CNET

See Bluey at Disneyland and Disney World

Bluey and her family are now hosting a stage show and themed area at the original Disney park. Debuting in March, Bluey’s Best Day Ever is located at the Fantasyland Theatre next to Mickey’s Toontown, which has been transformed into Bluey’s school classroom and grounds, including a gnome village and fairy garden.

Bluey and her sister, Bingo, appear several times each day, along with actors and musicians, to “bring to life the popular music and games emblematic of beloved Bluey episodes.” Those games include “keepy uppy” and the “grannies,” as well as appearances by Chattermax and Unicorse.

There are also puzzles, games and photo ops throughout the Bluey area, and Disneyland is serving up Bluey-themed foods at Troubadour Tavern.

The hugely popular Australian cartoon about a family of dogs is a worldwide hit, and Disney is slated to release a Bluey movie in 2027. (In the meantime, you can watch Bluey episodes and minisodes on Disney Plus.)

Disney World is also hosting Bluey and Bingo meet-and-greets and a show at the Conservation Station in Animal Kingdom.

Disney Parks

Star Wars Galaxy’s Edge: Old characters, new Mandalorian missions

The Star Wars-themed land at Disneyland has expanded its timeline to include Luke Skywalker, Leia Organa and Han Solo. The original trio arrived on Batuu on April 29 and now interact with guests and other characters. To help integrate them into the existing land, Galaxy’s Edge also has new props, merchandise, graphics and music featuring John Williams’ legendary score.

“Black Spire Outpost will roll back in time several decades, thoughtfully introducing beloved characters from across the Star Wars timeline,” the Disney Parks Blog announced in April. “Each era will be brought to life with the same care and attention to detail that the land was originally designed with, masterfully weaving together stories from across time and space in one location.”

Darth Vader has also joined the fun, and you can still see Ahsoka Tano, The Mandalorian, Grogu, Rey, Chewbacca and R2-D2.

Disneyland (and Hollywood Studios at Disney World) has also added Mandalorian and Grogu missions to the Millennium Falcon: Smuggler’s Run ride in Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge, tying in with the release of The Mandalorian and Grogu in cinemas. The new missions launched on May 22.

Disneyland expansion

Concept art of the new pedestrian bridge that will cross Harbor Boulevard. Disney

More than five years after unveiling plans for the expansion, Disneyland is expected to spend a couple of years completing the project, which will extend the park beyond its current boundaries, past Downtown Disney and into nearby parking lots. It’ll also transform “a portion of the current Hollywood Backlot area,” leading to the closure of the Monsters Inc. attraction permanently in 2027.

A new esplanade entry “experience” will replace the current walkway entry at the east side of Disneyland, as well as a new parking structure and pedestrian bridge over Harbor Boulevard. Construction on this begins this fall.

The biggest part of the expansion will be adding an Avatar-themed land, based on the second film, The Way of Water, as well as the third film, Avatar: Fire and Ash. It will include a dark boat ride much like Pirates of the Caribbean, “taking guests all the way to the wide-open seas of Pandora.” Disney has no dates or details yet on when it’ll be complete, and mentions of the Avatar area were notably absent at D23 in August.

Corinne Reichert/CNET

Disney Cruise Line: New ships

Disney has been all in on launching cruise ships over the last few years, including the Disney Wish in 2022, the Disney Treasure in 2024 and the Disney Destiny in 2025.

The Disney Adventure sailed on its maiden voyage from Singapore on March 10, the first of four new ships set to embark soon. Disney’s next cruise liner, the Disney Believe, was unveiled by new CEO Josh D’Amaro on March 18. The Believe will set sail next year with Tinker Bell on the bow, Woody and Buzz Lightyear on the stern and Moana as the Grand Hall icon.

A new class of ships — larger than the classic ships but smaller than the Wish-class vessels — is also coming in 2029.

Tech.title: Yes, You’re Probably Paying More for Phone Service. Here’s Where Your Money Is Going
Tech.content:
Everything is getting more expensive bit by bit, and it’s not just gas or grocery prices. T-Mobile just increased the price of a pair of fees that get added on top of what customers pay for their mobile phone plans, and it’s not the only carrier doing this.

Over the past year and a half, the big three US cellular providers have raised prices in small ways that may not seem consequential month to month, but add up over the year.

More costly fees, taxes and plans

For a while, a lot of carriers’ plans rolled taxes and fees into them as a competitive advantage — when you know you’re paying a fixed amount each month, it’s easier to budget. Unfortunately, those days are over, at least among the big three US carriers: AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon.

More from CNET

The new fee increases are so small that you probably won’t notice them on your bill. Effective Oct. 12, T-Mobile’s Regulatory Programs and Telco Recovery fees increased for every line on a customer’s account. For voice lines, it’s an increase of $1.00 for the combined fees (previously $4.49 a month, now $5.49 a month). Mobile internet lines, such as those for smartwatches or tablets, went up $0.50, from $2.10 to $2.60 a month.

T-Mobile is increasing some of its fees. Jeff Carlson/CNET

T-Mobile previously raised the cost of these fees in April 2025, from $3.49 to $3.99 and $1.40 to $1.60, so in a year and a half, customers are paying $2 more per voice line and $1 more per mobile internet line per month.

Even if your plan has a multi-year price guarantee, that applies to the main plan itself, not miscellaneous taxes and fees that are added on top of the plan’s cost. Carriers can, and do, increase those fairly regularly.

For Roger Entner, analyst and founder of Recon Analytics, the problem isn’t that carriers regularly raise fees like this. It’s that they spread out the increases.

“I don’t understand why they [don’t] only piss you off once a year, but instead sometimes choose to piss you off four times a year,” Entner said in a conversation with CNET. “It doesn’t make sense unless you want to be hated.”

T-Mobile isn’t the only one that’s increased these fees. AT&T raised its Administrative and Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee from $3.99 to $4.99 per line in August; that was after a December 2025 increase from $3.49. Verizon raised its fees in August 2025, from $3.50 to $3.78 per month for voice lines and from $1.60 to $3.97 per month for data-only lines.

As for the prices of the plans themselves, they’ve been relatively consistent. The exception is Verizon, which announced holiday deals in December 2025 and carried the pricing all the way through August when it announced the Simplicity plan. The myPlan plans, which include Unlimited Welcome, Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Ultimate, now cost $10 more per line for new customers than they did at the beginning of 2026.

Are these costs enough to inspire customers to look elsewhere? “We’ve done research on what makes people [switch carriers],” Entner said. “Five dollars and below doesn’t matter. People shrug it off. … Where the outrage [would be] is if your price would go up by $15, $20, and nobody’s doing that.”

Retiring legacy plans

When AT&T revamped its unlimited phone plan lineup in March this year. It also announced that prices would be increasing for many of its “retired” plans, as much as $20 for an account (not per line). Then, in August, the increases were applied to more legacy plans, which included the ones that the new 2.0 plans had just replaced a few months earlier.

At the time, an AT&T spokesperson said, “This increase reflects the real cost of continuing to deliver the speed, reliability and support our customers expect every day.” I think it’s also safe to say that this type of increase can also serve as an incentive for customers to migrate to current plans.

AT&T’s mobile app. Jeff Carlson/CNET

In June, however, T-Mobile announced it would unilaterally move some customers to new plans in order to get their old ones off the books. Although T-Mobile said that most plans would be comparably priced to what the customers were paying before, in some cases it meant increases of up to $6 per line per month.

The new plans were variations of T-Mobile’s existing lineup, such as Experience More with Appreciation Savings versus the straight-up increase that switching to the Experience More plan entails.

The move wasn’t optional, and at least one customer filed an informal complaint with the FCC. That’s one step below a formal complaint, which would involve fees and lawyers.

Price guarantees have almost evaporated

In April of last year, Verizon made a big deal about offering a three-year price guarantee on all of its plans. However, the guarantee slipped away in August when the company introduced its Simplicity plan. T-Mobile one-upped Verizon with a five-year price guarantee on its plans, which is now available only on the Experience Beyond 2.0 and Experience More 2.0 plans.

The people who signed up for plans under those terms still enjoy the price protection, but customers looking to jump to a new carrier won’t necessarily get the same deal now.

For existing customers, price guarantees can also act like handcuffs. If they want to move to another Verizon plan, for example, they’ll have to give up that price stability.

Looking at the bigger picture, though, wireless service has gotten cheaper

When I was researching for this article, I came across one written by Entner for LightReading that takes a longer-term view of wireless pricing. It highlights that we’re actually paying less for phone service now than we used to. In “Inflation mostly skipped the wireless bill,” Entner uses industry and government data to show that wireless service has gotten cheaper in real terms since 2007 (the year the iPhone was released).

“The dollars that you spend, yes, it’s going up,” Entner said in our conversation. “When we calculate it as part of your wallet share, [the] percentage of your monthly disposable income, it goes down.”

How can you save money on your phone bill?

A couple bucks in fees here and there doesn’t sound like a lot, but if you have four lines on an account, for example, that’s an extra $8 per month you weren’t paying before. And for people looking for the most economical plan, it’s a larger percentage of their phone bills.

So what options are there to offset the increases or reduce your monthly expense?

One option is to shop around for a prepaid plan. Companies such as Cricket, Mint Mobile and Visible run on the carrier’s networks and can cost less, especially if you’re currently paying for perks such as streaming services or hotspot data you’re not using. (Those three are all actually owned by the big three: Cricket is AT&T, Mint Mobile is T-Mobile and Visible is Verizon). Another option is US Mobile, which lets you choose whichever network is strongest in your area.

A single line on T-Mobile’s Essential Saver 2.0 plan, for example, costs $50 and includes 50GB of high-speed data. Mint Mobile’s 12-month Unlimited plan works out to $30 a month when you prepay $360 for the entire term, and it also includes high-speed data that may be slowed after you use 50GB. It includes up to 20GB of mobile hotspot usage, too.

Although it’s a bigger one-time lift, prepaying for an entire year for a plan like this means you won’t have to wonder how much next month’s bill will be.

You may not be in a position to switch providers, particularly if you’ve financed a phone from your current carrier. But you may be able to drop back to a less expensive plan with fewer features.

Verizon’s Simplicity plan at $45 a month, for example, is $20 less expensive than its Unlimited Welcome myPlan for a single line. (Verizon touts the $30 a month price, but that’s just for new customers who bring their own phone with them.) And Simplicity actually gives you better performance, because you can connect using the faster 5G Ultra Wideband (or 5GUW) if your phone has the hardware for it; Unlimited Welcome is limited to regular 5G speeds.

But Simplicity has an important catch: If you have a multi-line Verizon plan and one person switches to Simplicity, every other line must also switch to it. For a family of four, that means paying $180 a month (at the $45 rate), which is $10 more expensive than the Unlimited Plus myPlan and includes less high-speed mobile hotspot data.

As another example, AT&T’s modular Build-A-Plan costs as little as $15 a month when you bring your own unlocked AT&T-compatible and eSIM-capable phone. That gives you just 1GB of data — and that’s it, but you can add more data and hotspot capability for additional costs.

Then there’s the free option. If you don’t mind ads and the restriction of using a single app for all your communications, TextNow gives you calling, texting and data for email, maps, ride-sharing and finance apps. Unlimited data and calling plans can be purchased for the day ($3), week ($9) or month ($36).

If you’re thinking of switching providers, don’t forget that each one has limited programs to let you test out the speed and coverage in your area. T-Mobile offers a free three-month Network Pass, Verizon has a 30-day “trial” program and AT&T has its own 30-day eSIM free trial program.

It’s never fun to find the bill for your wireless phone service — an expense that feels like a modern necessity — is going up. But there are plenty of alternative options that can save you money, if you know where to look.

Tech.title: This Is My Favorite Microsoft 365 Replacement and It’s Free on Linux, Mac and Windows
Tech.content:
Earlier this year, I ended one of my longest relationships. After more than a decade, I broke up with Microsoft 365. I’d like to say I ditched the office suite for some nuanced reason — like I don’t want Microsoft’s AI assistant Copilot because I find it distracting and unhelpful — but really, I just wanted to save some money. And LibreOffice has been a great, free alternative that has everything I need, and it’s available on Linux, Mac and Windows.

LibreOffice has roots that trace back to 1985, with the release of the word-processing program Star-Writer I. In 2010, the independent, nonprofit German foundation The Document Foundation launched the free, open-source software suite LibreOffice. Since then, the foundation says, government offices around the world have saved money by migrating to the office suite.

In addition to being free and open-source, LibreOffice offers other benefits, such as greater document privacy than Microsoft 365 or Google Docs, but there are also drawbacks, such as no native cloud access for those documents. Here’s what to know about LibreOffice if you’re considering switching from Microsoft 365 or Google Docs, as I did.

More from CNET

LibreOffice has programs similar to the ones you already use

LibreOffice includes six applications, and most of them will feel familiar to anyone who has used Microsoft 365 or Google’s suite of office apps like Docs and Sheets.

Writer, Calc, Impress, Draw and Base are analogs to the Microsoft programs Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Visio (for creating flowcharts and diagrams) and Access (or designing business apps and templates), respectively. LibreOffice also has a mathematics program called Math that allows you to create and edit formulas to be used within other LibreOffice programs.

You can easily edit PDFs and other file types in LibreOffice. LibreOffice/Screenshot by CNET

LibreOffice runs on a variety of devices

You can install LibreOffice on Windows, MacOS and Linux devices. So you can download this onto a MacBook, a Microsoft Surface laptop and many other desktops or laptops. But there’s no mobile app.

LibreOffice also offers a portable app, meaning you can keep a self-contained copy of the productivity suite on a flash drive to use between your different computers. You don’t even need to have LibreOffice installed on a device to run it, as long as you have it installed on a flash drive.

LibreOffice offers a lot of value at no cost

LibreOffice has some advantages over other office suites, including its nonexistent price tag. Here are some of the pros of LibreOffice.

You get some privacy and security benefits

Because LibreOffice is open-source, anyone with enough technical understanding can look into its source code to identify vulnerabilities or bugs. And if you’re savvy enough, you can fix the issue yourself and provide a patch for others to use. Additionally, some elements of LibreOffice can make it more private and secure than other office program suites.

LibreOffice says it doesn’t collect or send your user data without your consent. The organization also says it doesn’t create a user profile for you or track how you interact with documents.

By comparison, Microsoft 365 collects two different types of data: what it calls required and optional. A lot of the data Microsoft 365 gathers is hardware- and software-related, which could be used for basic fingerprinting — like understanding the hardware and software being used. But it might also collect client IP addresses. Your public IP address is like a home address in that it gives a general sense of your geographical location, along with information about your internet provider. While the info that Microsoft 365 aggregates may not pose as much of a threat if leaked as personal data like passwords and usernames, it’s more information than LibreOffice collects, which is nice for privacy peace of mind. And you can always use a VPN to mask your public IP address and other information.

LibreOffice saves documents locally on your device — not in the cloud or with a third-party — and it lets you assign a password or encrypt a file using a GNU Privacy Guard key. So even if your device is stolen or someone gains remote access to it, there are measures in place to keep your files secure.

On the whole, LibreOffice is a great alternative to similar products from big tech that don’t collect unnecessary data.

LibreOffice has a few privacy benefits you might appreciate. Tatiana Maksimova/Getty Images

LibreOffice is compatible with many file types

LibreOffice is compatible with many documents, including Microsoft Word, Excel and Apple Pages files. You might run into compatibility issues with some font types, like multicolored fonts, when rendering in LibreOffice.

One Reddit user also found that you might encounter issues if you exchange complex documents multiple times between LibreOffice and other office suites, like Microsoft 365. If you use LibreOffice and you exchange a document with someone who uses Microsoft 365, you might have to change the file type in order for the document to be readable in your chosen office suite. This can cause some issues with the document, but to avoid this, you could save the file in a common format, like .doc.

If you aren’t planning on sending LibreOffice files to others, though, you shouldn’t have an issue. I’m not planning on using LibreOffice for anything beyond budgeting and personal writing, and I don’t want anyone outside my household to see either of those things. But if you plan to use LibreOffice for work documents or other high-stakes files, maybe keep backups in multiple file formats, just in case.

LibreOffice’s Calc has similar functionality to Microsoft’s Excel. LibreOffice/Screenshot by CNET

It’s highly customizable

LibreOffice allows you to customize the functionality of its programs through an extensive collection of extensions and templates in the LibreOffice Extension Center. Here you can find free plugins and extensions, like MLA format templates that let you easily add citations, different language spellcheckers and even a Snake game. Because who doesn’t want to insert a game of Snake into a spreadsheet?

Did I mention it’s free?

LibreOffice is completely free, and there’s no subscription fee. This was a huge draw for my household as we look to cut unnecessary costs around our home. We couldn’t justify Microsoft 365’s price for how little we use it.

Google also offers office productivity apps, like Docs and Sheets, for free, but unlike LibreOffice, it requires a Google account to use it, meaning you’re handing over some personal data.

While LibreOffice is free and therefore enticing, it has some downsides

There are compelling reasons to use LibreOffice over its rivals, but it has some disadvantages compared with other apps, such as Microsoft 365 or Google Docs.

It might not be as user-friendly as other programs

Some people might feel that LibreOffice is more complex than other similar office suites. Google Docs, for example, is a fairly straightforward word processor that almost anyone can jump into and use. LibreOffice’s interface might feel intimidating to new users by comparison to other office suites.

For example, the interface for LibreOffice’s Writer felt cluttered to me as symbols for options, like inserting footnotes and basic shapes, framed a ring around my blank document. It was a lot to take in at once, but I realized that some of these options were present in a Microsoft Word document under tabs like Insert and Layout. Having all those options present on one screen was slightly overwhelming for me, but it didn’t take long for me to get used to the busy-looking workplace.

LibreOffice/Screenshot by CNET

There’s no cloud integration

LibreOffice doesn’t offer native cloud support or integration, which can be disappointing if you want to work on a document from multiple devices. This also means you can’t collaborate in real time on a document with someone else if you aren’t in the same location or using the same computer.

If you wanted to work on a document on multiple devices, you could load the file onto a flash drive, sync files using a cloud storage service like Dropbox or email yourself the file, but those require extra steps and equipment.

LibreOffice has limited mobile device support

There aren’t mobile versions of LibreOffice available at this time — just desktop apps.

“The Document Foundation has limited resources and focuses on the desktop LibreOffice application,” the organization wrote online.

There is a read-only app available for Android devices with what the organization calls “experimental editing support.” Because of its experimental nature, I would not advise relying on this mobile app for document editing, as it might be buggy.

Customer support is virtually nonexistent

The Document Foundation doesn’t provide technical support to individual LibreOffice users. So if you need customer support, you can file a bug report or consult the LibreOffice community assistance page. By contrast, if you’re using another office suite, like Microsoft 365, you should be able to contact customer support more easily.

Should you switch to LibreOffice?

That depends. I’m a simple man and like that LibreOffice is free without losing the basic functionality of a word processor — which is all I need it for. But the options to customize LibreOffice with new, free templates and extensions that can add more functionality make it feel like I’m getting a good deal. Some users on Reddit find LibreOffice is just as good as Microsoft Word, enjoy how customizable it is or appreciate that it’s open-source.

So if you want a customized experience with helpful extensions, want more privacy for your documents and enjoy free stuff, give LibreOffice a try. If you want an office suite that’s easy to virtually collaborate with others on, want a mobile app or just don’t feel like learning a new program, then LibreOffice might not be for you.

For more, check out how to get Microsoft 365 for free, the best free VPNs and the best free antivirus software. You can also check out the best data removal services.

Tech.title: I Test Home Security Tech. Here Are 4 Devices I Rely on to Guard My Porch
Tech.content:
Your front door is your first line of defense against, well, anything you don’t want in your home. It’s also one of the first places burglars check when they’re looking for an easy break-in, and the spot porch pirates watch if they think lucrative packages are going to show up. That means your door is also the best place to start improving home security, especially as the holidays ramp up and you get more visitors and deliveries.

Here’s the technology I use to protect my front door and porch, in four easy steps anyone can start with. You don’t need to install a full security system or pay a high monthly subscription for home monitoring with these devices, either. Setup is totally DIY and takes very little time, too. See which you should start with.

A smart lock to control access from anywhere

Smart locks add a new dimension to your security. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Old deadbolts do well, but any entryway can get a powerful upgrade by adding digital features via a smart lock. Smart locks allow you to control your front door lock from anywhere using your phone, as well as creating temporary passes for guests. They can support digital wallet keys for touchless unlocking, and many have keypads or fingerprint readers. Plus, you can enable settings like auto-locking, so you never have to worry about forgetting to lock the door.

More from CNET

Smart locks come in two flavors: retrofits that leave your deadbolt largely intact and only replace your indoor thumb turn, and full deadbolt replacements that give you new locking power, inside and out. Don’t worry about installation: If you’ve never installed a deadbolt before, the process is generally easy and doesn’t take much time. I have a full guide where you can find more details.

What models do you recommend?

A video doorbell for smart alerts about what’s happening

Tapo’s large doorbell offers unique visual options. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Say goodbye to dusty doorbells of the past. Today’s high-tech doorbells do far more than chime: Video doorbells keep an eye on your front porch, while also giving you a two-way audio intercom right on your phone to hold a conversation — or even let an LLM do the talking for you.

Video doorbells also have particularly useful object recognition features, sometimes even for free. That includes recognizing packages and alerting you whenever one shows up at your door, or when one suddenly vanishes. Video storage options can save recordings of key events, so you can check who came to the door if you need to.

These advanced doorbells come in both wired and wireless versions. I’m a fan of the battery-powered, wireless models, which you can set and angle to get just the right look at your porch, doormat and other key places. Many can also work with your current door chime, although you probably don’t need it anymore with phone-based chimes.

What models do you recommend?

A delivery box to protect packages

Yale’s delivery boxes are larger, so you need room for them in the right spots. Tyler Lacoma

Package theft concerns have reignited a centuries-old tradition of protecting mail. Today’s modern delivery boxes are specifically designed to allow delivery people to put packages inside, but make it difficult or impossible for thieves to take packages out, through clever lock models, auto-locking, smart controls and other various tricks.

I’ve been using a delivery box myself for a couple of years and find it very handy, as long as you have the space by your door. Some versions even come weighted or screwed down if you’re worried about a porch pirate absconding with the entire box. It’s a good idea to put notes in your deliveries to use the box, since despite signs not all delivery people will notice it’s there.

As a final plus, these boxes also keep your packages protected from the elements, which is nice when you live in an area that gets frequent winter snowstorms, as I do.

What models do you recommend?

A smart bulb for powerful lighting

Smart bulbs are cheap, support multiple voice assistants and have lots of fun tricks. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Where front doors exist, there’s usually a light nearby, like an overhead porch light or a wall-mounted lamp, to illuminate the entryway and surrounding area. These lights can also get a major makeover if you switch to an LED smart bulb, which are available as both BR30 floodlights and standard A19 home bulbs.

These lights also give you phone app controls, which is more important than it might seem. With my apps, I can control brightness, set schedules for bulbs to turn on or off, and even adjust the color to whatever I want, say for a holiday event. All it takes is screwing in the bulb and connecting it to Wi-Fi, so you can be done in seconds.

If you feel like experimenting, you can usually link smart bulbs to other devices, too. For example, you could set the light to turn on automatically when a smart lock is unlocked, or when a security system is disarmed.

What models do you recommend?

Now that your front porch is up to date, take a look at the latest home AI tricks I’ve found are actually worth using and how to get them.

Tech.title: How I Captured These Tricky Macro Photos for a Major CNET Feature Story
Tech.content:
My favorite image from the series. This was a combination of around 20 focus-stacked images for the main body of the watch, with separate images shot of my hand in different positions. I then composited these together in Photoshop. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

My CNET colleague Katie Collins wrote a superb feature about the repairability of wearable devices, in particular Google’s most recent Pixel Watch 4. It’s a wonderful read, but my task was to produce the photos and video to accompany the story. From shooting close-up macro photos with specialist lenses to transforming my home into a studio to shoot the video, there was a massive amount of work for me to do.

I’m thrilled with the results — and especially pleased that my main photo, seen above, has been shortlisted for a major photography award, and the images look great on the page. Here’s how I put it all together.

Macro photography: The camera equipment I used

While I love my Leica Q3 43 for out-and-about photography, my main camera for most of my studio product photography and macro work is my Canon R5. It’s high-resolution and has accurate autofocus and in-body stabilization, which can be a real boon.

My secret weapon for this shoot was the DZO Films X-Tract probe lens. This specialist macro photography lens looks weirdly long and thin, but it lets me get super close-up on objects while still providing a wide-angle view. The result is dramatic macro images, so I used this lens pretty much exclusively for the “hero” images in the piece. You can see more about how I used it in my behind-the-scenes video, which is embedded below.

But the right lens can only take you so far. I also used a Zhiyun Molus G300 LED light with a wide, narrow strip box modifier on the front. This turns that small LED light source into a wide light, which gives a great spread over the watch. I angled this to get a clean-looking edge light on some images, or a more even flood of light in others. I accented this using a variety of reflectors to “bounce” that light back into the product — in some cases, even small pieces of paper were enough to help create a nice reflection on the shiny watch.

Canon R5 Mirrorless Camera $2,600 at Best Buy

Macro photography: Taking the images

I’d already decided on a visual style for these images, with a stark, high-contrast aesthetic, somewhat reminiscent of Apple’s OS X-era product photography. I wanted the images to be eye-catching and actually illustrative of what’s going on to ensure they fit well within the article itself.

The probe lens let me get close up on the subject. As I didn’t have enough hands free, I’d secured the pincers in place using multiple rigging arms and a grip that’s supposed to be used for holding test tubes in laboratories. The finished shot is below. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

To help achieve this, I used both static product imagery of the watch and my own hand coming into the frame using pincers to remove components like the battery or display. I mostly figure out a strong visual look for an image series in advance of a photoshoot. This can be one of the best ways to elevate your photos from simple snaps to something that stands out and tells a story. It takes a bit more time to think about, but the results will speak for themselves.

Once I had my scenes set up, I got the camera and the long probe lens into position and dialed in my settings: That’s usually around ISO 200 on my camera, an aperture between f16 and f32 on the lens and a shutter speed around 1/15 of a second. It’s quite slow, so I had to ensure the camera was locked down on a tripod to make sure there was no movement that would cause blur in the image. I used a remote shutter release cable so I didn’t have to touch the camera and risk moving it.

The finished image. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

To ensure the whole product was perfectly sharp, I used a technique called focus stacking. This involved taking many images — usually around 20 — focusing first on the closest part of the watch and adjusting the focus with each image to move the focus point farther and farther away. I then stitched those images together using a dedicated piece of software called Helicon Focus.

Finally, I took the focus-stacked shot into Adobe Photoshop for some retouching, including dust removal, color correction and, in some shots, removing the big LED softbox from the image. I also composited some images together, blending a frame of the watch with a separate frame of my hand using the pincers. While I sometimes like to try and take these images as a single shot, I simply didn’t have that many hands available at once, so I had to blend multiple images together.

I used two pieces of white card as reflectors, bouncing some of the light from the overhead LED back into the shiny body of the watch. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Filming the feature video: More macro fun

Some of the clips in the video were shot much the same way as the still images above — I simply switched my camera to video mode and pressed record. But there was a lot more to do besides.

The main thing to film was Katie’s piece to camera, where she (expertly) presented her script. For this, I shot using a BlackMagic Pocket Cinema Camera 6K Pro paired with a 35mm Arles Prime cinema lens from DZO Film. I used a pink paper backdrop (because I love the color) and used the same LED light as before as the main light on Katie’s face, with a SmallRig RC 450B LED as a fill light on the other side of her face to help soften the shadows and give a more even look to the scene.

Blackmagic Design Pocket Cinema Camera 6K Pro $2,835 at B&H Photo

I recorded the audio using two microphones: a Rode VideoMic NTG shotgun mic on a boom arm just out of shot above Katie’s head (wirelessly connected using a DJI Mic 2 transmitter) and a separate DJI Mic 2 transmitter used with its own built-in mic clipped to Katie’s shirt collar and hidden by her hair.

To film Katie’s piece to camera I used a BlackMagic Cinema camera, two microphones and two large LED light sources. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Then came the Pixel Watch 4 teardown section, which I filmed using much the same setup. I repositioned the lights and switched the 35mm prime lens for a 75mm DZOFilm Arles Prime cine lens to allow me to get a much closer-up view on the intricate work Katie was doing, without having to get the camera (or lens) in the way of her work.

The video was then edited by expert CNET producer JD Christison, and finally, all of the pieces were ready to go.

If that sounds like a lot of effort, it’s because it was. My work on this took place over multiple late nights and an entire weekend. Product and macro photography can be a precise form of photography, requiring a lot of setup and a huge amount of attention to detail. When you’re focusing so close up, every tiny adjustment makes a massive difference in your image, so there’s a vast amount of trial and error.

There was a lot of setup to achieve this look. Andrew Lanxon/CNET

And sure, it also requires a lot of equipment and a fair amount of space to set everything up. I’ve given over a large bedroom in my house to convert into a studio space for shooting photos and videos for CNET, so I don’t have to worry too much about making a mess. I installed specialist shelving and wall-mounted backdrop supports so I could use the admittedly compact space as a regular production studio. If you’re planning to recreate this sort of thing in your own home, be prepared for a lot of cleanup after each shoot.

But as this feature is a major piece for CNET, I wanted to ensure that the imagery we used looked as good as it can, so spending this amount of time and effort on these visuals is absolutely worth it. I’ve been a journalist at CNET for 15 years now, but it still gives me a great sense of pride to see my own images used in stories like this.

Tech.title: An Entire Swedish TV Show Got Deleted, and AI Got Blamed
Tech.content:
Fans of TV4’s international edition of The Challenge, which features Swedish celebrities competing in physical and mental contests, will have to wait a while longer for another season. A TV4 system failure wiped out hundreds of hours of work, and Sweden’s Aftonbladet newspaper reported that an AI agent was at fault, citing unnamed sources at the production company, called Mastiff. The network airing the show refuted that AI agents are to blame.

The Swedish series was due to return on Nov. 22, but has been delayed indefinitely, TV4 said in a statement. “We have to recut it from scratch. All the raw material is still there, and all that,” program director Mia Lindqvist said on the network’s website.

The TV4 network denies the Aftonbladet report that an AI agent deleted the episodes. “We don’t have the exact details of what happened yet, but it’s not true that this was caused by an AI agent. The main issue is that the production company’s backup system failed caused by a human error,” Lindqvist told CNET by email.

More from CNET

The program features stars of other Swedish reality programs, such as the country’s version of The Bachelor and Farmen, a reality show about (wait for it…) contestants on a farm. The Challenge: Sweden first aired in 2023.

AI is increasingly a part of editing and production workflows across movies and television, with entertainment giants, including Netflix, leaning on the technology to produce content more quickly and at lower cost. How much AI is involved in production and at which stages it’s used has been unclear.

If an AI agent were somehow responsible, that would seem to have negated any of AI’s time-saving benefits for The Challenge: Sweden and its production team, who now have to spend time rebuilding the episode edits that were lost. But technical issues caused by human error have a long history in TV and film, including the notorious Pixar incident in which a stray file system command wiped out 90% of Toy Story 2 during production (which was only recovered thanks to a supervising director who had taken her work home after a pregnancy, as The Next Web recounted).

Worries about AI agents taking unwanted action have spiked in recent months. The biggest flash point came over the summer when it was discovered that an OpenAI agent hacked the Hugging Face software repository. Shortly after that, the Australian government said that an agent, also from OpenAI, hacked into a government health site.

While TV4 said an AI agent was not to blame, it did not clarify whether another type of AI might have had some role in the deletion.
